event_model_payload.headline: Why Can’t My Running Pods Be Reached? Our Journey to kube-proxy nftables Mode
event_model_payload.summary:
Hi, I’m Karin, and I’m on the Cluster squad within SRE at Karrot. Our team designs and runs the Kubernetes platform that every service at Karrot runs on. We take responsibility for everything that keeps our clusters observable and reliable, from monitoring infrastructure all the way to the service mesh and security, along with the policies and roadmaps that keep it all maintainable. In this post, I’ll share how we migrated kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode.

kube-proxy runs on every node in a Kubernetes cluster and programs network rules into the Linux kernel so that traffic sent to a Service reaches the actual Pods. For years, our clusters ran kube-proxy in iptables mode to provide this core feature. Below, I’ll walk through how we moved to nftables, its more efficient successor, and what we learned along the way.

1. kube-proxy latency was hurting service reliability

In Kubernetes, nodes come and go and Pods spin up all the time. That’s just how it works. But when a Pod lands on a fresh node and the app starts up, is it actually ready to talk to other services?

kube-proxy manages the network rules (just “rules” from here on) on each node that let traffic headed for a Service reach the actual Pods. On a new node, if an application starts up while those rules are still being prepared, its DNS lookups and calls to other services can fail.

kube-proxy rule sync lag had been creeping up for a while. We’d been watching the metrics since 2024, and latency was noticeably higher in our production cluster in the Korea region, the largest of all the regions we serve. But we judged it wasn’t serious enough to cause operational problems, and in practice, it never actually turned into an incident.

Then, in the first half of this year, we made a big change: we adopted Karpenter. Now that we could scale out nodes quickly, we stopped using the Overprovisioner that used to keep spare nodes ready for Pods. As a result, Pods were landing on freshly created nodes much more often, which also raised the odds that an application would try to talk to something before rule sync had finished.

Soon after, we started getting reports like the ones below, and most of them boiled down to “my Pod can’t talk to anything.”

Putting our kube-proxy metrics from 2024 and 2026 side by side made it obvious how much heavier kube-proxy’s workload had gotten in just two years. Our service footprint and NAT rule count had grown noticeably, and Pods were being created and terminated far more often. Every time a Pod changes, the Service’s Endpoints (the IPs of the Pods that receive its traffic) change with it, so the number of changes kube-proxy had to apply grew right along with it. Rule sync latency got several times worse, and endpoint changes pending, which tracks Endpoint changes not yet reflected in the rules, went from occasional brief spikes to a steady backlog.

In the first half of 2026, our service cluster had roughly 1,400 Services and 27,000 Pods, with about 80,000 iptables NAT rules. With Endpoints constantly churning from deploys and autoscaling, and nodes repeatedly being torn down and spun up, the initial rule sync on a new node sometimes took as long as 4 minutes and 20 seconds. (That’s over four minutes with no working Service or DNS traffic!)

Once we confirmed this was actually affecting production, we had to fix it. After some intense discussion with the team, we decided to try switching kube-proxy from iptables mode to nftables mode. Here’s how the two modes differ.

In iptables mode, kube-proxy creates rules for every Service and every Endpoint. When a packet comes in, it’s first matched against the Service rules one by one, top to bottom, to find the destination Service, and then against that Service’s Endpoint rules, again one by one, to pick a Pod. Both steps are sequential scans, so the more Services and Endpoints behind them you have, the more rules a packet has to walk through. That makes lookup cost O(N): it grows linearly with the number of Services and Endpoints.

The bigger problem is updating those rules. The total rule count grows with the number of Services and Endpoints, and the more rules there are, the longer each update takes. Since Endpoints change every time a Pod does, updates happen constantly, and changes that hadn’t been applied yet kept piling up. On top of that, right after kube-proxy starts, it does a full sync that rewrites every rule from scratch, and at the scale Karrot’s clusters had grown to, that sometimes took over four minutes.

nftables mode uses maps for both steps: finding the Service and picking an Endpoint. It looks up destination IP . protocol . port in a map to jump straight to the right Service, and it picks an Endpoint directly from that Service's own map, instead of scanning a list. So lookup cost stays close to O(1) no matter how many Services or Endpoints you add. Updates only apply the Services and Endpoints that changed since the last sync, so the cost scales with the amount of change, not the total size. The more Endpoints you have and the more often they change, the bigger the difference.

But before switching modes, we had some questions. What exactly was slowing down rule sync? Was it the sheer number of Services and Endpoints? The frequency of changes? How much would nftables actually help? And could we switch to nftables safely?

To answer these, we set up experiments on a test cluster: vary the conditions, measure latency, and compare iptables against nftables. We figured initial sync needed to come in under 20 seconds to actually solve the problem, and we set out to verify that through experiments.

2. Four goals for the experiment

Before diving in, we nailed down four things we wanted to learn.

1. Find out which conditions slow rule sync down, and by how much

Having lots of Services and Endpoints is a different condition from having Endpoints that change constantly. And deploying the same number of Pods might have a different impact depending on whether you replace them gradually or all at once. We decided to isolate scale, change frequency, and deployment pattern, and measure how each one affects latency.

2. Compare iptables and nftables under identical conditions

nftables has a reputation for better performance, but we wanted to see for ourselves how much it would help in Karrot’s environment. So we generated the same load on a test cluster and compared the two.

3. Confirm it’s safe for production

Getting faster in a test doesn’t mean you flip the switch in prod. We needed to make sure it would play nicely with our add-ons like the VPC CNI and Istio, and check whether any known issues applied to our setup.

4. Decide whether to keep the current kube-proxy version or upgrade alongside

At the time, our EKS clusters were on v1.34, but we had pinned kube-proxy at v1.31 because of an issue (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323) we’d found in v1.34 (more on this in section 6). Since nftables mode was also available in v1.31, we considered two options: switch only the mode, or upgrade to v1.34 and switch at the same time. Performance and known issues can vary by version, so we wanted to weigh the improvement against the operational risk before deciding.

3. First, defining what we’re measuring

Before getting into the experiments, let’s go over what kube-proxy does and what the metrics we tracked actually mean.

When Endpoints change, node rules have to change too

kube-proxy watches Services and EndpointSlices for changes and updates the network rules on each node. That’s what makes a request to a Service address reach an actual destination Pod.

But the moment an Endpoint changes and the moment that change lands in a node’s rules are not the same. It takes time to receive the change and update the rules, and kube-proxy may also batch several changes together.

We split our experiments into two scenarios: applying changes on a node that’s already running, and kube-proxy performing its initial sync on a freshly started node. Since the initial sync is directly tied to the connectivity problems on new nodes, we measured it separately.

The kube-proxy metrics we watched

rule sync latency is how long a single sync run takes. network programming latency is the delay from the recorded time of the triggering change until the rules are applied, so time spent delivering the change and waiting to be processed counts toward it too. The trigger time is taken from the endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time annotation of an EndpointSlice resource.

addressType: IPv4
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - 10.10.10.10
    nodeName: ip-10-11-11-11.ap-northeast-2.compute.internal
    targetRef:
      kind: Pod
      name: test-server-7d6969fdd-xf9w2
      namespace: test-server
    zone: ap-northeast-2a
metadata:
  annotations:
    endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time: '2026-03-27T00:00:00Z'
...

Normally the EndpointSlice controller sets it, but if you create EndpointSlices yourself for a selector-less Service, as we did in these experiments, you have to set the annotation yourself.

For example, if a change waits 10 seconds before a sync picks it up and the rules take 2 seconds to apply, it took about 12 seconds for the change to take effect. If you only look at sync duration, you miss those first 10 seconds.

pending is the number of Endpoint changes kube-proxy has received but hasn't yet picked up for a sync.

We measured initial sync time from the elapsed value in each kube-proxy Pod's first SyncProxyRules complete log line. kube-proxy writes this line every time it applies the cluster's Service and Endpoint state to the node's rules, and elapsed records how long that took. When kube-proxy first starts, it has to build every rule from scratch, so the very first log line tells you how long it took to build the entire rule set.

I0301 12:02:44.082722 1 proxier.go:822] “SyncProxyRules complete” ipFamily=”IPv4" elapsed=”1m24.368581138s”

Some metrics couldn’t capture the real maximum

During the experiments, rule sync latency kept topping out at 16.4 seconds. Yet the initial sync logs showed runs taking over a minute, and in one experiment, 5 minutes 33 seconds. A flat 16.4s while syncs were clearly taking much longer seemed off, so we dug in.

The bucket layout of the kube-proxy metric explained it. The largest finite bucket boundary in the classic histogram we were using was 16.384 seconds. Anything longer lands in the +Inf bucket, and when the quantile falls there, histogram_quantile() simply returns 16.384 seconds.

In other words, 16.4 seconds was not the actual maximum. Long syncs were still being recorded; the bucket layout just couldn’t tell them apart. Going deeper would take us off topic, so for the rest of this post, just read “16.4s” as “at least 16.4s, probably more.”

(Reference: kube-proxy metrics docs: https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubernetes@v1.31.0/pkg/proxy/metrics)

So we compared recurring syncs using metrics, and tracked initial sync time, the one that mattered most here, separately through logs.

With our dashboards set up, we ran and observed the experiments many times over, across a bunch of different scenarios 💪🏻

4. What slows rule sync down? (Goal 1)

We started by looking for the conditions that make latency climb in iptables mode. Is it the number of Services and Endpoints? Or a big batch of Endpoints changing at once?

To find out, we wrote a benchmarking tool in Go for load-testing kube-proxy and set it up on a test EKS cluster. Instead of running tens of thousands of real Pods, we created selector-less Services with test EndpointSlices. Adding or swapping IPs in those EndpointSlices makes kube-proxy detect the change and update its rules. This let us generate pure rule-management load with no application traffic involved.

What happens as scale grows? (iptables mode)

The first round varied the number of Services and Endpoints and how they were distributed, for example, putting 5,000 Endpoints behind a single Service versus spreading them across many. With around 16,000 NAT rules, p99 sync latency mostly stayed under a second.

But that didn’t explain what we were seeing in production. So we mixed small and large Services and gradually scaled up.

Once we scaled up, the difference became clear. p99 went from 1.7s at around 29,000 NAT rules to 14.6s at around 79,000. At around 96,000, peak pending also jumped to 600.

Latency that barely registered at small scale showed up once we got close to production scale.

Same number of Endpoints, different latency

Next, we simulated deployments on top of an existing rule set, mimicking a real environment where workloads are constantly being rolled out. We ran new deployments (adding Endpoints incrementally) and rolling updates (replacing existing IPs with new ones) separately. Combining three baseline loads with nine deployment conditions gave us 27 test cases in total.

The factor that stood out most was how many Endpoints were added at once. Holding steady at about 84,000 NAT rules, we added 500 Endpoints in total, n at a time, every 2 seconds.

The total was 500 Endpoints either way. But adding them 250 at a time made sync times balloon and let far more changes pile up.

This showed us that it’s not just overall scale that matters, but also the pattern in which changes arrive. Next, we ran the same load in nftables mode.

5. How much faster does nftables handle the same load? (Goal 2)

To see how the two modes compare, we first switched kube-proxy to nftables mode on v1.34 (up from v1.31) and reran the 27 deployment cases. (Note that this comparison includes both the mode change and the version change. I’ll cover the experiment that keeps the version and only switches the mode later on.)

Adding many Endpoints at once

Let’s start with the condition that showed the biggest gap. We kept the same Service and Endpoint setup that had produced about 84,000 iptables rules, and added 500 Endpoints, 250 at a time.

Sync time dropped dramatically, and far fewer changes piled up. That said, nftables wasn’t faster in every scenario. In the 10-at-a-time case, nftables p99 sync latency hit 15.6s at one point.

So rather than judging on a single deployment pattern, we also measured the thing that mattered most for this project: initial rule sync time.

How much did initial sync time improve?

Here we kept a configuration equivalent to about 83,000 NAT rules and restarted the kube-proxy Pod. Comparing elapsed from the first SyncProxyRules complete log line, iptables took about 66 seconds and nftables about 1.3 seconds.

Since we restarted kube-proxy on an existing node, this doesn’t reproduce the full new-node bootstrapping process. What we compared here is the initial sync kube-proxy performs after it starts.

Overlapping deployments with initial sync

So what happens when deployments are in flight at the same time? Next, we recreated a production-like situation with lots of overlapping changes. While keeping the baseline load, we ran all of the following at once:

  • Rolling update of Service A (1,000 Endpoints)
  • Rolling update of Service B (500 Endpoints)
  • New deployment of Service C (500 Endpoints)
  • Restarting kube-proxy on a different node roughly 15, 30, and 60 seconds after the deployments began

The initial sync times tell a clear story.

iptables took over a minute all three times, with the worst run at 5 minutes 33 seconds. nftables came in around 1.3 seconds every time. In this experiment, initial sync wasn’t just faster. It was also far more consistent.

Change propagation latency during the deployments dropped as well.

p99 change propagation latency improved by about 12x, from 84.5s to 6.8s. Beyond the initial sync, nftables was also applying changes that came in during deployments much faster.

A quick note on methodology: early versions of our benchmarking tool set the wrong annotation key for the change timestamp, so network programming latency wasn’t recorded in the earlier runs. We fixed it before this experiment, which is why this is the first place those numbers show up.

That wraps up confirming the benefits. Next, we looked at whether we could get these gains safely in production.

6. Is it safe for production? (Goals 3 and 4)

We’d confirmed the performance gap between iptables and nftables. But before rolling it out to production, we needed to make sure existing traffic paths would keep working and that no new issues would bite us. This was also where we decided whether to bump kube-proxy from v1.31 to v1.34.

Checking compatibility with our existing setup

First, we checked the Service configuration on a dev cluster that mirrors production. We paid special attention to ingress-nginx and the Istio ingress gateway, where inbound traffic first reaches our cluster. Both Services use NodePort with externalTrafficPolicy: Local, and requests come in through an NLB to the node's primary IP and NodePort.

We checked this path because NodePort behaves a bit differently in nftables mode. By default, nftables mode only handles NodePort requests that arrive on the node’s primary IP, and it doesn’t support access via localhost. Both Services receive traffic from the NLB on the node's primary IP, so they weren't affected.

We didn’t find any compatibility concerns with the other components either.

But a conntrack issue shaped our version choice

There were conditions our benchmarks couldn’t reproduce. The big one was conntrack, the kernel’s connection tracking. Our test environment had about 4,000 entries, while production had about 166,000. Even with comparable Endpoint counts, the actual connection state differed by roughly 40x.

So separately from the experiments, we reviewed known issues, and that’s where we found a critical one.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323

The biggest factor in our version decision was a conntrack cleanup performance regression introduced after v1.32. With lots of UDP connections piled up, cleanup could take a long time whenever Endpoints changed. And if cleanup drags on, subsequent rule updates can get delayed too. The fix landed in v1.36, but kube-proxy can’t run a newer version than the control plane, so it wasn’t an option on our EKS v1.34 clusters.

The public issue confirmed the impact in both iptables and nftables modes, so switching to nftables alone wouldn’t fix it. And since our test environment’s conntrack table was small, we couldn’t judge the production risk from benchmark results alone.

So we had one more question to answer: would keeping v1.31 and switching only the mode be good enough?

v1.31 or v1.34?

In kube-proxy v1.31, nftables mode was still in beta, so we needed to validate its performance and stability.

We reused the high-load scenario from earlier and ran it multiple times on each setup: v1.31 iptables, v1.31 nftables, and v1.34 nftables.

v1.34 nftables was faster on initial sync. But even on v1.31, a sync that used to take over 100 seconds dropped to about 5 seconds. Peak pending and peak CPU came down too.

p99 programming latency varied quite a bit, anywhere from 5.7s to 15.9s. We didn’t try to rank the two nftables versions based on this alone. What we wanted to know was whether v1.31 could deliver a meaningful improvement on its own, and we had the evidence for that.

Based on these results, I decided to stay on v1.31 and switch to nftables mode. It let us sidestep the conntrack regression, and even in beta, it delivered more than enough performance.

Preparing for the switch and day-2 operations

The rollout procedure was simple: update the kube-proxy config to nftables mode and restart the kube-proxy DaemonSet. We also prepared a rollback plan: switch the mode back to iptables and restart again. Flipping the setting is easy, but each node still has to clean up the old rules and set up the new ones, so we reviewed the traffic impact during that window too.

The CLI commands engineers relied on changed as well. So we wrote a separate runbook showing how to do the familiar iptables-save | grep KUBE-, iptables -nvL, and TRACE workflows in nftables, complete with real output from our nodes, and walked the team through it in a session.

The goal was to make sure we could still find Service rules, check destination Endpoints, and trace packet paths after the switch.

7. Adding observability and rolling out in stages

To know whether the switch actually worked, we needed a direct view of the problem we were trying to fix. The key question was how long kube-proxy spends on its initial rule sync on a new node. Our existing metrics couldn’t isolate the initial sync, so we turned the value we’d been pulling from logs into a metric.

The setup is simple. A CronJob runs every minute and looks up kube-proxy Pods created within the last 120 seconds. It extracts elapsed from the first SyncProxyRules complete line in each Pod's logs and records it as a metric called kubeproxy_first_sync_seconds.

Now we can track initial sync time per node without digging through logs. We started collecting it before the switch, so we could compare iptables and nftables on the same metric.

We also widened the rollout gradually. After confirming no issues in our alpha environment, we went region by region, from lower-traffic regions to higher-traffic ones. Our production cluster in the Korea region, the most critical of them all, was switched over during an early-morning maintenance window.

The plan covered more than just the mode switch. After switching, we restarted large Deployments to make sure traffic stayed healthy under heavy Endpoint churn, just like a real deploy, and then watched the metrics for about an hour. In the end, the migration went smoothly with no major issues.

8. And the results are in!

After rolling out to our production cluster in the Korea region, the first thing we checked was initial sync time on new nodes. What used to take 70–90 seconds at peak hours dropped to around 4–5 seconds.

We saw changes on the application side too. Previously, Istio was logging tens of thousands of ca request failed errors every day while requesting certificates. From the day of the switch, that count dropped to zero.

istio-proxy requests certificates through the istiod Service’s ClusterIP, and that request has to go through the node’s kube-proxy rules to reach an istiod Pod. Requests sent before the initial sync finished on a new node were failing, and once sync time came down, those failures disappeared too.

We also checked whether day-to-day changes were being handled more smoothly, comparing dashboards for the same window (8 AM to 6 PM) on the day before and the day of the switch. Network programming volume was about the same, but latency spikes became much less frequent. Peak endpoint changes pending also dropped from about 60,000 to 14,000.

Resource usage didn’t match our experiments, though. In production, kube-proxy CPU usage roughly doubled and memory went up about 20%. But overall usage was still low, so we didn’t consider it a problem.

In the end, we safely solved the problem we set out to fix: Pod connectivity failures caused by slow kube-proxy rule sync on new nodes.

9. Wrapping up

This project started with a problem we didn’t think was urgent, until cluster growth and changes in how we run nodes turned it into a real reliability issue. From deciding on the fix through benchmarking, adding observability, and finishing the rollout, it took about a month.

Since we were changing how node networking works, the fear of “what if this breaks connectivity?” kept us running more experiments, which stretched things out. But thanks to a shared belief on the team that, as SREs, you can never be too thorough with safety checks, we were able to move carefully, one step at a time.

Personally, this was a really rewarding and fun adventure. I uncovered metric pitfalls I never knew existed and got a much deeper understanding of how kube-proxy works. Watching the metrics shift as we added new experiment scenarios was a fun little bonus, too.

The mode switch went smoothly, with none of the issues we’d worried about. If you run kube-proxy and have been thinking about making it faster, I hope this post helps.

Thanks for reading!

Why Can’t My Running Pods Be Reached? Our Journey to kube-proxy nftables Mode was originally published in 당근 기술 블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: 파드는 떴는데 왜 통신이 안 될까? kube-proxy nftables 전환 여정
event_model_payload.summary:
안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 클러스터 파트에서 일하고 있는 Karin(카린)이에요. 클러스터 파트는 당근 내부의 모든 서비스가 운영되는 쿠버네티스 환경을 설계하고 관리해요. 쿠버네티스 환경의 가시성과 서비스 안정성을 확보하기 위해 모니터링 인프라부터 서비스 메시, 보안까지 여러 방면에서 정책과 로드맵을 설계하고 적용해요.

이 글에서는 kube-proxy를 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환한 이야기를 해보려고 해요. kube-proxy는 쿠버네티스의 모든 노드에서 동작하면서, Service로 들어온 트래픽이 실제 Pod로 전달되도록 리눅스 커널에 네트워크 규칙을 설정하는 컴포넌트예요. 이 규칙을 관리하는 방식으로 오랫동안 iptables를 써왔는데, 이를 더 효율적인 후속 도구인 nftables로 바꾼 과정과 그 과정에서 배운 점을 공유하려고 해요.

1. kube-proxy latency가 서비스 안정성에 영향을 미쳤어요

쿠버네티스에서 노드가 새로 생기고 Pod가 뜨는 것은 매우 자연스러운 일이죠. 그런데 새 노드에 Pod가 스케줄링되고 애플리케이션이 시작되었다고 해서, 다른 서비스와 통신할 준비도 모두 끝난 걸까요?

kube-proxy는 각 노드에서 Service로 향하는 트래픽이 실제 Pod에 도달할 수 있게 네트워크 규칙(이하 ‘규칙’)을 관리하는데요, 새 노드에서는 이 규칙을 준비하는 동안 애플리케이션이 먼저 시작하면 DNS 조회나 다른 서비스와의 통신에 실패할 수 있어요.

kube-proxy의 규칙 동기화가 느려지고 있다는 것은 예전부터 알고 있었어요. 2024년부터 지표를 지켜보니, 다른 리전보다 규모가 큰 한국 프로덕션에서 유독 지연이 높았거든요. 그러나 운영상 문제가 될 정도는 아니라고 판단했고, 실제로도 이슈로 이어진 적은 없었어요.

하지만 올해 상반기에 Karpenter를 도입하는 큰 변화가 있었어요. 노드를 빠르게 scale-out할 수 있게 되면서 Pod가 사용할 노드를 미리 준비하던 Overprovisioner를 더 이상 사용하지 않게 됐어요. 그 결과 새로 생성된 노드에 Pod가 곧바로 스케줄링되는 상황을 더 자주 마주했어요. 규칙 동기화가 끝나기 전에 애플리케이션이 통신을 시도할 가능성도 커진 거죠.

이후에 아래와 같은 문의가 들어오기 시작했고, 대부분은 ‘Pod가 통신이 안 된다’라는 제보였어요.

2024년과 2026년의 kube-proxy 지표를 나란히 놓고 보니, 2년 사이 kube-proxy의 부담이 크게 늘어난 걸 뚜렷하게 확인할 수 있었어요. 서비스 규모와 NAT 규칙 수가 눈에 띄게 늘었고, Pod가 생성되고 종료되는 일도 잦아졌어요. Pod가 바뀔 때마다 Service의 목적지를 나타내는 Endpoint, 즉 트래픽을 받을 Pod의 IP도 함께 바뀌기 때문에 kube-proxy가 반영해야 할 변경도 그만큼 늘어났어요. 그 결과 규칙 동기화 지연은 이전보다 몇 배 커졌고, 아직 규칙에 반영되지 못한 Endpoint 변경을 나타내는 endpoint changes pending 지표도 과거에는 잠깐씩 튀던 값이 지속적으로 쌓이는 모습으로 바뀌었어요.

2026년 상반기 당시 서비스 클러스터에는 약 1,400개의 Service와 27,000개의 Pod가 있었고, iptables의 NAT 규칙은 약 80,000개에 달했어요. 배포와 오토스케일링으로 Endpoint가 계속 바뀌는 가운데, 노드가 반복적으로 종료되고 생성될 때는 첫 규칙 동기화에 최대 4분 20초가 걸리기도 했어요. 4분 넘게 Service와 DNS 통신이 안 되는 상태였던 거예요!

실제 서비스 운영에 영향을 주는 문제라는 것을 확인했기 때문에 이 문제를 해결해야 했어요. 팀원들과 개선 방안을 치열하게 의논한 결과 iptables 모드에서 nftables 모드로 전환해 보기로 했어요. 두 모드의 차이점은 다음과 같아요.

iptables 모드에서 kube-proxy는 Service마다, 그리고 Endpoint마다 규칙을 만들어요. 패킷이 들어오면 먼저 Service 규칙을 위에서부터 차례로 비교해 목적지 Service를 찾고, 다시 그 Service의 Endpoint 규칙을 차례로 비교해 보낼 Pod를 골라요. 두 단계 모두 순차 비교라서 Service가 많을수록, 그리고 Service 하나에 붙은 Endpoint가 많을수록 비교할 규칙이 늘어나 조회 비용이 O(N)이에요.

더 큰 문제는 규칙을 갱신할 때예요. 전체 규칙 수는 Service와 Endpoint 수에 비례하고, 규칙이 많을수록 갱신 시간도 길어져요. 그런데 Endpoint는 Pod가 변경될 때 함께 바뀌어서 갱신이 자주 일어나다 보니, 반영하지 못한 변경이 점점 쌓였어요. 특히 kube-proxy가 시작한 직후에는 전체 규칙을 새로 쓰는 full sync를 하는데, 규모가 커진 당근 클러스터에서는 이 시간이 4분을 넘기도 했어요.

nftables 모드는 Service를 찾는 단계와 Endpoint를 고르는 단계를 모두 map 기반으로 처리해요. 목적지 IP . 프로토콜 . 포트를 키로 map을 조회해서 해당 Service로 바로 이동하고, Endpoint도 목록을 하나씩 훑지 않고 map에서 바로 골라요. 그래서 Service나 Endpoint가 늘어나도 조회 비용은 O(1)에 가깝게 유지돼요. 갱신할 때도 지난 동기화 이후 바뀐 Service와 Endpoint만 반영하므로, 비용이 전체 규모가 아니라 변경량에 비례해요. Endpoint가 많고 자주 바뀌는 환경일수록 이 차이가 크게 드러나요.

하지만 모드를 변경하기 전에, 몇 가지 질문이 있었어요. 무엇이 규칙 동기화를 느리게 만들고 있었을까요? Service와 Endpoint가 많아서일까요? 변경이 자주 발생해서일까요? nftables로 바꾸면 얼마나 개선될까요? nftables 모드로 ‘안전하게’ 전환할 수 있을까요?

이 질문에 답하기 위해, 테스트 클러스터에서 조건을 바꿔가며 latency를 측정하고 iptables와 nftables를 비교하는 실험을 해보기로 했어요. 첫 동기화 시간을 20초 이내로 줄여야 한다고 판단했고, 실험으로 이를 검증하고자 했어요.

2. 실험의 네 가지 목표

실험을 시작하기 전에, 이 프로젝트에서 무엇을 확인할지 네 가지로 정리했어요.

1. 조건에 따른 규칙 동기화 지연 시간 확인

Service와 Endpoint가 많은 것과, 그 Endpoint가 자주 바뀌는 것은 다른 조건이겠죠? 같은 수의 Pod를 배포하더라도 조금씩 교체할 때와 한꺼번에 교체할 때의 영향이 다를 수 있고요. 규모, 변경 빈도, 배포 패턴을 나눠서 각각 latency에 어떤 영향을 주는지 측정해보기로 했어요.

2. 같은 조건에서 iptables와 nftables를 비교

nftables의 성능이 좋다고 알려져 있어도, 당근의 운영 환경에서 얼마나 개선될지는 직접 확인하고 싶었어요. 테스트 클러스터에서 같은 부하를 만들어 성능을 비교하기로 했어요.

3. 프로덕션에 안전하게 적용할 수 있는지 확인

테스트에서 빨라졌다고 바로 전환할 수는 없겠죠? 당근에서 사용하는 VPC CNI, Istio 등의 addon 구성과 충돌 없이 동작하는지, 알려진 이슈 중 우리 환경에 해당하는 것은 없는지 살펴봐야 했어요.

4. kube-proxy 버전을 유지할지, 함께 업그레이드할지

당시 EKS는 v1.34이지만, kube-proxy는 v1.34에서 이슈(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323)가 발견되어 v1.31을 유지하고 있었어요. v1.31에서도 nftables 모드를 사용할 수 있었기 때문에, 모드만 변경하는 방법과 v1.34로 올리면서 변경하는 방법을 모두 검토했어요. 버전마다 성능과 알려진 이슈가 다를 수 있으니, 개선 폭과 운영 위험을 함께 비교해 결정하고자 했어요.

3. 먼저, 무엇을 측정하는지 정리했어요

본격적인 실험에 앞서, kube-proxy가 어떤 일을 하고 우리가 보려는 지표가 무엇을 의미하는지 짚어볼게요.

Endpoint가 바뀌면 노드의 규칙(rule)도 바뀌어야 해요

kube-proxy는 Service와 EndpointSlice의 변경을 관찰하고, 각 노드의 네트워크 규칙을 갱신해요. 애플리케이션이 Service 주소로 요청하면 실제 목적지인 Pod로 전달되도록 하는 거예요.

하지만 Endpoint가 바뀌는 시점과 노드의 규칙에 반영되는 시점은 달라요. 변경을 전달받고 규칙을 갱신하는 데 시간이 필요하기 때문이에요. 여러 변경을 모아서 처리하기도 하고요.

이번 실험에서는 두 상황을 구분했어요. 운영 중인 노드에서 변경을 반영하는 상황과 새로 시작된 노드에서 kube-proxy가 첫 동기화를 수행하는 상황이에요. 특히 첫 동기화는 새 노드의 초기 통신 문제와 연결되므로 따로 측정했어요.

kube-proxy 메트릭을 관측했어요

rule sync latency는 한 번의 동기화 작업에 걸린 시간이에요. network programming latency는 기록된 변경 원인 시각부터 규칙 적용까지의 지연이에요. 여기서 '변경 원인 시각'은 EndpointSlice에 붙는 endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time annotation 값이에요.

addressType: IPv4
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - 10.10.10.10
    nodeName: ip-10-11-11-11.ap-northeast-2.compute.internal
    targetRef:
      kind: Pod
      name: test-server-7d6969fdd-xf9w2
      namespace: test-server
    zone: ap-northeast-2a
metadata:
  annotations:
    endpoints.kubernetes.io/last-change-trigger-time: '2026-03-27T00:00:00Z'
...

평소에는 EndpointSlice 컨트롤러가 이 값을 기록하지만, 이번 실험처럼 selector가 없는 Service에 EndpointSlice를 직접 만들면 annotation도 직접 넣어야 해요. 변경 전달과 처리 대기 시간도 rule sync latency에 영향을 줘요.

예를 들어, 동기화 전까지 10초가 걸리고 규칙 적용에 2초가 걸렸다면 변경 반영까지는 약 12초가 걸린 셈이에요. 동기화 시간만 보면 앞의 10초를 놓칠 수 있어요.

pending은 Pod 수나 규칙 수가 아니에요. 동기화 작업이 변경 목록을 가져가면 초기화되므로, 0이라고 규칙 적용까지 끝났다는 뜻은 아니에요.

첫 동기화 시간은 kube-proxy Pod의 첫 번째 SyncProxyRules complete 로그에 찍힌 elapsed 값으로 확인했어요. kube-proxy는 클러스터의 Service와 Endpoint 정보를 노드의 규칙에 한 번 반영할 때마다 이 로그를 남기고, elapsed에는 그 반영에 걸린 시간이 기록돼요. kube-proxy가 처음 뜰 때는 모든 규칙을 처음부터 만들어야 해서, 첫 번째 로그가 전체 규칙을 만드는 데 걸린 시간을 보여줘요.

I0301 12:02:44.082722 1 proxier.go:822] “SyncProxyRules complete” ipFamily=”IPv4" elapsed=”1m24.368581138s”

특정 메트릭은 실제 최댓값을 측정할 수 없었어요

실험 중 rule sync latency가 16.4초에서 더 올라가지 않는 모습이 반복됐어요. 하지만 첫 동기화 로그에는 1분 이상, 특정 실험에서는 5분 33초가 걸린 기록도 있었어요. 이렇게 동기화가 오래 걸리는 상황에서 16.4초라는 일정한 값이 찍히는 게 이상해서 찾아봤어요.

kube-proxy 메트릭의 bucket 구성을 보니 원인을 알 수 있었어요. 당시 사용한 classic histogram의 마지막 유한 경계는 16.384초예요. 그보다 긴 관측값은 모두 +Inf 구간에 들어가요. 지표가 이 구간에 해당하면 histogram_quantile()은 16.384초를 반환해요.

즉, 16.4초는 실제 동기화 시간의 최댓값이 아니었어요. 긴 동기화도 기록되지만, 이 bucket 구성으로는 해당 구간의 수치를 구분해서 표현할 수 없었던 거예요. 이 내용을 자세히 다루기에는 글의 주제와 맞지 않아서, 이 글에서 **‘16.4초로 기록된 값은 실제로 그 이상일 수 있다는 점’**을 참고해 주세요.

(참고자료: kube-proxy metric 문서: https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/kubernetes@v1.31.0/pkg/proxy/metrics)

그래서 반복되는 동기화는 메트릭으로 비교하고, 이번 문제에서 중요한 첫 동기화 시간은 로그로 따로 확인했어요.

실험을 위한 대시보드 구성을 마친 뒤, 여러 상황을 가정하며 수차례 실행과 관찰을 반복했어요 💪🏻

4. 어떤 상황에서 규칙 동기화가 느려질까요? (실험 목표 1)

먼저 iptables 모드에서 지연이 커지는 조건을 찾아보기로 했어요. Service와 Endpoint가 많아서일까요? 아니면 한꺼번에 많은 Endpoint가 바뀌어서일까요?

이를 확인하려고 Go를 사용해 kube-proxy 부하 테스트를 할 수 있는 벤치마크 도구를 만들고, 테스트용 EKS 클러스터에 벤치마크 환경을 구성했어요. 실제 Pod를 수만 개 띄우는 대신, selector가 없는 Service와 테스트용 EndpointSlice를 생성했어요. EndpointSlice의 IP를 추가하거나 교체하면 kube-proxy가 변경을 감지하고 규칙을 갱신해요. 이 방식으로 애플리케이션 트래픽 없이 규칙을 관리하는 부하를 만들었어요.

규모가 커지면 어떤 일이 생길까요? (iptables 모드)

첫 실험에서는 Service와 Endpoint의 수, 분배 방식을 바꿔봤어요. Endpoint 5,000개를 하나의 Service에 모으거나, 여러 Service에 나누는 식이에요. NAT 규칙이 약 16,000개인 범위에서는 sync latency의 p99가 대체로 1초 이내였어요.

이 정도로는 프로덕션의 지연을 설명하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 작은 Service와 큰 Service를 섞고, 전체 규모를 점차 늘려봤어요.

규모를 키우자 차이가 드러났어요. NAT 규칙이 약 29,000개일 때 1.7초였던 p99가, 약 79,000개에서는 14.6초까지 올라갔어요. 약 96,000개인 조건에서는 pending 피크도 600까지 증가했어요.

규모가 작을 때는 잘 드러나지 않던 지연이 프로덕션과 비슷한 규모에서 발견됐어요.

같은 수의 Endpoint도 한꺼번에 바꾸면 달랐어요

다음에는 기존 규칙이 있는 상태에서 배포를 시뮬레이션했어요. 워크로드가 활발히 배포되는 현실의 상황을 가정한 거예요. Endpoint를 순차적으로 추가하는 신규 배포와, 기존 IP를 새 IP로 교체하는 롤링 업데이트를 나눠서 실행했어요. 세 가지 기본 부하에 아홉 가지 배포 조건을 조합해 총 27개 케이스를 확인했어요.

그중 차이가 뚜렷했던 것은 한 번에 추가하는 Endpoint 수였어요. NAT 규칙 약 84,000개를 유지한 상태에서, 총 500개의 Endpoint를 n개씩 2초 간격으로 추가했어요.

총 500개를 추가한다는 점은 같았어요. 하지만 250개씩 추가했을 때는 동기화 시간이 크게 늘고, 처리할 변경도 더 많이 쌓였어요.

이 결과로 전체 규모뿐 아니라 변경이 들어오는 패턴도 중요하다는 것을 확인했어요. 다음에는 같은 부하를 nftables 모드에서도 실행해보기로 했어요.

5. nftables에서는 같은 부하를 얼마나 빨리 처리할까요? (실험 목표 2)

두 모드의 성능에 어떤 차이가 있는지 확인하기 위해 먼저 kube-proxy를 (v1.31 →)v1.34의 nftables 모드로 바꾸고, 앞의 27개 배포 케이스를 반복했어요. (이 비교에는 모드와 버전 변경이 함께 포함돼 있어요. 버전을 유지하고 모드만 바꾸는 실험은 뒤에서 따로 소개할게요.)

한꺼번에 많은 Endpoint를 추가했을 때

차이가 컸던 조건부터 볼게요. 약 84,000개의 iptables 규칙을 만들었던 Service·Endpoint 구성을 유지하고, Endpoint 500개를 250개씩 추가했어요.

동기화 시간이 크게 줄었고, 처리할 변경도 덜 쌓였어요. 다만 모든 조건에서 항상 빨랐던 것은 아니에요. 10개씩 추가한 조건에서는 nftables의 sync latency p99가 15.6초까지 올라간 기록도 있었어요.

그래서 한 가지 배포 패턴만으로 판단하지 않고, 이번 프로젝트에서 가장 중요했던 첫 규칙 동기화 시간도 확인했어요.

첫 동기화 시간은 얼마나 줄었을까요?

위 실험에서는 NAT 규칙 약 83,000개에 해당하는 구성을 유지한 채 kube-proxy Pod를 재시작했어요. 첫 SyncProxyRules complete 로그의 elapsed를 비교하니, iptables는 약 66초, nftables는 약 1.3초였어요.

기존 노드에서 kube-proxy를 재시작한 실험이므로 새 노드의 생성 과정을 모두 재현한 것은 아니에요. 여기서는 kube-proxy가 시작한 뒤 수행하는 첫 동기화 작업을 비교했어요.

배포와 첫 동기화를 겹쳐봤어요

그렇다면 배포가 겹치는 동안에는 어떨까요? 다음 실험에서는 프로덕션처럼 여러 변경이 겹치는 상황을 만들었어요. 기본 부하를 유지하면서 아래 작업을 동시에 실행했어요.

  • Endpoint 1,000개인 Service A의 롤링 업데이트.
  • Endpoint 500개인 Service B의 롤링 업데이트.
  • Endpoint 500개인 Service C의 신규 배포.
  • 배포 시작 후 약 15초, 30초, 60초에 서로 다른 노드의 kube-proxy 재시작.

먼저 첫 동기화 시간을 보면 차이가 뚜렷해요.

iptables에서는 세 번 모두 1분을 넘겼어요. 가장 긴 기록은 5분 33초였고요. 반면 nftables는 세 번 모두 1.3초 안팎이었어요. 이번 실험에서는 첫 동기화 시간이 짧아졌을 뿐 아니라, 측정값 사이의 편차도 작아졌어요.

배포 중 변경 반영 지연도 함께 줄었어요.

변경 반영 지연의 p99는 84.5초에서 6.8초로 약 12배 감소했어요. 첫 동기화뿐 아니라, 배포 중에 들어오는 변경도 더 빠르게 반영하고 있었어요.

여기서 측정 과정의 수정 사항도 하나 짚고 갈게요. 초기 벤치마크 도구에는 변경 시각을 기록하는 annotation 키가 잘못 설정돼 있었어요. 이를 수정한 위 실험부터 테스트 변경의 network programming latency를 정상적으로 측정했어요. 따라서 앞선 실험에서 이 지표가 없었던 것을 “지연이 없었다”는 뜻으로 해석하지 않았어요.

여기까지는 전환 효과를 확인하는 과정이었어요. 다음에는 이 개선을 프로덕션에서도 안전하게 얻을 수 있는지 살펴봤어요.

6. 프로덕션에서도 안전하게 사용할 수 있을까요? (실험 목표 3, 4)

iptables와 nftables의 성능 차이는 확인했어요. 하지만 프로덕션에 적용하려면 기존 통신 경로가 유지되는지, 새롭게 영향을 받을 이슈는 없는지 확인해야 했어요. kube-proxy 버전을 v1.31 → v1.34로 올려도 될지도 이 과정에서 판단했어요.

기존 구성과 호환되는지 확인했어요

먼저 프로덕션과 같은 구성을 사용하는 개발 환경 클러스터의 Service 설정을 확인했어요. 특히 외부 요청을 받는 ingress-nginx와 Istio ingress gateway를 살펴봤어요. 두 Service는 NodePort와 externalTrafficPolicy: Local을 사용하고 있었어요. 요청은 NLB를 거쳐 노드의 primary IP와 NodePort로 들어왔어요.

이 경로를 확인한 이유는 nftables 모드에서 NodePort 동작이 일부 달라지기 때문이에요. nftables 모드는 기본적으로 노드의 primary IP로 들어온 요청만 NodePort로 처리하고, localhost를 통한 접근은 지원하지 않아요. 두 Service 모두 NLB를 거쳐 노드의 primary IP로 트래픽을 받고 있어서 영향이 없었어요.

그 외 컴포넌트의 호환성을 확인해 봤을 때 문제 될 만한 것은 없었어요.

설정 검토와 함께 개발 환경에서의 전환 후 동작도 확인했어요. 당시 개발 환경에서는 문제가 발견되지 않았어요.

하지만, conntrack 이슈가 버전 선택에 영향을 줬어요

벤치마크에서 재현하지 못한 조건도 있었어요. 대표적인 것이 커널에서 연결 상태를 추적하는 conntrack이었어요. 테스트 환경의 entry는 약 4,000개, 프로덕션은 약 166,000개였어요. Endpoint 규모를 비슷하게 만들어도 실제 연결 상태의 규모는 약 40배 차이가 났어요.

그래서 실험 결과와 별도로 알려진 이슈를 검토하던 중, 크리티컬한 이슈를 발견했어요. (이슈 링크: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135323)

버전 선택에 가장 큰 영향을 준 것은 v1.32 이후의 conntrack cleanup 성능 저하 이슈였어요. 많은 UDP 연결이 쌓인 상태에서 Endpoint가 바뀌면 정리 작업이 오래 걸릴 수 있었어요. 이 작업이 길어지면 후속 규칙 갱신도 늦어질 수 있고요. 해당 이슈는 v1.36부터 해결되었는데, kube-proxy는 컨트롤 플레인보다 높은 버전을 쓸 수 없어서 EKS v1.34 클러스터에는 적용할 수 없었어요.

이 문제는 nftables 모드로 바꾸는 것만으로 해결되지 않았어요. 공개 이슈에서는 iptables와 nftables 모두에서 영향을 확인했어요. 테스트 환경의 conntrack 규모도 작았기 때문에, 벤치마크 결과만으로 프로덕션의 위험까지 판단하기는 어려웠어요.

그래서 한 가지 더 확인해 보기로 했어요. v1.31을 유지하고 모드만 바꿔도 충분히 개선될까요?

v1.31 vs v1.34 무엇을 선택할까요?

kube-proxy v1.31에서 nftables 모드는 Beta stage였기 때문에, 성능이나 안정성 면에서 검증이 필요했어요.

비교에는 위에서 실험한 고부하 시나리오를 그대로 활용했어요. 이 실험에서는 v1.31 iptables, v1.31 nftables, v1.34 nftables 각각의 환경에서 시나리오를 여러 번 실행했어요.

첫 동기화는 v1.34 nftables가 더 빨랐어요. 하지만 v1.31에서도 100초 이상 걸리던 작업이 약 5초로 줄었어요. Pending과 CPU 피크도 낮아졌고요.

Programming latency의 p99는 5.7초에서 15.9초 정도로 편차가 있었어요. 이 결과만으로 nftables 두 버전의 우열을 단정하지는 않았어요. 이번에 확인하려던 것은 v1.31에서도 충분한 개선을 얻을 수 있는지였고, 그 근거는 확보했어요.

실험 결과를 바탕으로 저는 v1.31을 유지하면서 nftables 모드로 전환하는 것으로 결정했어요. 당시 검토한 conntrack 성능 저하 이슈를 피하면서, Beta stage이지만 충분히 좋은 성능을 보여줬기 때문이에요.

전환과 이후의 운영을 준비했어요

전환 절차는 EKS add-on의 모드를 변경하고 kube-proxy DaemonSet을 재시작하는 방식으로 정리했어요. 문제가 생기면 모드를 iptables로 되돌리고 다시 재시작하는 롤백 절차도 준비했어요. 설정을 바꾸는 작업은 간단하지만, 각 노드에서 기존 규칙을 정리하고 새 규칙을 준비하는 과정은 필요해요. 이때의 통신 영향도 검토했어요.

운영자가 사용하는 명령어도 달라져요. 익숙한 iptables-save | grep KUBE-, iptables -nvL, TRACE 작업을 nftables에서 어떻게 수행할지 별도 운영 가이드로 정리했어요. 노드에서의 실제 출력도 넣고 팀 세션에서 공유했어요.

전환 후에도 Service 규칙을 찾고, 목적지 Endpoint를 확인하고, 패킷 경로를 추적할 수 있도록 준비한 거예요.

7. 지표를 보강하고 순차적으로 전환을 진행했어요

전환 효과를 확인하려면, 우리가 해결하려던 문제를 직접 관측할 수 있어야 했어요. 특히 중요했던 것은 새 노드에서 kube-proxy가 첫 규칙 동기화에 얼마나 시간을 쓰는지였어요. 기존 지표만으로는 첫 동기화만 분리해서 보기 어려웠기 때문에, 로그에서 확인하던 값을 메트릭으로 만들었어요.

수집 방식은 단순해요. CronJob을 1분마다 실행해서, 최근 120초 이내에 생성된 kube-proxy Pod를 조회해요. 각 Pod의 로그에서 처음 등장하는 SyncProxyRules complete의 elapsed를 추출하고, kubeproxy_first_sync_seconds라는 메트릭으로 기록했어요.

이제 로그를 일일이 열지 않아도, 노드별 첫 동기화 시간을 편하게 관측할 수 있게 됐어요. 전환 전부터 수집을 시작해서 iptables와 nftables의 차이를 같은 지표로 확인할 준비를 했어요.

적용 범위도 단계적으로 넓히기로 했어요. 알파에서 문제가 발견되지 않은 것을 확인한 뒤, 트래픽이 적은 리전부터 큰 리전까지 순차적으로 진행했어요. 가장 중요한 한국 프로덕션은 새벽 작업으로 진행했어요.

작업 계획에는 모드 전환뿐 아니라, 전환 후 큰 Deployment를 재시작하는 검증도 포함했어요. 실제 배포처럼 Endpoint가 많이 바뀌는 상황에서 통신에 문제가 없는지 확인하고, 약 1시간 동안 지표를 관찰하도록 했어요. 결과적으로 큰 이슈 없이 순탄하게 전환이 완료되었어요.

8. 전환 결과는!

한국 프로덕션에 적용한 뒤, 먼저 새 노드의 첫 동기화 시간을 확인했어요. 피크 시간대에 70~90초가 걸리던 작업이 4~5초 수준으로 줄었어요.

애플리케이션 쪽에서도 변화가 보였어요. 기존에는 Istio가 인증서를 요청하는 과정에서 ca request failed 로그가 매일 수만 건 이상 발생했었어요. 전환 당일부터 이 로그가 0건으로 집계됐어요.

istio-proxy는 istiod Service의 ClusterIP로 인증서를 요청하는데, 이 요청은 노드의 kube-proxy 규칙을 거쳐야 istiod Pod에 도착해요. 새 노드에서 첫 동기화가 끝나기 전에 나가던 요청이 실패했던 건데, 동기화 시간이 줄면서 이 실패도 함께 사라진 거예요.

운영 중에 발생하는 변경도 더 원활하게 처리하는지 살펴봤어요. 전환 전날과 당일의 같은 시간대인 오전 8시부터 오후 6시까지 대시보드를 비교했어요. Network programming 양은 비슷한 수준이었지만, 지연이 크게 치솟는 빈도는 줄었어요. endpoint changes pending도 피크 시간대에 약 60,000에서 14,000 수준으로 감소했어요.

자원 사용량은 실험과 다른 결과가 나왔어요. 프로덕션에서는 kube-proxy의 CPU 사용량이 약 2배, 메모리 사용량이 약 20% 증가했어요. 하지만 여전히 리소스 사용량이 적었기 때문에 문제 상황으로 보지는 않았어요.

결론적으로, 우리가 목표했던 ‘새 노드의 kube-proxy 규칙 동기화 시간 지연으로 인한 Pod 통신 오류’ 문제를 안전하게 해결했어요.

9. 마치며

이번 프로젝트는 시급하지 않다고 생각했던 문제가 클러스터의 성장과 노드 운영 방식의 변화에 따라 서비스 안정성에 영향을 주면서 시작됐어요. 개선 방법 결정과 벤치마크 실험, 지표 보강과 전환 완료까지 약 1개월의 시간이 걸렸어요.

노드 네트워크 방식을 바꾸는 큰 작업이다 보니 ‘통신이 안 되는 사고가 발생하지 않을까’ 하는 우려에 실험이 반복되고 작업이 더 길어졌다고 생각해요. 하지만, SRE 엔지니어로서 안전 점검은 철저히 할수록 좋다는 팀원들과의 공감대 덕분에 차근차근 안전하게 진행할 수 있었어요.

개인적으로도 매우 유익하고 재미있는 과정이었어요. 평소에 몰랐던 지표의 오류도 발견하고, kube-proxy의 동작 방식도 깊이 알게 되었어요. 실험 시나리오를 추가하며 지표가 변하는 것을 보는 것도 소소한 재미였어요.

걱정했던 것과 달리 kube-proxy 모드 전환은 큰 이슈 없이 순조롭게 진행되었어요. kube-proxy를 운영하며 속도 개선을 해볼까 고민하던 분들에게 제 글이 도움이 됐으면 좋겠어요.

긴 글 읽어주셔서 감사합니다.

파드는 떴는데 왜 통신이 안 될까? kube-proxy nftables 전환 여정 was originally published in 당근 기술 블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Flags SDK now works on Vercel without FLAGS_SECRET
event_model_payload.summary:
With flags@4.5.0, projects on Vercel can use Flags Explorer and precompute without FLAGS_SECRET. That cuts out a setup step for new projects and removes the need to keep a shared secret in sync across microfrontends.

Vercel signs Flags Explorer discovery requests and overrides, and the SDK encrypts flag values shown in the Vercel Toolbar with Vercel’s public key.

Existing projects keep using FLAGS_SECRET while the environment variable is set or the secret is passed in code. Upgrading alone doesn't switch them to Vercel-managed keys. To use Vercel-managed keys for these features, remove the environment variable and any code that passes the secret explicitly. For local development, run vercel env pull.

Precomputed codes created without a secret work only in the deployment that created them. Precompute without a secret requires Vercel system environment variables, which are enabled by default. Prebuilt deployments and codes that must work across deployments still need a secret; use FLAGS_PRECOMPUTE_SECRET if only precompute needs one. If you use a build cache, see the precompute documentation for the required configuration.

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Agents can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP
event_model_payload.summary:
Your agent can now manage AI Gateway through Vercel MCP. Ask it in plain language to:

  • Manage virtual models: Create reusable model IDs with saved settings, then list, inspect, update, or restore them.

  • Configure routing rules: View, add, and update team-wide rules that redirect requests to another model or block them.

  • Set spending budgets: View and set budgets for your team, projects, and members, and configure defaults.

To create a virtual model, for example, ask your agent:

Create a virtual model named coding-agent that uses anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 with Zero Data Retention enabled.

Your apps and coding agents using AI Gateway can then use vmc/coding-agent as the model ID. You can change its model or settings later without updating those clients or redeploying your app.

To get started, connect your agent to Vercel MCP with team-level access and the required AI Gateway permissions. Your Vercel team permissions still apply.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Delete a run's data on demand in Workflow SDK
event_model_payload.summary:
The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads.

Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata: the run is still listed in observability. Attributes, hook tokens, and timings for steps and events can still be inspected.

You can delete a run's data from the Vercel Dashboard, or via the CLI:

You can also delete a run's data programmatically from your code:

Deletion applies to finished runs only, so a run that is still going is skipped and keeps running. If you want to delete a run's payload as soon as it finishes, use the retention settings instead.

Upgrade to workflow@5.7.0 or higher to use this feature. Learn more in the deleteRuns() reference.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Coworker rejects PR (one month in) because it does not meet his standards
event_model_payload.summary:
just joined this new team about 1 year into their development. Demoed the work to the team about two weeks ago (half way in). Work is practically complete & runs well no issues. I create PR & assign the two PR reviewers (one my rank another a rank above me). one colleague (the one at my level) leaves some constructive comments no functional changes. The other colleague (one rank above me) says something equivalent to "does not meet our standards" "do not do x pattern since we have used y (which has a huge limitation)" to use Y pattern I would basically need to change most of the logic and it would be about 70% waste. I demoed my code with this pattern two weeks ago and there were no issues/comments from the team. The code is concise and easy to read. I had a call with the colleague and explained the code and why I used it, and showed him some other parts of the codebase where this pattern should be used, his only defense was that "it does not meet our standards because it uses X rather than y pattern, since we used y pattern in the past, we should only use y pattern" while x pattern is very similar only removing the limitation that was causing the code to be difficult to maintain etc. This "standard requirement" is written nowhere as a hard requirement and the codebase is barely one year old, with only one of the codebase founders still on the team.... I'm going to have a chat with the manager tomorrow morning.

event_model_payload.headline: Piramal Finance Scales Its Internal Agentic AI Assistant With MongoDB
event_model_payload.summary:
Piramal Finance Limited is a retail-led upper-layer NBFC with a pan-India presence. It offers a diverse portfolio of retail lending products spanning affordable housing loans, loan against property, microfinance, personal loans, insurance solutions, and more, as well as wholesale lending, which provides asset-backed, data-driven financing solutions across real estate and select non-real estate sectors.

As of June 30, 2026, the company has over ₹ 1,00,000 Cr of assets under management; it operates 780 branches and serves over 6 million customers across 26 states.

The company operates a distinctive phygital model combining high-touch engagement with high-tech capabilities, including machine learning models, agentic AI tools, and real-time dashboards. Underpinning this breadth of services is Piramal Finance’s "high-tech, high-touch" strategy. Unlike other financial institutions that rely on off-the-shelf software, Piramal Finance’s team built the company’s entire tech stack in-house.

MongoDB has been core to Piramal Finance’s tech stack since the company’s early days. Today, MongoDB Atlas’ flexible document model—combined with built-in capabilities like MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search—powers over 80% of Piramal Finance’s services, including its loan management system, which was migrated from PostgreSQL.

Building on this solid data foundation, Piramal Finance recently set out to solve its next big challenge: empowering its workforce with generative AI.

Building an internal agentic AI assistant for 18,000+ employees

In 2024, Piramal Finance decided to invest in agentic AI to help improve productivity and job satisfaction for its more than 18,000 employees. The company aimed to empower employees across the company—including those from engineering, operations, HR, and customer service—with AI tools.

Piramal Finance’s team wanted to build an intuitive, enterprise-wide agentic AI assistant that would serve as a one-stop shop for employees, from querying policies and tracking performance metrics to resolving customer issues and interacting with internal systems. The idea was to democratize access to AI and allow even non-technical staff to leverage state-of-the-art AI, without complex prompts or technical training.

Initially, Piramal Finance's team started building an architecture that stitched together several specialized third-party tools:

  • Neo4j, a graph database that stores data as nodes and the relationships between them, managed the dynamic permissions model. Because permissions depended on a user's position in the organizational hierarchy and their associations with other entities—and because those relationships changed in real time—access had to be evaluated at runtime rather than precomputed.

  • pgVector, an open-source extension that adds vector storage and similarity search to PostgreSQL, handled the vector workloads powering AI features.

  • PostgreSQL, an open-source relational database, handled operational data and analytical queries.

However, this setup introduced significant complexity and inefficiencies, and it didn't lend itself to running complex AI workloads at scale.

Piramal Finance’s team saw MongoDB Atlas as the best solution to move away from PostgreSQL’s credential management. Using MongoDB’s built-in authentication and authorization features, Piramal Finance was able to map MongoDB Atlas’s access control directly to its enterprise single sign-on and Active Directory, so employees could log in securely with their standard corporate credentials. Meanwhile,MongoDB Atlas’s built-in role-based access control (RBAC) capabilities automatically restricted sensitive data based on Piramal Finance employees’ job roles.

Piramal Finance soon realized that the power of the MongoDB Atlas platform could solve many of the other challenges that its fragmented database stack presented.

From a fragmented to a unified AI data layer: The power of MongoDB Atlas

As Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI Assistant's enterprise knowledge base grew, the data architecture became increasingly complex. Although this separation allowed each database to specialize in its workload, it introduced significant operational overhead and complexity, as Piramal Finance explained in a recent conversation at MongoDB .local Mumbai.

Data had to be synchronized across multiple systems through ETL pipelines, resulting in update latencies of over 30 minutes before newly ingested content became searchable.

Figure 1. Piramal Finance’s data architecture before migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

As Piramal Finance explored options to unify its data foundation, it realized that MongoDB Atlas was both inherently built for AI workloads (thanks to its flexible document model), and that it had all the capabilities needed to scale an agentic AI solution on a single platform.

Kaushik Deb, Head of AI engineering, Piramal Finance, said: “An AI agent is only as good as the data behind it. MongoDB gives us one platform for all our data, which makes our AI simpler to build, easier to maintain, and more reliable in production.”

Figure 2. Piramal Finance’s data architecture after migrating to MongoDB Atlas.

During the architecture review, Piramal Finance’s team realized that most of the graph queries involved bounded traversals such as reconstructing document hierarchies, identifying parent-child relationships, and retrieving connected metadata—operations that did not require a dedicated graph database. The data model was redesigned to represent these relationships within MongoDB itself, using the flexibility of MongoDB Atlas’ document model and MongoDB’s aggregation framework capabilities.

The $graphLookup aggregation stage became central to the implementation, enabling recursive traversal of document relationships directly within MongoDB collections. Combined with operators such as $lookup, $facet, $unwind, and $project, Piramal Finance was able to replace Neo4j traversals with efficient aggregation pipelines, all while expressing complex relationship queries entirely within MongoDB.

MongoDB Atlas also allowed the team to consolidate structured metadata, document storage, relationship traversal, and search into a single platform. MongoDB Search handled keyword retrieval, while the aggregation framework combined metadata filtering, graph traversal, and ranking into unified retrieval pipelines, reducing application-side joins and simplifying backend services.

Today, there are 25+ MongoDB MCP servers live, powering Piramal Finance’s agentic AI assistant, which, combined with MongoDB Vector Search, allows for unstructured documents (e.g., 500-page policy PDFs) to be processed through Piramal Finance’s in-house pipeline (.score), chunked, embedded using in-house embedding models, and stored directly in MongoDB Atlas. MongoDB Vector Search delivers 3x faster retrieval performance compared to Piramal Finance’s former Postgres setup.

An incredibly efficient, smart agentic assistant

Since the launch of Piramal Finance’s internal agentic AI assistant, employee performance and productivity across all functions have improved, which has in turn improved customer experience and satisfaction.

Today, over 80% of Piramal Finance's 18,000 employees use the internal agentic AI assistant on a weekly basis, with an average of 15,000 daily queries handled by the platform.

Teams from all across the organization are benefiting from using the agentic AI assistant. HR teams experience a significant reduction in routine internal support tickets regarding benefits, travel policies, and payroll, as new hires and staff turn to the agentic solution for instant answers, supporting agents. Support agents who previously spent extensive time manually combing lengthy and complex policy manuals during live calls are now able to ingest real-time customer data and policy docs into the agentic assistant. This has drastically reduced handle times, improving first-contact resolution and customer satisfaction. Furthermore, sales representatives using the internal agentic AI assistant have seen a 2x improvement in performance compared to non-users during contest periods.

Piramal Finance’s tech team, including developers, are also greatly benefiting from using MongoDB Atlas. Knowledge graph and document updates that previously took up to 30 minutes in legacy setups now execute in just 15 seconds, eliminating operational downtime.  Working with MongoDB and being able to use MongoDB Atlas’ built-in capabilities such as MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search has also made developers’ jobs much easier.

With MongoDB, Piramal Finance has been able to turn what was initially a pretty simple AI assistant into a full agentic solution that orchestrates workflows across the entire organization. MongoDB Atlas has become the single source of truth for the internal agentic AI assistant, providing a simpler architecture and a scalable foundation for semantic retrieval, richer metadata, and future AI-powered knowledge discovery.

Looking to the future, Piramal Finance plans to use MongoDB’s capabilities to further expand its internal agentic AI assistant into a personalized, proactive coach for every employee in the company.

event_model_payload.headline: GitLab Dedicated: A go-live guide
event_model_payload.summary:
GitLab Dedicated is a single-tenant SaaS solution that is fully isolated, deployed in your preferred AWS cloud region, and hosted and maintained by GitLab. GitLab Dedicated and compliance covers why regulated organizations choose a single-tenant instance operated by GitLab, and serves as a starting point for evaluation. In this article, you'll learn what to do after you sign on to GitLab Dedicated, including understanding which responsibilities GitLab takes on and which remain with your teams, as well as what controls each team needs to put in place.

Teams arriving from any self-managed source-control or CI/CD platform bring an operating model built around upgrade runbooks, pre-flight checks, staging environments, and rollback plans. On GitLab Dedicated, many of those responsibilities move to GitLab, and the ones that stay with you look different.

Division of responsibility

GitLab Dedicated splits platform operation between GitLab and the customer.

GitLab ownsYou own
Version validation and testingPipeline configuration
Security patchingScripts and services calling the GitLab API
Database migrationsWebhooks and integrations
Monitoring and observabilityRunner configuration
Backup and regional recoveryMigration away from deprecated features

The right-hand column is where most of your team's work now sits. GitLab operates the platform. Your teams operate what runs on it.

What you configure in Switchboard

Switchboard is the administration portal for GitLab Dedicated. From there, you manage:

  • IP allowlists for inbound access
  • SAML and instance authentication
  • Operational email addresses
  • Access to your application logs, which GitLab delivers to a private Amazon S3 bucket
  • AWS PrivateLink connections and bring-your-own-key encryption
  • Hosted runners

Switchboard has two roles: Admin edits instance configuration and manages Switchboard users; Read-only views instance data.

Some capabilities must be enabled on your tenant by GitLab before they appear in Switchboard. If an option you expect is missing, contact your Customer Success Manager or Support before troubleshooting permissions.

GitLab Dedicated does not provide shell access to the infrastructure, feature flags, experimental features, or modified GitLab source. These constraints are what allow GitLab to carry the availability SLA and keep every instance on the supported upgrade path.

How upgrades work

GitLab Dedicated runs one minor version behind current GitLab, a model known as N-1. Your instance has a weekly maintenance window, chosen at onboarding. Most weeks that window carries patches and infrastructure work. Once a month, after each GitLab release, it carries the minor version upgrade. Each release has already run on GitLab.com before it reaches your instance.

Major versions arrive roughly once a year. Breaking changes are announced in the deprecations list in advance, typically with at least a month's notice. GitLab also identifies customers using features scheduled to change and contacts them ahead of the upgrade.

Upgrade validation

GitLab SREs validate each release against internal test environments before it reaches any customer instance. The pre- and post-upgrade health checks documented for GitLab Self-Managed don't apply to Dedicated, because they require infrastructure access that customers don't have. GitLab monitors your instance and contacts you if an upgrade causes a problem.

For teams used to running their own upgrade validation, this is the biggest change in the operating model. Upgrade testing moves from your team to GitLab's.

Maintenance windows and exceptions

Your maintenance window cannot be changed after onboarding. Two things can move an upgrade off your window:

  • Production change locks are declared by GitLab during periods of reduced GitLab staffing, such as major holidays. They pause all production changes, including Switchboard configuration. An upgrade due during a lock moves to the first window after it lifts. You can’t request a lock for your own change freeze.
  • Emergency maintenance covers urgent actions such as a platform outage, serious degradation, or a critical security fix. It’s applied outside your window and can’t be postponed.

For emergency security patches, GitLab withholds vulnerability details until disclosure because publishing early would expose customers that have not yet been patched. Details are published through the vulnerability disclosure process 90 days after release.

Reference architecture changes happen when your instance needs resizing, for example to support more load. GitLab schedules the change with you in advance. During the resize, content stays readable, but most writes, including Git pushes, fail and new CI/CD jobs don’t start. Plan for up to an hour per size step.

Rollback

Version rollback is not part of the GitLab Dedicated operating model. It is also not a supported operation on GitLab Self-Managed. Upgrades run post-deployment database migrations, and once those have run, earlier application versions are no longer compatible with the data. Rolling back a self-managed instance means restoring a database backup taken under the target version and losing all changes since.

GitLab Dedicated resolves regressions by rolling forward with patch releases. The N-1 lag, zero-downtime deployments applied one minor version at a time, and emergency maintenance for critical issues are the controls that reduce how often a fix is needed.

Disaster recovery

The disaster recovery documentation covers the headline objectives: an RTO of eight hours and an RPO of four hours, with failover typically completing in 90 minutes. These rest on four-hourly snapshots of every datastore, continuous log-based database backups for point-in-time recovery, and Geo replication of database, repository, and object storage to your secondary region. The full objectives apply only to instances configured with a secondary region when the instance is created. Without one, recovery relies on restoring from backup.

Failover limits

Some services behave differently after a failover. Plan for these:

  • Advanced search indexes are not continuously replicated and are rebuilt after failover. Basic search remains available in the meantime.
  • ClickHouse Cloud is provisioned in the primary region only.
  • Hosted runners are provisioned in the primary region only and are not rebuilt in the secondary.
  • PrivateLink connections must be repointed at the secondary endpoint. Create the secondary endpoint before a disaster. It can sit in your primary region and connect cross-region, so after a failover you change DNS and leave workloads where they are. The inbound PrivateLink Terraform module shows the setup.

Disaster recovery and accidental deletion

Disaster recovery on GitLab Dedicated is designed for platform-level failures. Recovering data a customer deleted is not a standard service process. For accidental deletion, use delayed project and group deletion, which retains deleted items for a period you configure.

This matters most for teams managing group and project structure with infrastructure-as-code. A Terraform plan that removes a group can remove everything beneath it. Controls on the customer side include plan review before apply, protected configuration repositories, and a deletion retention period long enough for the mistake to be noticed.

Testing changes without a staging environment

A common question from teams moving to GitLab Dedicated is how to test their own changes, such as pipeline updates, compliance policies, organization-level settings, and integrations, when there is a single instance.

A second GitLab Dedicated instance can serve as staging. Placed in an earlier maintenance window, it gives production a few days of soak behind it. It runs the same version as production, so it does not preview the next release, and it is a second environment at additional cost.

Several practices work on a single instance:

  • A sandbox group with its own projects, where pipeline and policy changes run before they reach production groups
  • Versioned CI/CD components and includes, so changes ship as new refs
  • Compliance frameworks applied to the sandbox group first, then promoted
  • Infrastructure-as-code for group and project structure, with mandatory plan review

What each team needs to know

Platform engineering. Instance configuration moves to Switchboard. Your team owns the integration surface: API consumers, webhooks, runner configuration.

Change and release management. The upgrade cadence and maintenance window are fixed. Build the change calendar around them, and keep releases and time-critical jobs out of the window. Performance degradation during the scheduled window does not count against the availability SLA. Hosted runners run on a separate schedule. GitLab upgrades them without downtime or interrupting running jobs, so those upgrades can happen outside your window.

Security and compliance. Patching is continuous and applied at zero downtime, and disclosure follows a published process. Both can be referenced directly in audit evidence. Encryption keys are another onboarding decision. Data at rest is encrypted with AWS-managed KMS keys by default. If you want customer-managed keys, you supply your own KMS key ARNs when the instance is created. That choice can’t be added, removed, or changed later.

SRE. Include the published RTO and RPO in recovery runbooks, along with the failover limits above. Pre-configure secondary-region network endpoints. Treat GitLab’s operational notifications as your failover signal, because GitLab doesn’t offer programmatic monitoring of failover events. Rehearse the steps you own, such as repointing PrivateLink and moving CI/CD jobs to your own runners if you rely on hosted runners.

Developers. Zero-downtime upgrades can include a brief interruption of under a minute when compute resources restart, and long-running connections may drop. Implement retries.

Getting started checklist

  1. Set operational contacts to a team distribution list. Operational contacts receive notifications regardless of individual Switchboard settings.
  2. Review the deprecations list each release.
  3. Maintain an inventory of API consumers, webhooks, and runner configuration.
  4. Standardize pipeline configuration migrated from other platforms before it reaches production groups.
  5. Add the published recovery objectives and failover limits to your DR plan.
  6. Put plan review and deletion retention in place for infrastructure-as-code that manages groups and projects.

Summary

GitLab Dedicated moves platform validation, patching, monitoring, and recovery to GitLab. Your teams keep ownership of pipelines, integrations, runners, and the structure of your groups and projects. Teams that map that split early, and set up the controls on their side of it, spend less time on surprises after go-live.

Learn more

  • GitLab Dedicated documentation
  • Maintenance and release schedule
  • GitLab Dedicated: Compliance for a new regulatory era
  • GitLab Migration documentation
  • Contact GitLab to discuss regions, networking, and migration

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Can I map all the arguments in a topic to "approach the truth"?
event_model_payload.summary:
Hi HN, I wanted to take a stance on these topics people have been arguing all around. There should be some sort of answer, right?

I used to go to debates for that end. But I often only see the repetition of the same points, the hardest objection being dodged, etc. I tried AI as well, but it only returns surface level arguments likewise.

Is there anyway to preserve debate's purpose in trying to see the deepest case, while getting over these “sophistry”?

Could I map all the arguments in controversial topics (continuously allowing new inputs), and rephrase and put them in a clear sequence, so fallacies, detours, and claims already have well-established answers could be cleared out, leaving only the real tradeoff standing?

I tried it: creating TruthTree (Truthtree.app). Anything it has missed, you can hit "Challenge this claim”, type your counter, and if it's spot on (through the AI, with a fallback checker), it will be on the tree.

For example, for abortion, the map currently filters out this unanswered crux: "knowingly creating a life that depends on your body gives you a duty to continue the pregnancy."(https://truthtree.app/abortion/responsibility)

Is that the answer to abortion? What’s the map missing?

Please also let me know if this format works, and if there’s anything that could be changed to make things easier!

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Anyone know someone at GitHub to help expedite a support request?
event_model_payload.summary:
Background: I've been working with a new company to help deliver a project. I got set up with a Google account for them (so I have myname@example.com), and I created a new Github account to associate with that email, and connected everything together.

For the first week everything was fine, I was fixing issues, putting up PRs, etc. One of the last PRs I was able to put up was a CI fix -- we had 10 CI checks that hadn't passed in months, and by fixing the underlying issue they started running. That ended up being an issue however -- they started running very long running tasks, and our Github Action minutes spiked up.

Soon after, my account was suspended, with no email, no warning, nothing. The CTO who had Github org admin access could see that I had been suspended, and nothing else. Both he on behalf of the Github Enterprise organization and myself personally submitted a ticket up, and got no response so far. We waited over the weekend, and still didn't get a response.

Since we had a deadline of before Thanksgiving, and we weren't hearing back anything from Github, my company spun me up a new Google account and Github account, just so I could start contributing. A few hours later, that account was banned as well.

It's very frustrating -- and even our Enterprise organization seems to get no recourse. Is there any good solution here?

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Harness vs. Feature Factories
event_model_payload.summary:
It seems to me the industry is at a divergence point, with strong forces pull in opposite directions.

In the "developers are team leads / checkpoint verifiers" corner we have:

- Microsoft, re "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product" (Nadella) and "become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work"

-- Microsoft has always championed "AI as a team member", even as a product.

- Salesforce

- Stripe

- Uber, Shopify, Spotify, Meta

In the "developers use harnesses to improve personal velocity and quality corner we have:

- Netflix

- Amazon

- ... Google, but it's hard to find more than anecdotal references

These two approaches, in my view, are not compatible. Fully, or even just semi-automated feature factories keep the context, leaving the developer to validate artifacts and manage the flow, shifting responsibility to specs and building automated verifiers. It lets less technical people into the product development loop but keeps the code an AI-only territory.

On the other hand, a harness keeps the developer in control, but sacrifices velocity and requires higher technical prowess, or at least understanding, of what's being generated.

Which way is the industry going to go? Are AI-only maintained code bases going to collapse under their own weight? Are "technical" developers going to be sidelined for higher delivery velocity? Will we see two types of businesses - features and infra, each taking a polar position in this? Or even within the same business, different teams?

event_model_payload.headline: Vibe-Hackers: Script kiddies, stronger?
event_model_payload.summary:
Hello, i am sharing a concern/opinion that i’ve been contemplating for the past couple of years. Today, we see how vibe coders with plain-english are building basic websites/webapps/mobile apps etc… you name it. Most of it is being used for good. Setting aside the quality, slop and everything else, this is not our concern. For me, the AI/agentic systems surge, directly empowered another group of people: Hackers, regardless of their nature (black hat, white hat etc…). Similar to software engineers, hackers required an immensive amount of theoretical knowledge, practical expertise and years of experience in order to be market ready (whether for an actual job or not). Script-kiddies as we know them, weren’t that meticulous in their craft , they understood some basics and executed pre-defined scripts. They didnt know how to change them, alter them or even create some their own. But today, in our new agentic-era, I believe English is the only requirement alongside a target. Considering the LLM being used is jailbroken/not safeguarded and restricted, they can literally break into systems, easily. So I was thinking to myself, a lot of people wanted to be hackers but they couldn’t (it required effort in studying, practicing etc…), today it doesnt need the same amount of effort anymore. So in the future, we are definitely going to see a surge in the number of hackers. The question comes here: How are we going to defend against malicious activities? Do we have AI-Powered systems that could act like a security analyst? Forensics? And how powerful are they? Are they deployed in reputable companies? How are they performing? Vibe-hackers are now stronger than ever, defense is required. Whether at org level or for individuals.
