event_model_payload.headline: Ubuntu 26.04 golden images on Hetzner with cloud-init
event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

The snapshot your team has cloned for two years was built by hand on Ubuntu 24.04. Nobody remembers which packages went in, the user-data file has grown to 200 lines, and the first reboot of every new server runs a slow apt upgrade. Ubuntu 26.04 golden images are the cleanest way to reset that, and the timing is right. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released on 2026-04-23, and its first point release, 26.04.1, is now out. Historically, the first point release is when Canonical opens LTS-to-LTS upgrades, and many teams wait for it before treating an LTS as safe for fleets.

Short answer: build a fresh 26.04 snapshot with Packer's hcloud builder instead of upgrading old snapshots. Bake slow, stable things (packages, hardening, agents) into the image. Leave per-server things (users, keys, hostnames) to cloud-init user-data at first boot. This applies to Hetzner Cloud fleets. If you install from ISO or on dedicated hardware, the autoinstall section below is the relevant path.

What changed and who is affected

Two mechanisms get confused here:

  • cloud-init configures an already-installed image at boot. This is what Hetzner Cloud uses.
  • Autoinstall is the Subiquity installer's unattended mode for installing Ubuntu from ISO. It uses an autoinstall.yaml with autoinstall: version: 1 and can embed a cloud-init user-data section.

Hetzner Cloud servers start from provider images or your snapshots. Autoinstall therefore matters only if you install from ISO, use a rescue-and-install flow, or run dedicated servers.

You are affected if any of these is true:

  • Your servers boot from a hand-made 24.04 snapshot that was never cleaned with cloud-init clean.
  • Your user-data installs packages at every boot, so scaling out is slow and depends on mirror availability.
  • Your provisioning scripts assume specific userland behavior, such as sudo flags or GNU coreutils output parsing. Recent Ubuntu releases have moved some core utilities toward Rust implementations. Check the 26.04 release notes against your scripts rather than assuming parity.

Cost: a snapshot is billed per GB per month, and you will hold at least two (old and new) during the migration. Treat the exact Hetzner image name for 26.04 as something to verify, not assume (see step 1).

Before/after config

The "before" pattern does everything at boot, on every server. It is slow and non-deterministic because it depends on the mirror state at that moment.

#cloud-config
# BEFORE: everything happens at first boot, on every server
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
packages: [fail2ban, unattended-upgrades, prometheus-node-exporter]
runcmd:
  - [sh, -c, "curl -fsSL https://example.com/harden.sh | sh"]  # unpinned, unaudited

🧪 Lab — try this in your browser

  • EOL Countdown — Check when your Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Node.js, Ubuntu… versions lose support. Paste command output or add versions — get status, days left and calendar reminders.

The "after" split keeps the slow work in the image and shrinks user-data to identity and secrets. This is the Packer template (HCL2) for the image:

packer {
  required_plugins {
    hcloud = {
      source  = "github.com/hetznercloud/hcloud"
      version = ">= 1.6.0"   # check the plugin releases for the current version
    }
  }
}

variable "hcloud_token" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
variable "server_type"  { type = string }   # pick from: hcloud server-type list

locals {
  build_ts = formatdate("YYYYMMDDhhmm", timestamp())
}

source "hcloud" "golden" {
  token         = var.hcloud_token
  image         = "ubuntu-26.04"            # verify: hcloud image list --type system
  location      = "fsn1"
  server_type   = var.server_type
  ssh_username  = "root"
  snapshot_name = "golden-ubuntu-2604-${local.build_ts}"
  snapshot_labels = { role = "golden", os = "ubuntu-26.04" }
}

build {
  sources = ["source.hcloud.golden"]
  provisioner "shell" {
    inline = [
      "cloud-init status --wait",   # let first-boot cloud-init finish before changing things
      "apt-get update && DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y dist-upgrade",
      "DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get -y install fail2ban unattended-upgrades prometheus-node-exporter",
      "cloud-init clean --logs --seed",   # re-arm cloud-init for the next boot
      "truncate -s 0 /etc/machine-id",    # avoid duplicate machine IDs across clones
      "rm -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*"         # host keys are regenerated on first boot
    ]
  }
}

Step-by-step migration to Ubuntu 26.04 golden images

  1. Confirm the base image. Run hcloud image list --type system | grep -i ubuntu and use the exact name it prints. If 26.04 is missing in your project or location, stop here. Do not upgrade a 24.04 box in place instead.
  2. Move user-data to identity only. Remove package installs and hardening scripts. Keep users, SSH keys, hostname and write_files for per-environment config.
  3. Build. Inject the token from your secret store or CI secret as an environment variable, never in the template or on the command line: export PKR_VAR_hcloud_token="". Then run packer init . && packer build -var "server_type=" .
  4. Validate user-data against the schema before using it. Run cloud-init schema --config-file user-data.yaml on any machine with cloud-init installed. The slim file looks like this:
#cloud-config
hostname: web-01
ssh_pwauth: false
users:
  - name: deploy
    groups: [sudo]
    shell: /bin/bash
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"   # tighten if your policy requires a password
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... deploy@ci
  1. Canary first. Point one non-critical server at the new snapshot ID and keep the rest on the old one. Use the same workflow you already use for fleet changes (Ansible, OpenTofu or Terraform), so the image ID lives in one variable.
  2. Widen gradually by replacing servers, not upgrading them. Replacement is what makes rollback trivial.

If you do need autoinstall for ISO or dedicated installs, keep the same split:

  • A minimal autoinstall.yaml for identity, SSH and storage layout.
  • Everything else in the embedded user-data.

The Subiquity documentation lists the current schema. Field names and defaults are version-dependent.

Verify and roll back

Create a throwaway server from the new snapshot. Check that cloud-init ran as a first boot, not a replay of the build:

hcloud server create --name golden-test --type  \
  --image  --ssh-key deploy \
  --user-data-from-file user-data.yaml

ssh deploy@ 'cloud-init status --long; sudo cloud-init schema --system; \
  cat /etc/machine-id; ls /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*; lsb_release -ds'

Expect:

  • status: done with no errors.
  • A schema validation message saying the config is valid.
  • A freshly generated, non-empty machine ID that differs from the build host.
  • New SSH host keys.
  • An Ubuntu 26.04 description string.

Also check /var/log/cloud-init.log for warnings. To confirm time-to-ready improved, compare cloud-init analyze blame and systemd-analyze output with a server on the old image. Record your own numbers; do not trust anyone else's.

Rollback means replacing servers back onto the previous snapshot ID. That only works if you do not delete the old snapshot. Label it (for example role=golden-previous) and keep it for at least one full release cycle of your own services. Roll back on a concrete signal:

  • Failed health checks on canaries.
  • cloud-init status reporting error.
  • A regression in your application's package set.

Gotchas after the switch

Watch out for a stale machine-id. If you skip the truncate step, clones can share an identity. That can break DHCP leases, log aggregation keyed on machine ID, and some monitoring agents. Check cat /etc/machine-id on two servers from the same snapshot.

Watch out for cloud-init not re-running. If the build left state in /var/lib/cloud, user-data may be silently skipped on new servers. That is why cloud-init clean --logs --seed is the last provisioning step. Check the flags with cloud-init clean --help on your installed version.

Other documented-behavior traps:

  • Do not hardcode datasource_list in the image unless you have a reason. The Hetzner datasource is detected automatically on Hetzner Cloud, and a hardcoded list breaks the same image elsewhere.
  • Snapshots age. Rebuild on a schedule (weekly or monthly) so unattended-upgrades is not the only thing patching a months-old base. Known patch state matters more now: since 11 September 2026, the EU Cyber Resilience Act requires manufacturers of products with digital elements to report actively exploited vulnerabilities (24h early warning, 72h notification).
  • Do not use this approach for stateful servers, such as databases with local disks. Rebuild-and-replace assumes data lives on volumes or elsewhere.
  • Pin what you download in provisioners with checksums. curl | sh inside a golden image bakes an unaudited script into every future server.

For schema details and module options, use the cloud-init documentation. For builder settings, use the Packer documentation.

Related

  • Ubuntu 26.04 Upgrade with Ansible: Migrate 24.04 Fleets Safely
  • Migrate Playbooks to ansible-core 2.22 Without Breaking Collections
  • Migrate nvm, pyenv and tfenv to one mise toolchain file

event_model_payload.headline: I built a Modbus simulator that Claude drives over MCP: test SCADA without a PLC
event_model_payload.summary:
Disclosure: I work on fieldpuppet, the open-source simulator in this post. It is maintained by the team behind PLCGateway.

Here is a prompt I can now type into Claude:

Set up 50 energy meters starting at port 6000. Make meter 12 stop answering for 30 seconds, then tell me which registers my SCADA read from it.

A few seconds later there are 50 Modbus TCP devices listening on my laptop, one of them goes silent on schedule, and I get a report of what my software polled. No PLC, no meter, no cabinet.

This post explains why I built it, how the MCP part works, and how to use it without any AI at all.

The problem: the hardware is never on your desk

If you write software that talks Modbus TCP (a SCADA screen, a gateway, a historian, a data collector), you know this situation. The code is ready, but the PLC is in a cabinet at the customer site, the energy meter has not shipped yet, and nobody will let you unplug a pump just to see how your software handles a timeout.

A register table that returns fixed numbers does not help much. Real testing needs:

  • Many devices at once, because polling 1 device and polling 200 behave very differently.
  • Values that move, so trends, alarms and scaling can be checked.
  • Faults on demand: slow answers, no answer, exception replies, dropped connections. These break software in the field and are the hardest to reproduce with real equipment.
  • A record of what your software asked for, so you can see whether it polls the registers you think it does.

Why MCP fits this job

Setting up test devices is boring, repetitive work: copy a register list from a manual, pick ports, write a fault timeline. It is exactly the kind of work an assistant does well if it has the right tools.

fieldpuppet is a single Rust executable of about 2 MB with an MCP server built in. It exposes 22 tools, such as create_device, set_signal, apply_scenario, inject_fault and get_traffic_log. Every tool carries read-only and destructive hints, so the client knows which calls change state.

For Claude Code it is one line:

claude mcp add fieldpuppet -- /full/path/to/fieldpuppet mcp

For Claude Desktop, each release has an .mcpb bundle you can install from the Extensions settings. Any MCP client that can start a local server over stdio works.

Things I ask it most often:

  • "Here is the register list from a device manual. Build a simulated device that matches it."
  • "Make the tank level rise from 20 % to 95 % over two minutes, then switch the high level alarm on."
  • "Pump 2 should answer with a device busy exception for the next 30 seconds."
  • "Which registers has my SCADA been reading from the drive in the last minute?"

A read-only web dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:5080 shows every device, its live values and a feed of everything the assistant changed, so you are never guessing what it did.

It works without AI too

Describe the devices in YAML:

devices:
  - id: pump-1
    template: pump
    port: 5020

  - id: dosing-skid
    port: 5021
    points:
      - name: chlorine_ppm
        table: input
        address: 0
        scale: 0.01
        unit: ppm
        value: 0.8
        signal: { type: random_walk, min: 0.5, max: 1.2, step: 0.02 }

Run it:

fieldpuppet run water-station.yaml

Point your own software at 127.0.0.1, port 5020 or 5021, unit id 1. The chlorine value drifts between 0.5 and 1.2 ppm like a real sensor would. Addresses are zero-based protocol addresses, so holding register 40001 is address 0.

Test the bad days, not only the good ones

Four fault types are available, each with an optional time limit:

  • delay: correct answers, but late
  • no_response: your client sees a timeout
  • exception: a Modbus exception such as device busy
  • disconnect: the connection closes on every request

This is how you find out whether your software reconnects, whether one dead device stalls the polling of the other 49, and whether stale values are marked as stale.

Limits

  • Modbus TCP only. No serial RTU or ASCII yet.
  • Devices do not model process behaviour. A pump does not stop because its run coil was cleared; a scenario or the assistant has to change the values.
  • Simulation only. It answers requests sent to it and never connects to real equipment.

Try it

The code is on GitHub under MIT / Apache 2.0: CybriantOps/fieldpuppet. It is a new project, so bug reports and feature requests are very welcome.

Which fault case has caused you the most trouble in the field?

event_model_payload.headline: What If Online Proctors Could Tell the Difference Between a Panic Attack and Cheating? Meet AegisPulse.
event_model_payload.summary:
Imagine this: You're halfway through a high-stakes exam that determines your university scholarship.

Your chest tightens. Your heart rate shoots through the roof. Your breathing turns shallow and rapid. You look frantically around your screen, trying to steady your racing thoughts.

Seconds later, a terrifying red box flashes:
🚨 SUSPICIOUS BIOMETRIC ANOMALY. EXAM TERMINATED FOR DISHONESTY.

You weren't cheating. You were having an acute panic attack. But today’s remote proctoring algorithms can’t tell the difference between a student suffocating under test anxiety and someone peeking at an answer key.

Every year, over 80 million students take exams online, and thousands of neurodivergent or anxious students face disciplinary hearings simply for having a nervous system. Meanwhile, actual cheaters with hidden phones slip right past basic face-detection software.

I built AegisPulse to fix this broken, punitive paradigm—turning proctoring into an ethical, privacy-preserving guardian powered by contactless physiological sensing.

What I Built

AegisPulse is the first ethical exam integrity and well-being platform that separates test anxiety from academic dishonesty in real time—completely on-device, with zero video or audio ever leaving the candidate's browser.

Instead of treating students like suspects in an interrogation room, AegisPulse acts like a compassionate proctor:

🫀 Contactless Biometric Baseline: In the first 5 seconds, it establishes your personal resting heart rate and respiratory baseline using contactless camera sensing.
🛡️ The Protected Panic Shield: If your heart surges to 138 BPM and your breathing spikes, but your eyes remain locked on the test paper, AegisPulse recognizes an acute anxiety episode. It automatically pauses the exam clock, suppresses false cheating penalties, and launches an interactive 4-7-8 resonant box-breathing reset.
📱 Catching Real Dishonesty: When resting vitals co-occur with a downward lap glance
pitch) and covert whispers, the system decomposes the anomaly in an Explainable AI forensic matrix.
👥 Proctor Collaboration Room: Proctors monitor room-wide telemetry live in a second tab and can grant +5m accommodations with one click.
🔒 Tamper-Proof Cryptographic Notary: At the end of the test, an immutable ECDSA P-256 certificate is signed right in the browser, verifiable by any university in a standalone portal.
Demo

Here is the full 1080p walkthrough showing live contactless cardiac waveforms, interactive 5-point gaze calibration, the panic attack intervention, and our cryptographic tamper test in action:

🎬 Watch / Download the AegisPulse 1080p Demo Video

https://youtu.be/tYxFTlTecYw

Code

The entire project is open-source, fully typed in TypeScript and Python, and designed to run entirely client-side:

GitHub repository- https://github.com/yuvanshankarm007/aegispulse
How It Responds to Human Signals

The real magic of AegisPulse lives in how it fuses the Presage SmartSpectra SDK with client-side computer vision:

We pipe four live physiological data streams over a local WebSocket bridge (ws://127.0.0.1:8765/smartspectra):

Cardiac Pulse (BPM) — Sub-surface facial chrominance rPPG.
Respiration Rate (RPM) — Subtle chest and nasal optical motion flow.
Heart Rate Variability (HRV RMSSD) — Autonomic nervous system vagal tone.
Signal Quality Index (SQI %) — Telemetry confidence scoring.

When anxiety strikes, the candidate’s physiology goes wild, but their gaze stays centered on the test. AegisPulse rewards that focus by pausing the clock and opening a gentle, harmonic box-breathing circle to help them regain composure.

Conversely, when someone looks down at a phone under their desk, their heart rate stays normal, but their gaze vector plunges
and our 36-band acoustic FFT spectrogram isolates covert speech frequencies (300−3400Hz).

It's fair, explainable, and grounded in real human physiology.

Prize Categories
🌟 Best Thoughtful Real-World Use

Online exams shouldn't feel like a police state. Millions of students struggle with anxiety disorders, neurodivergence, or high-stress panic. AegisPulse is built specifically to protect them:

Calibrated to the individual: It doesn't rely on arbitrary global thresholds; it personalizes baselines in 5 seconds.
Dignity first: When a student is overwhelmed, it pauses the exam and guides them back to calm without academic penalty.
Human in the loop: Proctors can grant extra time or send reassuring messages directly through a dual-tab BroadcastChannel.
🎨 Most Creative or Delightful Use

Proctoring is universally despised for being invasive and cold. AegisPulse flips the entire experience into something genuinely delightful:

Smooth in-browser 5-point reticle calibration that maps your unique cranial anatomy in seconds.
A soothing, resonant 4-7-8 breathing circle that synchronizes with your heartbeat.
A standalone verification portal where admissions officers can run an interactive "1-Byte Tamper Test" to watch cryptographic signatures break in real time!
Consent and Data Handling

We took an uncompromising stance on student privacy: Zero Data Retention (ZDR).

Clear, Opt-In Onboarding: The test cannot begin without the candidate explicitly reviewing and accepting the biometric consent gate.
100% On-Device & Ephemeral: Raw video frames and microphone streams are processed exclusively in browser memory. Not a single frame or audio buffer is ever written to disk or sent over the internet.
No Biometric Storage: The system never creates facial recognition vectors, biometrics IDs, or face templates.
Wellness, Not Diagnostics: AegisPulse is designed purely as an educational wellness and exam integrity aid; it makes zero medical claims or clinical diagnoses.
Cryptographic Proofs Over Surveillance: Instead of saving hours of student video recordings, universities receive an anonymized cryptographic JSON certificate signed with ECDSA P-256, mathematically proving the test was taken legitimately without storing the student's personal data.

event_model_payload.headline: epub_rtl: a pure-Flutter EPUB parser and reader for right-to-left books
event_model_payload.summary:
An EPUB file is a zip archive of XHTML chapters with a manifest, a reading order and a table of contents. For an Arabic book, a reader has more to get right than opening the zip. The book declares that its pages progress from right to left, and the reader has to swipe the other way. A paragraph mixes Arabic with an English word or a number, and the bidi algorithm needs the right isolates to keep the sentence in order. The table of contents should open from the right side. The body text needs an Arabic font.

On the Flutter side, the README notes the state of the usual packages: epubx has had no release since June 2023, and epub_view depends on it and on the archived scrollable_positioned_list.

epub_rtl is a pure-Flutter EPUB 2/3 parser and reader that handles right-to-left books. It is built for Arabic and other RTL texts, and it uses no WebView.

What it does

The package has three layers. You can use the parser alone, the parser with the content model, or all three.

The parser

It is pure Dart and depends only on archive and xml.

  • It finds the package document through META-INF/container.xml, then reads the OPF: metadata (titles, creators with role and file-as, languages, identifiers, publisher, date, description, dcterms:modified and the cover image), the manifest, and the spine with linear and page-progression-direction.
  • EpubBook.isRtl uses the spine direction, and falls back to the book language when the spine declares none.
  • For navigation, it reads the EPUB 3 nav document (toc, landmarks, page-list), and falls back to the EPUB 2 NCX with the guide element as landmarks.
  • Content is read by href, with relative paths, percent-encoding and fragments resolved.
  • Reading is lazy. Only the zip directory is read up front. Each chapter or resource is inflated when it is requested, and it is not cached. EpubBook.openFile reads entries from disk on demand.

Malformed books throw a typed EpubException with an EpubErrorKind. With lenient: true, the parser recovers from common real-world errors and records them in warnings: a missing or misplaced mimetype, a missing NCX or nav document, missing or unknown media types, dangling spine references and wrong letter case in paths.

A book with DRM listed in META-INF/encryption.xml is refused with EpubErrorKind.encrypted. A book whose only encrypted resources are obfuscated fonts opens in lenient mode, and those fonts are unreadable.

The content model

EpubChapter turns a chapter's XHTML into a flat list of blocks. Each id maps to a block index, which is what locations point to.

  • Blocks: headings, paragraphs, pre, images (including SVG-wrapped covers), lists, blockquotes, basic tables and rules.
  • Inline content: emphasis, bold, underline, strike, sup/sub, code, links and basic ruby.
  • dir and lang are inherited, and dir="auto" uses the first strong character.
  • Inline dir is wrapped in bidi isolates (LRI/RLI … PDI), bdi in FSI … PDI, and bdo in LRO/RLO … PDF.
  • A CSS subset is read from linked stylesheets, style elements and style attributes: text-align, font-style, font-weight, margins, text-indent, direction and display: none, with tag, class, id and descendant selectors.

The reader

EpubReaderView is a Flutter widget with two modes. scroll is one continuous vertical scroll through the whole book. paginated shows one chapter per page, swiped in the book's reading direction, so RTL books advance with a right swipe.

The reading position is an EpubLocation: spine index, element index and an offset fraction. You can serialise it with toJson or encode, restore it with initialLocation, and follow it through onLocationChanged and the controller.

EpubReaderController has jumpTo, jumpToHref (for TOC entries and internal links), nextChapter and previousChapter. EpubTocDrawer is a table-of-contents drawer laid out in the book's direction.

EpubReaderSettings covers font size and line height, light, sepia and dark themes, justification, and arabicFontFamily, which is used for RTL-language runs and placed first in the fallback list.

Internal links jump inside the book, and external links go to your onExternalLink callback. Jumps inside a chapter use GlobalKeys and Scrollable.ensureVisible, so the package does not depend on scrollable_positioned_list.

How to use it

Add it from GitHub:

dependencies:
  epub_rtl:
    git: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/epub_rtl

It needs Flutter 3.24 or later. A complete reader screen, from the README:

import 'package:epub_rtl/epub_rtl.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

class ReaderScreen extends StatefulWidget {
  const ReaderScreen({super.key, required this.bytes, this.saved});

  final List<int> bytes;
  final String? saved; // a previously stored EpubLocation.encode()

  @override
  State<ReaderScreen> createState() => _ReaderScreenState();
}

class _ReaderScreenState extends State<ReaderScreen> {
  late final EpubBook book = EpubBook.fromBytes(widget.bytes, lenient: true);
  final controller = EpubReaderController();

  @override
  void dispose() {
    controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(title: Text(book.metadata.title)),
        drawer: EpubTocDrawer(book: book, controller: controller),
        body: EpubReaderView(
          book: book,
          controller: controller,
          mode: EpubReaderMode.paginated,
          settings: const EpubReaderSettings(
            fontSize: 20,
            theme: EpubReaderTheme.sepia,
            arabicFontFamily: 'Amiri', // bundle the font in your app
            justify: true,
          ),
          initialLocation:
              widget.saved == null ? null : EpubLocation.tryDecode(widget.saved!),
          onLocationChanged: (location) {
            // Persist location.encode() or location.toJson().
          },
          onExternalLink: (url) {
            // Open with url_launcher, for example.
          },
        ),
      );
}

If you only need the parser:

final book = EpubBook.fromBytes(bytes);
print(book.metadata.title);
print(book.spine.pageProgressionDirection); // PageProgressionDirection.rtl
for (final entry in book.navigation.toc) {
  print('${entry.title} -> ${entry.href}');
}
final chapter = EpubChapter.fromBook(book, 0);
print(chapter.blocks.length);

Coming from epubx or epub_view

The README has a mapping table. The main lines: EpubReader.readBook(bytes), which is async and loads everything, becomes EpubBook.fromBytes(bytes), which is sync and lazy. book.Title becomes book.metadata.title. chapter.HtmlContent becomes book.chapterHtml(i) or EpubChapter.fromBook(book, i). EpubView with its EpubController becomes EpubReaderView with an EpubReaderController, and EpubViewTableOfContents becomes EpubTocDrawer.

One thing does not carry over: locations are not EPUB CFIs. Saved epub_view CFIs cannot be converted.

Things to know

  • DRM-encrypted books are refused. Obfuscated embedded fonts are not de-obfuscated, and embedded fonts are not loaded. Use fontFamily and arabicFontFamily with fonts bundled in your app.
  • Paginated mode is one chapter per page. The page scrolls vertically. The text is not split into screen-sized pages.
  • The CSS support is a small subset. No floats, positioning, colours, font sizes from CSS, pseudo-classes, >/+/~ selectors or @media rules.
  • Tables are basic: no colspan or rowspan. Ruby is shown as annotation-over-base, without full ruby layout.
  • Not rendered: SVG images, audio, video, MathML and scripts. Fixed-layout EPUBs are rendered as reflowable text.
  • Long chapters cost more. Each chapter is built as one widget subtree so that element keys exist for jumps. Very long single chapters cost more to lay out.
  • Web. EpubBook.openFile needs dart:io and is not available on the web. Use fromBytes there.
  • Test data. No third-party book content is bundled. The test fixtures and the example's sample book are generated in code, with text written for the package.

Why I built it

The README states the problem in two sentences: the existing parser has had no release since June 2023, and the existing viewer depends on it and on an archived scrolling package.

For an Arabic book, direction is not a setting you add at the end. It decides which way a swipe goes, which side the drawer opens from, how a mixed Arabic and Latin sentence is isolated, and which font the text falls back to. So I wrote the reader with direction read from the book itself, from the spine first and the language second, and applied at every level: the page view, the drawer, the paragraph and the inline run. Doing it with Flutter widgets instead of a WebView keeps the whole thing in one rendering system, with a reading position that can be saved as a small string and restored.

Get the code

The source, the migration table, an example app with a generated sample book and the tests are on GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/epub_rtl. It is MIT licensed.

Originally published at abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

event_model_payload.headline: I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem
event_model_payload.summary:
I Built a Python CLI to Tackle Oracle Cloud Ampere A1's "Out of Host Capacity" Problem

Getting an Oracle Cloud Ampere A1 instance can be frustrating.

You may have your OCI account configured, your network ready, your quotas checked, and your VM configuration prepared — but capacity availability can still get in the way.

I wanted a simpler way to handle this workflow.

So I started building a Python automation tool for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). What began as a personal automation script gradually evolved into a cross-platform CLI with interactive configuration, installation scripts, monitoring capabilities, safety checks, and support for AI coding agents.

!OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

Today, I'm sharing it with the developer community.

GitHub: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

The Problem I Wanted to Solve

Working with OCI A1 instances involves more than just clicking the Create Instance button.

Before attempting to launch an instance, there are several things worth checking:

Is A1 capacity currently available in my region and availability domain?
Are my OCPU and memory quotas sufficient?
Is my existing VCN and subnet configuration valid?
Is the selected image appropriate?
Am I staying within my intended compute and storage budget?
How can I monitor capacity without repeatedly doing the same manual checks?

I didn't want to build another cloud dashboard or a complicated infrastructure platform.

I wanted a lightweight tool that could automate repetitive checks and provide a manageable workflow from the terminal.

What I Built
OCI Always Free A1 VM Automation

A Python-based CLI designed to help OCI users inspect their environment, check A1 capacity, validate configuration, and optionally request one VM through an explicitly guarded workflow.

The project supports Windows and Linux.

What It Can Do

  1. A1 Capacity Monitoring

Check OCI A1 availability and monitor capacity using configurable retry and backoff behavior.

  1. Quota and Configuration Checks

Validate important settings such as:

Home region and availability domain.
Existing VCN and public subnet.
Compute and storage limits.
A1 instance configuration.
Image and SSH public-key settings.
Existing instances and resource usage.

  1. Interactive Terminal Interface

Instead of remembering every command, users can open the application and navigate through an interactive terminal menu.

  1. Guided Configuration

The configuration editor allows users to work through settings in organized groups, validate values, review changes, and save safely.

  1. Windows and Linux Installers

The project includes PowerShell and shell installers that create an isolated Python environment and initialize a safe starter configuration.

  1. AI Coding-Agent Support

The repository includes instructions and project memory for tools such as:

Claude Code
OpenAI Codex
Gemini CLI
GitHub Copilot
Other agentic development environments

The idea is to make it easier to understand, maintain, and extend the project with AI assistance.

Some Implementation Decisions I Found Interesting

This project was also a useful exercise in making an existing automation tool more reusable.

A few decisions shaped the architecture.

Keeping the Existing Engine

Rather than rewriting the original automation logic, I introduced a new oci-platform CLI layer around the existing Python engine.

This allowed me to preserve existing functionality while improving how users interact with it.

Handling Windows and Linux Differences

One portability issue came from using the POSIX-only fcntl module for process locking.

That approach wasn't suitable for Windows.

I replaced the unconditional platform-specific import with a cross-platform locking implementation.

It was a good reminder that cross-platform support needs to be considered at the application level, not just in the installer.

Making Configuration Safer

I didn't want setup to accidentally arm VM creation or overwrite an existing installation.

The installers refuse to overwrite an existing target directory, and the configuration workflow keeps VM creation disabled.

These are deliberate design decisions, not just documentation warnings.

Safety Is a Core Part of the Design

Because this application interacts with cloud infrastructure, I wanted the default behavior to be read-only.

VM creation requires three independent safeguards:

mode.creation_enabled=true in the local configuration.
The exact confirmation phrase LAUNCH_ONE_ALWAYS_FREE_INSTANCE.
The CLI flag --enable-create.

An actual launch also requires the operator's explicit authorization.

The application is designed around an existing network rather than automatically creating or modifying networking resources.

It does not upgrade OCI accounts, terminate existing instances, or promise guaranteed capacity or zero billing.

A capacity check is not a reservation, and Always Free eligibility must always be verified against your own OCI account and current Oracle terms.

Development and Testing

I wanted to validate more than just whether the Python code worked on my own machine.

The repository now has GitHub Actions workflows covering:

Python 3.11 and 3.12.
Windows and Ubuntu.
Application compilation and unit tests.
CLI startup and packaging.
Installer safety checks.
A fresh Linux installer integration test.

The Linux integration test checks installation in a clean temporary directory, verifies the installed commit, confirms the starter configuration keeps creation disabled, and checks that existing directories are preserved.

I also encountered an environment-related problem while trying to run a Linux installation test in an isolated Debian container: DNS resolution for raw.githubusercontent.com failed.

Instead of marking that attempt as successful, I added hosted Ubuntu integration coverage to the CI workflow.

The latest main commit passed all six CI jobs.

I also tested a fresh Windows installation and the interactive CLI on a second PC; that result was reported by the operator.

There is still work to do around live OCI validation, so I am not claiming that every real-world tenancy or capacity scenario has been verified.

Getting Started

You need:

Git
Python 3.11 or newer
Windows (PowerShell)

Download the installer:

powershell
Invoke-WebRequest "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.ps1" -OutFile install.ps1

Review the installer:

powershell
Get-Content .\install.ps1

Run the installer:

powershell
.\install.ps1

Linux

Download the installer:

bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM/main/install.sh

Review the installer:

bash
less install.sh

Run the installer:

bash
bash install.sh

Launch the Interactive CLI

Windows:

powershell
$cli = "$HOME\oci-automation-platform.venv\Scripts\oci-platform.exe"
& $cli

Linux:

bash
CLI="$HOME/oci-automation-platform/.venv/bin/oci-platform"
"$CLI"

Start with local configuration and diagnostics before connecting to your OCI environment.

The installer creates a starter configuration with VM creation disabled. Follow the detailed instructions in the repository before running live OCI checks.

What's Next?

The initial V1 code-delivery milestone is complete, but I see this as the beginning of community testing rather than the end of development.

Some areas I'd like to improve through feedback:

More real-world OCI A1 edge-case testing.
Better diagnostics and operator feedback.
Additional installation and configuration testing across environments.
Improvements to monitoring and retry behavior.
More useful workflows for AI-assisted maintenance.

I also want to keep the project lightweight rather than turn it into a large platform with unnecessary services.

I'd Love Your Feedback

I'm especially interested in hearing from developers who use Oracle Cloud, Python automation, or cross-platform CLI tools.

A few questions:

Would you find a tool like this useful for managing OCI A1 capacity?
What edge cases should I test before a wider release?
Is the interactive terminal experience a good approach, or would you prefer a different workflow?
What would you improve in the current architecture?

Feedback, bug reports, and contributions are welcome.

Explore the Project

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/mudassir-93/OCI-Always-Free-VM

Thanks for reading!

event_model_payload.headline: Where Open-Source Tools Quietly Fail: The Authentication Chain
event_model_payload.summary:
Where Open-Source Tools Quietly Fail: The Authentication Chain

Database security writing loves the database: accounts, grants, encryption at rest. I spend my weeks auditing a different layer — the open-source tools that sit next to the database. Admin consoles, BI panels, backup agents, report engines. The tools that hold production credentials and whose CVEs keep tracing back not to the login form itself, but to the chain behind it.

The useful mental model is to stop treating "authentication" as a feature and start treating it as a chain of five links. Every component I've audited fails at exactly one of them — and only one of them is the password check.

Link 1: The login form

Everyone tests the login form. The failures here are quieter than SQL injection:

  • Default accounts that survive upgrades. The installer creates admin, the upgrade script doesn't remove it, and the docs never mention it. Check the migration scripts, not just the docs.
  • Password comparison in code. Somewhere between the form and the database, a comparison happens. When it's a string equality on a fetched hash instead of a constant-time verify on a computed one, you have a timing oracle — and more commonly, a hashing scheme chosen in 2015 that nobody revisited.

Link 2: The token

The login succeeds and the component mints a token. This is where I find the most per-issue impact:

  • JWT secrets committed to source. Still, in 2026. Grep the repository for signing keys before reading anything else.
  • alg confusion. The library accepts more algorithms than the code intends. Rare in mature projects, endemic in young ones.
  • Sessions that never expire because expiry is a config key nobody sets. The default value is zero, zero means "no expiry," and no test catches this because tests log in and log out.

Link 3: The remember-me cookie

Remember-me is a serialization feature disguised as a convenience feature. State goes into a cookie, the server trusts the cookie later. When the "state" is a serialized object graph, you're one gadget chain away from a much worse CVE than "session forgery." When it's a signed user ID, check what signs it — I've found remember-me cookies signed with the same key as the JWT, which means forging one forges the other.

Link 4: The password reset flow

The reset flow is the authentication chain running without a password, which makes it the most security-critical code in the component and, consistently, the least reviewed:

  • Reset tokens that double as session tokens. The token resets the password and then logs you in. Now the token's lifetime is the session's lifetime, and the token was sent over email.
  • Host header injection in the reset email. The link in the email is built from the request's Host header. An attacker who can get a request to the server with a chosen Host header sends the victim a poisoned reset link. It's a one-line bug that keeps being shipped.

Link 5: The service account

The last link is the one no user ever sees: the API key the component uses for its own operations, and the ones it issues for integrations. Shared by all users, no expiry, and in several published cases, one of them authenticates as admin. When you audit, list every key type — user keys, integration keys, internal keys — and check the middleware that validates them. The gap between "valid key" and "this key may do this" is where the whole chain collapses.

The chain-shaped audit

Read the chain in order, and do it from source:

  1. Find the login handler. Read the comparison.
  2. Find the token mint. Find the expiry check. Grep for the signing key.
  3. Find the remember-me serializer. Check what it trusts and what signs it.
  4. Read the reset flow end to end, including how the email link is built.
  5. List every API key type. Find the middleware. Check what "valid" means for each.

Five links, five afternoons, no lab, no exploit server. The bugs you find this way are the ones that get CVEs later — you're just reading them first.

I'm collecting these patterns — each link anchored to real, patched public CVEs — into Auditing Open-Components: A Practitioner's Field Guide, an early-access book about auditing deployed open-source middleware from source alone.

Argon2id turns a password into a key that is slow to guess on GPUs; XChaCha20-Poly1305 seals the file so any change is detected. This post walks through the format of skull-locker, an open-source file locker, and the one rule that keeps your original safe: never delete it until the locked copy has been opened and checked.

The rest: the README's "Why another file locker" table and the "Use" section, then a link to https://github.com/skull-org/skull-locker.

event_model_payload.headline: HTTP 413 Request Entity Too Large: nginx fix
event_model_payload.summary:
The request body (usually an upload) is larger than the limit nginx or a proxy in front of it allows – the request never reaches the application.

Common causes

  • client_max_body_size is not set; the nginx default is 1 MB.
  • The directive is in the wrong context or in a file that is not included.
  • A second proxy in front (load balancer, Docker proxy, Cloudflare with 100 MB on the free plan) has its own limit.
  • PHP limits upload_max_filesize and post_max_size are too small (usually an application error rather than 413).

How to check it

Find the effective value in the loaded config

nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -n client_max_body_size

Find 413 cases in the log

grep 'too large body' /var/log/nginx/error.log | tail -n 10

Check the PHP-FPM limits (not the CLI ones)

grep -rE 'upload_max_filesize|post_max_size' /etc/php/8.3/fpm/

What actually helps

  1. Set client_max_body_size 10G; in the right server or location block (0 disables the check).
  2. Test and reload: nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx.
  3. Raise the same limit on every proxy in front.

FAQ

Why doesn't changing php.ini help?

Because the 413 comes from nginx before PHP ever sees the request. Also, PHP-FPM uses a different php.ini than the CLI.

Is client_max_body_size 0 a good idea?

Only behind authentication. On public endpoints it allows arbitrarily large requests and makes simple resource attacks easy.

Full page with every command and the German/Italian version: daniele-michelin.com/en/errors/http-413-request-entity-too-large/

First published at daniele-michelin.com. The error lexicon covers HTTP, DNS, TLS, mail, database, PHP, nginx, systemd and Nextcloud, in German, English and Italian.

event_model_payload.headline: Actively exploited this week: 9 new CISA KEV entries (16 November to 22 November 2026)
event_model_payload.summary:
Every week CISA adds vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue. The bar for getting on that list is not "severe on paper" but "attackers are using it now". For a small team with limited patching hours, that makes KEV the most useful priority list there is.

Below: every entry added between 16 November and 22 November 2026, copied from the catalogue and linked to its NVD record, plus what Romania's national cyber security directorate and Have I Been Pwned published in the same days. Nothing is estimated or rewritten.

The 9 actively exploited vulnerabilities added this week

Added Product CVE Known ransomware use
20 Nov Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability CVE-2026-76466 not known
20 Nov Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 not known
20 Nov Broadcom VMware vCenter: VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 not known
20 Nov SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability CVE-2025-42884 not known
18 Nov Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 not known
18 Nov Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 not known
18 Nov BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 not known
18 Nov Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2024-10441 not known
17 Nov Perforce Puppet Enterprise Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 not known

What Romania's DNSC flagged the same week

Alerts from DNSC, Romania's national cyber security directorate, with their original titles in Romanian:

  • ALERTĂ: Vulnerabilitate critică la nivelul VMware, 20 November
  • ALERTĂ: Vulnerabilități critice identificate la nivelul NGINX, 19 November
  • ALERTĂ: Vulnerabilitate critică la nivelul Java, 18 November

When a national authority and CISA point at the same product in the same week, that product goes to the top of the queue.

Breaches added to Have I Been Pwned

  • Careers360: 3,609,421 accounts, added 20 November. Check the breach page
  • Too Lost: 724,323 accounts, added 20 November. Check the breach page

If your team's work addresses may be in one of these, check the breach page and the password reuse question, not only the address.

How to use a list like this in an hour

  1. Start with what faces the internet. VPN and access gateways, firewalls, routers, mail servers and public web platforms are how many ransomware incidents start.
  2. Search your inventory by product name, not by memory. "We don't run that" is a claim, and the asset list is the evidence.
  3. Patch or apply the vendor mitigation, then confirm the version. A patch that was downloaded but not applied reads as done in a ticket and is still exploitable.
  4. If you cannot patch today, reduce exposure: restrict the management interface to known addresses, disable the affected feature, or put the service behind an access gateway you trust.

Where this comes from

A small collector reads official sources every hour: DNSC, CERT-EU, CERT-FR (ANSSI), CERT-Bund (BSI), the UK NCSC, CISA KEV, Have I Been Pwned and three specialist newsrooms. It copies each item exactly, with its source link.

Nothing in this post is written by a model. A security page that paraphrases an advisory wrongly does more harm than no page at all.

Sources: CISA KEV catalogue (dateAdded 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22), DNSC alerts, Have I Been Pwned. Generated from the sources on 2026-11-23.

event_model_payload.headline: I built a tiny programming language for Halloween — then made property tests prove it behaves
event_model_payload.summary:
This post is part of Kiroween 2026 — it's the story of my Skeleton Crew entry, CurseEngine.

The idea started with a grumble: every automation tool I rely on asks me to trust rules I can't read. Moderation bots, reminder workflows, digest jobs — the rule fires on real people, and the person accountable for it gets a settings page, not a sentence.

So I built the opposite. CurseEngine is a small language where a rule is one line of near-English:

curse spam-strikes: when message where count(message by same author flagged) >= 3 within 7 days -> mute author for 1 day; escalate to owner

A hand-written parser compiles that to an inspectable graph. A sandboxed executor runs it — no eval, no LLM making the call. And because a rule you can't rehearse is still a gamble, the same executor doubles as a simulator: run it over history and see what would have happened, with zero side effects. Every real action lands in an append-only log — the grimoire — where undo appends a reversal instead of erasing history.

One engine, three hosts: GrimMod (chat moderation — a raid bot muted on its third flagged message), Deadbeat (invoice chasing at 7/14/21 days, exactly once per tier), and a standup-digest rule-pack. After the engine's baseline commit, the apps were added with zero changes to the engine package. That diff is the whole Skeleton Crew argument, and it's checkable in the git history.

The part I did not expect: the property-based tests found the best bug. The suite runs 1,500 generated event streams through the live executor and the simulator and demands identical outcomes. On the first run it shrank a disagreement about stacked mutes down to a tiny example — a wrong assumption that my hand-written tests shared, which is exactly why they would never have caught it. The generators are wider now (hostile regex patterns, wrong-typed fields, webhook and timer curses), and the parity count is asserted inside the test so it can't silently shrink.

The build itself was spec-first in Kiro: four specs, steering files with three inviolables (no exfiltration, the simulator never executes side effects, every action is reversible), and a hook that re-runs the whole property suite every time a curse or fixture is saved — a hook I trust because we deliberately broke a fixture once and watched it fail. Total agent cost: about 50 of the 4,000 hackathon credits. Writing the decisions down turned out to be the cheap part's best friend.

Try it live: GrimMod and Deadbeat are both running (links in the repo), and the code is MIT at github.com/pintu544/curseengine. If you run a small community or chase invoices solo, I'd genuinely like to know which curse you'd write first.

event_model_payload.headline: Why fnmatchcase Matters for Cross-Platform Python Tools
event_model_payload.summary:
In toml-sort, a configuration override for servers.Beta could also apply to servers.beta on Windows. On Linux, it didn't.

The input file and configuration were identical. The difference came from Python's fnmatch.fnmatch(), which toml-sort used to match TOML key paths.

An Override That Shouldn't Match

toml-sort lets you override sorting options for individual TOML tables. For example, this configuration enables key sorting globally but disables it for servers.Beta:

[tool.tomlsort]
sort_table_keys = true

[tool.tomlsort.overrides."servers.Beta"]
table_keys = false

Now consider a table whose name differs only in case:

[servers.beta]
z = 1
a = 2

TOML keys are case-sensitive. The override for servers.Beta shouldn't apply to servers.beta, so the keys should be sorted:

[servers.beta]
a = 2
z = 1

With toml-sort 0.25.0, the original order could remain unchanged on Windows because the override matched despite the case difference. On Linux, the keys were sorted.

This could also affect toml-sort --check: the same file and configuration might pass the check on one platform and fail on another.

How fnmatch() Caused the Difference

Python's fnmatch.fnmatch() supports shell-style wildcard matching. Before matching, it passes both the input string and pattern through os.path.normcase().

On Windows, normcase() converts uppercase characters to lowercase. On Linux, it leaves the case unchanged.

For example:

import fnmatch

fnmatch.fnmatch("servers.beta", "servers.Beta")

This returns True on Windows and False on Linux.

That behavior is documented, but toml-sort wasn't matching filenames. It was matching dotted TOML key paths, whose case-sensitivity shouldn't depend on the operating system.

The relevant code was in _find_config_override().

It first looked for an exact match:

path_string = ".".join(path)

if path_string in self.sort_config_overrides:
    return self.sort_config_overrides.get(path_string)

If that failed, it tried the configured patterns:

matches = [
    config
    for pattern, config in self.sort_config_overrides.items()
    if fnmatch.fnmatch(path_string, pattern)
]

The exact lookup was already case-sensitive. The fallback wasn't consistently so.

Even servers.Beta, which contains no wildcard, could match servers.beta through that fallback on Windows.

The fix in PR #110 changed one function call:

- if fnmatch.fnmatch(path_string, pattern)
+ if fnmatch.fnmatchcase(path_string, pattern)

Unlike fnmatch(), fnmatchcase() doesn't normalize the strings through os.path.normcase(). It performs case-sensitive matching regardless of the host platform.

Wildcard support and the existing exact-match priority were preserved.

The fix was released in toml-sort 0.26.0 on November 14, 2026.

Reproducing Windows Matching on Linux

The regression test needed to catch a Windows-specific problem even when running on Linux.

A normal case-sensitivity test on Linux wouldn't have done that. The original fnmatch() call already behaved correctly there.

Instead, the test uses ntpath, Python's Windows-oriented path module, together with pytest's monkeypatch fixture:

import ntpath
import os

monkeypatch.setattr(os.path, "normcase", ntpath.normcase)

This replaces the normalization function used by fnmatch() with the Windows implementation.

With the original code, patterns that differ only in case can now match on Linux as they would on Windows. The updated fnmatchcase() call is unaffected.

The upstream test covers five patterns against the TOML path servers.beta:

Pattern Expected match
servers.beta Yes
servers.* Yes
servers.Beta No
Servers.* No
servers.[A-Z]* No

The last case checks a case difference inside a character class, rather than ordinary text.

The test also checks toml-sort's sorting behavior. It creates a small TOML document with unsorted keys and supplies an override that disables sorting when the pattern matches.

If the pattern should match, the keys must remain in their original order. Otherwise, they must be sorted.

Before the fix, the simulated Windows normalization made the three case-mismatched patterns select the wrong override. With fnmatchcase(), all five expectations are satisfied.

The test doesn't emulate an entire Windows environment. It replaces the specific normalization step responsible for this bug.

That makes the platform-dependent failure visible to Linux CI without needing a Windows runner for this particular check.

Matching the Data, Not the Platform

fnmatch() isn't inherently the wrong function. Its platform-dependent normalization can be useful when that's the intended matching behavior.

For TOML identifiers, however, it introduced a dependency on the operating system that the format itself doesn't have.

In this case, switching to fnmatchcase() made override selection consistent, and the regression test checked that consistency through the resulting sorting behavior.

References

  • toml-sort repository
  • PR #110 — Match TOML override patterns case-sensitively
  • Original implementation (v0.25.0)
  • Fixed implementation (v0.26.0)
  • Python documentation — fnmatch
  • TOML v1.0.0 specification
  • toml-sort on PyPI

event_model_payload.headline: A pre Black Friday monitoring checklist (do it this afternoon, not Thursday night)
event_model_payload.summary:
Black Friday is coming up this Friday. Assuming you are running an online shop, or a SaaS that online shops depend on, this is the weekend when "the site was a bit slow for a while, or down" turns into lost revenue you can actually count.

Most of what goes wrong isn't exotic. It's a certificate that expired, a checkout that returns a friendly 200 while being broken, or an alert that went to someone who was asleep. Here's a checklist that takes an afternoon. Every item comes from a failure that has actually happened.

1. Things that expire

TLS certificates, on every hostname. That means www, shop., api., the checkout subdomain, the callback URLs your payment provider calls, and any custom domain on your CDN.

Two things changed recently that make this more likely to bite:

  • Since March 15, 2026, publicly trusted certificates are valid for at most 200 days (down from 398), and the limit drops to 100 days in March 2027. Renewals happen more often, so a broken renewal job shows up sooner.
  • Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry-warning emails in June 2025. If your renewal job quietly broke, nobody will tell you.

Check every hostname now:

for h in www.example.com shop.example.com api.example.com; do
  end=$(echo | openssl s_client -servername "$h" -connect "$h:443" 2>/dev/null \
        | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)
  echo "$h -> $end"
done

Anything that expires before mid-December, renew it this week.

Domains. In 2017 Marketo forgot to renew marketo.com, and it took the site and its customers' tracking links down with it. If a company that size can do it, so can anyone.

whois example.com | grep -i expir

2. Monitor what makes money, not just /

A homepage check tells you the homepage works. Customers don't pay you on the homepage.

  • Cart, checkout and sign-up. Check each one for text that only renders when the page really works, such as "Order summary" or "Payment method". A cached page, a maintenance page or an error template can all return 200 OK. 
  curl -fsS https://shop.example.com/cart | grep -q "Order summary" \
    && echo "OK" || echo "BROKEN"
  • Every API the storefront depends on: stock, shipping rates, payments, search. Check your own health endpoint as well, and check what the body says, not only the status code.
  • Response time. Set a threshold. A checkout that takes 9 seconds is down for most shoppers, even though it's technically up. 
  curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'total: %{time_total}s\n' https://shop.example.com/checkout

3. The jobs nobody watches

Stock sync, price feeds, abandoned-cart emails, nightly backups: they run from cron or a scheduler, and when one stops, nothing turns red. You find out when a customer buys something you don't have.

Make each job report in when it finishes, and alert when the report doesn't arrive (a "heartbeat" or "dead man's switch" check):

# last line of the job: only runs if everything before it succeeded
/usr/local/bin/sync-stock.sh && curl -fsS -m 10 https://your-heartbeat-url >/dev/null

Set the expected interval a little longer than the job's schedule, and send the alert to the same on-call person as everything else.

4. Detect fast, without crying wolf

  • Shorten your check intervals for the weekend. Five minutes between checks is a long time when the checkout is down.
  • Confirm from a second location before alerting. A blip on one network path shouldn't wake anyone up at 3 a.m. If people learn to ignore alerts in November, they'll ignore the real one in December.

5. People

  • Write down who is on call from Thursday to Monday, with phone numbers, and make sure they know.
  • Set up escalation. If the first person doesn't acknowledge within N minutes, the alert goes to the next one. Holiday weekends are exactly when "I didn't see the notification" happens.

6. A change freeze

  • No deploys, no plugin updates, and automatic updates off from Wednesday.
  • Take a full backup, and test the restore. A backup you've never restored is a hope, not a backup.

7. Communication

  • Have a status page, so customers can check whether it's you without opening a ticket. Every ticket you don't get is one less thing to answer while you're fixing the problem.
  • Write the message for "our hosting or CDN provider is down" now. You won't write a good one at 2 a.m.

When Fastly failed on June 8, 2021, one customer's valid config change triggered a latent bug, and 85% of Fastly's network returned errors. Every site on it went down at the same moment. You can't fix that kind of outage, but you can be the one who tells your customers first.

8. Know your providers' status pages, and don't rely on them

During the 2017 AWS S3 outage, AWS couldn't update its own status dashboard for about two hours, because the dashboard depended on S3. In June 2025, Google Cloud's status page lagged by about an hour for a similar reason.

Bookmark your providers' status pages, but your own external checks are what tell you first.

The short version

  • [ ] Every certificate is valid until mid-December or later
  • [ ] Domains are renewed, with auto-renew on
  • [ ] Cart, checkout, sign-up and APIs are monitored, with keyword checks
  • [ ] A response-time threshold is set
  • [ ] Every scheduled job reports in when it finishes
  • [ ] Shorter check intervals, with confirmation from a second location
  • [ ] On-call rota and escalation are written down
  • [ ] Change freeze from Wednesday, backup tested
  • [ ] Status page is ready, and the "provider is down" message is written

Got something to add to my list? Tell me in the comments.

Sources: Let's Encrypt ends expiry emails · Certificate validity changes · Marketo domain · Fastly, June 8 2021 · AWS S3, 2017 · Google Cloud, June 2025

If you want external checks running before Friday: code BLACKFRIDAY gives 3 months of 12happy Pro free, no card, for the first 100 accounts until December 1 (details).

I'm Eli, part of the team behind 12happy, an uptime monitoring and status page service with a free plan of 50 monitors. This post was drafted with AI assistance, and reviewed and edited by me.

event_model_payload.headline: I Think Mathematicians and Software Engineers Will Be the Same in the Future
event_model_payload.summary:
I now feel that the math world will eventually become like the programming world: responsible for all kinds of strange hypotheses and creations.

Then let AI verify them, do the work, get the results, and reinvent the wheel over and over again, but every wheel is made differently.

There are millions of ways to implement a feature, and the same goes for proving a mathematical conjecture.

I really miss the time before AI, the feeling of being immersed in writing code and the sense of achievement after completing a feature.

And being able to happily share with others the methods I found during development and my design ideas.

But now, I can only pursue features and rough design directions. It's become like having meetings with AI every day to discuss features.

But I can't go back to the old-fashioned way of programming anymore, because I can no longer purely immerse myself in writing a program.

Because I know that whatever I write, AI can do it in a few seconds, and do it better. I can't get any sense of achievement, and the time I spend becomes purely a waste of time.

I've already given up now. I'm not some top student from a top university, or some top talent who has worked at a top company.

The ambition I used to have is gone. All that's left is the thought of "destroy everything together, then create completely new rules and a new world."

event_model_payload.headline: AI Gateway now runs canary ZDR audits
event_model_payload.summary:
AI Gateway now runs canary audits against inference providers to detect when prompt content is read outside the inference path.

Contractual Zero Data Retention (ZDR) agreements and point-in-time security audits establish how a provider should handle your data, but production infrastructure changes continuously. Canary audits add a detection layer on top.

Each canary audit run:

  1. Mints unique URLs that exist nowhere else, each mapped privately to a specific provider, model, and audit run.

  2. Sends prompts containing those URLs through the normal inference path, with ZDR requested for covered providers and non-ZDR pairs included as positive controls.

  3. Watches for traffic. A ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, so a canary URL should never receive a request.

  4. Records any request to a canary URL, identifying the provider, model, and run for investigation.

Canary audits complement contractual ZDR agreements and independent audits rather than replacing them.

Read more about AI Gateway security and compliance measures in the documentation.

event_model_payload.headline: Vercel日本法人の代表に花尾和成が就任いたしました
event_model_payload.summary:
（本記事は、英語版の就任発表の日本語訳に、花尾本人の就任のご挨拶を加えたものです。）

Vercel日本法人の代表に、花尾和成が就任いたしました（東京拠点）。今後、Vercelは花尾とともに国内のチームを拡充し、日本市場への投資をさらに進めていきます。

弊社が10年以上前に公開したNext.jsを、日本の開発者の皆さまはいち早く使い始めてくださいました。そして現在、日本では三菱商事、富士通、U-NEXT、ディー・エヌ・エーといった大企業から、SANUや令和トラベルといったスタートアップまで、幅広い企業にVercelをご利用いただいています。

花尾はこの10年間、日本でソフトウェア企業の運営にリーダーシップを発揮してきました。前職ではPendoの日本法人社長を務め、それ以前にはHashiCorpの日本事業を立ち上げ、Pivotalの東京オフィスで営業部門を統括しました。

就任にあたり、花尾から皆さまへのメッセージをご紹介します。

このたび、Vercelの日本法人代表に就任いたしました花尾和成です。私は20年以上IT業界に身を置き、そのうち10年以上は、開発者が開発そのものに集中できるようにするプロダクトに携わってまいりました。この経験を活かし、日本の開発者の皆さまと、その先にあるビジネスの価値を最大化することに貢献してまいります。

Vercelには、CEOのギシェルモ・ラウチを筆頭に、日本を好きなメンバーが数多くいます。こうした仲間の後押しを受けながら素晴らしいチームをつくり、Vercelが日本市場にとってかけがえのない存在となることを目指します。そして究極的には、直接的にも間接的にも、Vercelが日本のあらゆる場所で使われている世界を実現したいと考えています。

今後ともご指導ご鞭撻のほど、よろしくお願い申し上げます。

ここからは、私（Nick Bogaty, CRO）が聞き手を務めた花尾へのインタビューをお届けします。日本市場にどのような可能性を感じているのか、Vercelへの入社を決めた理由とあわせて伺いました。

Vercelが日本でさらに成長できるとお考えなのは、なぜですか？

日本のソフトウェア開発は、まさに転換期を迎えています。日本には革新的な企業が多く、高い技術力を持つ開発者の皆さまが活躍されています。一方で、多くの企業では既存のシステムが複雑になり、最先端のAIの導入がなかなか進んでいません。その結果、AIを十分に活用できていないケースもあります。

日本企業がAIのポテンシャルを引き出すには、AIを試す段階から本番運用へ進む必要があります。Vercelは、その一歩を後押しできると考えています。AIアプリケーションを大規模に、安全かつ安定して、効率よく運用できるよう支える。これはまさに、Vercelが強みを発揮できる領域です。

そして、AIにかかるコストをどう管理するか、どんなルールで運用するか、セキュリティをどう確保するか。いまやどれも技術部門だけでなく、経営陣にとっても優先課題です。最近お会いした経営幹部の方々も、こうした課題に取り組んでいると口をそろえておっしゃっていました。この点でも、Vercelは日本企業の力になれると考えています。

Vercelへの入社を決めた理由をお聞かせください。

複雑なことをシンプルにし、企業がもっとすばやく動けるようにする。以前から、そんなテクノロジーに魅力を感じてきました。Vercelなら、これまで私が取り組んできたことを、さらに大きな規模で実現できると思ったのです。いま、AIはソフトウェアの開発から運用まで、そのあり方を変えつつあります。そのなかで、Vercelは次世代のアプリケーションを支える基盤になれると考えています。

入社の決め手になったのは、Vercelのビジョンと、開発者の皆さまを第一に考える文化です。そして、日本で一から事業をつくっていけることにも惹かれました。私がやりがいを感じるのは、事業を立ち上げ、優れた人材を集め、チームが主体的に難しい課題に挑める環境をつくることです。Vercelでは、私自身が可能性を信じている技術を軸に、そうした仕事に取り組めると思いました。

グローバル企業の日本事業を立ち上げるなかで、何を学ばれましたか？

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway
event_model_payload.summary:
AI is now used in every part of a business, and as a result, companies send source code, customer records, and regulated data through inference providers.

The assurance that no data is retained after processing is still publicly unverified. Payment platforms, cloud infrastructure, and most other layers that handle data this sensitive have a way to prove their controls to outside parties, and inference will follow the same path.

Today we are introducing Audited ZDR on AI Gateway. A provider is labeled Audited ZDR only after an independent security firm tests its zero data retention claims against its code, infrastructure, and live traffic, then publishes the report. Baseten, Modal, and Wafer are launch partners that have already begun audits, and more providers are encouraged to join to help raise the bar for security and privacy.

Audited ZDR builds on two steps we took toward stronger governance earlier this year:

  • We launched team-wide Zero Data Retention (ZDR) so teams could route traffic exclusively to providers stating a ZDR policy.

  • We completed our ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, which put Vercel’s own AI systems under independent third-party audit.

We are now asking inference providers for the same thing we asked of ourselves: independent verification.

Why a contract is not enough

ZDR guarantees rely on contracts and self-attestation. A provider agrees not to retain prompts or completions, and customers take that commitment on faith.

For teams sending proprietary code, customer information, or regulated data through models, self-reported ZDR contracts don't provide enough assurance.

  • Are prompts landing in debug logs, crash dumps, or tracing pipelines?

  • Can a rate limit push a request marked ZDR to a non-ZDR endpoint?

  • Can a support engineer's debugging tools surface a customer's prompt?

Answering these questions means running a bespoke security review for every provider and the models they host. An audit answers them in public.

What Audited ZDR verifies

To qualify for Audited ZDR on AI Gateway, an inference provider engages an independent security firm, chosen from among respected third-party auditors, to run the audit. The firm then tests the provider's zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic.

The audit confirms that customer data is never written or retained on durable storage in any system. Customer data means prompts, completions, system prompts, embeddings, files, images and audio, tool and function-call payloads, and any derived data that could identify them. Coverage spans request logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, prompt caches, abuse monitoring, analytics, backups, support tools, and training, fine-tuning, and evaluation datasets.

The audit confirms that once a response is returned to AI Gateway, that content is deleted from the inference provider’s systems. Where a request uses caching, such as a KV cache, the cache stays in RAM only, is never written to disk, and the behavior is disclosed.

The audit also confirms:

  • That a request marked ZDR never fails over to a non-ZDR endpoint, tool, or feature

  • That no human or automated process accesses customer data outside handling the request itself

  • That sub-processors with access comply with all of the above

  • That no training on customer data occurs

Auditors verify this by reviewing the inference provider's serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then running live tests. They send marked prompts through AI Gateway and search the provider's logging, caching, and storage systems for any trace of them.

Every passing provider publishes the report under the auditor's name. It covers scope, methodology, dates, findings, and fix status, with any exceptions disclosed and redactions limited to exploit detail. AI Gateway links directly to the report.

Canary monitoring between audits

An independent audit checks a provider's code and infrastructure at a point in time, but production systems change. To add a detection layer between independent audits, Vercel also runs canary audits against inference providers on AI Gateway.

Each run sends prompts containing unique, unindexed URLs mapped privately to a provider, model, and run. Because a ZDR provider should never retain, inspect, or crawl prompt content, any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved. Canary checks cannot detect prompts written to disk and never read, so they complement independent code and infrastructure audits rather than replacing them.

How Audited ZDR works in AI Gateway

We are adding an independently Audited ZDR provider tier and a team-wide toggle in AI Gateway policy settings. When enabled, AI Gateway routes and fails over your team's requests only across providers with published audits that meet the bar.

Launch partners have started their audits, and each provider enters the tier as soon as its report is published. Launch partner reports are expected to be published by December 8, 2026.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries and failover for higher uptime than connecting to providers directly. It reflects provider pricing with no markup and charges no platform fee on inference, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. Read the AI Gateway documentation to get started.

The audited tier works alongside AI Gateway's other compliance controls. Regional inference pins where a provider runs inference to the US, EU, Australia, or Japan, per request or team-wide, and any data the provider stores at rest stays in that region. If AI Gateway can't honor the region, the request fails rather than running elsewhere.

Provider headquarters filters routing by who owns the provider, so a request only reaches providers whose parent company is headquartered in a country you allow.

Private inference connects your own self-hosted or fine-tuned model endpoints to AI Gateway, called as private/ with the same SDKs, auth, and observability as catalog models and scoped to your team.

event_model_payload.headline: Catch missing feature flags before they reach production
event_model_payload.summary:
Vercel Flags can now block a deployment from reaching production if you’ve declared a flag in code but haven’t created it in your project. Without that definition, your app can silently fall back to the flag’s default value, even if that turns on a feature you meant to keep off.

The Flag Definitions Present Deployment Check runs when a deployment is ready. If any flags are missing, the check fails and lists them in the results, where you can create each one before redeploying.

The check reads your Flags SDK discovery endpoint. With flags@4.5.0 or later on Vercel, it works without FLAGS_SECRET; earlier versions still require the secret.

To turn on blocking, teams on all plans can enable the check in their project’s Build and Deployment settings and mark it as required. See the Deployment Checks documentation for setup details.

event_model_payload.headline: Choose AI Gateway providers by headquarters country
event_model_payload.summary:
Provider headquarters sends your AI Gateway requests only to providers headquartered in countries you choose, so you can meet compliance and procurement rules about where your AI vendors are located.

You can configure provider headquarters to be an allowlist of the countries to use, or a denylist of the countries to block. AI Gateway skips providers in blocked countries and routes requests to the rest of the list, so a model stays accessible as long as it is available in one of its allowed provider locations.

Use provider headquarters with regional hosting and regional inference to control where a request is received, where the model runs, and who runs it.

Set provider headquarters for your team

Pro and Enterprise customers can apply their provider headquarters list to every AI Gateway request across their team. Configure the list in AI Gateway settings.

Provider headquarters settings are applied automatically as AI Gateway adds models and providers. Providers without a headquarters country on record never receive your requests.

Set provider headquarters per request

On any plan, set headquarters in the gateway provider options to restrict a single request. Pass country codes for an allowlist, or prefix every code with ! for a denylist, as in ['!US']. If your team has a list, a request can only narrow it.

In the examples below, requests are only sent to providers based in the US and Germany:

Both settings filter providers, so a model stays available as long as one of its providers is based in an allowed country. If no provider is available in an allowed country, AI Gateway tries your fallback models. If no fallback models are available in allowed countries, or if no fallback models are configured, the request will fail without trying to route to providers in other locations.

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
event_model_payload.summary:
I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives.

A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company.

Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares

Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid.

For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison.

This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?
