event_model_payload.headline: 3-Tire WordPress website Deployment on AWS
event_model_payload.summary:
Deploying WordPress on AWS with a 3-Tier Architecture

Hosting WordPress on one server works until that server crashes, traffic spikes, or the database is exposed to the internet. This article walks through how I built WordPress the way real companies do: a secure, scalable 3-tier architecture on AWS, step by step and in plain language.

The project is split into six parts, which this article follows in order:

  1. Project Overview
  2. Networking Setup: create a V
  3. Networking Setup: create a NAT Gateway and security groups
  4. Database Setup: create a MySQL database and EFS in AWS
  5. Compute Setup: set up EC2 instances and an Application Load Balancer
  6. Conclusion and Clean-up What is a 3-tier architecture? A 3-tier architecture splits an application into three layers, and each layer has one job. Think of a restaurant: customers meet the host at the door, the kitchen prepares the food, and the storage room keeps the ingredients. Customers never walk into the kitchen or the storage room. Tier Restaurant analogy In this project Presentation The front door and host Application Load Balancer in public subnets Application The kitchen Two EC2 instances running WordPress in private subnets Data The storage room Amazon RDS (MySQL) in private subnets This separation is what makes the design secure and reliable. Only the Load Balancer faces the internet, so the servers and the database cannot be reached directly from outside. Part 1: Project Overview The goal is a live WordPress website that stays available if one server or one data centre fails, and that keeps its servers and database hidden from the public internet. The build has five main pieces: • Network setup: a VPC with 2 public and 4 private subnets. An Internet Gateway gives the public subnets internet access, and 2 NAT Gateways in the public subnets give private resources outbound-only access. • Load balancing: an Application Load Balancer (ALB) receives visitor traffic and spreads it across the servers. • Compute layer: two EC2 instances in private subnets host the WordPress application. • Database layer: an Amazon RDS MySQL instance in the private subnets stores the site data. • Routing and security: route tables and security groups control which traffic may flow where. Visitors enter through the Internet Gateway and reach the Load Balancer, which forwards requests to the WordPress servers. The servers use EFS for files and RDS for data, and the NAT Gateways give the private subnets outbound-only access. Services used Service What it does here Category Amazon VPC Isolated network with subnets, route tables and NAT Gateways Networking Internet Gateway Gives public subnets access to the internet Networking NAT Gateway Lets private instances download updates without being exposed Networking Application Load Balancer Distributes incoming traffic across the EC2 instances Load balancing Amazon EC2 Runs the WordPress application Compute Amazon RDS Managed MySQL database for WordPress data Database Amazon EFS Shared file storage so both servers see the same WordPress files Storage IAM roles and policies Secure permissions between AWS services Permissions Route tables Direct traffic between subnets, gateways and the internet Networking Security groups Fine-grained firewall rules for each resource Security What the finished project delivers • A live WordPress website reachable through the ALB DNS name • Secure traffic routing, with EC2 instances kept in private subnets • An integrated Amazon RDS database for dynamic content • A scalable, production-style 3-tier architecture Part 2: Networking Setup, VPC with Public and Private Subnets The VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own isolated network inside AWS, and every other resource in this project lives inside it. I split it into 2 public and 4 private subnets, spread across two Availability Zones so that an outage in one zone does not take the site down. The CIDR ranges below are an example layout. Use any non-overlapping ranges you prefer. Subnet Type Availability Zone Purpose Example CIDR public-1 Public AZ 1 Load Balancer, NAT Gateway 10.0.1.0/24 public-2 Public AZ 2 Load Balancer, NAT Gateway 10.0.2.0/24 private-app-1 Private AZ 1 EC2 instance running WordPress 10.0.3.0/24 private-app-2 Private AZ 2 EC2 instance running WordPress 10.0.4.0/24 private-db-1 Private AZ 1 RDS database 10.0.5.0/24 private-db-2 Private AZ 2 RDS database 10.0.6.0/24 Steps
  7. Create the VPC. In the VPC console, create a VPC with a CIDR block such as 10.0.0.0/16 and give it a clear name tag.
  8. Create the six subnets. Create each subnet from the table above, choosing the right Availability Zone for each one.
  9. Create and attach an Internet Gateway. The Internet Gateway (IGW) is the door between the VPC and the internet. Attach it to your VPC.
  10. Create a public route table. Add a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway, then associate this route table with the two public subnets. A subnet is only "public" because its route table points to the Internet Gateway. The private subnets have no such route, which is why nothing on the internet can reach them directly. The private subnets still need to download packages and updates, which is what the NAT Gateways in the next part are for. Part 3: Networking Setup, NAT Gateways and Security Groups Private servers cannot be reached from the internet, but they still need to go out to it for software updates and WordPress packages. A NAT Gateway allows outbound connections from private subnets while blocking inbound ones. Security groups then act as firewalls around each layer. Create the NAT Gateways
  11. Allocate two Elastic IP addresses, one for each NAT Gateway.
  12. Create a NAT Gateway in each public subnet, so there is one per Availability Zone. If one zone fails, the other zone's servers keep their outbound access.
  13. Create two private route tables, one per Availability Zone. In each, add a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway in the same zone.
  14. Associate each private route table with the private subnets in its zone. Create the security groups The rule of thumb is least privilege: each layer accepts traffic only from the layer directly in front of it. Security group Attached to Allows inbound from Port alb-sg Application Load Balancer Anywhere on the internet 80 (HTTP), plus 443 if you add HTTPS web-sg EC2 WordPress instances alb-sg only 80 db-sg RDS MySQL database web-sg only 3306 efs-sg EFS file system web-sg only 2049 (NFS) Because each group references the previous one instead of an IP range, a visitor can only reach WordPress through the Load Balancer, and only the WordPress servers can reach the database. Part 4: Database Setup, MySQL Database and EFS WordPress stores two kinds of data, and each gets its own managed service. Amazon RDS holds the content (posts, users, settings), and Amazon EFS holds the files (themes, plugins, uploads). With two web servers, shared storage matters: an image uploaded through one server must also appear on the other. Create the MySQL database on RDS
  15. Create a DB subnet group that contains the two private database subnets, one in each Availability Zone.
  16. Create the database. Choose the MySQL engine and a small instance class to keep costs low. Set the database name, the admin username and a strong password, and write them down, because WordPress needs them later.
  17. Place it in the VPC. Select your VPC and the DB subnet group, and turn off public access.
  18. Attach the db-sg security group so that only the WordPress servers can connect on port 3306.
  19. Copy the database endpoint once the instance is available. You will enter it into the WordPress configuration. Create the EFS file system
  20. Create an EFS file system in the same VPC.
  21. Create a mount target in each private application subnet, using the efs-sg security group.
  22. Note the file system ID. Both EC2 instances will mount it to share the WordPress files.

Amazon RDS
Amazon EFS
Stores
Posts, pages, users, settings
Themes, plugins, uploaded media
Type
Managed MySQL database
Shared network file system
Reached by
EC2 on port 3306
EC2 on port 2049 (NFS)
Why it matters
Content stays safe and backed up
Every server shows the same files
Part 5: Compute Setup, EC2 Instances and Application Load Balancer
This part brings the site to life. Two EC2 instances run WordPress in private subnets, and an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets is the only door visitors use.
Launch and configure the EC2 instances

  1. Launch two EC2 instances, one in each private application subnet. Attach the web-sg security group and do not assign a public IP address.
  2. Attach an IAM role to the instances so they can work securely with other AWS services.
  3. Install the web stack. Install a web server (Apache or Nginx), PHP and the MySQL client. The NAT Gateways make these downloads possible.
  4. Mount the EFS file system on the WordPress directory so both servers share the same files.
  5. Install WordPress and point its configuration file at the RDS endpoint, database name, username and password from Part 4. Create the Application Load Balancer
  6. Create a target group for HTTP on port 80 and register both EC2 instances. The health check lets the Load Balancer stop sending traffic to an unhealthy server. WordPress often redirects the home page, so accept redirect codes in the health check if it reports unhealthy.
  7. Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the two public subnets with the alb-sg security group.
  8. Add a listener on port 80 that forwards traffic to the target group.
  9. Open the ALB DNS name in your browser. When both targets show as healthy, the WordPress setup page appears. Complete the WordPress installation through the ALB DNS name rather than an instance address, so the site URL WordPress saves is the one visitors will actually use. How a visitor request travels
  10. The visitor's browser sends a request to the ALB DNS name.
  11. The Load Balancer picks a healthy EC2 instance and forwards the request.
  12. WordPress on that instance reads the content from RDS and the files from EFS.
  13. The page returns to the visitor through the Load Balancer. Part 6: Conclusion and Clean-up The result is a production-style WordPress site: visitors reach it through the Load Balancer, the servers and database stay private, and two Availability Zones keep it running if one fails. What I learned • Networking is the hardest and most important part. Most problems come from route tables or security groups, so check those first when something does not connect. • Private subnets are a big security win. Nothing sensitive is reachable from the internet. • Shared storage matters. Without EFS, two WordPress servers would show different files. • High availability means duplication. Two zones, two NAT Gateways and two servers remove single points of failure. Clean up to avoid charges NAT Gateways, the RDS database and the Load Balancer are billed by the hour, even when idle. Delete resources in this order, because AWS blocks deleting something that another resource still depends on:
  14. Delete the Application Load Balancer, then its target group.
  15. Terminate both EC2 instances.
  16. Delete the RDS database.
  17. Delete the EFS mount targets, then the EFS file system.
  18. Delete both NAT Gateways, then release the Elastic IP addresses.
  19. Delete the custom security groups and route tables.
  20. Detach and delete the Internet Gateway.
  21. Delete the subnets, then the VPC. Finally, open the Billing console the next day and confirm no unexpected charges are appearing. Final thoughts Building a 3-tier architecture turned AWS from a long list of services into one system I understand. If you are learning cloud or DevOps, it is one of the best hands-on projects to start with.

event_model_payload.headline: The 20 biggest open-source AI agent projects on GitHub (November 2026)
event_model_payload.summary:
AI agents are the fastest-moving corner of open source. We track 576 agent projects on GitHub with more than 500 stars in the AI-Sovereign directory, and refresh their numbers every day. Here are the 20 biggest on 22 November 2026, ranked by stars, with what each one actually does.

The top 20

# Project Stars Language What it does
1 ECC 308K JavaScript Performance system for agent harnesses: skills, instincts, memory, security
2 DeepSeek Harness 285K TypeScript DeepSeek's agent harness, built so everything is a plugin
3 Hermes Agent 265K Python Nous Research's personal agent that grows with its user
4 Firecrawl 206K TypeScript Search, scraping and data access so agents can read the web
5 Ponytail 196K JavaScript Makes coding agents write less code ("the best code is the code you never wrote")
6 Graphify 152K Python Turns a codebase, docs and schemas into a queryable knowledge graph
7 LangChain 150K Python The agent engineering platform
8 Orca 132K TypeScript Runs a fleet of coding bots on your own subscriptions
9 Browser Use 122K Python Library for AI agents that drive a real browser
10 Taste Skill 120K JavaScript Gives coding agents design taste: art direction, references, a browser check
11 claude-mem 119K TypeScript Persistent memory across agent sessions
12 Paperclip 116K TypeScript Open-source app for managing agents at work
13 Agent Reach 114K Python Lets agents read and search social platforms and video sites
14 Gemini CLI 109K TypeScript Google's open-source terminal agent
15 Archify 99K JavaScript Agent skill that turns ideas and code into interactive diagrams
16 RAGFlow 95K Go Retrieval engine that grew into context infrastructure for agents
17 OmniRoute 89K TypeScript Free AI gateway: one endpoint for many model providers
18 HyperFrames 88K TypeScript Open-source AI video editor driven by text
19 Crawl4AI 88K Python Web crawling and extraction built for agents
20 DeerFlow 86K Python ByteDance's long-horizon agent that researches, codes and creates

What the list says

The harness is the product now. All of the top three are not models or apps but harnesses: the layer that wraps a model with tools, memory, skills and rules (ECC, DeepSeek Harness, Hermes Agent). The model is becoming a replaceable part; the harness decides how good the agent feels.

Skills are a category of their own. Ponytail, Taste Skill and Archify are not agents at all. They are packaged know-how that you drop into an existing coding agent to change how it works. Three of them sit in the top 15.

Agents need eyes and memory. Five projects in the top 20 exist to give agents access to the outside world or a memory of the past: Firecrawl, Crawl4AI and Agent Reach for web data, claude-mem and Graphify for memory and knowledge. A model alone does not know what happened today or what you told it last week.

Python and TypeScript split the field. Across all 576 agent projects we track, 182 are written mainly in Python and 177 in TypeScript, far ahead of JavaScript (45), Rust (39) and Go (35).

Almost everything ships under a permissive license. 19 of the top 20 use MIT or Apache 2.0; Firecrawl is the notable AGPL exception.

Methodology

We collect GitHub repositories tagged with agent topics that have more than 500 stars, rank them by stars and refresh the numbers every day. Each project page shows its stars, forks, language, license, last commit and its 24-hour and 7-day change once history builds up. See the live ranking on the AI Agents page and the wider open-source AI ranking, and read how AI-Sovereign ranks projects.

Originally published on AI-Sovereign, the daily ranking of AI models, APIs, agents and open-source projects.

event_model_payload.headline: Building a Kubernetes CI/CD Pipeline Without Giving GitHub Actions a Kubeconfig
event_model_payload.summary:
Hi guys! In the previous part of this Kubernetes series, I discussed how I used MetalLB, Envoy Gateway, and Gateway API to give multiple applications one shared entry point.

At that stage, I could route a request to the frontend or backend. But there was another problem I didn't want to ignore. My onprem was considered alive.

Every time someone changes the application, who should be responsible for deploying that change to Kubernetes?

I could keep building an image locally, pushing it to a registry, and manually updating a Deployment. That works for the first few tests, it did wonderfully. However, it isn't the workflow I wanted for a platform that would host more applications.

1. The problem wasn't building a Docker image

I already had application containers and a Kubernetes cluster that could run them. The application also had ClusterIP Services and an HTTPRoute, so the traffic side had a place to go.

The problem was the release process.

I didn't want the normal deployment path to look like this:

Developer changes code
        |
        v
Build an image manually
        |
        v
Push image to registry
        |
        v
SSH to a server / access cluster
        |
        v
kubectl set image or kubectl apply
        |
        v
Hope the live state matches what is in Git

It has a lot of problem to be honest, like manually building image? okay

It has a lot of problem to be honest, like manually building image? okay, but the last step is the real problem. Once a person changes a live Deployment manually, the cluster might be ahead of, or simply different from, the version recorded in the repository.

That also makes rollback confusing. Am I reverting a Git commit? Reusing an older image? Or undoing someone's manual change? too much headache.

I wanted a simpler answer:

Application repositories produce artifacts. The GitOps repository declares desired versions. Argo CD owns reconciliation.

That is not a magical security boundary, by the way. A pipeline with permission to modify the GitOps repository can still influence what the cluster will deploy. But at least it doesn't need a direct Kubernetes API credential to perform the normal delivery path.

2. Three repositories, two kinds of responsibility

My application was split into a frontend and a backend. Each had its own source code, Dockerfile, and CI workflow. A separate cluster-management repository held the Kubernetes manifests.

The intended flow was:

FRONTEND SOURCE REPO                  BACKEND SOURCE REPO
       |                                     |
    push main                             push main
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
  GitHub Actions                        GitHub Actions
  test / build                          test / build
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
  GHCR frontend                         GHCR backend
  image: sha-FE                         image: sha-BE
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
 frontend-image.yaml                   backend-image.yaml
       \                                     /
        \                                   /
         +----- cluster-management --------+
                         |
                         v
                      Argo CD
                         |
                         v
                Kubernetes staging
               frontend + backend

There are two separate concerns here.

Component What it owns What it should not own in this design
Frontend GitHub Actions Frontend checks, image build, GHCR publish, frontend image reference update Direct Kubernetes deployment
Backend GitHub Actions Backend checks, image build, GHCR publish, backend image reference update Frontend image reference or direct Kubernetes deployment
GHCR The published container images Which release is currently desired in staging
cluster-management Git repository Kubernetes configuration and desired image references Building application images
Argo CD Reading desired state, rendering manifests, and reconciling Kubernetes Building source code or deciding an image tag on its own

Notice that the frontend release and backend release have different commit IDs.

That seems obvious when you look at the two source repositories. But it matters when you design the automation. There is no reason to pretend that both services share one source commit.

3. Why I didn't give GitHub Actions a kubeconfig

I considered the direct model first: build an image in CI, then run kubectl set image from the GitHub Actions runner.

It would have been relatively straightforward. But it also meant giving the CI workflow Kubernetes credentials and making the runner part of the cluster deployment control path.

I didn't want that as the default for this project.

Instead, the access model in my runbook separated three relationships:

GitHub Actions  ---> GHCR
    publishes the application image

GitHub Actions  ---> GitOps Git repository
    writes only the application's desired image reference

Argo CD         ---> GitOps Git repository
    reads the desired state

Argo CD         ---> Kubernetes API
    reconciles the workload

So no kubeconfig, Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, or Argo API token needed to be copied into the application CI workflow for the normal deployment process.

However, I want to be precise about what that does, and doesn't, improve.

Removing direct cluster credentials from CI reduces one class of exposure. It doesn't make a compromised CI runner harmless.

If a workflow has permission to modify the GitOps repository, an attacker who compromises that workflow could potentially change the desired state that Argo CD eventually applies. So the GitOps write credential is still a form of deployment authority, even if it doesn't directly access the Kubernetes API.

But there is another side to this.

Because my GitOps repository is private, Argo CD also needs GitHub credentials to read it. Ideally, those credentials should only have read access.

And since Argo CD is running inside my on-premises Kubernetes cluster, I also have to consider what happens if that environment gets compromised.

An attacker who gains access to Argo CD's repository credentials could potentially use them according to the permissions assigned to those credentials. If those permissions are broader than read-only, the impact could be greater. A compromise of Argo CD itself could also expose its Kubernetes access, which is a separate concern.

So technically, I'm not eliminating credential-related risks. I'm separating responsibilities and trying to limit what each component is allowed to do.

In my case, some repository access relied on temporary, account-linked SSH credentials because of restrictions on using deploy keys. That was an acceptable workaround for getting this non-production lab running, but I wouldn't consider it an ideal long-term permission model.

After all, a credential tied to a personal GitHub account could inherit permissions beyond what the workflow or Argo CD actually needs.
For a more mature implementation, I would prefer a dedicated GitHub App or similarly constrained identity, protected branches or approval gates as appropriate, and short-lived credentials where available. I would also limit Argo CD's destinations and resource permissions through an AppProject. None of these safeguards should be assumed to exist just because GitOps is installed.

That distinction is important to me. I don't want to call something "least privilege" merely because the YAML looks neat.

4. The real design problem: two CI pipelines editing the same file

Originally, I could describe frontend and backend images together inside the staging kustomization.yaml:

images:
  - name: ghcr.io/example/frontend
    newTag: sha-FRONTEND
  - name: ghcr.io/example/backend
    newTag: sha-BACKEND

That is a perfectly valid Kustomize pattern.

But if the frontend and backend pipelines both update the same file, a small timing problem appears:

12:00  Frontend CI checks out GitOps commit A
12:01  Backend CI checks out GitOps commit A
12:03  Frontend CI updates the shared YAML, pushes commit B
12:04  Backend CI tries to push its edit based on A
12:04  Push rejected: the remote branch changed

This doesn't automatically mean data loss. Git rejected the non-fast-forward push. But now the pipeline needs to reconcile its change with the remote branch.

I didn't want both pipelines repeatedly rewriting the same shared image list. So I split the ownership into two small patch files.

cluster-management/
  apps/
    marketplace/
      base/
        frontend/
          deployment.yaml
          service.yaml
        backend/
          deployment.yaml
          service.yaml
      overlays/
        staging/
          kustomization.yaml
          patches/
            frontend-image.yaml    <- frontend CI owns this
            backend-image.yaml     <- backend CI owns this
          routing/
            httproute.yaml

The base contains the reusable workload definitions. The overlay contains staging-specific configuration, including the selected images.

In the staging kustomization.yaml, the relevant part is:

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

namespace: demo-staging

resources:
  - ../../base

patches:
  - path: patches/frontend-image.yaml
  - path: patches/backend-image.yaml

These are simplified examples. A real overlay may also include ConfigMaps, NetworkPolicies, routes, and other resources, which need to be declared in the appropriate base or overlay.

The frontend's patch can be as small as:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: frontend
          image: ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-FRONTEND_COMMIT

The backend has a separate file with its own Deployment, container name, and image.

One technical detail here: a strategic-merge patch identifies the container entry by its name. That name must match the actual container name in the base Deployment. I would validate the rendered manifest rather than assume the patch changed the right thing.

Splitting the files does not make concurrent Git pushes automatically safe. It just means that when one runner rebases on top of the other's commit, the edits are usually independent and easier to merge.

5. The image tag is a release record, not latest

I wanted the deployed image reference to point to a specific source revision.

Each source workflow publishes an image tagged with its own commit SHA:

ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-
ghcr.io/example/backend:sha-

So staging might contain this combination:

Frontend = sha-a1b2c3...
Backend  = sha-d4e5f6...

The backend does not need to restart just because the frontend changed. Their Deployment Pod templates change independently.

A commit-based tag is also easier to trace than latest. However, a tag is still a mutable registry reference unless the registry prevents overwrites. For stronger artifact immutability, image digests such as @sha256:... are preferable. The source design used SHA-based tags; it should not be described as having guaranteed digest-pinned deployments.

There is another limitation: the frontend in this project was built with Vite, so environment values such as the API base URL may be embedded during npm run build. Those VITE_* build arguments are not a substitute for Kubernetes runtime Secrets. I have to validate the target environment when building an artifact for staging.

6. What the pipeline actually needs to do

I don't think the most useful article is one that pastes 300 lines of GitHub Actions YAML without explaining anything.

The important sequence is:

  1. Run the source repository's checks.
  2. Build and publish the appropriate image to GHCR.
  3. Check out the GitOps repository with Git write permission.
  4. Update only the component's image patch.
  5. Render Kustomize and confirm the intended image appears.
  6. Commit and push that desired-state change, handling a concurrent push safely.
  7. Let Argo CD detect and reconcile the new Git revision.

For the GHCR part, the workflow needs only the permissions appropriate for publishing the package. A representative excerpt is:

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

# In a build job after source checkout and tests:
# - authenticate to ghcr.io with the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN
# - build for the intended node architecture
# - push ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-${{ github.sha }}

That is a workflow sketch, not a complete GitHub Actions file. GitHub's official container-publishing documentation describes GITHUB_TOKEN with packages: write for this use case.

I deliberately kept the GitOps write key separate from the GHCR authentication. The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN is normally scoped to the repository running the workflow; it is not automatically authorized to write to an unrelated private GitOps repository.

Validate the change before committing it

Before pushing a new image reference, I would render the overlay:

cd cluster-management

kubectl kustomize apps/marketplace/overlays/staging \
  > /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

test -s /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

grep -n 'image:' /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

I would then confirm that both rendered Deployments contain the intended image references. That also catches mistakes in patch names, paths, and Kustomize structure before Argo CD sees the commit.

This test is static validation. It does not prove that Kubernetes pulled the image, started a Pod, or served a request.

What about simultaneous GitOps updates?

GitHub Actions' concurrency setting can serialize jobs or runs within one repository. But my frontend and backend workflows were in different repositories, so a concurrency group in the frontend repository does not coordinate with the backend repository's group.

A simplified push strategy is:

# Run from the GitOps checkout after committing a component patch.
# This assumes a clean commit that can be safely rebased.

for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  git fetch origin main
  git rebase origin/main || {
    echo 'Rebase conflict: stop and investigate.' >&2
    exit 1
  }

  if git push origin HEAD:main; then
    echo 'GitOps update pushed.'
    break
  fi

  if [ "$attempt" -eq 5 ]; then
    echo 'GitOps push still failing after retries.' >&2
    exit 1
  fi

done

Why not just force-push? Because force-pushing from a CI pipeline risks overwriting the other component's deployment update. In the normal case, separate patch files let Git rebase independent commits cleanly. A genuine rebase conflict should stop the pipeline rather than be hidden.

This is still only one approach. A pull request into a protected GitOps branch would offer stronger review and audit gates, at the cost of another approval step. For staging, the source runbook intentionally favored direct automation.

7. Argo CD owns the cluster-facing part

For this project, Argo CD itself was managed with Helm. That was a platform installation decision. The application's desired state was managed with Kustomize and watched by an Argo CD Application.

The relationship was:

Helm: install/manage Argo CD itself
                  |
                  v
Argo CD Application: watch the GitOps source
                  |
                  v
Kustomize: render staging resources
                  |
                  v
Kubernetes: reconcile Deployments and Services

Argo CD natively supports Kustomize sources. The application points at the desired repository path; I didn't need a separate kubectl apply -k command in the application pipeline.

A reduced Application example would look like this:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: demo-staging
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: staging
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/cluster-management.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/marketplace/overlays/staging
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: demo-staging
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      enabled: true
      selfHeal: true
      prune: false

That example assumes the AppProject, repository credentials, namespace, and required RBAC already exist. A private repository also needs appropriate credentials. The repoURL shown here is illustrative, not a live repository.

There are two Argo CD settings I didn't want to treat casually:

  • selfHeal allows Argo CD to reconcile certain live-cluster drift back toward Git's desired state.
  • prune allows deletion of resources that are no longer present in the desired state when automated pruning is enabled.

I preferred starting with manual sync and no automatic pruning, inspecting the diff, then introducing automated sync and self-healing only after the repository accurately represented the existing application. Pruning was a later, separate decision.

That order matters. Automatically reconciling an incomplete or incorrect Git repository can break an application very efficiently.

One more point: Synced is about the relationship between the desired and live resource state. Healthy is a separate assessment. Neither one alone proves that the application's user-facing endpoint works correctly.

8. What I would verify end to end

My runbooks contain detailed acceptance procedures, including a frontend test before activating the backend workflow. They don't contain complete captured logs for every step, so I will describe the validation procedure and expected outcome, not invent a passed test transcript.

Check Command or location What it proves if successful
Source validation GitHub Actions job logs The relevant checks completed
Image published GHCR package and tag An image reference exists in the registry
Desired state updated GitOps repository commit and patch diff CI wrote the intended source SHA into Git
Manifests render kubectl kustomize The selected overlay produces valid YAML and intended image references
Argo has accepted source kubectl get application -n argocd Argo CD sees the desired revision and reports sync/health status
Pod template updated kubectl get deployment -o jsonpath=... The workload spec contains the new image reference
Rollout completes kubectl rollout status The Deployment rollout reached Kubernetes' completion criteria
App responds App-specific HTTP health/smoke tests The tested endpoint responded through the selected route

For example, in an example namespace:

kubectl get application demo-staging -n argocd

kubectl get deployment frontend -n demo-staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}'

kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend \
  -n demo-staging --timeout=180s

Then I would repeat the test with the backend, checking that a backend-only change does not modify the frontend's desired image reference.

There is also a useful negative test: deliberately modify a managed Deployment in the cluster only in a disposable test environment, and check whether self-healing restores the value declared in Git. That's a controlled test of reconciliation, not a suggested operating habit.

The important distinction is that a successful build doesn't mean a successful release. Publishing an image is not the same as writing desired state, and writing desired state is not the same as confirming a healthy application.

9. Two problems that belong in the GitOps story

So while creating it, i have noted some issues that appeared when Argo CD took ownership of existing resources and private repositories.

The first was an application that repeatedly appeared OutOfSync. When developing this, I had included a system-managed metadata.generation value in a Deployment manifest. That value is maintained by Kubernetes rather than being application desired configuration. My note records removing it from the declarative manifest. I would check the live diff and refresh result before treating that as a universally proven root cause for any OutOfSync condition.

The second was a private repository access problem. So I recorded an SSH-agent-related error while Argo CD tried to resolve a Git revision. A repository Secret had also been scoped to a particular Argo CD project, while other Applications needed the same repository. That was a reasonable permission-scope hypothesis to investigate, not enough evidence by itself to say that every SSH_AUTH_SOCK error is caused by project scoping.

These two examples gave me a practical reminder: GitOps introduces its own layer of configuration and debugging. The source revision, rendered manifest, repository credential, AppProject, and live Kubernetes object all need to be inspected separately.

10. The trade-offs I would keep visible

This architecture improved clarity, but I wouldn't call it perfect.

Direct-to-main staging: The workflow I created deploys staging candidates from main. There was no pre-merge review gate in that model. A failing CI job stops that image from becoming the next desired version, but it doesn't remove the bad commit from the source branch.

Temporary Git credentials: I used a dedicated SSH key associated with a personal GitHub account. That should be treated as technical debt, with access narrowed and credentials rotated when an organization-approved service identity is available.

Two independent source repositories: A separate image patch per component reduced file contention, but the pipelines still shared one GitOps branch. A push/rebase retry or an approved merge workflow was needed to handle concurrency.

Tags versus digests: SHA-based tags improved traceability. They did not by themselves prove registry immutability.

Database migrations: I intentionally kept automatic database migration out of the first application-image workflow. Database schema changes need their own compatibility, execution, and recovery strategy. A separate migration Job can be introduced later once that contract is clear.

Rollbacks: Reverting a GitOps image change can trigger Argo CD to redeploy an earlier application image. That does not automatically undo a database migration or guarantee compatibility with external dependencies.

11. What I learned

For me, the interesting part wasn't that GitHub Actions could run a Docker build. That's the easy part, and of course that the world of devops is huge.

The more useful decision was defining who was allowed to change what.

GitHub Actions could produce a frontend or backend image and propose the intended version through Git. Argo CD was responsible for translating that version into a Kubernetes deployment. And the two source repositories needed separate release records so one team's change wouldn't accidentally replace another component's desired version.

I would still tighten the credentials and add stronger release gates before applying this model to more sensitive environments. But for this non-production platform, separating build, desired state, and reconciliation gave me a structure I could reason about.

The next article will move from who is allowed to deploy to which network connections workloads are allowed to receive: testing Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rather than assuming namespace separation provides isolation.

References

  • Argo CD: Automated Sync Policy
  • Argo CD: Kustomize
  • GitHub: Publishing Docker Images
  • GitHub: Control Workflow Concurrency
  • GitHub Actions: Secure Use Reference

event_model_payload.headline: From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline
event_model_payload.summary:
Quick answer: Replace FTP deploys with Git-based atomic releases: build in CI, upload to a new timestamped release directory, symlink shared storage and .env, run migrations, then switch a "current" symlink. Move crontab entries one by one into Laravel's scheduler with locks and logging. Keep the old path working until each piece is proven.

In Part 4 we moved auth and sessions without logging anyone out. The next thing that tends to break legacy modernization is not the code. It is how the code reaches the server. If production is "whatever someone last uploaded with FileZilla", you cannot reason about what is running, you cannot roll back, and the new Laravel modules from Parts 1–3 end up deployed the same fragile way.

I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi, and at Loop Origin we inherit a lot of these apps. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked the commands against the Deployer, GitHub Actions and Laravel scheduler documentation.

📚 Series Navigation — Modernizing Legacy PHP Without a Rewrite

  • Part 1: Strangler Fig for Legacy PHP: Run Old and New Side by Side
  • Part 2: Untangling Dependency Cycles in a Modular Laravel Monolith
  • Part 3: Upgrading Old PHP Versions Safely With Rector and CI
  • Part 4: Replacing Legacy Auth & Sessions Without Logging Everyone Out
  • Part 5 (This Post): From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline
  • Part 6: Decommissioning the Old App: Shadow Traffic, Flags & Final Cutover

Related earlier posts: Backups That Never Restored: Automated Restore Drills · Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Laravel & Node.js SaaS

Step 0: find out what production actually is

Before changing anything, I take an inventory. Production often differs from any repository you were given.

# On the server, read-only
cd /var/www/legacy-app
find . -type f -newer composer.json -not -path "./storage/*" | head -50   # files edited after last known deploy
crontab -l -u www-data > ~/cron-inventory.txt
sudo ls /etc/cron.d/ >> ~/cron-inventory.txt
php -v; php -m > ~/php-modules.txt
~~~{% endraw %}

Then I download a full copy of the web root and diff it against the repository. Every difference is either a hotfix that never got committed (commit it) or junk like {% raw %}`index_old2.php`{% endraw %} (note it and remove it later). Uploaded user files and generated caches get listed separately; they must never live inside the code directory again.

## FTP deploys vs a real pipeline

| Concern | FTP / manual upload | Atomic release pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| What is running? | Unknown mix of files | One Git commit SHA per release |
| Half-uploaded state | Yes, for minutes | No, symlink switch is instant |
| Rollback | Re-upload old files from memory | Point symlink to previous release |
| Dependencies | Vendor folder uploaded by hand | {% raw %}`composer install --no-dev`{% endraw %} in CI |
| Secrets | Edited live in config.php | Shared .env outside releases |
| Audit trail | None | CI run, commit, who approved |

## The release directory layout

This is the layout I use on plain VPS servers. It works for old procedural PHP and Laravel alike.{% raw %}

~~~text
/var/www/app/
  current -> releases/20261122-0715-a1b2c3d
  releases/
    20261121-1930-9f8e7d6/
    20261122-0715-a1b2c3d/
  shared/
    .env
    storage/
    public/uploads/
~~~{% endraw %}

Each release is a fresh checkout. Shared folders and the env file are symlinked into it. Nginx points at {% raw %}`/var/www/app/current/public`{% endraw %}, and PHP-FPM is reloaded after the switch so OPcache drops stale paths.

## The CI pipeline

I build artifacts in CI, not on the server. Here is a trimmed GitHub Actions workflow:{% raw %}

~~~yaml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # requires manual approval in repo settings
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.3' }
      - run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader
      - run: vendor/bin/phpunit --testsuite=smoke
      - run: tar czf release.tgz --exclude=.git --exclude=tests .
      - name: Upload and activate
        env:
          SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}
        run: ./deploy/activate.sh release.tgz "$GITHUB_SHA"
~~~{% endraw %}

The {% raw %}`activate.sh`{% endraw %} script is short and boring on purpose:{% raw %}

~~~bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
REL="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)-$(echo "$2" | cut -c1-7)"
ssh deploy@app "mkdir -p /var/www/app/releases/$REL"
scp "$1" deploy@app:/tmp/release.tgz
ssh deploy@app bash -s <<EOF
set -e
cd /var/www/app/releases/$REL && tar xzf /tmp/release.tgz
ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/.env .env
rm -rf storage && ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/storage storage
php artisan migrate --force
php artisan config:cache && php artisan route:cache
ln -sfn /var/www/app/releases/$REL /var/www/app/current
sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm
ls -1dt /var/www/app/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs rm -rf   # keep 5
EOF
~~~{% endraw %}

Two cautions. Migrations run before the switch, so they must be backward compatible with the release still serving traffic; that is the expand-and-contract pattern from my zero-downtime migrations post. And keep the deploy user's sudo rights limited to reloading PHP-FPM, nothing else. If you would rather use a tool, Deployer does the same release/symlink dance with less shell.

## Rollback is one command{% raw %}

~~~bash
ssh deploy@app 'cd /var/www/app && PREV=$(ls -1dt releases/* | sed -n 2p) && ln -sfn "$PWD/$PREV" current && sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm'
~~~

Rollback does not undo database migrations. That is another reason to keep migrations additive until the old code is gone.

## Taming the crontab

Old apps hide business logic in cron: invoice emails at 2 a.m., a CSV import every 10 minutes, a cleanup script that nobody dares touch. My rule is to move them one at a time into Laravel's scheduler, wrapping the old script first rather than rewriting it.{% raw %}

~~~php
// routes/console.php (Laravel 11+)
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::exec('php /var/www/app/current/legacy/cron/send_invoices.php')
    ->dailyAt('02:00')
    ->timezone('Asia/Karachi')
    ->withoutOverlapping(30)
    ->onOneServer()
    ->appendOutputTo(storage_path('logs/cron-send-invoices.log'))
    ->onFailure(fn () => report(new RuntimeException('send_invoices failed')));
~~~{% endraw %}

Then the crontab shrinks to a single line, {% raw %}`* * * * * php /var/www/app/current/artisan schedule:run`{% endraw %}. For each migrated job I disable the old crontab line in the same change, never before and never after, so it cannot run twice or not at all. {% raw %}`withoutOverlapping`{% endraw %} fixes the classic bug where a slow import starts again before the last one finished. Later, each wrapped script can be rewritten as a proper command or queued job when someone actually needs to change it.

## Diagnostic checklist

- [ ] Production web root diffed against Git; hotfixes committed
- [ ] Uploads, logs and caches moved to a shared directory outside releases
- [ ] Secrets in a shared .env, not in committed config files
- [ ] CI builds the artifact and runs at least a smoke test suite
- [ ] Releases are timestamped directories with a {% raw %}`current`{% endraw %} symlink
- [ ] PHP-FPM is reloaded after each switch
- [ ] Rollback tested on staging this month
- [ ] Crontab reduced to {% raw %}`schedule:run`{% endraw %}, every job has locking and logs
- [ ] FTP access disabled once the pipeline is proven

## FAQ

### Can I do this on shared hosting without SSH?
Partly. Many hosts now offer SSH or Git deploy. If yours has neither, that is a strong reason to move to a small VPS; atomic releases depend on symlinks and shell access.

### What about apps that write files into the code directory?
Find every write path first, from the inventory step, and point them at {% raw %}`shared/`{% endraw %}. Until that is done, atomic releases will lose user data on each deploy.

### Do I need Docker for this?
No. Containers are a fine next step, but release directories plus CI give you most of the safety with far less change to an old app.

### How do I handle the first deploy safely?
Deploy the pipeline's first release to a new path, point a staging hostname at it, compare behaviour, then switch Nginx for production. Keep the old document root intact for a week.

### What if a cron job must never run twice?
Use `withoutOverlapping` with a reasonable expiry, `onOneServer` when you have more than one app server, and make the script itself idempotent where you can.

### When can I turn off FTP?
After two or three clean pipeline deploys and one tested rollback. Remove the FTP accounts rather than just changing passwords.

## What's next

Part 6, the finale, covers decommissioning the old app: shadow traffic, feature flags and the final cutover. If you would like help setting up deploys and servers for an inherited app, this is the [server setup and maintenance](https://looporigin.com/services/server-setup-maintenance?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=ftp-deploys-cron-to-pipeline) work we do at Loop Origin, and our [pricing page](https://looporigin.com/pricing?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=ftp-deploys-cron-to-pipeline) shows how we scope it. For the Laravel side of the modernization, see our [Laravel development services](https://looporigin.com/services/laravel-development?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=ftp-deploys-cron-to-pipeline).

---

### Follow & Connect

- **Website:** [Loop Origin](https://looporigin.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=ftp-deploys-cron-to-pipeline)
- **Watch on YouTube:** [Resume Boost AI](https://www.youtube.com/@resume-boost-ai) · [PixelValut](https://www.youtube.com/@pixel-valut) · [Daily AI News By Ali](https://www.youtube.com/@AIDailyNewsByAli)

event_model_payload.headline: Uninstalling cleanly: registry, configs, drivers — the order that works
event_model_payload.summary:
Uninstalling cleanly: registry, configs, drivers — the order that works

Developer tooling is worst: PATH fragments, global package directories, kernel drivers, per-user configs — uninstallers claim maybe half.

Written in the order we actually hit the problems, so the fixes land in context.

Cleanup order that does not backfire

  1. Run the vendor uninstaller first — let it tear down what it knows about.

  2. Environment variables — dead PATH entries and custom *_HOME variables.

  3. User data — %APPDATA%, %LOCALAPPDATA%, ~/.config trees for the vendor or tool name.

  4. Services and drivers — still relevant for VM, VPN, and virtual-disk tooling:

Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.DisplayName -match 'ToolName'}
  1. Registry last — HKLM\Software and HKCU\Software vendor keys. Export before deleting anything you are not sure about.

Version swaps specifically

  • Back up config directories before downgrading — format migrations are usually one-way.

  • Re-check file associations after the swap; the old path will exist until someone updates it.

  • With a portable copy and an installer coexisting, identify which one owns double-click before debugging "my change did not take".

When deep cleaning is worth it

Routine tool swap → uninstaller plus PATH cleanup is usually enough.

Drivers, certificates, system services, VPN clients → full checklist plus reboot verification.

A machine with years of stacked versions → repairing the shared runtime (VC++ redist, .NET) often beats another registry pass.

Related resource

For the "can I re-verify this later" half of the workflow I keep GitVaults (https://gitvaults.com) open: every entry carries the upstream link, file size, and SHA-256, with a cloud mirror as the reachability fallback.

maotoumao musicfreedesktop 0 0 8 → https://gitvaults.com/download/2025/10/26/maotoumao-musicfreedesktop-0-0-8/en

That page puts version, architecture, and digest on one screen — download, compare the hash, then install. The catalog has another hundred-plus entries in the same format if you need neighbors.

Caveat

This is what works in our environment; your constraints may differ. If you have a sturdier sequence, corrections are welcome in the comments.

event_model_payload.headline: Build a CI/CD Pipeline for the 2048 Game using AWS CodePipeline, ECS and ECR
event_model_payload.summary:
Overview

Manual deployments do not scale. Each release requires building an image, tagging it, pushing it to a registry and updating a running service, and each step is a chance for human error.

This article documents a complete continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline on AWS. A containerized web application (the 2048 game, served by Nginx) is built, versioned and deployed automatically whenever code is pushed to GitHub.

The project is based on the "CI/CD Pipeline for the 2048 Game" lab from Tech With Lucy's 5 Advanced AWS Cloud Projects course. The implementation notes, code samples and recommendations below are my own.
Effort Approximately 2-3 hours
Estimated cost About $1 or less, provided resources are cleaned up
Compute model Serverless containers (AWS Fargate)

Objectives

  • Package the application as a Docker image
  • Store versioned images in a private registry (Amazon ECR)
  • Run the workload on Amazon ECS with the Fargate launch type
  • Trigger build and deployment automatically on every push to main
  • Apply least-privilege access between services using IAM

Architecture

The workflow is as follows:

  1. A developer pushes code to the GitHub repository.
  2. The push triggers AWS CodePipeline.
  3. AWS CodeBuild retrieves the code, builds the Docker image and tags it.
  4. The image is pushed to Amazon ECR.
  5. CodePipeline updates the ECS service. A new task starts with the new image and replaces the old task.

Services and responsibilities

Service Responsibility
AWS CodePipeline Orchestrates the source, build and deploy stages
AWS CodeBuild Builds the Docker image and pushes it to ECR
Amazon ECR Private container registry
Amazon ECS (Fargate) Runs and manages the container
Amazon S3 Stores build artifacts passed between stages
AWS IAM Controls access for each service

Prerequisites

  • An AWS account and an IAM user with programmatic access
  • Docker, Git and the AWS CLI installed and configured (aws configure)
  • A GitHub account

If you prefer not to install tools locally, a small EC2 instance accessed over SSH works equally well.

Implementation

1. Containerize the application

The application consists of static files, so a lightweight Nginx image is sufficient.

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

Validate locally before involving AWS:

docker build -t 2048-game .
docker run -p 8080:80 2048-game

2. Publish the first image to ECR

ECS requires an existing image before the service can start, so the first image is pushed manually.

aws ecr create-repository --repository-name 2048-game-repo --region <REGION>

aws ecr get-login-password --region <REGION> \
  | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.<REGION>.amazonaws.com

docker tag 2048-game:latest <ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.<REGION>.amazonaws.com/2048-game-repo:latest
docker push <ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.<REGION>.amazonaws.com/2048-game-repo:latest

3. Deploy to ECS Fargate

  1. Create an ECS cluster using the Fargate infrastructure.
  2. Register a task definition with a container named 2048-container, the ECR image URI and port 80.
  3. Create a service with one task, the default VPC and subnets, a public IP, and a security group allowing inbound HTTP (port 80).

Opening the task's public IP in a browser confirms that the manual deployment works. This gives a known-good baseline before automation is added.

4. Create the source repository

Push the project, including the Dockerfile and buildspec.yml, to a new GitHub repository on the main branch. This repository becomes the pipeline's source.

5. Configure CodeBuild (continuous integration)

CodeBuild reads its instructions from buildspec.yml:

version: 0.2

phases:
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - aws ecr get-login-password --region $AWS_DEFAULT_REGION | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com
      - REPOSITORY_URI=$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.amazonaws.com/$IMAGE_REPO_NAME
  build:
    commands:
      - docker build -t $REPOSITORY_URI:latest .
  post_build:
    commands:
      - docker push $REPOSITORY_URI:latest
      - printf '[{"name":"%s","imageUri":"%s"}]' $CONTAINER_NAME $REPOSITORY_URI:latest > imagedefinitions.json

artifacts:
  files:
    - imagedefinitions.json

The generated imagedefinitions.json maps the container name to the new image and is consumed by the deploy stage.

Supporting configuration:

  • IAM service role: permissions to push to ECR, write artifacts to S3, write logs, and update the ECS service
  • S3 bucket: a globally unique bucket for build artifacts
  • Build project: connected to the GitHub repository, using the buildspec file and the environment variables AWS_ACCOUNT_ID, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, IMAGE_REPO_NAME and CONTAINER_NAME
  • Privileged mode: must be enabled, as Docker builds require it

Run a manual build first. A successful build produces a new image in ECR and imagedefinitions.json in S3.

6. Configure CodePipeline (continuous deployment)

Create a pipeline with three stages:

Stage Provider Configuration
Source GitHub Repository, branch main
Build AWS CodeBuild The build project from the previous step
Deploy Amazon ECS Cluster, service and imagedefinitions.json

The pipeline runs automatically after creation and again on every push.

Validation

To verify the full workflow, the page heading was changed from 2048 to 2048 by :

git add .
git commit -m "Update game title"
git push origin main

CodePipeline started within moments of the push. Source, Build and Deploy completed without intervention, and once the new ECS task was running, the updated title was visible at the service's public IP.

During the Deploy stage, ECS starts a new task with the new image, then stops the old one, so the application stays available throughout.

Note that each new Fargate task receives a new public IP. For a stable endpoint, place an Application Load Balancer in front of the service.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Resolution
Docker build fails in CodeBuild Privileged mode disabled Enable Privileged mode
Push to ECR denied Missing registry permissions Add ECR push permissions to the build role
Deploy stage fails Container name mismatch Make CONTAINER_NAME match the task definition exactly
Application unreachable Port 80 blocked or no public IP Update the security group and enable public IP
Task exits immediately Image or tag missing in ECR Verify the image URI and tag

Security recommendations

  • Grant each IAM role only the permissions it needs, scoped to specific resources, rather than broad full-access policies.
  • Treat access keys as secrets. Never post them in chats, screenshots or repositories. If a key is exposed, deactivate and delete it in IAM immediately and issue a new one.
  • Prefer short-lived credentials and IAM roles over long-lived access keys where possible.

Cost management and clean-up

Costs are low, but resources keep billing until removed. After testing, delete:

  1. The CodePipeline pipeline
  2. The CodeBuild project
  3. The ECS service and cluster
  4. The ECR repository
  5. The S3 artifact bucket
  6. IAM roles, policies and access keys created for the project
  7. Any EC2 instance used to run commands

Key takeaways

  • Automating build and deployment makes releases faster, repeatable and less error-prone.
  • Fargate removes the need to manage servers for container workloads.
  • Most failures trace back to IAM permissions, Privileged mode, or a mismatched container name, so check these first.

Recommended next steps

  • Add an automated test stage (unit tests or health checks) before deployment
  • Put an Application Load Balancer and HTTPS in front of the service
  • Add monitoring and alarms with Amazon CloudWatch
  • Define the infrastructure as code with Terraform or AWS CloudFormation

Thanks for reading. If you have questions or improvements, please share them in the comments.

event_model_payload.headline: Building Sentinel: Uptime Monitoring with Signed Reports and Quorum
event_model_payload.summary:
The problem with a single uptime checker

Most uptime monitors are one process making one HTTP request from one location. That is enough to catch most outages, but it has two blind spots: the checker itself can go down, and regional network problems look like global outages. If my checker is in us-east and an ISP there has a routing issue, I could page my team at 3 AM for a problem that only a small share of users can see.

I built Sentinel to explore whether a small network of independent validator nodes, each checking the same target from a different region and each signing its report, could reach a verdict by majority agreement and avoid false alarms from single-region noise. Here is what I learned.

How it works 

  node-us-east  --+
  node-eu-west  --+   signed reports    +-----------------------+
  node-ap-south --+------------------->  |          HUB          |
  node-us-west  --+   POST /reports     |  - validates sig      |
                                         |  - aggregates window  |
                                         |  - runs quorum        |
                                         |  - stores verdict     |
                                         |  - fires alerts       |
                                         +-----------------------+
                                                    |
                                               PostgreSQL

One report's lifecycle, end to end:

  1. Check (node/src/validator-node.ts). On every tick the node fetches its assignments from the hub, runs HttpHealthChecker.check(url, timeoutMs), and gets back { status, httpStatus, latencyMs, error }.

  2. Build and sign (node/src/report-builder.ts, shared/crypto.ts). A ReportBuilder assembles the payload, including the current window_id and a random UUID nonce. signReport() then serializes the payload in a fixed key order and signs it with the node's Ed25519 private key using Node's built-in crypto module.

  3. Ingest (hub/src/ingestion/report-ingestion-service.ts). The hub passes the signed report through a Chain of Responsibility of five validators: schema check, signature check, clock-skew check, replay-guard check, rate-limit check. Only then does it write to Postgres.

  4. Aggregate (hub/src/consensus/window-aggregator.ts). A background loop runs every second. Time is split into 30-second windows, and the window_id is the current time divided by the window length, rounded down, so every node computes the same integer for the same period. A window closes when all live nodes have reported or the deadline has passed. The hub then gathers that window's reports and passes them to ConsensusEngine.decide().

  5. Verdict and alert (hub/src/consensus/, hub/src/alerts/). The engine runs the configured strategy, stores the verdict, and feeds it to a TargetStateMachine. When the state machine sees enough consecutive verdicts of a new status, it fires an alert through an Observer chain.

Key design decisions

1. Quorum instead of trusting one node

Problem: a single node can be wrong because of its network path, its region's ISP, or the node process itself.

Decision: a verdict needs at least quorumK reports, and the winning status must hold a strict majority of the reports received.

// hub/src/consensus/simple-quorum-strategy.ts
const quorumMet = reports.length >= context.quorumK;
const hasMajority = agreeing.length > reports.length / 2;

Trade-off: with N nodes I set quorumK to floor(N/2) + 1, which is 2 for 3 nodes. If at most f nodes are faulty and N >= 2f + 1, honest nodes outnumber faulty ones, so a majority of the reports still reflects the truth. With 3 nodes, the system tolerates 1 faulty node. This is not full Byzantine fault tolerance: it assumes the faulty nodes are a minority. If a majority lie, the verdict will be wrong.

2. Signatures prove identity, not truth

Problem: I needed to know that a report came from a registered node and was not tampered with in transit.

Decision: every report is signed with the node's Ed25519 private key over a canonical payload. The hub verifies the signature against the registered public key before accepting the report.

// shared/canonical.ts
const PAYLOAD_KEYS = [
  'node_id', 'target_id', 'window_id', 'timestamp', 'nonce', 'status',
  'http_status', 'latency_ms', 'error'
] as const satisfies readonly (keyof ReportPayload)[];

export function canonicalReportBytes(payload: ReportPayload): Buffer {
  const ordered: Record<string, string | number | null> = {};
  for (const key of PAYLOAD_KEYS) ordered[key] = payload[key];
  return Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(ordered), 'utf8');
}

Trade-off: a signature only proves who sent the report, not that the result is accurate. A node running with FAULT_MODE=lie signs a correctly formed report with a flipped status. The quorum is what handles that: if one node lies and the rest agree, the verdict follows the majority.

3. INCONCLUSIVE instead of guessing

Problem: if only 1 of 3 nodes reports before the window deadline, what verdict should the hub emit?

Decision: if reports.length < quorumK, the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE. No alert fires and no state transition occurs.

Trade-off: this is an explicit "I don't know" rather than a guess. A test covers it:

// hub/src/consensus/window-aggregator.test.ts
it('waits before deadline, then closes partial reports with an inconclusive verdict', async () => {
  const nodes = [node('n1','ACTIVE'), node('n2','ACTIVE'), node('n3','ACTIVE')];
  expect((await build(nodes,[report('n1')],34_000).closeIfReady(target,'0')).closed).toBe(false);
  const result = await build(nodes,[report('n1')],35_000).closeIfReady(target,'0');
  expect(result.closed).toBe(true);
  expect(result.verdict?.status).toBe('INCONCLUSIVE');
});

The cost is that when the hub cannot collect enough reports, the target looks "unknown" instead of triggering an alert. I chose that over a wrong alarm.

4. Region-aware quorum to avoid single-region false DOWN

Problem: if the us-east nodes see DOWN but eu-west and ap-south see UP, the target is probably fine globally and us-east has a routing problem.

Decision: the region-aware strategy applies the simple majority check and adds one rule: if the verdict would be DOWN but fewer than requiredRegions distinct regions agree, it becomes DEGRADED.

// hub/src/consensus/region-aware-quorum-strategy.ts
decide(reports: VerifiedReport[], context: ConsensusContext): Verdict {
  const verdict = majorityVerdict(reports, context, this.name);
  if (verdict.status !== 'DOWN' || verdict.regionsAgreeing >= context.requiredRegions) return verdict;
  return { ...verdict, status: 'DEGRADED', reason: 'single-region failure' };
}

Trade-off: strategies are chosen per target. A simple internal service may not need region awareness, while a globally used API probably does. A ConsensusStrategyFactory lets me register a new strategy without modifying the engine.

5. Windowed aggregation and heartbeat-based failure detection

Problem: nodes check on their own schedule, and the hub needs to know when a period's results are in without waiting forever.

Decision: the aggregator closes a window when all live nodes have reported, or when the deadline (window end plus a grace period) has passed. Node liveness is tracked through heartbeats and a State pattern (ActiveState, SuspectState, DeadState). Dead nodes are excluded from the expected reporters, so they do not stall aggregation.

Trade-off: dead nodes shrink the effective quorum. The aggregator caps quorumK at min(target.quorumK, live_nodes). If most nodes die, the system is left with a dangerously small quorum. I list this under limitations below.

6. Replay protection and idempotent ingestion

Problem: a node may retry a failed POST, and the hub could see the same report twice.

Decision: two guards in sequence. First, an in-memory nonce check catches exact replays. Second, a window-uniqueness check on node_id:target_id:window_id stops a node from submitting a second report for the same window even with a fresh nonce. Postgres UNIQUE constraints back both as the durable layer. A 409 response is treated as success by the node.

// hub/src/ingestion/validators.ts
async claim(node: string, nonce: string, target: string, window: string): Promise<boolean> {
  const nonceKey = `${node}:${nonce}`, windowKey = `${node}:${target}:${window}`;
  if (this.nonces.has(nonceKey) || this.windows.has(windowKey)) return false;
  this.nonces.add(nonceKey); this.windows.add(windowKey); return true;
}

Trade-off: InMemoryReplayGuard does not survive a hub restart. After a restart, a replay is only caught when the Postgres constraint rejects the insert. Running multiple hub replicas would need a shared store such as Redis for the in-memory layer.

7. Hysteresis to prevent alert flapping

Problem: a target that alternates between UP and DOWN on every window would generate a storm of alerts.

Decision: TargetStateMachine requires hysteresisCount (default 2) consecutive verdicts of a new status before it triggers a transition. An INCONCLUSIVE verdict resets the counter without triggering anything.

// hub/src/alerts/target-state-machine.ts
this.consecutive = this.candidate === verdict.status ? this.consecutive + 1 : 1;
this.candidate = verdict.status;
if (this.consecutive < this.hysteresisCount) return undefined;

Trade-off: alerts are delayed by hysteresisCount windows (by default 2 x 30s = 60s) in exchange for filtering out transient noise. It is a trade between alert latency and false positives.

Design patterns in the code

Node liveness: State (shared/liveness.ts). ActiveState, SuspectState and DeadState each own their transition logic and answer countsTowardQuorum(), so the aggregator never inspects a status string directly.

// shared/liveness.ts
export class ActiveState implements NodeLivenessState {
  readonly status = 'ACTIVE' as const;
  afterMissedHeartbeat(age: number, suspect: number, dead: number): NodeLivenessState {
    return age >= dead ? new DeadState() : age >= suspect ? new SuspectState() : this;
  }
  countsTowardQuorum(): boolean { return true; }
}

Circuit breaker: State (hub/src/alerts/webhook-circuit-breaker.ts). ClosedState, OpenState and HalfOpenState hold the retry timestamp and decide whether to allow a probe, so there is no central if (state === 'Open') block.

Validation: Chain of Responsibility (hub/src/ingestion/report-validator.ts). BaseReportValidator.validate() calls check() and then delegates to next. A test proves the short-circuit: the signature validator's verify throws 'must not run' if the schema check fails first.

Repository observability: Decorator (hub/src/ingestion/report-repository-decorators.ts). LoggingReportRepository and MetricsReportRepository wrap the real repository and add structured logging and counters without touching the core insert logic.

Testing with fault injection

Any node process can run in one of three fault modes through FAULT_MODE:

// node/src/validator-node.ts
if (this.faultMode === 'offline') continue;
if (this.faultMode === 'slow') await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, target.timeoutMs * 2));
if (this.faultMode === 'lie') result.status = result.status === 'UP' ? 'DOWN' : 'UP';

The consensus unit tests cover the key scenarios: one liar among three nodes still produces UP, a single-region DOWN under region-aware produces DEGRADED, and fewer than quorumK reports produces INCONCLUSIVE. A mock-target service exposes POST /toggle to flip between 200 and 503, so I can watch the full pipeline produce a DOWN verdict and then recover.

Future scope: blockchain integration

The next step I want to explore is settling verdicts on a blockchain. Publishing each verdict on-chain would give a tamper-proof record of what the network decided, and adding staking and slashing would give node operators an economic reason to report honestly. That would make the system suitable for an open network where nodes are run by people who don't trust each other.

The extension point is already in the code: VerdictPublisher in shared/ports.ts. The current implementation, LoggingVerdictPublisher, writes the verdict to the structured log on state transitions. A blockchain publisher would be a new implementation of the same interface that serializes the verdict (batched, to keep gas costs down) and submits it to a smart contract. The consensus engine would not need to change.

// shared/ports.ts
export interface VerdictPublisher { publish(verdict: Verdict): Promise<void> }

Other planned additions on this path are stake-weighted consensus as a new ConsensusStrategy, and a reputation score per node.

Limitations and what I would do next

Current limitations:

  • The hub is a single point of failure. One process and one Postgres. If it goes down, aggregation stops.
  • InMemoryReplayGuard is not shared across restarts or replicas. The Postgres constraints are the real guard.
  • quorumK shrinks as nodes die. If 3 of 4 nodes die, quorumK becomes 1, and a single node can produce a verdict. There should be an absolute minimum quorum floor.
  • No TLS between nodes and hub. Signatures authenticate reports, but the transport is plaintext.
  • No authentication on the hub API. Anyone who can reach the hub can register a node or add a target.

What I would do next:

  1. Add TLS (or mTLS) between nodes and hub.
  2. Replace InMemoryReplayGuard with a Redis-backed implementation for multi-instance deployments.
  3. Add a minimum absolute quorum floor, independent of the live node count.
  4. Implement an on-chain VerdictPublisher (see Future scope above).
  5. Replace assignment polling with a push model (long-poll or SSE).

Takeaways

  • Signatures authenticate the sender, not the content. A lying node can sign a false report correctly. Only agreement across independent nodes handles that.
  • An explicit "I don't know" beats a guess. Returning INCONCLUSIVE and requiring consecutive verdicts before alerting kept the system from raising alarms it could not justify.
  • State machines compose well. Liveness, target status and the circuit breaker each own exactly one lifecycle, so each is easy to test on its own and their interactions stay small.

GitHub: https://github.com/shiven16/Sentinel

event_model_payload.headline: Rustidian 0.1.7: try my Rust notes app with npx
event_model_payload.summary:
Rustidian is a Markdown notes app I'm building in Rust for Linux. It opens Obsidian-format vaults as plain folders, with a native egui interface instead of Electron. Version 0.1.7 went out this morning, and the main change is that you can now try it without picking a package format first.

One line to try it 

npx rustidian

Or keep it installed with npm i -g rustidian. Both need Linux x86_64.

I didn't want npm to become a second build of the app. So the package is a small Node script, about 140 lines. On the first run it downloads rustidian-linux-x86_64.tar.gz and SHA256SUMS from the matching GitHub release. Then it hashes the archive and compares the result with the checksum file. If they match, it extracts the archive into one folder and starts the binary. Later runs skip the download and start right away. The binary you get is the same one that the .deb and the tarball ship, built and checked by the release workflow.

The launcher source is short if you want to read it before you run it.

What changed in the app

  • It remembers where you were. Reopening Rustidian brings back the last vault, its tabs, and the scroll position of each page.
  • Links outside the vault. A link to a note in another folder, or through a symlink, opens as a tab next to the note you're reading. Before, it went to the browser.
  • Rendering fixes. Inline data: images show up instead of "Image unavailable". SVG text uses Rustidian's fonts, draws off the UI thread, and stays crisp at the page's size.
  • Numbered lists. Enter on a numbered item now renumbers the items below it, so no number repeats.
  • A new icon. The pink Signature logo, without the inner glow, is now the icon in the packages.

A contributor's fix

The AppImage had no writable demo vault to open on first launch. Oikantik Basu (Golden007-prog) sent PR #8. It copies the bundled demo vault into the app's data folder, so you can open the AppImage and start editing at once. It came with tests, and it's in this release. Thank you, Oikantik.

Other ways to install

The Debian package is still the main route. Download the .deb and SHA256SUMS, then run:

sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
sudo apt install ./rustidian-linux-amd64.deb
rustidian

The release page also has the AppImage and a portable tarball. You need glibc 2.39 or newer, so Ubuntu 24.04 or later.

What it doesn't do yet

Obsidian community plugins don't run, and Canvas and Bases are missing. Try it on a copy of your vault first. If something breaks, an issue helps a lot, and PR #8 shows that a first contribution can be small and still matter.
