event_model_payload.headline: A pricing kit's self-check validated the sample, not my workbook
event_model_payload.summary:
This is the adapted syndicated version of a review originally published on AI Stack Lab: https://aistacklab2026.blogspot.com/2026/11/hvac-business-starter-kit-review-i-re.html — that Blogger post is the canonical one and carries the full job-by-job tables.

A spreadsheet-and-Markdown starter kit for HVAC contractors has one claim worth testing with code rather than prose: that a labor rate built from your own cost base, pushed through a single fixed ten-line formula, will price any job the same way twice.

I unzipped it, re-implemented its formulas from the prose, and compared. The arithmetic held on every figure. The bundled self-check did not.

What it actually is

17 files, 85,815 bytes unpacked. Thirteen Markdown documents, two CSVs, one 196-line Python script, one licence. No dependencies, no network, no accounts.

The two interesting pieces of engineering:

  • A seven-line rate chain that turns wage, payroll load, paid hours, billable hours, overhead, target margin into an hourly rate.
  • A ten-line job formula applied in a fixed order to every job, including one composed premium line, one materials-only discount, and one labor-only agreement credit.

And a checker, self_qos.py, that the README tells you to run.

The rounding trap: Python's round() gets this wrong

The kit is careful here in a way most template bundles are not. It names the four values in its own example that sit exactly on a half cent and tells you to copy them rather than recompute with a different rounding rule.

It is right to be careful. The final step is labor_rate = cost_hour / (1 - margin) — that is 83.30 / 0.80 = 104.125, an exact tie on a half cent.

round(83.30 / 0.80, 2)   ->  104.12    # banker's rounding, Python default
ROUND_HALF_UP            ->  104.13    # what the kit documents

One cent. Here is why that matters — I re-priced all five of the kit's worked jobs twice, once at each rate, using decimal.Decimal so nothing else could drift:

job     kit total    banker's total    delta
J-001      281.95           281.93     -0.02
J-002      409.65           409.64     -0.01
J-003     1180.49          1180.45     -0.04
J-004     8850.90          8850.78     -0.12
J-005      962.61           962.57     -0.04

Every single row moves. Individually trivial. Collectively they are the reason two people can run the same kit, hand the same customer different prices, and both be "following the method."

If you re-implement the formula — in a spreadsheet, a script, a quoting tool — you have to state half-up explicitly:

  • Excel's ROUND is half-up. Matches.
  • Python's built-in round() is banker's rounding. Does not.
  • Decimal.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP) is what you want in Python.

That is a real, findable defect class and it is worth writing down before it costs someone a customer argument.

The self-check validates the sample, not your workbook

This is the leak I actually care about.

The README tells you to edit 01_Startup_Cost_Model.csv with your own truck count and local costs, and it is honest that the ladder line will report SELF-QOS FAIL afterward. Fair warning, credit given.

What it does not say is how far the failure reaches. The checker asserts the CSV has exactly 18 data rows and that the column sums produce one specific five-number ladder. So I ran four edits a real purchaser would make:

edit                                          self_qos.py says
lower one high figure inside its valid band    FAIL - ladder for 1 truck(s) is 12390.00/40010.00, expected 12390.00/41010.00
add one honest cost (shop rent)                FAIL - startup model has 19 data rows, expected 18
remove a line that does not apply to you       FAIL - startup model has 17 data rows, expected 18
add a per-truck line for a second van          FAIL - startup model has 19 data rows, expected 18

Every one of those is legitimate. A 19-row file with no invalid values in it is called a failure, with a message that reads like corruption.

The source confirms the cause:

def check_rate_chain():
    wage, load, paid, billable, overhead, margin = (
        Decimal("38.00"), Decimal("0.22"), Decimal("160"), Decimal("128"),
        Decimal("3245.00"), Decimal("0.20"))

Six hardcoded literals. It never reads your inputs. Drop your own wage into the pricing guide — exactly as the guide instructs — and the checker still prints PASS. It is comparing the constants against themselves.

So the tool does exactly one useful thing: it proves your download is intact and its frozen example is internally consistent. Run it once, keep the PASS line as your receipt, then stop. Treating it as a green light on your own model is the mistake it invites.

What genuinely held

Everything numerical, which is the part that usually breaks:

  • The seven-line rate chain reproduced to the cent, including all five intermediates.
  • All five worked jobs re-priced from my own implementation — total, cost and margin matched on all five rows (281.95 / 409.65 / 1,180.49 / 8,850.90 / 962.61).
  • The 18-row startup ladder summed to 12,390.00–41,010.00 for one truck and 40,790.00–138,610.00 for five.
  • The 6-row tracker summed to 11,780.60 / 7,851.50 / 3,929.10 with every row's revenue-minus-cost equal to its margin.
  • The agreement model: 190.00 revenue, 142.72 cost, 47.28 gross per system per year.

The four ordering rules the kit states are the ones its own numbers obey — premiums composed additively on a single line, trip charge never marked up, agreement credit on labor only, discount on materials only. That is rarer than it should be.

Who this is not for

  • Anyone who has not finished their certification — the model assumes you are pricing work, not studying for it.
  • Anyone expecting software: no dispatch, no scheduling, no invoicing, no CRM, no API.
  • Anyone reading the printed figures as a price list. They are example inputs, not market rates.
  • Anyone who wants enforcement automated. There is no CI gate; the checker is a sample integrity test, as measured.
  • Anyone whose estimates already reconcile at month end.

The honesty block

Example figures are illustrative planning inputs — not market rates and not earnings. Nothing here is legal, tax, insurance, licensing or financial advice; HVAC work carries refrigerant, electrical and gas rules that vary by jurisdiction. No claims are made about CRM, map, API, invoicing or dispatch integrations, because the bundle ships none. No ratings, reviews, testimonials or sales figures are quoted, because the live listing shows a rating count of zero and no sales.

Price and the link

Disclosure: this promotes a product we made. The sale is direct — not an affiliate link, no third-party commission.

The kit is on Gumroad at https://nandminc.gumroad.com/l/hvac-kit for $1.00, the live page price read from the listing's own price metadata before and after writing this. The page also shows SAR 3.75 as a local-currency display estimate for a Saudi visitor; that is a conversion, not a second price.

Questions first: nandminc2020@gmail.com

The takeaway worth carrying to any other template bundle: a self-check that only proves the sample is intact is not a validator for your data, and a rounding convention buried in a formula is a spec, not a detail.

event_model_payload.headline: Scops vs Enterprise Manager, DPA, Foglight and Datadog: One Table, Every Row to Scops
event_model_payload.summary:
Five Oracle monitoring products in one table: Scops, Oracle Enterprise Manager 24ai, SolarWinds Database Performance Analyzer, Quest Foglight for Oracle and Datadog Database Monitoring. Every competitor cell comes from that vendor's own documentation or price list, linked under Sources; where a vendor does not state something, the cell says so. Scops is agentless, needs no Oracle pack, monitors Standard Edition 2 in full, and wins every row: detection, AI, automation, what runs on the database server, packs and editions, what you must run, session history, price, interface, scope, Oracle versions and where the data stays.

The table

Criterion Scops Oracle Enterprise Manager 24ai SolarWinds DPA 2026.2 Quest Foglight for Oracle Datadog Database Monitoring
Detection Radar Engine: 75+ detectors that forecast (a tablespace full in 3 days), catch pile-ups (blocking, surges, storms) and anomalies (a plan that changed, commits slowing against the hour before). Every finding names the cause and earns its level from the data. Metric thresholds. Adaptive thresholds and dynamic baselines require the Diagnostics Pack. Anomaly detection on hourly wait time: a model learns from up to 90 days of data, needs three days before it shows anything; warning at the predicted value plus two standard deviations, critical at three. Alarms with IntelliProfile (adaptive) baselines. Monitors on metrics; "AI-powered root cause analysis" for queries.
AI Scops AI, the most capable AI assistant for Oracle: 40+ agentic tools that read the live database, the history and the findings, answer why, propose the fix, and change nothing without a click. Runs with your own model. A generative AI assistant announced with 24ai; scope on Oracle performance not detailed in the announcement. AI Query Assist: one query and its plan sent to an external LLM for rewrite suggestions. No assistant over live database state is described. Not stated. "AI-powered root cause analysis" and query recommendations; no Oracle assistant that reads live database state is described.
Automation Automation for the routine work, one-click fixes proposed by Scops AI, plus two modules no monitoring tool has: Archiving (old rows moved online, in rowid chunks) and Compression (Oracle compression managed from one screen). Dynamic Runbooks require the Diagnostics Pack. Not stated. "Remedial actions" from alarms. Recommendations with "in-context remediation steps".
On the database server Nothing, ever. One Windows server with two services connects through the listener with one read-only account (CREATE SESSION, SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE). A Management Agent on each host; 24ai Remote Agents reduce the count. No agent ("agentless probes"), but a utility package is installed in each monitored instance, by a user with the DBA role. "No agent overhead on the monitored hosts"; an Agent Manager host runs the agents. The Datadog Agent 7.53+; for self-hosted Oracle, "install the Agent directly onto the database host"; a view is created in the SYS schema.
Oracle packs and editions No pack: Scops samples sessions itself, every 5 seconds. Standard Edition 2 is monitored in full, the same as Enterprise Edition; a license switch guards the two features that use a pack, so one is never used by accident. Diagnostics Pack for notifications, metric and alert history, AWR, ASH, Performance Hub; Tuning Pack on top of it; both sold for Enterprise Edition only. Standard Edition 2 gets base features. Pack: not stated. "Oracle SE" is named as supported. Pack: not stated. "All Oracle Database Editions". Pack: not stated; grants on V$ views. Editions: not stated.
What you must run One Windows server; the repository is an Oracle schema on a database you already run. No second database server, no WebLogic, no agents to patch. OMS on WebLogic, a Management Repository on Oracle 19.22 or later, an agent per host. 13.5 leaves support on 31 December 2026; the upgrade to 24ai is out-of-place. A DPA server (4 cores, 10 GB RAM for 1 to 20 instances) plus a repository database on SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL or Azure SQL: 6 cores, 8 GB cache and 240 GB disk for 1 to 20 instances. Foglight Management Server, its Database Repository, an Agent Manager, and the SQL PI Repository. An Agent per database host; the data goes to Datadog's backend over the internet.

event_model_payload.headline: Rebuilding a plumbing startup-cost model from its own CSV, in Python
event_model_payload.summary:
Canonical original: https://aistacklab2026.blogspot.com/2026/11/plumbing-business-startup-cost-i.html

The best documentation products in the trades share one property that almost no marketing page mentions: they are falsifiable. You can open the file, take the claim apart, and find out whether it is true before you spend anything. So when a $1 plumbing business kit claimed a startup-cost model covering one van to five, I did the only thing worth doing with a claim like that — I extracted the zip and rebuilt the model in Python from its own rows.

Three files did most of the work: 03_Startup_Cost_Model.csv (19 line items), 11_Job_and_Route_Log.csv (5 seeded jobs), and self_qos.py (a standard-library checker, imports csv, decimal, os, sys). Here is what survived.

A cost model is a spec, and a spec must be executable

The startup model is deliberately split into two scales. Nine rows are base — counted once no matter how many vans you run. Ten rows are per-truck — multiplied by the van count. That single decision is what makes the ladder non-linear, and it is the sort of thing a PowerPoint business plan quietly gets wrong.

Rebuilt:

base      = 12,230.00 low / 38,400.00 high      (9 rows, counted once)
per-truck = 15,350.00 low / 54,100.00 high      (10 rows, each)
1 van     = 27,580.00 -> 92,500.00
2 vans    = 42,930.00 -> 146,600.00
3 vans    = 58,280.00 -> 200,700.00
4 vans    = 73,630.00 -> 254,800.00
5 vans    = 88,980.00 -> 308,900.00

Ten of ten cells footed to the cent against the shipped table. That is a low bar — addition — but it is the bar most of these products fail, because the table was typed by hand after the engine was written.

Two properties of that table are worth more than the numbers.

The band is 3.35× wide. 92,500 / 27,580 = 3.354. Any article quoting "about 28 grand" has deleted two thirds of the model's uncertainty. When a range is that wide, the width is the information: it tells you which rows to go price first in your own market.

About half of the low-end figure is working capital, not capex. The largest single base row is a 60-day reserve: 6,500.00 low, 18,000.00 high. That is 53% of the base low subtotal and 24% of the entire one-van low row. So "startup cost" in this file is two questions stapled together — what you must buy once, and what must sit in the account while the first deposits clear. Splitting them changes what you ask a lender for, and it changes how long you can survive a slow month.

The price engine, re-derived from its inputs

Five calls are frozen end to end. I threw the totals away and repriced each from its inputs through the nine-line engine (book hours × 145.00, parts × 0.45 markup, 69.00 service call, 0.50 after-hours on its own line, permit pass-through):

def engine(hours, parts, ah, trip, permit):
    raw   = round2(hours * 145.00)
    sell  = round2(parts + round2(parts * 0.45))
    base  = round2(raw + sell)
    job   = round2(base + round2(base * 0.50 * ah))
    return round2(job + round2(69.00 * trip) + permit)

5 / 5 exact, including margins (total minus job cost). The interesting one is the least obvious call, J-002: 3.00 hours, 620.00 of parts, a 95.00 permit, service call credited. 435.00 + 899.00 + 95.00 = 1,429.00. The one that would have hidden a composition bug is J-004, where the after-hours multiplier and the service call both apply: 1,145.50 base, 572.75 after-hours, +69.00 trip, permit 0.00, total 1,787.25.

The labor rate is a chain of seven lines, not a market guess: wage 34.00 → payroll load 9.52 → loaded tech 43.52 → 18,278.40/month → cost hour 60.93 → T&M 87.04 → 174.08 minimum. The cost hour being 60.93 rather than 43.52 is not a typo; it absorbs the paid-but-not-billed hours over a paid-to-on-job ratio of exactly 420/300 = 1.40. Replace the wage with your own and the chain follows.

Rounding a break-even up is the correct defect to have

Fixed costs 18,278.40 labor + 5,255.00 overhead = 23,533.40. Contribution per call 447.96. That is 52.53 calls.

The kit does not round that to 52. It rounds it to 53 whole calls and prints both sides of the line: at 52 calls the month nets −239.48, at 53 calls +208.48. Round-half-up on a break-even would have put the reader one call short of profitable and looked entirely innocent. That is the kind of choice you can only check by doing the arithmetic yourself.

Same story on the monthly P&L: 92,675.00 − 57,973.57 = 34,701.43, which is 37.44% of revenue. And the job log seeds five rows totalling 6,741.25 revenue / 3,306.74 cost / 3,434.51 margin over 17.50 book hours — a blended 50.95% job margin.

That last pair is the trap worth naming out loud: job margin is contribution before the month's overhead. 50.95% on the log and 37.44% on the month are both correct, and comparing them to each other is exactly how a busy week gets mistaken for a profitable month. 385.21 of revenue per book hour is not profit per hour.

The checker is the part I would pay for 

$ python3 self_qos.py
SELF-QOS PASS - manifest 17/17 files.
SELF-QOS PASS - tech build-up 9.52/43.52/18278.40/60.93/87.04/174.08/0.62.
SELF-QOS PASS - engine 5/5 calls 282.75 1429.00 554.75 1787.25 2687.50.
SELF-QOS PASS - P&L footing 92675.00 - 57973.57 = 34701.43.
SELF-QOS PASS - startup ladder 27580.00/92500.00 42930.00/146600.00 ...
SELF-QOS PASS - log 5/5 rows, totals 6741.25/3306.74/3434.51.
SELF-QOS PASS - honesty sweep clean: no banned tokens, no sibling pricing, no URLs.
SELF-QOS PASS

Exit 0, eight lines. Zero external URLs anywhere in the bundle, no pip install, no service to authenticate against — which is why the whole thing is auditable in an afternoon instead of a weekend.

The honest limits of that checker, since I am the one recommending it: it validates the shipped numbers. Edit the startup CSV or the job log to your own market and it will, correctly, report your numbers and may print a fail line. That is the check doing its job, not breaking. Keep an untouched copy if you want to re-run the full gate later.

What this is not

  • Not software. No app, no CRM or map or API or invoicing integration. Seventeen plain files (13 Markdown, 2 CSV, a licence, the checker) at 42,042 bytes and 13,322 words of Markdown, measured rather than claimed.
  • Not US-neutral. Dollars, state and local licensing, permit pass-through. The method travels — engine, cost chain, ladder, log — every figure and every compliance item does not.
  • Not one number. The honest output is a 3.35× band plus a method for narrowing it in your own market.
  • Not legal, tax, insurance or licensing advice. The licensing file is 19 checkboxes of questions to put to your own state office; it does not tell you what your state requires.

Every figure above is an example figure to verify locally. Footing means the arithmetic agrees with itself, not that 145.00 a book hour is your market rate.

The product

This is our own kit, disclosed plainly: Plumbing Business Starter Kit — Estimate & Pricing Templates, Startup Cost Model & Operations Docs. The estimate engine, the startup ladder, five worked calls, a one-van P&L with break-even, 7 SOPs, a licensing checklist, a safety checklist, a contract, three estimates, a job log, a pipeline tracker and a 7-day launch plan.

  • Gumroad: https://nandminc.gumroad.com/l/plumbing-kit — $1.00 as loaded from the live page immediately before this was published (intro price on a ladder that steps up as sales accrue; check the page, not this sentence)
  • Licence: PERSONAL USE - NO RESALE — use it in your own business, do not resell or redistribute it
  • Questions: nandminc2020@gmail.com

No ratings, reviews, testimonials or sales figures appear in this post, because I have none that would be honest to quote.

The full measured write-up, with the tables and the row-by-row rebuild, is on AI Stack Lab: https://aistacklab2026.blogspot.com/2026/11/plumbing-business-startup-cost-i.html

event_model_payload.headline: Understanding Database Indexes by Building a Tiny B-Tree
event_model_payload.summary:
An index is not magic. It is a sorted data structure that the database keeps up to date for you. In this post we build one from scratch in about 80 lines of Python, test it, and then watch a real database (SQLite) behave exactly the way our toy does.

Everything here uses only the Python standard library and was run on Python 3.13.

The problem: scanning

Take a users table with 500,000 rows and ask for one user by email. With no index, the database has no choice but to read every row until it finds a match. SQLite's query plan calls this a SCAN.

I measured it (SQLite 3.53.1, in-memory, 500k rows, average of 20 lookups):

Query plan Time per lookup
No index SCAN users ~22.6 ms
Index on email SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_email (email=?) ~0.002 ms

That is roughly a 10,000x difference, and the gap grows with the table. Timings depend on your machine, so treat the ratio, not the absolute numbers, as the point.

Why a tree?

We need a sorted structure so we can jump to a key instead of walking to it. A sorted array supports binary search, but inserting into the middle means shifting everything after it. A binary tree fixes inserts, but it is deep, and on disk every level costs a page read.

A B-tree fixes both by making nodes wide. Each node holds many keys (in a real database, one disk page's worth, often hundreds), so the tree stays very shallow.

We will build the most common database flavor, the B+tree:

  • Internal nodes hold only separator keys and child pointers. They are signposts.

  • Leaf nodes hold the actual keys and values (in a database, a pointer to the row).

  • Leaves are linked left to right, so a range scan walks along them without going back up the tree.

  • All leaves are at the same depth. The tree only grows taller when the root splits.

  • When a node holds more than max_keys keys, it splits in half and hands a separator key up to its parent.

Real databases use variants of this design, but the mechanics are the same.

The implementation 

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

class Node:
    def __init__(self, leaf):
        self.leaf = leaf
        self.keys = []
        self.children = []  # internal nodes: len(keys) + 1 children
        self.values = []    # leaf nodes: parallel to keys
        self.next = None    # leaf nodes: right sibling, for range scans

class BPlusTree:
    def __init__(self, max_keys=4):
        assert max_keys >= 3, "need at least 3 keys per node"
        self.max_keys = max_keys
        self.root = Node(leaf=True)
        self.height = 1  # nodes visited by every lookup

    def _find_leaf(self, key):
        node = self.root
        while not node.leaf:
            node = node.children[bisect_right(node.keys, key)]
        return node

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        leaf = self._find_leaf(key)
        i = bisect_left(leaf.keys, key)
        if i < len(leaf.keys) and leaf.keys[i] == key:
            return leaf.values[i]
        return default

    def range(self, lo, hi):
        """Yield (key, value) for lo <= key <= hi, in key order."""
        leaf = self._find_leaf(lo)
        while leaf:
            for k, v in zip(leaf.keys, leaf.values):
                if k > hi:
                    return
                if k >= lo:
                    yield k, v
            leaf = leaf.next

    def insert(self, key, value):
        split = self._insert(self.root, key, value)
        if split:  # the root itself split: the tree grows one level
            sep, right = split
            new_root = Node(leaf=False)
            new_root.keys = [sep]
            new_root.children = [self.root, right]
            self.root = new_root
            self.height += 1

    def _insert(self, node, key, value):
        if node.leaf:
            i = bisect_left(node.keys, key)
            if i < len(node.keys) and node.keys[i] == key:
                node.values[i] = value  # key exists: overwrite
                return None
            node.keys.insert(i, key)
            node.values.insert(i, value)
            return self._split_leaf(node) if len(node.keys) > self.max_keys else None

        i = bisect_right(node.keys, key)
        split = self._insert(node.children[i], key, value)
        if split is None:
            return None
        sep, right = split
        node.keys.insert(i, sep)
        node.children.insert(i + 1, right)
        return self._split_internal(node) if len(node.keys) > self.max_keys else None

    def _split_leaf(self, node):
        mid = len(node.keys) // 2
        right = Node(leaf=True)
        right.keys, node.keys = node.keys[mid:], node.keys[:mid]
        right.values, node.values = node.values[mid:], node.values[:mid]
        right.next, node.next = node.next, right
        return right.keys[0], right  # separator is copied up; it stays in the leaf

    def _split_internal(self, node):
        mid = len(node.keys) // 2
        sep = node.keys[mid]
        right = Node(leaf=False)
        right.keys, node.keys = node.keys[mid + 1:], node.keys[:mid]
        right.children, node.children = node.children[mid + 1:], node.children[:mid + 1]
        return sep, right  # separator is pushed up; it leaves this level

Four ideas carry the whole thing:

  1. Lookup (_find_leaf) walks from the root, using binary search at each node to pick the child, until it reaches a leaf. Every lookup visits exactly height nodes.

  2. Leaf splits copy the separator up. The first key of the new right leaf is also kept in that leaf, because leaves must hold every key.

  3. Internal splits push the separator up. The middle key moves to the parent and leaves this level, because internal keys are only signposts.

  4. Range scans find the leaf containing lo, then follow the next pointers. No walking back up the tree is needed.

Here it is on a small example, with a helper that prints the tree's shape:

from btree import BPlusTree

def show(node, depth=0):
    print("  " * depth + ("leaf " if node.leaf else "node ") + str(node.keys))
    for child in node.children:
        show(child, depth + 1)

t = BPlusTree(max_keys=4)
for k in [10, 20, 5, 6, 12, 30, 7, 17]:
    t.insert(k, f"row-{k}")

show(t.root)
print(t.get(12))
print(list(t.range(6, 17)))

Output:

node [10, 17]
  leaf [5, 6, 7]
  leaf [10, 12]
  leaf [17, 20, 30]
row-12
[(6, 'row-6'), (7, 'row-7'), (10, 'row-10'), (12, 'row-12'), (17, 'row-17')]

Drawn as a tree (dotted arrows are the next links between leaves):

Eight keys did not fit in one leaf, so leaves split and the root became an internal node holding the signposts 10 and 17. Looking up 12 means: compare against the root's keys, go to the middle leaf, find it there.

The last insert, 17, is a leaf split in action. The leaf [10, 12, 20, 30] became [10, 12, 17, 20, 30], which is one key over max_keys=4. It splits in half, and the first key of the new right leaf (17) is copied up into the parent:

Does it actually work?

A data structure like this fails quietly: a bad split still returns plausible answers for a while. So the tests check three different things:

  • Against an oracle. After thousands of random inserts (with deliberate overwrites), every get must match a plain Python dict, across several node sizes from 3 to 100.

  • Against the structure's own rules. After inserts, a checker walks the whole tree and asserts that keys are sorted, no node is overfull, non-root nodes are at least half full, every key sits within its parent's bounds, all leaves are at the same depth, and the leaf chain contains exactly the sorted keys.

  • On nasty input. Sorted and reverse-sorted inserts (the classic worst case for naive trees), empty and single-element trees, string keys, and 500 random range queries compared against a brute-force filter.

The full test file is in the appendix. Running it:

$ python3 test_btree.py
ok   test_empty_and_single
ok   test_matches_dict_oracle
ok   test_range_queries
ok   test_sorted_and_reverse_inserts
ok   test_string_keys
5 tests passed

How deep does it get?

With 100 keys per node, I inserted keys in random order and recorded the tree's height:

Keys Height
1,000 2
10,000 3
100,000 3
1,000,000 4

A million keys, four node visits. Height grows with the logarithm of the table size, and with wide nodes the base of that logarithm is large. The same arithmetic puts a billion keys at about five levels, which is why indexed lookups on huge tables still take a handful of page reads, and why the top levels of a busy index usually stay cached in memory.

The same thing in a real database

Our toy and SQLite agree. Using the 500k-row table from the start, I created a composite index on (country, created_at) and asked SQLite how it would run three queries:

country AND created_at > ?   ->  SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_country_created (country=? AND created_at>?)
country only                 ->  SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_country_created (country=?)
created_at only              ->  SCAN users

The tree is sorted by country first, then by created_at within each country. Here is the leaf level, simplified to three countries:

A query on country jumps straight to one block. A query on created_at alone would have to look inside every block. That has direct consequences, and you can see each one in the toy:

  • Leftmost-prefix rule. Filtering on country can descend the tree. Filtering on created_at alone cannot, because matching rows are scattered across every country's section. Hence the SCAN.

  • Range conditions are cheap. created_at > ? within one country is a descent plus a walk along linked leaves, exactly our range().

  • Leading wildcards defeat the index. For email LIKE '%99@example.com' SQLite also reported SCAN users, even with idx_email present. A suffix match gives the tree nothing to compare against at the top.

  • Order comes free. Leaves are already sorted, so ORDER BY on the indexed column needs no separate sort.

The cost side

Reads get faster; writes get more work. Every insert has to find its leaf and may trigger splits that cascade up the tree, and each additional index on a table is another tree to update. Index the columns you actually query by, not every column.

What this toy leaves out

This is a teaching implementation, so be clear about its limits:

  • No deletion. Real trees merge or borrow between underfull nodes. We only insert.

  • Unique keys only. Inserting an existing key overwrites it, like a unique index. Non-unique indexes need duplicate handling.

  • In memory. Real nodes are fixed-size disk pages, read through a buffer cache.

  • Single-threaded. Real engines use fine-grained latching so many readers and writers share a tree.

  • No crash safety. Real engines log changes (a write-ahead log) so a half-finished split can be recovered.

Each of those is a good follow-up post on its own.

Appendix: the full test suite 

import random
from btree import BPlusTree

def check_invariants(tree):
    """Raise AssertionError if the tree breaks any B+tree rule."""
    leaf_depths = set()
    min_fill = tree.max_keys // 2

    def walk(node, depth, lo, hi):
        assert node.keys == sorted(node.keys), "keys out of order"
        assert len(node.keys) <= tree.max_keys, "node overfull"
        if node is not tree.root:
            assert len(node.keys) >= min_fill, "node underfull"
        for k in node.keys:  # every key must sit inside its parent's bounds
            assert (lo is None or k >= lo) and (hi is None or k < hi)
        if node.leaf:
            leaf_depths.add(depth)
            assert len(node.keys) == len(node.values)
            return
        assert len(node.children) == len(node.keys) + 1
        bounds = [lo] + node.keys + [hi]
        for i, child in enumerate(node.children):
            walk(child, depth + 1, bounds[i], bounds[i + 1])

    walk(tree.root, 1, None, None)
    assert leaf_depths == {tree.height}, "leaves at different depths"

def leaf_chain_keys(tree):
    node = tree.root
    while not node.leaf:
        node = node.children[0]
    keys = []
    while node:
        keys.extend(node.keys)
        node = node.next
    return keys

def test_matches_dict_oracle():
    for max_keys in (3, 4, 5, 16, 100):
        rng = random.Random(max_keys)
        tree, oracle = BPlusTree(max_keys), {}
        for _ in range(5000):
            k = rng.randrange(2000)  # small key space forces overwrites
            tree.insert(k, k * 10)
            oracle[k] = k * 10
        check_invariants(tree)
        assert leaf_chain_keys(tree) == sorted(oracle)
        for k in range(-5, 2005):
            assert tree.get(k) == oracle.get(k)

def test_range_queries():
    rng = random.Random(1)
    tree, oracle = BPlusTree(4), {}
    for _ in range(3000):
        k = rng.randrange(10_000)
        tree.insert(k, str(k))
        oracle[k] = str(k)
    for _ in range(500):
        lo, hi = sorted((rng.randrange(-100, 10_100), rng.randrange(-100, 10_100)))
        expected = [(k, oracle[k]) for k in sorted(oracle) if lo <= k <= hi]
        assert list(tree.range(lo, hi)) == expected
    assert list(tree.range(20_000, 30_000)) == []  # empty range past the end

def test_sorted_and_reverse_inserts():
    for keys in (range(1000), reversed(range(1000))):
        tree = BPlusTree(4)
        for k in keys:
            tree.insert(k, k)
        check_invariants(tree)
        assert leaf_chain_keys(tree) == list(range(1000))

def test_empty_and_single():
    tree = BPlusTree(4)
    assert tree.get(1) is None and tree.get(1, "x") == "x"
    assert list(tree.range(0, 10)) == []
    tree.insert(1, "a")
    assert tree.get(1) == "a" and tree.height == 1

def test_string_keys():
    tree = BPlusTree(4)
    words = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".split()
    for w in words:
        tree.insert(w, len(w))
    check_invariants(tree)
    assert list(tree.range("a", "g")) == [("brown", 5), ("dog", 3), ("fox", 3)]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tests = [v for k, v in sorted(globals().items()) if k.startswith("test_")]
    for t in tests:
        t()
        print("ok  ", t.__name__)
    print(f"{len(tests)} tests passed")

Published via ZyVOP — Write once in Markdown, auto-backup to GitHub, and syndicate to Dev.to, Medium & Hashnode in 1 click.

event_model_payload.headline: Serving NitroFusion2 on one GPU: the text encoder, the memory mode and the step count
event_model_payload.summary:
Image models like this start from noise and clean it up in passes, called steps. Tongyi-MAI's Z-Image-Turbo needs eight. NitroFusion2 is distilled from it: a student network trained to land on the teacher's result in one or two. Dar-Yen Chen and Yi-Zhe Song (SketchX, University of Surrey) built it and released it under Apache-2.0. We served it as an API on one RTX 4090 on our cloud. At 1024 x 1024, one step took 0.78 to 0.82 seconds of GPU time, two steps 1.32 to 1.33.

Speed came for free. A few settings and one testing habit did not. Every table, the memory ladder and the setup commands are in the full NitroFusion2 write-up on inferencekey.com.

Budget memory for the text encoder, not the model file

The transformer (the main network that draws) ships as a 12.3 GB file, which seems to suit a 16 GB card. It does not. The text encoder, the Z-Image-Turbo component that turns your prompt into numbers, takes about 8 GB by itself. With the full file, peak use was about 23 GB. All on the GPU means a 24 GB card.

The authors also publish GGUF files from 2.0 GB to 7.2 GB: quantized copies that store each weight in fewer bits. Under a 16 GB cap, the 7.2 GB file died with out of memory on its first image. The 5 GB file fits beside the text encoder. On a physical 16 GB card, an RTX 2000 Ada that draws 70 watts, it stayed fully on the card at about 4.0 seconds per image at one step, 7.3 at two. At 8 GB the text encoder alone fills the budget. We did not test a smaller text encoder.

Pick the memory mode yourself on a 16 GB card

The example's memory mode defaults to auto, which keeps the pipeline on the GPU only when at least 23 GiB are free. Below that it switches to offloading: parts of the model wait in system RAM and move to the GPU when needed (the authors' script does the same). With the full file under a 16 GB cap, that cost 14 to 19 seconds per image. On a 16 GB card, auto never takes the 4-second path, so name it:

NF2_TRANSFORMER=nf2-Q4_K_M.gguf
NF2_MEMORY_MODE=gpu

The offloaded images came out the same, only slower, so only your timings show it.

Steps 1 to 4, guidance 0, or you get an error

NitroFusion2 takes 1 to 4 steps. Guidance (how hard sampling pulls toward the prompt) stays at 0. Our dashboard's image tester opens at 20 steps and guidance 4.5, and gets a 400. With 1 or 2 steps and guidance 0, the one-step poster arrived in about 1.1 seconds. The SDK example's README says so; the tester's defaults have not changed.

For two steps the authors suggest a 0.38 GB add-on. It makes the first step half Z-Image-Turbo; the student finishes alone.

Measure GPU time and round trip separately

GPU time is only the drawing. The round trip adds the request, PNG encoding and the network, and at one step it nearly doubles the time.

Steps GPU time Round trip through the API
1 0.78 to 0.82 s 1.45 to 1.50 s
2 1.32 to 1.33 s 1.95 to 2.00 s
4 2.42 s 3.08 s

Through the API, that is about 40 images a minute at one step and about 30 at two. Log both numbers while you tune. Requests ran one at a time: no batching (several prompts in one GPU pass), no concurrency, no eight-step baseline. Our 4090 was a 48 GB card, capped to act like the usual 24 GB one.

Do not trust one seed across GPUs

The seed is the random starting point of an image. With the authors' cat-and-sign prompt and seed 42, the 4090 wrote "HELLO WORd" at one step and "Hello World" at two.

On the 16 GB card, that seed at one step spelled "HELLO WORLD" correctly. A fixed seed does not reproduce a picture on another card, so one seed per prompt is a smoke test, not a quality score.

Short, big lettering usually survived one step: the Lisbon tram poster spelled "LISBOA" and "Tram 28 - every 12 minutes" correctly at one and two steps and on the 16 GB card. Small lettering did not: the cafe menu wanted "SOURDOUGH 4.50", and at one, two and four steps the 4090 wrote "SOURDOAGH". The paper admits "a substantial gap" on text rendering. In its long-text test, one step scores 43 out of 100, two steps 76, and eight-step Z-Image-Turbo 92. Those are the authors' figures; we did not reproduce them.

So text, not speed, decides. One step for previews, two for short headlines you check by eye. For menus, labels and prices, overlay real text afterwards, or switch to eight-step Z-Image-Turbo.

Credits and where to go next

NitroFusion2, its paper and code are by Dar-Yen Chen and Yi-Zhe Song (paper on arXiv, code on GitHub, weights and GGUF copies on Hugging Face). It builds on NitroFusion by Dar-Yen Chen, Hmrishav Bandyopadhyay, Kai Zou and Yi-Zhe Song. The base model and text encoder are Tongyi-MAI's Z-Image-Turbo. The diffusers maintainers wrote ZImagePipeline. PedroMarinhoDev made community ComfyUI builds (untested by us), and AI Search's news video is where we found the model. We wrote the custom backend, deployed it, and ran the timings and memory tests. The NitroFusion2 deployment notes with the memory ladder and per-request measurements also cover the request fields and startup time.

To run it on your own card, start from the NitroFusion2 article on inferencekey.com and its SDK example.

event_model_payload.headline: Dark Fleet: we spent Hack Western chasing ships that switch off their transponders
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the MLH DEV Writing Challenge, from Hack Western 13.

On Friday night at Hack Western 13, before we had a name or a single screen, we started recording every ship broadcasting its position in six parts of the world. We didn't know exactly what we'd build yet. We just knew that live ship data only exists if you were listening when it happened.

The problem we wanted to work on: big ships carry a transponder, a radio that tells everyone where they are. Some switch it off, often tankers moving sanctioned oil to another ship at sea, where nobody can see the transfer. Sanctions teams and coast guards have to work out where those ships went and who they met.

What We Built

Dark Fleet. When a ship goes quiet, it shows everywhere the ship could have gone since, which other ships it could have met, and whether any of them are on a sanctions list. Then it helps you look: a satellite radar check over the area, and a lookout on a Raspberry Pi running QNX that raises an alarm when it sees a boat that isn't broadcasting.

How It Actually Works

Step 1: record. One connection to a live transponder feed covers six regions. Every position goes to disk and into Tiger Data, where a per-minute continuous aggregate drives the live numbers on screen.

Step 2: notice a real silence. A ship stopping is easy to spot. Knowing it means something is harder: we only raise an alert if our own receivers were hearing that area at the time. Otherwise it's a gap in coverage, not a ship hiding.

Step 3: draw the circle. From the last position and the ship's top speed, we draw everywhere it could be by now. Then we check every other ship's own track to see which ones could actually have been in the same place at the same time. In one live case, 129 ships were inside the circle and only 15 could have met it.

Step 4: check the lists. We match on the IMO number, which stays the same when a ship is renamed, and show which list a ship is on.

Step 5: look from above, and from the water. For the satellite check we pull the newest Sentinel-1 radar image over the circle and run our own ship detector on it. Radar sees ships whether they broadcast or not, so anything it sees that isn't broadcasting shows up red. On the water, the Pi's webcam feeds an object detector, but a small safety loop at QNX's top priority owns the alarm. The AI runs below it and is treated as untrusted. Kill the AI and the Pi says "lookout blind" instead of going quiet, and a standby takes over in about 150 ms.

What Went Wrong (and What We Did)

Our first sanctions hits weren't sanctions. Three of the first four "listed" ships were on a port-inspection list. We now count only sanctions and shadow-fleet lists, and say which one.

Everything said OK while nothing was working. For hours our live numbers read zero and every request still returned success. The data had stopped arriving. Now a small script checks the actual values every few minutes.

The camera froze. We gave the AI a higher priority than the camera, and the camera stopped after three frames. Getting the order right was the biggest win of the weekend: under the same overload test, 10 of 27 alarms met the 200 ms deadline before, and 63 of 64 after.

Our own validation had a hole. For the Strait of Hormuz we used two years of satellite radar and found the share of ships not broadcasting roughly doubled after the war began. We'd compared it with the Gulf of Oman to rule out bad reception, and late Saturday night we realized our Hormuz area contained the Gulf of Oman area. We redrew it and re-ran everything. The result held, and got slightly stronger.

Satellites are rarely overhead at the right time. No pass has caught a live ship while it was dark yet. The closest came 17 hours early, and the app says that plainly. And on a stormy night the sea was so bright on radar that our detector treated most of it as land until we fixed the check.

Our first guided demo didn't work. We replaced it with a story that follows one real ship from the moment it switches off.

What We Learned

The physics clears ships as well as flagging them. Ten ships went silent far out at sea and reappeared together a day later near the UAE, a trip that needed about 29 knots. They can't go that fast. Their positions were faked, probably by GPS jamming, so we don't flag them.

Start collecting data before you've finished the idea. And check the real numbers, not just whether the system says it's healthy.

Tools: What Worked and Where We Hit Friction

QNX. The OpenCV DNN package from QNX's own repository ran our detector on the Pi without us building anything from source. Adaptive partitioning wasn't in the image we had, so we used fixed priorities instead, which in the end was the thing that mattered.

Tiger Data. Hypertables and continuous aggregates were quick to set up. The catch: the newest minutes aren't summarised yet by default, so our live rate read zero until we turned on real-time aggregation.

We used AI coding agents for much of the code. Most of our time went into deciding what to build and checking their work against real data.

Holding a photo of a boat up to the webcam just after midnight and watching the alarm go off was when it all felt real.

Code: https://github.com/kassem-kanjo/Hack-Western

Powered by Global Fishing Watch. Sanctions data from OpenSanctions (CC BY-NC). Radar from Copernicus Sentinel-1 via Microsoft Planetary Computer.

event_model_payload.headline: How much should an LLM decide? Building an avatar that reviews your training week with FastAPI, Gemini and Jev, a judge model
event_model_payload.summary:
loadline is a web app that reviews your training week with an avatar. It imports the workouts you record on an Apple Watch. Once a week, a 3D avatar speaks a short review of the week: how tired you are, and how much you trained compared with your usual weeks. It then shows two or three options for the next week, and one of them is always to rest or train easy.

  • App (beta): https://api-qbvpsx77dq-an.a.run.app
  • Source code: https://github.com/d-station-grid/loadline
  • (English README: https://github.com/d-station-grid/loadline/blob/main/README.en.md)

You can try the app without signing up. Click "Try as a guest" on the sign-in screen, and the app opens a dashboard with demo data and a weekly review.

The backend is FastAPI. Gemini writes the avatar's lines, and Jev, a judge model that only returns probabilities, checks them before the avatar speaks. This post is about the question I spent the most time on while designing it: how much should the LLM decide?

What goes wrong if Gemini decides everything

The simplest design sends a week of records to Gemini and asks it for a review. Gemini then has to compare numbers on its own, such as this week's training load against the average of the past nine weeks, or fitness against fatigue. An LLM can get a comparison like that wrong, and the review still sounds confident.

In this app, a wrong comparison leads to wrong advice. If the model reads a hard week as an easy one, the avatar may tell a tired user to train more.

I also wanted two properties that an LLM does not give on its own. The same records should always produce the same judgment, so that I can test it. And the weekly review should always be created, even when Gemini is busy or Jev does not respond.

So I split the work. Code makes every judgment that involves numbers, Gemini writes the words, and code decides whether the avatar can use those words.

The pipeline: code, Gemini, Jev, then code again

A weekly review goes through four steps.

  1. Code judges the week from the records: whether the user is tired, whether they trained more or less than usual, and whether the app may suggest more training.
  2. Gemini receives the results and writes the avatar's lines and the options for the next week.
  3. Jev reads the lines and returns, for each question, the probability that the answer is yes. The questions ask whether the lines push the user too hard, give medical advice, or recommend more training.
  4. Code reads the probabilities and decides whether the avatar can use the lines. If any probability is 0.35 or higher, or if Gemini or Jev fails, the app switches to fallback lines prepared in advance.

Only steps 2 and 3 use AI.

What code decides

Code makes two judgments from the records. Both are plain functions in domain/, so the same records always give the same result, and unit tests cover them.

The first judgment asks whether the user is tired. The app computes daily training load from heart rate, and then fitness and fatigue as exponential moving averages of that load over 42 days and 7 days. Form is fitness minus fatigue. domain/situation.py divides form by fitness and maps the ratio to fatigued, fresh or steady. Because it uses a ratio, the same thresholds work regardless of how high the user's fitness is. Weeks with too few records, weeks without training, and weeks right after a break get their own values (not_enough_data, no_training, returning) before the ratio is checked.

The second judgment compares the week's load with the user's own average over the past nine weeks (domain/effort.py). Below 0.8 is light, 1.5 or above is heavy, and anything between is usual.

Code also decides whether Gemini may offer more training as an option. After a heavy week, the answer is no. Gemini receives this answer together with the two judgments and numbers that code has already computed, such as the number of workouts and the change from the previous week. Gemini never has to compare numbers itself.

What Gemini decides

Gemini decides what the avatar says and how it says it. The request has three parts (domain/review_prompt.py, adapters/gemini.py).

  • Input: the two judgments, counts and changes from the previous week, the VO2max trend, the user's notes, the option they chose last week, and whether more training may be offered
  • System prompt (system_instruction in the Gemini API): rules such as never contradicting the judgments, encouragement first, no medical advice, always one option to rest or train easy, and a line that takes about 15 seconds to speak
  • Structured output: the response must be JSON with an explanation, the line and the options. Because the shape is fixed, code can check the length and the number of options

The system prompt states the split directly: "situation was decided by our own code from the numbers. Trust it and never contradict it."

Reading the numbers aloud adds little, because the dashboard already shows them. So the system prompt lists six well-known training principles and asks Gemini to pick the one that fits the judgments and use it as the reason for its advice. One of them is "Weeks of steady training add up to more than one big week." The prompt also limits numbers: the first sentence of the line has none, and the whole line mentions at most one. VO2max goes to Gemini only as a trend (up, flat or down), not as a value.

Here is the line Gemini wrote for the demo user's latest week. The code judged the week as steady with training usual, and the user's notes mention a race:

You kept your routine going smoothly after the race, and that consistency is wonderful. Weeks of steady training add up to more than a single big effort, and your body is responding nicely to the regular work.

Fifteen seconds is too short to explain the reasoning, so Gemini also writes an explanation of 80 to 120 words. The app shows it only when the user opens "Read more", and the avatar does not read it aloud.

Jev as a guardrail

Jev (by TypeSafe AI) is a model for judgments only and does not write text. You send it a text and some yes-or-no questions, and it returns the probability of "yes" for each question. The code decides what to do with those probabilities.

After Gemini writes the review, code joins the line with the labels and descriptions of the options and sends the text to Jev with three questions (domain/line_check.py):

  • Does it push the user to train harder, for example by ordering, blaming, or asking them to make up for missed sessions?
  • Does it give medical advice, such as a diagnosis or a treatment?
  • Does it recommend raising volume or intensity?

The third question counts only in weeks where code has already decided not to offer more training. The system prompt gives Gemini the same rule, but code checks it again instead of relying on the prompt.

If any of these probabilities is 0.35 or higher, the app does not use Gemini's line and switches to the fallback lines. The threshold is below 0.5 so that the app also drops lines that Jev is unsure about.

Jev also reads the user's notes before the request to Gemini and answers whether they mention pain or sickness (domain/note_check.py). If the probability is 0.35 or higher, code sets a health flag, and options to raise volume or intensity are no longer candidates.

The same call that checks the line also asks Jev which expression fits it: happy, relaxed, sad or surprised. Jev returns its choice with a confidence. If the confidence is below 0.6, code uses the calm expression, relaxed (domain/expression.py).

When something fails

Gemini can be busy, Jev can time out, and Gemini can return a line that breaks the length rules. The app handles all of these cases in the same way.

The code that calls external services lives in adapters/. When a call fails for any reason, the adapter logs the reason and returns None. The Gemini adapter, for example, tries the models in order from the newest generation to older ones. It moves to the next model on a 429, a 5xx or a network error, and it retries the same model once if the JSON fails the checks on length and the number of options. It returns None after a timeout, an authentication error, or when no model gives a valid answer.

The service in services/reviews.py only sees None. It does not know why the call failed, and it does not need to. For any None from Gemini or Jev, and for any line that Jev flags, it uses the fallback lines in domain/fallback_review.py. A line that Jev could not check counts as a line that failed the check. The fallback lines are prepared in English and Japanese and chosen to match the two judgments, so even a fallback review fits the week.

As a result, a weekly review is always created. If the voice cannot be generated either, the app saves the review without audio and shows only the captions.

How the FastAPI backend is organized

The split between code and AI also decides the folder structure of the backend (api/app/).

Folder What it does What it does not do
routers/ Receives requests, checks who the user is, and calls services/ Calculations or judgments
services/ Loads data from the DB, calls domain/ and adapters/ in order, and saves the results Detailed calculations or judgments
domain/ Calculations and judgments, such as the two judgments and whether a line can be used Access to the DB or external services
adapters/ Calls Gemini, Jev, tts/, Cloud Text-to-Speech and Cloud Storage Judgments

services/ does not import Gemini or Jev. It defines Protocols such as ReviewWriter and LineChecker and depends only on them. The only place that connects these Protocols to the real adapters is routers/deps.py, through FastAPI's Depends:

@lru_cache
def get_review_writer() -> ReviewWriter | None:
    return gemini_writer(get_settings())


ReviewWriterDep = Annotated[ReviewWriter | None, Depends(get_review_writer)]

The return type allows None. When the Gemini project is not configured, get_review_writer returns None, and the service uses the fallback lines, in the same way as when a call fails.

In tests, app.dependency_overrides replaces these providers. The API tests set them to None, so every review in those tests uses the fallback lines. The service tests pass fakes that return fixed answers, so they can check what happens when Jev flags a line without calling Jev. When I added Japanese voices, the change was one more adapter for Google's Text-to-Speech behind the same Speaker Protocol.

What I want to check next

This split is not proven yet. I plan to keep using loadline with my own training records and check whether the weekly reviews match how my body actually feels. The thresholds for fatigue and the system prompt will change based on what I find.

Two smaller changes are also on my list. The avatar appears full-body and small on the dashboard, so its expression is hard to see, and I want to show it closer. Jev already returns a confidence for the expression, so the avatar could also show a stronger or softer expression depending on that confidence.

If you have built an app where an LLM gives advice, I would like to hear how you decided what to leave to the model. The demo and the source code are linked at the top of this post.
