event_model_payload.headline: Browser Use in DSH Agent Enhancer: Click, Debug, and Replay Saved Flows
event_model_payload.summary:
dsh-agent-enhancer is a desktop plugin for DSH. Its Browser Use layer gives your agent a dedicated browser. It can click, type, and submit. Login state stays in its own profile, so your everyday browser is left alone.

You do not need scripting or API knowledge. Do the task once in the dedicated window, and the agent can follow the same steps. Save the recording as a flow, rerun it by name, and hand it to a scheduled task without approving every action.

The practical rule: if you click through the same web admin every day or every week, it is worth handing over. Here are scenarios that work right after install:

Role Repetitive work How it helps
E-commerce ops Export yesterday's orders, refunds, and inventory at 8:00 every day Three saved flows plus the built-in scheduler, running unattended
Finance / reconciliation Export admin data and statements on the 1st of each month, then reconcile three tables Automated except for the password step; if it gets stuck, it leaves a record
Recruiting / HR Go through new resumes and filter by keywords every Monday Read-only tabs: it can read, but cannot change anything
Marketing / competitive research Check competitor pricing and campaign pages every morning Extract plus screenshots, with changes written straight into the chat
Dev / QA Re-click the same reproduction steps in the admin UI Record once, rerun by name during regression; fix once after a redesign
Handover / onboarding Explain "where to click first" again and again A teammate demos once; the steps become a flow anyone can run next month

Three patterns cover most of these:

  • Turn repetitive work into one sentence. Record once, save, run on schedule, and check the result in the morning.
  • Read-only pages that must not change. Order details, reports, production dashboards: it can read and scroll, but clicks do nothing.
  • Keep the "how" around. A teammate demos once, the steps become a flow; when the site changes, it finishes the job and you click Remember once.

Under the hood, the actions come from a set of browser_* tools: browser_navigate opens a page, browser_snapshot reads it, browser_click / browser_type operate it, browser_scroll / browser_wait / browser_extract handle long pages, browser_list_tabs / browser_follow_tab switch tabs, browser_network / browser_console / browser_emulate debug it, browser_demonstrate records a demo, and browser_demo_recipes manages saved flows. When you need to take over and log in yourself, use browser_ask_user; there are also browser_screenshot and browser_status.

This post starts with what it can do, then walks through six areas: operation, troubleshooting, demo recording, saved flows, scheduled tasks, and boundaries. Each section ends with a concrete use case.

Operation: multiple tabs, read-only tabs, idle cleanup

Say "open the browser" in the chat, or Alt-click (Option-click on Mac) a link in the conversation, and the dedicated window starts. It has its own profile, so you log in once and stay logged in. On Mac it uses Chrome or Safari; on Windows, Chrome or Edge. It is completely separate from your daily browser. On Mac, selecting Safari drives the WebKit engine, not the Safari app you use every day.

Multiple tabs. The sidebar lists every tab; click one to switch. When navigating, you can choose to open a new tab. If a task needs to compare orders, inventory, and shipping, you do not have to cram everything into one page.

Read-only tabs. One click in the sidebar makes a tab read-only: the agent can look, but it cannot click, type, or navigate within that tab. Opening a new tab and scrolling still work. Check-only pages — reports, order details — are the safest place to use it. Even a saved flow replay is blocked by this restriction.

Idle cleanup. Idle tabs can close automatically after 10, 30, or 60 minutes, or never. The tab you are currently viewing, session-bound tabs, and the last remaining tab are never closed. The dedicated window does not pile up.

Use it for: reconciling orders across three admin pages. Open orders, inventory, and shipping in separate tabs; make inventory read-only so nobody accidentally clicks "Adjust stock"; come back from lunch and idle tabs are gone, but the login is still there.

Troubleshooting: debug tools and page emulation

When the Export button does nothing, guessing is the worst approach. Turn on Debug & Page Emulation in settings (off by default):

  • Network: method, URL, status code, duration, failure reason;
  • Console: output, uncaught exceptions, source location;
  • Page emulation: dark mode, reduced motion, viewport size.

It reads only what it needs: no request headers, cookies, or response bodies. Tokens and codes in URLs, plus links in the console, are redacted.

Startup failures do not require digging through logs either. The status bar and sidebar show the reason and the next step: feature not enabled, browser not started, WebKit missing, no usable browser on the machine, profile directory locked, and so on.

Use it for: a dead Export button. Check whether the network call returns 500 or times out, then look for console errors. Switch to a narrow viewport to rule out an overlay covering the button. Once you know the cause, change the agent's action instead of trying blindly.

Demo recording: do it once, it remembers

Some admin tasks are easier to show than to describe. Turn on Demo Recording in settings (off by default), click "Start demo" in the sidebar, and use the dedicated window normally. When you are done, click "End and view steps".

It records clicks, typing, Enter presses, and page navigations. It can record across tabs, and other tabs opened during the demo are captured. When finished, you can copy the steps or click "Send to agent" to insert them into the input box (the current conversation needs at least one message first, otherwise it asks you to send one). You can also say "let me show you" in the chat, and the agent can start a recording itself.

Password, CAPTCHA, token, and card-number fields are stored as *** only. It does not take screenshots or record network requests.

Use it for: handing over monthly reconciliation. Ask a teammate to demo it once: open the reconciliation page, pick the month, export, download, and check the three tables. Send the steps to the agent, and next month nobody has to ask "where do I click first?"

Saved flows: from a one-off demo to a reusable run

After recording, click "Save as flow" and give it a name, such as "Weekly report export". There are three ways to run it:

  • Click Run under "Saved flows" in the sidebar;
  • Say Run "Weekly report export" in the chat. The agent finds it by name and asks for approval once per run by default; Full Access or unattended mode stops the repeated prompts;
  • Hand it to the built-in Automation Tasks with unattended mode, and it runs on schedule. The next section explains how to wire that up.

It works across sessions and restarts. If the current page is not the page where recording started, it returns there first. Data stays local and only redacted steps are stored; password fields remain ***.

The sidebar row keeps only Run and "⋯"; rename and delete live in the menu, and delete asks for confirmation. Expanding the row shows editable values, run mode, and steps. Replay supports dropdowns and checkboxes. If several controls share a name and cannot be distinguished, it stops and lists the candidates instead of clicking the first one by name.

Parameters: plain language, not variable names

After saving, values worth changing — dates, email addresses, search terms — are detected automatically. Parameter names come straight from the page labels ("Start date"), so you do not have to invent variable names.

Date fields get a date picker. You can also say "last week", "this month", or "last quarter", and the agent converts it to a real date. When a value is missing, it asks in plain language: "Which start date should I use this time?"

Each value's default and display name can be changed; it can be set to "Ask me each time" or switched back to a fixed value. Every change goes into version history, and the last change can be undone.

Repair: when the site changes, it finishes the job

If the site renames a control or inserts an extra dialog, the flow gets stuck. The agent finishes the task, then offers a suggestion:

"The control in step 4 changed; it is now called 'Start date'. Remember this for next time?"

  • Remember: write the repair back into the flow and use it next time;
  • Just this once: leave the flow as it was.

Repair changes only how the control is located. It does not change values or step order. Password fields do not participate, and are never stored in the flow. Every write-back creates a version that can be undone.

Run results: what happened last time

Each saved flow records its last run: time, success / stopped at step N / failure. If it did not finish, the row shows a "Last run incomplete" badge. It stores counts and the reason it stopped, not page content.

Use it for: a weekly report export. Record once, save "Weekly report export", set "Start date" to Ask me each time, say Run "Weekly report export" with last week's start date on Monday morning, and check the run result. If the site changes, repair it once, remember it, and the next run uses the fix.

Scheduled tasks: a flow is not "placed inside" a task

First, a common misconception: a saved flow is not an asset you drag into a scheduled task. When the schedule fires, the task only says one sentence.

The built-in Automation Tasks scheduler creates a new session with fixed permissions: Workspace Modify with approval prompts. The task itself cannot change permissions. So when our flow runs, an approval prompt will appear — and nobody is there to click it. The task stalls.

The fix is not to loosen global permissions. Turn on Unattended for that one flow. It applies only to the site recorded in that flow, with a default budget of 20 minutes / 30 actions. When time or actions run out, it goes back to per-action approval. It is off by default; it cannot be enabled if the flow has no recorded site; password fields still stop and wait; it does not apply to another site or another session; if a run is denied, the site grant is revoked immediately.

These two numbers can be changed in Settings → Agent Enhancer → Features → Browser Agent: authorization duration 5–60 minutes, action limit 10–200. Defaults stay unless you change them.

Putting "Weekly report export" on a schedule (5 steps)

  1. Run it manually once. Sidebar "Saved flows" → expand "Weekly report export" → Run. Confirm it finishes within the authorization window and does not ask for input.
  2. On the same flow, click "Allow unattended". The "Unattended" badge appears next to the name.
  3. Create a built-in task. Open "Automation Tasks", create one, and set it to Monday 08:00.
  4. The prompt is one sentence: Run "Weekly report export". You can include the site: Run "Weekly report export" on example.com. It checks the site recorded in the flow and refuses to run on the wrong one.
  5. Check the result on Monday morning. Expand the flow in the sidebar; "Run mode" shows the last run time and whether it succeeded, stopped at step N, or failed.

What actually happens when the schedule fires

  • The task creates a new session; permissions are still Workspace Modify with approval.
  • The agent finds the flow by name and issues a temporary site pass for the site recorded in the flow (default 20 minutes / 30 actions).
  • The dedicated browser launches itself. Login state is still in its own profile; no need to sign in again.
  • The flow replays in the recorded order, and the result is written back to the flow.
  • If a site change blocks it, the agent finishes the remaining steps and leaves a repair suggestion. Unattended mode does not write the repair back automatically; click Remember when you have time.
  • On a password or CAPTCHA, it stops and records the step where it stopped. That step is never auto-approved.

Three easy traps

  • The flow is too long. The default pass covers 30 actions. Raise "Action limit" in settings (max 200); if that is still not enough, split "Export orders / Export refunds / Export inventory" into smaller flows. At the default budget, a 40-step flow falls back to per-action approval halfway through and then stalls.
  • A parameter is still set to "Ask me each time". Nobody is there to answer during a scheduled run, and the agent will not invent a value. For scheduled flows, either fix the value or put it in the prompt: Run "Weekly report export" with start date set to last week.
  • No site recorded. Older flows that did not record a site have "Allow unattended" grayed out. Record the flow again to enable it.

Use it for: an automatic weekly report at 8:00 on Monday. Enable unattended only for "Weekly report export", tune the budget to that flow, and check the run result afterward. Other tasks and other sites still require approval each time.

If the session already uses Full Access, actions no longer prompt one by one; Auto Review goes through the built-in reviewer; View Only is refused with an explanation.

Boundaries: what it won't do

It can act, but it does not have unlimited permission. By default, every action that changes external state needs approval. It stops at a login wall and waits for you to click "I'm done, continue"; it does not bypass it.

Demo recording captures actions only: no screenshots, no network requests. Debugging does not read request headers, cookies, or response bodies; URL parameters are redacted. Saved flows live locally and contain only redacted steps; passwords never enter a flow and never participate in repair. Read-only tabs prevent changes at the entry point, and flow replays are subject to the same restriction. Turn the feature off and it removes the tools and closes the dedicated window; no background window is left behind.

The dedicated window does not label itself as an automation environment, so sites with login bot checks, such as Bilibili, no longer reject it for that reason. This is not a generic anti-detection patch; sites that check more signals still need a separate look.

Use it for: hand a read-only report page to the agent for checking; when a submission is needed, let it stop and wait for you; give a scheduled task one flow and a limited window. Narrow permissions are what make it safe to let go.

Up and running in 5 minutes

  1. Settings → Plugins, search dsh-agent-enhancer → install or update to the latest version, then restart the desktop app when prompted.
  2. On the plugin page, confirm "Agent Enhancer" is enabled. Then go to Settings → Agent Enhancer → Features → Browser Agent (off by default) and turn it on. Choose the dedicated browser: on Mac, Auto / Chrome / Safari; on Windows, Auto / Chrome / Edge. Before selecting Safari (WebKit) on Mac, run npx playwright install webkit; the status bar tells you if it is missing.
  3. In the chat, say "open the browser", or Alt-click (Option-click on Mac) a link. Run one demo recording first; if it feels right, save it as a flow.
  4. Run the flow manually once. When it is stable, enable "Allow unattended", raise the budget in settings if needed, and create a built-in Automation Task with Run "flow name".
  5. Do not start with Full Access.

Command line (installs the latest version by default):

dsh plugin --profile desktop add dsh-agent-enhancer

Compatible with DSH desktop 0.2.2.x.

Start by walking it through one demo recording. After that, it remembers the run for you.

Links

  • GitHub
  • npm
  • Changelog

event_model_payload.headline: Running a video-by-code agent on one RTX 4090: the context budget is the real limit
event_model_payload.summary:
Run an open model as a long agent (a model that calls tools in a loop on its own) on one card and the weights are rarely what stops you. The budget around them is: how much the agent can keep in view, and how long one answer may be.

We learned that with SenseNova 6.8 Code2Video, SenseTime's open 27B model that makes video by writing code. We drove it with Claude Code on one 24 GB RTX 4090 on our cloud. Ten minutes in, it had a full 12-second clip. Forty minutes in, it had no finished film. The logs and frames are in the full research write-up on running Code2Video on one RTX 4090. Here I focus on the settings.

Your settings are not the authors' settings

The SenseNova team publishes a Claude Code skill called code-video and six complete production runs. They serve the full-size model across four GPUs. Their context window (the text the model can see at once, counted in tokens, which are word pieces) is 512K tokens, and one answer may run to 64K. Their films needed between 261 and 876 turns each.

We used bartowski's 4-bit GGUF, a compressed copy of the weights (17.2 GB) for the llama.cpp server, plus a 0.93 GB vision part so the model can see images. Three Claude Code variables encode the gap:

CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS=98304   # authors: 524288
CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=80     # same as the authors
CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS=16384    # authors: 64000

Without the first one, Claude Code assumes 200K for a model it does not recognize.

The trap: compaction needs room to write

Compaction is how Claude Code survives a full context. Once the window passes 80%, it has the model write a recap, throws the old history away and continues from the recap alone. The recap is a normal reply, so the output cap applies to it too.

Our 98,304-token window was full after about 19 minutes. Three recap requests followed. All three ran into the 16,384-token ceiling, none produced a usable summary, and together they ate 21 minutes until our 40-minute limit killed the run with no final film.

Compaction can work: four of the authors' six runs cleared contexts of 167K to 492K tokens, under a 64K cap. On our side two settings are under suspicion. One is the 16,384-token cap. The other is hidden reasoning, the thinking the model writes before its visible answer, which we left on and which draws from the same cap. The logs cannot tell them apart, though in a separate single request the same 4-bit file burned all 8,192 output tokens thinking and wrote no page. A bigger window, a bigger cap or reasoning off might fix it; we tried none of them.

So when you size a single-card agent, measure two things before you trust it: when the context will hit the compaction threshold, and whether one summary fits under your output cap with reasoning on.

The file check passed a wrong picture

Self-review did its job. The model opened 21 of its own stills as images, spotted two bugs and fixed both. All on-screen text matched the brief word for word.

The one fact that mattered was still wrong. The brief asked for 30 dots in a 5 by 6 rectangle. We located each dot centre in the 7.2-second frame with numpy and scipy and got 5 rows of 7 columns, one cell empty per row. The skill's file check still said yes. It only looks at resolution, frame rate and duration, never at what is drawn.

Add a check that knows what the clip should show.

Two pieces of plumbing to verify first

Claude Code speaks Anthropic's Messages API format, so whatever sits in front of the model has to translate it. Ours lost the frames: each image either vanished or arrived as a block of text, and the model reviewed its work blind. Fixed in our test build, not yet on the hosted service. With any gateway, send one PNG first and check the model describes it.

Second, time. Our first call waited for the full answer instead of streaming it piece by piece. The worker, the process on the GPU machine that forwards requests to the server, gives up after 120 seconds, and the model was still thinking. Raising that to 30 minutes fixed the run, and the example now streams.

What fits on smaller cards

The 4-bit run peaked at 20.9 GiB. Smaller copies, one short request each:

Budget Copy Peak Result
16 GB 3-bit, 32K 13.7 GiB page renders, one dot visible at a time
12 GB 2-bit, 16K 10.0 GiB page cut off at 8,192 tokens

These ran on the 4090, not real 16 or 12 GB cards, with one sample each. The memory ladder, launch command and step-by-step setup for the Code2Video test have the rest. See also our earlier test of another SenseTime model, SenseNova-Loop-9B.

Credits and the honest limit

The SenseNova team at SenseTime built the model, the skill, the prompt template and the production runs, starting from the Qwen team's base model (model card, skill repository). bartowski made the GGUF quants and the llama.cpp maintainers made the server. Anthropic made Claude Code and Claude Opus 5.5, which drafted the brief from the authors' template. We first saw the model in an AI Search news video. We handled the deployment, fixed the image path, ran the sandboxed agent and counted the pixels.

This was one attempt at one brief under tight limits we chose. Logs, timings, the full VRAM table and the SDK example are in the complete Code2Video research post on inferencekey.com.

event_model_payload.headline: Cline Review 2026: The Open-Source AI Agent for VS Code
event_model_payload.summary:
What Is Cline?

Cline (formerly Claude Dev) is an open-source AI coding agent that runs as a VS Code extension. Unlike Copilot's inline suggestions, Cline can plan multi-step changes, create and edit files, run terminal commands, and use a browser — all autonomously within your project. It is the open-source alternative to Cursor's agent mode.

Cline at a Glance

Area What it does Who it suits
Reviewability Shows every prompt, tool call, and diff in the session Teams that require audit before merge
Execution control Proposes a plan, you approve each write Review-first, quality-first developers
Model choice Bring your own provider or a local model Cost- and privacy-conscious teams
Open source Inspect and fork the extension itself Security teams and maintainers

How Cline Works

You describe a task in natural language. Cline analyzes your project structure, plans the implementation, and executes it step by step. It can create files, edit existing code, run tests, read error messages, and iterate until the task is complete. You approve each action or let it run autonomously.

Key Features

  • Multi-step task execution: Plans and implements complex changes across multiple files
  • Terminal access: Runs commands, installs packages, executes tests
  • Browser tool: Can check web documentation and API references
  • Model flexibility: Works with Claude, GPT-4, Gemini, DeepSeek, and local models via OpenAI-compatible APIs Context awareness: Reads your entire project structure before acting

What Cline Does Well

Transparency by design

Its defining trait is that you can see exactly what the agent chose. Every tool call, the file it edits, and the prompt that drove it are part of the session. When a change is wrong, you read the audit and correct a specific step, instead of spending an afternoon reconstructing what the model guessed. For a review-heavy team, that audit habit de-risks every merge.

Explicit, diffable edits

Cline proposes a diff you can inspect before it modifies anything. You are not asked to trust a single accept-all click. Seeing and editing each change before it lands is the meaningful difference between an agent that "just did it" and one you actually supervise.

Open source, so you can audit it

Because Cline is open source, the tool is transparent too. You never depend on an endpoint you cannot examine, which matters for a security-conscious team or a careful open-source maintainer.

Bring your own model

You decide which model presides. That keeps control of cost and privacy in your hands and fits teams that want to route smaller or self-hosted models into the same loop without changing tools.

Cline vs Cursor Agent Mode

Cursor's agent mode is more polished with better UI and faster iteration. Cline is open-source, works with any model, and runs in your existing VS Code setup. If you already use VS Code and do not want to switch editors, Cline is the practical choice. See our Cursor IDE Review for the full Cursor comparison.

Cline vs GitHub Copilot

Different tools entirely. Copilot suggests code as you type. Cline executes multi-step tasks autonomously. Copilot is passive assistance; Cline is active agency. They complement each other rather than compete. See our GitHub Copilot Review.

Real-World Results

Adding auth to a Next.js app — 12 minutes

Cline created the auth middleware, login/signup pages, API routes, and updated the navbar. Required one correction (wrong redirect URL). Solid result for a task that would take 30+ minutes manually.

Writing unit tests for a React component — 8 minutes

Generated comprehensive tests with React Testing Library. 85% pass rate on first run. Fixed the 2 failing tests automatically on the next iteration.

Refactoring a Python API — 15 minutes

Split a monolithic route file into separate modules. Cline understood the dependency graph and updated all imports correctly. Impressive architectural understanding.

A Realistic Workflow with Cline

A healthy daily loop with Cline starts with a small, well-scoped task. You open Cline, point it at the relevant files, describe the change you want in a sentence or two, and let it read the project and propose a plan. You read that plan the same way you read a teammate's design note: is the approach right, is it too broad, does it touch files it should not? Only then do you let it draft the diff, and only when you approve does the edit land. This sounds slower than an accept-all flow, but it shifts the cost to the moment of the decision, catches a bad direction before a single edit is written, and leaves a clean audit of every step. Teams that run it this way consistently report that time moves from rework to review, which is a net win for the codebase.

The other habit worth building is a regular grounding pass. After Cline finishes a batch, run the project tests and your linter, then read the diff once more with fresh eyes before you push. The point is not to distrust Cline; it is to make sure the tool's work is a proposal you have verified rather than an assumption you accepted. Over a few weeks this discipline turns Cline from something a skeptical reviewer fears into a dependable assistant whose judgment you trust because you check it.

Pros

  • Open-source and free — bring your own API key
  • Works with any model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, local models)
  • Integrates into existing VS Code workflow Autonomous multi-step execution saves significant time

Cons

  • Less polished than Cursor's agent mode
  • Can get confused on very large codebases
  • API costs add up on long autonomous sessions Requires manual approval for safety (or careful auto-approve settings)

Pricing

Cline itself is free and open-source. You pay for the underlying model API. A typical coding session with Claude Sonnet costs $0.50-2.00. With GPT-4o, about the same. With local models like DeepSeek Coder, effectively free after hardware costs.

Final Verdict

Cline is the best open-source AI coding agent available. It does not match Cursor's polish, but the model flexibility and zero licensing cost make it a compelling choice for developers who want AI agency without vendor lock-in. Rating: 7.5/10

Related reading on PikVue:

  • OpenCode Review 2026: The Open-Source AI Coding Agent With 100K GitHub Stars
  • OpenCode vs Aider vs Cline 2026: Which Open-Source CLI Coding Agent Should You U
  • Best Offline Coding Setups for Developers in 2026: Local Models, Ollama, and Ope

Originally published at pikvue.com — independent 2026 reviews and comparisons of developer tools, AI products, and SaaS platforms.

event_model_payload.headline: How Many Users Can Your VPS Actually Handle? A Practical Guide to Capacity Planning
event_model_payload.summary:
Every developer knows this moment.

You just deployed a clean Laravel app on a $6 DigitalOcean Droplet. Everything feels fast. Then your client or your business lead sends a message: "Hey, we're launching a marketing campaign next week. How many people can use the site at once before it crashes?"

Most of us freeze for a second and guess. "Uh, maybe a few hundred? We can just upgrade the server if it gets slow."

Guessing works fine until it doesn't. If you overestimate, your site goes down right in the middle of a paid ad campaign. If you underestimate, you end up paying for a massive server you don't even need yet.

In the industry, solving this problem is called Capacity Planning. It sounds like a heavy enterprise buzzword, but you don't need expensive monitoring tools to do it. You can SSH into your VPS right now, run four safe commands, do three lines of simple math, and get a realistic answer in under five minutes.

Here is how to measure what your server can actually handle and how to turn those numbers into a real server budget.

Step 1: Pull Your Real Numbers From the Server

Before you calculate anything, you need to know what your server is doing right now. SSH into your VPS and run these four commands.

1. Check your CPU, RAM, and disk space 

echo "CPU Cores: $(nproc)" && free -m && df -h /

Look at the available RAM column (in MB) and your CPU core count. That available RAM is the main ceiling for how much traffic your server can take.

2. Check how much RAM each PHP-FPM worker uses

This is the most important number for a PHP or Laravel stack. Every incoming request needs a PHP worker to process it, and each worker eats a slice of your RAM.

ps aux | grep '[p]hp-fpm: pool' | awk '{sum+=$6; n++} END {if(n>0) printf "Active Workers: %d | Avg RAM/Worker: %.2f MB\n", n, sum/n/1024; else print "No workers found"}'

This tells you how many workers are currently running and the average megabytes each one consumes.

3. Check your Redis memory usage

If you use Redis for caching on the same VPS, you need to know how much RAM it's taking and whether it has a limit set.

redis-cli info memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human"

If maxmemory_human says 0B, it means Redis has no memory cap. Keep an eye on that an uncapped Redis instance can quietly eat into the RAM your app needs.

4. Measure your request processing time (TTFB)

Now, measure how long your server actually takes to generate a response. This is called Time to First Byte (TTFB).

Replace your-domain.com with your actual domain. Run it once on a light, cached page (your best-case scenario) and once on a heavy, database-driven page like a dashboard or search page (your worst-case scenario):

# Best-Case (light or cached page)
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "Best-Case -> Server Time (TTFB): %{time_starttransfer}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" https://your-domain.com/

# Worst-Case (heavy or dynamic page)
curl -o /dev/null -s -w "Worst-Case -> Server Time (TTFB): %{time_starttransfer}s | Total: %{time_total}s\n" https://your-domain.com/heavy-page-url

Step 2: Do the Math Yourself

Once you have those four outputs, you don't need a black-box calculator. You can verify everything by hand in three steps.

1. Find your safe number of PHP workers ($W$)

Never plan to use 100% of your available RAM. Leave at least 20% as a safety buffer for the operating system, Nginx, and Redis. Divide the remaining 80% by the average RAM per PHP worker:

(Tip: If you only have 1 CPU core, don't push $W$ too high even if you have spare RAM too many workers fighting for one core will just slow everything down.)

2. Calculate Requests Per Second ($RPS$)

Divide your safe worker count by your server processing time (TTFB in seconds):

Run this twice:

  • Best-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your light, cached page.
  • Worst-Case RPS: Use the TTFB from your heavy, dynamic page.

3. Estimate concurrent active users

Real people don't click a new link every single second. After a page loads, a user usually spends 5 to 10 seconds reading, scrolling, or filling out a form before clicking again. Performance engineers call this Think Time.

A quick real-world example

Think of your server like a small ticket counter.

Suppose your math gives you $W = 5$ workers (5 staff members behind the counter). If your app is well-cached and takes 0.2 seconds to handle a request:

If each visitor spends an average of 5 seconds reading a page before clicking again:

That means your small server can comfortably handle around 125 people browsing at the same time.

Now flip it to the worst case. If a heavy page with unoptimized database queries takes 1.0 second to load, your capacity drops to 5 RPS meaning only 25 to 50 active users before people start waiting in line and seeing 502 Bad Gateway errors.

Step 3: How Tech and Business Teams Turn This Into a Budget

Knowing your server's limit is great for debugging, but it becomes even more useful when you sit down with a business developer or client to plan server costs. Here is how experienced tech leads bridge the gap between terminal outputs and a budget spreadsheet:

  1. Start with a baseline: Use the math above to establish a clear benchmark for example, "Our current $6/month VPS comfortably handles 100 active users."
  2. Apply the 3x Peak Traffic Rule: If the business team expects 50 active users on a normal Tuesday, don't budget for 50. During a holiday sale, a viral post, or an ad push, traffic easily spikes to 3x the normal load (150 users). Always size your server for the peak, not the average.
  3. Stick to the 70% Safety Threshold: Never wait until your RAM or CPU hits 100% to upgrade. Plan your budget so that once sustained peak traffic crosses 70% of your server's capacity, you automatically move up to the next tier.
  4. Calculate Cost per Active User: Once you know your baseline, you can tell the business team exactly what it costs to support every 100 or 1,000 active users. That makes it easy for them to factor infrastructure costs directly into product pricing or marketing budgets.

event_model_payload.headline: I built Diviso — a local-first AI agent that runs on your own machine, even on a phone
event_model_payload.summary:
Most AI agents I tried wanted an account, a subscription, and my data on someone else's server. I wanted the opposite, so I built Diviso.

It's a Python agent that runs entirely on your own machine. Point it at a local model through Ollama, or plug in OpenAI, Claude, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek or OpenRouter with your own key. No Diviso account, no server of mine in the middle.

What's inside

  • ReAct loop + a planner, with hard step and cost caps on every run
  • Persistent memory (SQLite + a plain MEMORY.md) and TF-IDF search over your local files
  • A small multi-agent team (Researcher / Coder / Reviewer)
  • Tools for Python, JavaScript and Bash, file edits, tests, read-only git, web fetch — all behind an approval gate and a workspace sandbox
  • MCP client, a guarded scheduler, checkpoint/resume after every step
  • CLI + a small web dashboard

The part I'm happiest with

The core is standard-library-only Python, so the same code runs on a GPU PC, an old laptop, and an Android phone under Termux. It detects your hardware and picks a lite / balanced / pro profile with model sizes that actually fit.

Honest limits

It's v0.1.0. No token streaming yet, and the cloud providers are implemented against their documented APIs — the offline test suite (74 tests, CI green) runs on a deterministic mock provider. Local Ollama is the main path I test by hand.

Repo: https://github.com/Neuzant/diviso-agent

Feedback very welcome — especially from anyone who runs it on weird hardware.

event_model_payload.headline: The stock client is already post-quantum
event_model_payload.summary:
I probed github.com's SSH service twice in one week, with the same tool and the same options. The first run, from my Ubuntu 24.04 laptop, said two post-quantum key exchanges worked only with the experimental Open Quantum Safe client. The second run, from a Debian 13 container, said the stock client and the experimental client negotiate identically.

GitHub had not changed anything. My client had. Debian 13 ships a newer OpenSSH, and that release already does what I was using an experimental build for.

This post is about that shift: stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH now negotiate post-quantum key exchange out of the box, which changes what a "stock versus experimental" comparison can tell you, and what a post-quantum audit should actually measure.

Part 4 of a series on building pqc-probe. Earlier: part 1, part 2, part 3.

What changed in the stock clients

Post-quantum key exchange arrived in the mainstream tools in a few releases:

Date Release Post-quantum key exchange
Apr 2025 OpenSSH 10.0 mlkem768x25519-sha256 becomes the default
8 Apr 2025 OpenSSL 3.5.0 default TLS key shares become X25519MLKEM768 and X25519
19 Sep 2024 OpenSSH 9.9 adds mlkem768x25519-sha256, enabled by default; adds the name sntrup761x25519-sha512
Apr 2022 OpenSSH 9.0 sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com becomes the default

The OpenSSL change is easy to miss because it is one line in the source. The 3.5 default group list begins with ?*X25519MLKEM768, and the * means the client sends an ML-KEM hybrid key share in every handshake, next to a classical X25519 one. A server that understands ML-KEM can complete a post-quantum handshake without a single extra round trip. OpenSSL 3.0, still common on long-term-support distributions, has no ML-KEM at all.

OpenSSH went further in 10.1, which by default warns the user when a connection is not using a post-quantum key exchange.

Same server, two client machines

GitHub's SSH service offers three post-quantum key exchanges: mlkem768x25519-sha256, sntrup761x25519-sha512 and its older name sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com. Here is what pqc-probe reported against it from each machine:

Ubuntu 24.04 laptop Debian 13 container
Stock SSH client OpenSSH 9.6p1 OpenSSH 10.0p2
mlkem768x25519-sha256 with the stock client not implemented completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512 with the stock client not implemented under this name completed
sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com with the stock client completed completed
Stock versus OQS client diff 2 algorithms "only experimental" none

The laptop's OpenSSH 9.6 predates 9.9, so it lacks ML-KEM and the newer sntrup name. It still completes a post-quantum exchange through the older @openssh.com name, which every OpenSSH since 9.0 uses by default. The Debian container's 10.0 does all three.

The report from the laptop was correct; it described the laptop. Read naively, though, it suggested that GitHub needs an experimental client for ML-KEM, which is not true for anyone on a current OpenSSH.

What the diff still tells you

A "stock versus experimental" diff measures the gap between two clients against one server. When the stock client was classical-only, that gap was a fair stand-in for "what the server supports beyond the mainstream". With post-quantum stock clients, it splits into two different findings, and pqc-probe now labels them apart:

  • Newer mainline, not experimental. An algorithm only the OQS client negotiates may simply be one your stock client is too old for. pqc-probe marks these with the first mainline release that has them, for example mlkem768x25519-sha256 (stock OpenSSH since 9.9). The fix is to update the client, not to adopt an experimental build.
  • Genuinely experimental. Names such as frodokem-976-shake-sha384 or the @openquantumsafe.org hybrids exist only in OQS builds. A server that offers them is running experimental software, which is worth knowing for a different reason.

For TLS the effect is stronger. A stock OpenSSL 3.5 client already completes X25519MLKEM768 wherever the server allows it, so an empty TLS diff no longer means the server is classical. When the stock client itself negotiated a post-quantum group, pqc-probe says so in the report (vanilla_pq_capable), because the diff then says little about the server.

What it means for an audit

A connection is post-quantum only when both ends support it. A server audit answers half the question; the clients that actually connect answer the other half.

  1. Measure the server with a current client. Use OpenSSL 3.5+ and OpenSSH 10+ (or pqc-probe's Docker image, which carries both). An old client makes a capable server look incapable.
  2. Know your client population. Long-term-support systems keep their versions for years: Ubuntu 24.04 ships OpenSSH 9.6, which has sntrup761 but no ML-KEM, and OpenSSL 3.0, which has no post-quantum key exchange at all. Build agents, deploy scripts, backup jobs and the SSH clients on your own servers count too. Until they are upgraded, a server's ML-KEM support does nothing for their TLS connections, and their SSH connections stay on the older sntrup761 exchange.
  3. Record the client with the result. A finding such as "ML-KEM not negotiated" is meaningless without the client version that produced it. pqc-probe's JSON reports include the client versions for exactly this reason.

The practical consequence: "our servers support post-quantum key exchange" and "our connections are post-quantum" are two different claims, and only the second one protects traffic today against harvest-now, decrypt-later collection.

The comparison is shrinking, and that is good news

When I started pqc-probe, the interesting output was the diff: what the experimental client could do that the stock one could not. For the most common algorithms, that gap has largely closed. ML-KEM hybrids are in stock OpenSSL and OpenSSH, on by default, and negotiated without anyone asking for them.

That moves the useful question from "can it be done?" to "is it being done, by every client that matters?" The answer now depends far more on how old your clients are than on anything exotic on the server, and the cheapest post-quantum upgrade available to most teams is a routine package update.

Next in the series: shipping two liboqs builds in one container, and two GCC 14 bugs found on the way.

event_model_payload.headline: PHP's November 2026 Security Release: How to Check, Patch and Restart (and What's New in PHP 8.6)
event_model_payload.summary:
On November 19, 2026, PHP shipped PHP 8.6.0 and, on the same afternoon, security releases for every supported branch: 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36. The security releases fix 17 vulnerabilities, seven rated critical. PHP says the critical ones need non-default settings or uncommon setups, but several can lead to running code on the server.

The ones most likely to matter:

  • CVE-2026-129289, PHP-FPM request smuggling. If nginx (fastcgi_keep_conn on) or Apache (enablereuse=on) reuses FastCGI connections, leftover bytes from a request body can be read as a second, forged request that can run code. Standard setups that close the connection aren't affected by the demonstrated attack.
  • Three session bugs (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129481), including the upload-progress issue PHP warned about in October. Session upload progress is now off by default.
  • Two PHP 8.5-only bugs in the new fatal-error backtraces. The production setting zend.exception_ignore_args=1 blocks the demonstrated attack.
  • CVE-2026-129291, which can turn a compromised FPM worker into root when catch_workers_output is on, as it is in the official Docker images.

Check properly. Ubuntu and Debian backport fixes without changing the version, so a patched Ubuntu 24.04 still reports PHP 8.3.6. Look for the CVE in the package changelog instead: zcat /usr/share/doc/php*-common/changelog.Debian.gz | grep -m1 CVE-2026-129289. The fixed Ubuntu 24.04 package is 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.14.

Then update and restart PHP-FPM (or Apache for mod_php). Docker users should rebuild on the new php: images.

If you skipped October's release, this matters even more: the PHP2Shell bugs it fixed have been on CISA's list of exploited vulnerabilities since October 26, and this update covers them too.

PHP 8.6 brings partial function application, a \Time\Duration class, clamp(), a SortDirection enum and readonly property defaults. Patch first and test 8.6 later. The exception is PHP 8.2, whose support ends on December 31, 2026.

  • GHSA-8mjj-2r7p-4hg2: Use-after-free in magic method backtraces (CVE-2026-129474)

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing ONCSS: A Lightweight CSS-in-JS Library for Modern JavaScript Applications
event_model_payload.summary:
I've been working on ONCSS, a CSS-in-JS library designed to make styling modern web applications simple, flexible, and developer-friendly.

Instead of writing separate CSS files for every component, ONCSS lets you define styles directly in JavaScript using a familiar object-based API.

Why ONCSS?

ONCSS provides a css() function that generates and injects CSS dynamically.

Here's a quick example:

import css from "oncss";

const button = css({
  backgroundColor: "#2563eb",
  color: "#fff",
  padding: "10px 20px",
  borderRadius: "8px",

  "&:hover": {
    backgroundColor: "#1d4ed8",
  },

  "@media (min-width: 768px)": {
    padding: "14px 28px",
  },
});

function Button() {
  return <button className={button}>Click mebutton>;
}

Features

  • Object-based CSS styling
  • Nested selectors and pseudo-classes
  • Responsive media queries
  • Custom breakpoints
  • Dynamic keyframes and animations
  • Global styles
  • CSS at-rules: @media, @container, @layer, @supports
  • Custom aliases and CSS property transformations
  • Configurable style injection
  • TypeScript support
  • Server-side rendering support

Installation 

npm install oncss

Built for flexibility

ONCSS also supports customization through configuration options such as classPrefix, breakpoints, aliases, injectStyle, and custom property handlers.

It also provides CSSFactory for collecting generated styles during server-side rendering.

I'm building ONCSS as an open-source project and would appreciate feedback from developers who work with React and modern JavaScript styling.

Check it out:

  • GitHub: https://github.com/devnax/oncss
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/oncss

If you try it, I'd love to hear what you think and what features you'd like to see next.

event_model_payload.headline: How do we get 1 TW a year of orbital compute by 2035?
event_model_payload.summary:
- 50k Starship V4 launches a year, each carrying 200 t (20 MW of compute). That’s 137 a day, one every 2 minutes in two windows of roughly 5–7am and 5–7pm local. As Earth spins, the launch site passes under that target orbit twice a day, at local dawn and local dusk. Globally we’re at about 1 launch a day right now.

- The always-sunlit orbit needs launches heading north or south over open water. On US coasts only south works, and packing every usable spot with Starship pads gets us to just 25–30 launches a day. We need 5× that.

- So we will go out to sea, 300 km off central California. Inside the US EEZ, clear of Cape Mendocino, between the air routes to Hawaii and Asia. Open water both ways gives us both daily windows.

- We will place 35 floating pads in one 68 km row, so no rocket flies over another pad. The water is 4 km deep, so thrusters hold the pads in place.

- Need a huge daily supply: 190 kt of LNG, 680 kt of liquid oxygen, 27 kt of satellites. - About 7 LNG tankers and 10 liquid-oxygen tankers in constant rotation. - Roughly a container ship a day of satellites from LA, so 2–3 ships in rotation. - About 20 shuttles refilling pads between windows.

- The gas for all that is 2.5 times what all of California uses. The California Coastal Commission has really not been playing ball with such things so far.

- So we make it in Mexico. Baja’s Costa Azul terminal already turns US pipeline gas into LNG, so we expand that site with much bigger LNG production, a liquid-oxygen plant, new pipeline capacity from Texas to Baja and 20 GW of power. This would be one of the biggest natural gas sites on Earth.

Unexplored territory: - Terafab (we need at lesat 0.5M wafer starts per day, mostly memory. This is 10x more than TSMC makes today. maybe doable by 2035) - Starship V4 (scheduled for 2027) catching booster and ship at sea (Falcon boosters already do sea landings with legs) - large liquid-oxygen carriers (essentially an LNG carrier with oxidizer safety) - starship-scale floating pads (Sea Launch did this two decades ago. event_model_payload.headline: This Industrial Revolution Belongs to the Builders
event_model_payload.summary:
You've heard AI = Labor. Therefore Labor -> 0.

Some people think this means that only asset owners, people with lots of capital, will come out ahead.

They're wrong.

Because as a builder/founder, you create value.

Capital must capture some of this value to have a return.

The reason founders primarily need capital is to pay for labor (either employees or supplier overhead).

So this means that Capital ~= Labor.

But that's a problem for the "owners of capital will own everything" narrative, because now we have:

AI = Labor = Capital -> 0

In practice this will happen slowly as builders need less and less capital to build, capital will increasingly struggle to capture value created by builders.

Counterintuitively this means valuations will climb dramatically reflecting capital paying more and more to capture less and less value from builders.

As disruption accelerates, volatility increases while broader market wide returns start to stagnate.

The net will be a wholesale wealth and power transfer from capital holders to builders/founders, on the magnitude of what happened between the aristocracy and the capitalist class in the earlier industrial revolutions.

It's already started, companies are raising later and at higher valuations.

Most people accept that if superintelligence were created, capital would be useless, but what they often don't realize is that a class of builders armed with AI is already creating a distributed superintelligence that will have the same effect.

Interested if anyone else shares this perspective.

Some of the best technical insights come from sharing what you've built and what you've learned along the way.

That's one of the core ideas behind Unprompted, the blog we launched on Medium earlier this year to give Grafana Labs engineers and our broader OSS community a space to showcase their work. From behind-the-scenes engineering stories and technical deep dives to creative use cases for Grafana (a fishing dashboard, anyone?), it's a place to share ideas and learn from one another.

To give you a sense of what you'll find, we've rounded up a few recent posts covering everything from Grafana's architecture to monitoring your favorite reality TV show.

Behind the scenes at Grafana Labs

These posts explore some of the technical challenges our teams have tackled at Grafana Labs, including the decisions, tradeoffs, and lessons that shaped their work. 

Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding mode

Making an AI agent faster, more reliable, and less expensive takes a lot more than fine-tuning your prompts. Senior Software Engineer Dominik Broj shares how the team used production telemetry, offline evaluations, and Agent Observability to improve dashboarding mode in Grafana Assistant, reducing error rates by 73%, latency p95 by 50%, and cost by 18%.

How and why we're bringing data sources out of the Grafana monolith

Grafana data sources have historically been closely tied to the Grafana monolith. To make it easier to develop, maintain, and release data source plugins independently of Grafana's core release cycle, the team has been working to decouple them from the monolith. But what does that entail, exactly? Kate Vredenburgh, Senior Manager, Engineering, walks through it all, including the challenges of migrating existing code and how the team used AI agents to help along the way.

How we provision Grafana Play dashboards at scale with Git Sync and Terraform

event_model_payload.headline: Vercel Functions now support request bodies up to 20MiB
event_model_payload.summary:
Vercel Functions now accept inbound request bodies up to 20MiB, up from 4.5MB, in Public Beta.

To turn this on, set the VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_REQUEST_BODY=1 environment variable. The opt-in applies to the whole project in the environment where you set it, so you can test the larger limit on preview before enabling it in production. It requires the project's functions to use the performance memory setting of 4GB. It applies to functions on the Node.js, Python, and Bun runtimes, and to Routing Middleware. Functions and Routing Middleware on the Edge runtime keep the 4.5MB cap and return 413 on oversize bodies, so moving them onto the larger limit means switching to the Node.js runtime with runtime: 'nodejs', or proxy.ts in Next.js.

When a project opts in, Routing Middleware receives request headers and metadata but no request body, enforced at the project level. Middleware still runs and still sees every other request header, so body-dependent middleware behavior is the one thing that becomes unavailable. This avoids sending the body twice, to both middleware and the target function, which would raise cost and time to first byte.

When handling larger request bodies, read the body promptly and avoid holding it in memory to prevent backpressure and memory issues.

Learn more in the Vercel Functions limitations documentation.

event_model_payload.headline: How to let Claude Code, Codex or Cursor build a robot simulation
event_model_payload.summary:
Coding agents are good at writing Python, but robot simulation is a hard place for them: scenes fail in confusing ways, the first run compiles for minutes, and a simulation that quietly blew up can look like a success. This walkthrough sets up Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning, so an agent like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor can build and run simulations on its own, either through plain Python or through an MCP server.

pip install alloy-engine

1. Point the agent at docs written for agents

The package ships its docs, examples and a quick start written for agents. An agent can find them itself:

python -m alloy.docs          # prints three paths: the docs, the examples and AGENTS.md
python -m alloy.docs agents   # prints AGENTS.md, a quick start for agents

A good first prompt is simply: "Install alloy-engine, run python -m alloy.docs agents, and build me a scene where a robot arm pours water into a cup."

2. Or give it the engine as MCP tools

Alloy includes an MCP server, so the agent gets operations such as scene, build, run, state, check and render as tools instead of writing code. For Claude Code:

claude mcp add alloy -- alloy mcp

Other MCP clients (Cursor, Codex and so on) take the same command, alloy mcp, as a local stdio server.

3. The loop that keeps an agent honest

Two habits make agent-built simulations reliable: read the error's fix, and check the world after every run.

import alloy

scene = alloy.Scene(dt=0.01)
scene.add_ground()
scene.add_box("block", size=(0.05, 0.05, 0.05), pos=(0, 0, 0.1))
try:
    scene.add_box("thin", size=(0.05, 0.05))          # a typical agent mistake
except alloy.AlloyAPIError as e:
    print(e.message)
    print(e.fix)
sim = alloy.build(scene, device="cpu")
sim.run(0.5)
print(sim.check()["ok"], round(float(sim.state(world=0)["block.pos"][2]), 3))

size needs 3 finite numbers, got (0.05, 0.05)
pass size=(..., ..., ...) in m
True 0.025

Every error carries a message and a fix that names what to pass, so the agent can correct itself without guessing. After the run the block rests on the ground with its centre at 0.025 m, and sim.check()["ok"] is True.

Keep in mind

  • Tell the agent to print sim.check()["ok"] after every run: a frozen, broken world looks calm in a render.
  • The first run of each kind of scene compiles for minutes. Tell the agent not to stop it.
  • The docs keep the full list of limits.

Links

  • Docs page this is based on: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/how-to/coding-agents/
  • Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16312

event_model_payload.headline: A LangChain chat model that doesn't refuse your security tasks (Python and JS)
event_model_payload.summary:
Disclosure: I work on InterOdin, the API used in this tutorial. Any OpenAI-compatible provider plugs in the same way.

LangChain pipelines for security work, like log summarisers, alert enrichment or report drafting, break in an annoying way when the model refuses half the inputs. LangChain's OpenAI chat model accepts a custom base URL, so you can put Odin v1 behind an existing chain without touching the rest of it.

Python 

pip install langchain-openai

import os

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(
    model="odin-v1",
    base_url="https://api.interodin.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["INTERODIN_API_KEY"],
)

print(llm.invoke("Name three Norse gods.").content)

for chunk in llm.stream("Write a haiku about Odin."):
    print(chunk.content, end="", flush=True)

Tools and structured output 

from langchain_core.tools import tool
from pydantic import BaseModel


@tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the current weather for a city."""
    return f"14°C in {city}"


reply = llm.bind_tools([get_weather]).invoke("What is the weather in Cluj?")
print(reply.tool_calls)


class Person(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int


person = llm.with_structured_output(Person).invoke("Extract the person: Ana is 31.")
print(person)

Using langchain-anthropic instead

ChatAnthropic takes the origin, without /v1:

import os

from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

llm = ChatAnthropic(
    model="odin-v1",
    base_url="https://api.interodin.com",
    api_key=os.environ["INTERODIN_API_KEY"],
    max_tokens=1024,
)
print(llm.invoke("Name three Norse gods.").content)

JavaScript / TypeScript 

npm install @langchain/openai @langchain/core

import { ChatOpenAI } from '@langchain/openai'

const llm = new ChatOpenAI({
  model: 'odin-v1',
  apiKey: process.env.INTERODIN_API_KEY,
  configuration: { baseURL: 'https://api.interodin.com/v1' },
})

const reply = await llm.invoke('Name three Norse gods.')
console.log(reply.content)

for await (const chunk of await llm.stream('Write a haiku about Odin.')) {
  process.stdout.write(String(chunk.content))
}

Token usage is reported in response_metadata on each reply.

Limits

  • Built-in (hosted) tools are removed from the request; your own tools run.
  • Odin v1 is text-only; file inputs in the newest message fail with 400 unsupported_content.
  • Billing is prepaid credits per token, with no subscription. API prompts and completions are not stored.

Fewer refusals does not mean no rules: the Acceptable Use Policy forbids illegal and harmful uses, so keep it to systems and data you are authorised to work on.

The maintained version of this guide lives in the docs: https://docs.interodin.com/en/integrations/langchain

event_model_payload.headline: Ventoy: Turn One USB Stick Into an Installer for Almost Any OS
event_model_payload.summary:
Ventoy turns one USB stick into an installer for almost any operating system. Install it once, copy your ISO files onto the drive, and pick one from the boot menu. No reformatting, no extraction, no starting over every time a new distro comes out.

What Ventoy Is: One USB Stick, Every Operating System

Ventoy is a free open source tool to create a bootable USB drive for ISO, WIM, IMG, VHD(x), and EFI files, and it has 80,968 stars on GitHub with more than 17 million downloads. The idea is almost too simple to believe: install Ventoy on a USB stick once, and from then on you never format the drive again. You just copy image files onto it and boot them. It is licensed under GPL-3.0, it is 100 percent open source, and it runs on Windows and Linux. If you have ever kept a drawer full of USB sticks, one for Windows, one for Ubuntu, one for a rescue disk, Ventoy replaces the whole drawer with a single stick.

How It Works: Copy the ISO, Pick It From the Boot Menu

The normal way to make a bootable USB is slow and destructive. You pick an ISO, you run a flashing tool, the tool wipes the drive and writes the image, and the stick becomes a single-purpose installer until you wipe it again for the next ISO. Ventoy breaks that cycle. After the one-time install, the USB drive stays an ordinary drive. You copy as many image files onto it as fit, plug it in, and Ventoy shows you a boot menu to select one. The files do not even need to be stored in one continuous block on the disk, and there is no extraction step: Ventoy boots directly from the ISO, WIM, IMG, VHD(x), or EFI file as it sits on the drive. When a new distro version comes out, you delete the old ISO, copy the new one, and you are done. You can also browse ISO files stored on a local disk and boot them from there, without copying them to the USB at all.

1300+ ISOs Tested: Windows, Linux, and Everything Else

Ventoy supports most types of operating system, and the project has tested more than 1,300 ISO files. On the Windows side that means Windows 7, 8, 8.1, 10, and 11, plus Windows Server 2012 through 2025 and WinPE rescue environments. On Linux it covers Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, Manjaro, Linux Mint, Kali, Tails, Pop!_OS, NixOS, Gentoo, and more than 90 percent of the distros listed on DistroWatch. Unix systems like FreeBSD, pfSense, OPNsense, and TrueNAS work too, along with ChromeOS Flex and FydeOS, VMware ESXi, and Citrix XenServer. It supports x86 legacy BIOS, IA32 UEFI, x86_64 UEFI, ARM64 UEFI, and MIPS64EL UEFI, and both MBR and GPT partition styles. If you run a homelab, do IT support, or just like trying new distros, one Ventoy stick holds your entire toolkit.

Persistence, Secure Boot, and Auto Install

Ventoy is not just a boot menu. It supports Linux persistence, so a live distro can remember your files and settings between boots instead of resetting every time. It supports UEFI Secure Boot, which matters on modern laptops that refuse to boot unsigned media. It supports Windows and Linux auto installation, with variable expansion in the install scripts, so you can build a hands-off installer that sets up a machine exactly the way you want it. It handles ISO files larger than 4 GB, supports FAT32, exFAT, NTFS, UDF, XFS, Btrfs, and Ext2/3/4 on the main partition, and it can boot Linux vDisk images and Windows VHD files. There is a plugin framework behind all of this, plus VentoyPlugson, a graphical configurator for the plugins, so you do not have to hand-edit JSON to turn features on.

Password Protection and Themes: Make the Boot Menu Yours

A USB stick full of installers is worth protecting, and Ventoy has a password plugin that locks the boot menu behind a password you set. A weak password defeats the point, so generate a long one with a Random String Generator and store it somewhere safe before you set it. Ventoy also lets you reshape the menu itself: menu aliases and tips, a password prompt, a tree view mode instead of a flat list, and fully customizable themes for the legacy and UEFI boot menus. The menu can switch between list and tree view on the fly, and you can inject files into the runtime environment or replace boot configuration files dynamically. It is the rare utility that stays out of your way by default and still lets power users tune almost everything.

Installing Ventoy: Windows, Linux, and Upgrades

Getting started takes a few minutes. On Windows, download the release from the official website, ventoy.net, run the installer, pick your USB drive, and click install. On Linux, download the tarball and run the Ventoy2Disk.sh script from a terminal. The script needs to be executable before it will run, so if your system refuses it, a quick Chmod Calculator check gives you the exact permission number to set. Once installed, the USB drive still works as a normal drive for everyday files, and upgrading Ventoy later does not destroy your data: the upgrade keeps your ISO files and settings in place. You also never need to update Ventoy itself just because a new distro was released. Copy the new ISO, boot it, and move on.

FAQs

What is Ventoy?

Ventoy is a free open source tool that turns a USB stick into a bootable drive for ISO, WIM, IMG, VHD(x), and EFI files. Install it once, then copy image files onto the drive and pick one from the boot menu. You never need to format the drive again to switch operating systems.

Is Ventoy really free?

Yes. Ventoy is completely free and open source under the GPL-3.0 license. There is no paid version, no subscription, and no account. The project accepts donations, but every feature works without paying anything.

Can I put multiple ISOs on one USB stick with Ventoy?

Yes, that is the whole point. You can copy as many ISO, WIM, IMG, VHD(x), or EFI files onto the drive as fit, and Ventoy shows a boot menu to select one at startup. More than 1,300 ISO files have been tested with it.

Does Ventoy work with Windows 11 and Secure Boot?

Yes. Ventoy supports Windows 7 through Windows 11, plus Windows Server and WinPE, and it supports IA32 and x86_64 UEFI Secure Boot. It also supports legacy BIOS, ARM64 UEFI, and both MBR and GPT partition styles.

Does installing Ventoy erase my USB drive?

The first install does format the drive, so back up anything on it first. After that, adding or removing ISO files is just copying and deleting files, and upgrading Ventoy later is data nondestructive: your files and settings stay in place.

What is Ventoy persistence?

Persistence lets a live Linux distro remember your files and settings between boots instead of resetting every time. Ventoy supports Linux persistence through its plugin system, so a live USB can behave more like a real installed system.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/ventoy. Repo: ventoy/Ventoy.

event_model_payload.headline: Hackaday wrote about my STL to CAD tool, and the first bug report it brought was a good one
event_model_payload.summary:
This week Hackaday ran a short piece on mesh2cad, my open source tool that turns an STL of a simple mechanical part into STEP or an editable CadQuery, OpenSCAD or FreeCAD script: https://hackaday.com/2026/11/19/mesh2cad-automates-re-modelling/

The repo went from 14 to around 80 stars in a day, which is more than the previous month. More useful than the stars was the first proper bug report from someone I don't know.

What the report found

The reporter converted a noisy test plate (80 x 50 x 6 mm, four holes) and opened the STEP with OCP instead of trusting the exit code. The solid was inside-out. Negative volume, written with exit 0. On another seed the solid was valid but about 6 mm away from the mesh.

The cause was in the fallback path. When a least squares snap moved a vertex too far, the code projected that vertex onto the first fitted surface instead, with no distance check. On a thin plate the first surface was sometimes the opposite wall, so the top face got pulled down by the plate thickness.

What changed in 0.32.0

The projection is now guarded too: if it moves the vertex more than the snap limit, the original vertex stays. Then, before anything is written, the writer checks the signed volume. A reversed solid gets flipped. A snapped hybrid whose volume misses the mesh by more than 5%, or that sits too far from the mesh, is dropped and the plain faceted solid is written instead. An inside-out solid is never written.

The report also said one of the Original Prusa i3 parts came back faceted on 0.31.0. I could not reproduce that: on 0.22.0 and 0.32.0 it is exact (210 planes, 4 cylinders), and the sewing code did not change in between. I added a slow test that locks the face counts of all six Prusa parts, and asked for the reporter's OCP version.

Limits, same as before

mesh2cad is for brackets, plates and similar parts made of planes, cylinders and cones. Organic shapes, figurines and scans with heavy noise still come out faceted or are refused. That is on purpose: I would rather it say no than write a wrong solid, and this bug was exactly the case where it did not say no.

pip install -U mesh2cad
mesh2cad convert part.stl part.step

Repo: https://github.com/emirmrkaljevic/mesh2cad

If you have an STL that converts badly, an issue with the file attached helps more than anything else.
