event_model_payload.headline: 이런건어때 파일 용량을 줄여도 LCP가 줄어들지 않는 이유?
event_model_payload.summary:
글. 박수봉(Henby) / 서비스웹개발팀

안녕하세요. 서비스웹개발팀 헨비입니다.

이미지와 로딩 우선순위, JS 번들을 수정하여 상품 상세 페이지의 데이터 전송량을 26.3MB에서 10.8MB까지 줄였습니다. 총 59%를 감량했습니다.

그런데 대표 이미지가 화면에 뜨는 시간은 17.8초에서 16.0초로 줄어드는 데 그쳤습니다. 고작 1.8초(10%)였습니다.

전송량이 절반 넘게 줄어들었는데 당연히 속도도 비슷하게 빨라질 줄 알았습니다. 원인을 찾아가 보니 전송량도 이미지 크기도 아니었습니다. 실제로 수정한 것은 공용 이미지 컴포넌트의 두 줄입니다. 상용에 배포한 뒤 실제 브라우저에서 측정한 대표 이미지 표시 시간은 2.3초에서 0.48초가 됐습니다.

15MB를 줄였는데 왜 1.8초였을까요?

전송량은 59%를 줄였는데 LCP는 10%만 줄었습니다. LCP(가장 큰 콘텐츠가 그려지는 시점)는 보통 대표 이미지가 보이는 순간입니다. 그러니 이미지가 줄어들면 LCP도 그만큼 줄어든다고 생각하기 쉽죠. 저 또한 그렇게 생각했습니다.

Lighthouse는 LCP를 네 구간으로 나눠서 보여줍니다. 최적화 전후를 나란히 놓으면 아래와 같습니다.

측정 조건은 Lighthouse 12.8.2 CLI, 모바일(Moto G·4G), 5회 중앙값, 서드파티 스크립트 차단, 비로그인·콜드 캐시입니다. 실사용자 데이터(RUM)는 없고 전부 합성 측정값입니다.

Lighthouse는 기본으로 시뮬레이션 스로틀링을 씁니다. 위 숫자는 느린 기기와 4G 회선을 가정한 추정치라 사용자가 체감하는 절대 시간은 아닙니다. 이 글의 Lighthouse 숫자는 모두 같은 기준이라 서로 비교할 수 있습니다. 실제 브라우저로 측정한 값은 뒤에 따로 적었습니다.

최적화 전 상품상세. LCP 17.5초.

이미지 최적화가 직접 줄일 수 있는 구간은 Load Time 하나입니다. 3.11초에서 1.32초로 1.8초 줄었습니다. LCP가 줄어든 폭도 1.8초였죠.

줄이고 나서도 12초가 Render Delay로 남았습니다. 이미지를 다 받아 놓고 화면에 그리기까지 기다린 시간이라 이미지를 줄여서는 건드릴 수 없습니다.

26.3MB 열의 앞 세 구간을 더하면 5.2초입니다. 서버 응답부터 이미지 요청, 다운로드까지 다 더한 값이니 대표 이미지는 이때 이미 브라우저에 도착해 있었습니다.

그런데 화면에 보인 건 17.8초였습니다.

범인은 이미지 컴포넌트였습니다

미지는 5.2초에 도착했지만 화면에 나온 건 hydration이 끝난 17.8초였습니다.

Render Delay가 끝나는 시점을 찾아보니 TTI와 거의 겹치더라고요. React의 hydration이 끝나는 순간입니다.

잠깐, 용어 정리
SSR(서버 사이드 렌더링)은 서버가 화면을 HTML로 미리 그려서 보내는 방식입니다. 브라우저는 그 HTML을 먼저 띄우고, 뒤따라 받은 JS를 실행해 클릭이나 이미지 onLoad 같은 이벤트 핸들러를 붙입니다. 이 작업이 hydration입니다. 그 전까지 화면은 보이지만 눌러도 반응하지 않고, hydration이 끝나 페이지가 반응하기 시작하는 시점이 TTI입니다.

원인을 찾아 디자인 시스템의 이미지 컴포넌트를 열어봤습니다.

const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(true);   // ① 초기값 true
  style={{
    opacity: isLoading ? 0 : 1,                     // ② 그래서 처음엔 투명
    transition: 'opacity 0.3s ease-in-out',
  }}
  src={src}
  onLoad={() => setIsLoading(false)}                // ③ 이걸 붙이는 건 hydration 이후
/>

로딩 중에는 투명하게 두고 스켈레톤 박스를 보여주다가, 다 받으면 부드럽게 나타나게 하는 코드입니다. 화면만 보면 좋은 처리죠.

세 줄이 서버 사이드 렌더링과 만나면 이렇게 됩니다.

  1. isLoading의 초기값이 true입니다. 서버가 내려주는 HTML부터 이미 opacity: 0입니다.
  2. 브라우저는 그 를 보고 이미지를 받습니다. 이미지를 다 다운로드했지만 아직은 투명합니다.
  3. 이미지를 다시 표시해 주는 것은 onLoad 핸들러인데, 그 핸들러는 JS가 실행되고 hydration이 끝나야 붙습니다.

그래서 이미지가 아무리 빨리 다운로드되어도 JS가 다 실행될 때까지 기다리게 됩니다. LCP가 hydration 완료 시점이 됩니다.

다른 상품 상세 페이지도 같았습니다. 최적화를 전부 적용한 뒤 이미지는 2.7초에 도착했는데 LCP는 15.6초였습니다. 13초 가까이 기다린 겁니다.

이 구조가 흔한 이유

로딩 상태를 가진 이미지 컴포넌트는 웬만한 디자인 시스템에 다 있습니다. useState(true)로 시작하는 것도 자연스럽습니다. 아직 안 받았으니 true가 맞으니까요.

CSR이라면 맞는 코드입니다. 첫 렌더부터 브라우저에서 일어나니 onLoad 핸들러도 처음부터 붙어 있고, 이미지가 도착하면 바로 보입니다.

하지만 SSR에서는 초기값의 의미가 달라집니다.

그 opacity: 0은 서버가 내려주는 HTML에 박혀서 네트워크를 타고 날아가고 JS 번들이 도착해 실행될 때까지 유지됩니다. 코드는 같은데 어디서 렌더링되느냐에 따라 의미가 달라지는 셈입니다.

개발 환경에서는 이 문제가 잘 드러나지 않았습니다. 번들이 금방 로드되니 티가 안 났거든요. 전송량이나 Lighthouse 종합 점수로는 원인이 안 보였고, LCP를 구간별로 쪼개 보고 나서야 찾았습니다.

같은 코드베이스, 반대 결과

같은 컴포넌트를 쓰는 두 페이지가 서로 다른 벽에 막혀 있었습니다.

상용에서 배포 전에 잰 숫자에도 같은 구조가 보였습니다. 그때 상세 페이지에는 webp가 이미 적용돼 있었고 목록 페이지는 아니었는데, 두 페이지의 병목이 정반대였습니다.

(상용 모바일, 배포 전, 5회 중앙값)

목록 페이지는 이미지 109장을 원본으로 받느라 다운로드에만 27초를 썼습니다. 상세 페이지는 다운로드가 1~2초로 끝났는데도 LCP가 15초를 넘었고, 상세 페이지 A는 16.1초 중 10.6초가 표시 대기였습니다.

목록 페이지는 이미지를 줄이면 줄인 만큼 빨라질 거라고 봤습니다. 최적화를 상용에 배포한 뒤 다시 재 보니 예상대로였습니다.

(상용 모바일, 5회 중앙값. 이미지·로딩 우선순위·번들을 함께 배포한 당일 측정)

다운로드가 27.4초에서 2.5초로 줄면서 LCP도 15.2초 빠졌습니다. 같은 배포에서 상세 페이지 A는 0.3초 줄었고 B는 그대로였습니다.

대신 목록 페이지에서도 가장 긴 구간이 다운로드에서 표시 대기로 바뀌었습니다. 다운로드를 2.5초까지 줄이자 목록 페이지도 상세 페이지와 같은 자리에서 막힌 겁니다. 이미지 최적화로 얻을 수 있는 몫에는 천장이 있었습니다.

수단을 분리해서 측정하니 원인이 보인다!

세 수단을 같은 출발점에 각각 따로 적용하고 측정했습니다.

어느 최적화가 LCP를 움직였는지 가려낼 수 있었던 건 측정 방식 덕분이었습니다.

보통은 최적화를 차례로 코드에 적용하고 마지막에 한 번 측정합니다. 그러면 “좋아졌다”는 알 수 있지만 무엇 때문에 좋아졌는지는 모릅니다. 그래서 세 수단을 같은 출발점에 하나씩 따로 얹고 각각 측정했습니다.

S0 원본      아무것도 안 함
S1 현재      지금 상태 그대로
   ├── S2 이미지만          포맷·크기
   ├── S3 로딩 우선순위만   preload·lazy
   └── S4 번들만            배럴 import 제거·모달 지연 로드
S5 셋 다

전송량은 이미지가 거의 다 가져갔습니다. 그런데 LCP를 줄인 건 번들이었습니다. 세 페이지 전부 같은 방향으로요.

번들만 먹힌 이유도 앞에서 본 hydration 대기와 같습니다. JS가 가벼워지니 hydration이 빨라졌고 그만큼 이미지가 일찍 보였습니다. 바이트를 줄인 게 아니라 기다리는 시간을 줄인 것이었습니다.

줄이다가 되돌린 것, 감수한 것

로딩 애니메이션 플레이어(39KB)도 필요할 때 받도록 바꿔봤습니다. 상품상세의 TBT가 384ms에서 11ms로 줄었습니다.

그런데 스피너는 로딩 중에 떠야 합니다. 플레이어를 나중에 받게 하자 정작 로딩 중에는 스피너 코드가 아직 도착하지 않아서 빈 화면만 보였습니다. 그래서 롤백했고 39KB 절감과 TBT 11ms도 함께 포기했습니다.

반대로 감수하고 남긴 것도 두 가지 있습니다. 모달 12개는 열 때 코드를 받도록 바꿔서 처음 열 때만 아주 살짝 늦습니다. 갤러리는 앞뒤 한 장까지만 미리 받아서 아주 빠르게 넘기면 다음 사진이 잠깐 비어 보입니다. 실기기로 써보니 어색하지 않아서 그대로 뒀습니다.

측정값에는 오차가 있었습니다

표에서 +10.8초가 눈에 걸리실 겁니다. 이미지만 적용했더니 한 페이지의 LCP가 10.8초 늘었다는 값입니다. 이미지를 줄였는데 느려질 이유는 없으니 측정 오류로 봤습니다.

LCP가 17초쯤 나오는 페이지는 5회 측정한 중앙값을 써도 오차가 이만큼 납니다. 같은 조건에서 16.0초가 나온 적도 있고 25.1초가 나온 적도 있습니다. 한두 번 측정한 숫자로는 얼마나 줄었는지 판단할 수 없었습니다.

그래서 몇 초 줄었는지 대신 세 페이지 모두 줄었는지만 봤습니다. 이미지와 로딩 우선순위는 페이지마다 줄기도 하고 늘기도 했습니다. 세 페이지에서 모두 줄어든 건 번들뿐입니다. 이 측정으로 말할 수 있는 건 여기까지고, “얼마나”를 말하려면 실제 사용자 데이터가 필요합니다.

결국 두 줄만 수정하면 되었습니다

이걸 어쩌면 좋을까요? 고치는 방법은 세 가지가 떠올랐습니다.

  • 컴포넌트 전체를 바꾸기 — hydration 전에는 그냥 보여주고 마운트된 뒤에만 로딩 처리를 켭니다
  • 대표 이미지(LCP 후보) 한 장만 로딩 처리에서 빼기
  • opacity를 JS 상태에서 CSS로 넘기기

첫 번째가 가장 깔끔합니다. 하지만 그 컴포넌트는 공통 컴포넌트라 다른 서비스에서도 함께 씁니다. 로딩 스켈레톤이 떴다가 사라지는 흐름을 전제로 만든 화면이 어딘가 있을 수도 있고, 그걸 다 확인하는 건 이번 작업보다 큰 일이었습니다. 그래서 두 번째를 골랐습니다.

컴포넌트에는 이미 disableLoader라는 prop이 있었습니다. 스켈레톤을 숨기는 용도였는데, 여기에 “처음부터 보이게”를 얹었습니다.

- opacity: isLoading ? 0 : 1,
- transition: 'opacity 0.3s ease-in-out',
+ opacity: isLoading && !disableLoader ? 0 : 1,
+ ...(disableLoader ? {} : { transition: 'opacity 0.3s ease-in-out' }),

갤러리 쪽에서는 첫 장에만 disableLoader={index === 0}을 넘깁니다. 이제 서버가 내려주는 HTML에서 대표 이미지는 opacity: 1이고 페이드인도 없습니다.

상용 Lighthouse가 측정하면서 찍어 둔 화면을 꺼내 보면 차이가 눈으로 보입니다. 같은 0.75초에 수정 전에는 사진이 아직 거의 투명했고, 수정 후에는 이미 다 보였습니다.

이 화면은 CPU를 느리게 하지 않은 관측값이라 LCP가 1.05초에서 0.39초로 줄었습니다. 아래 실측은 CPU를 4배 느리게 한 값이라 숫자가 더 큽니다.

상용에서 다시 측정하기

배포 다음 날 같은 두 상품을 두 가지 방법으로 측정했습니다.

먼저 실제 브라우저입니다. CPU를 4배 느리게 하고 캐시를 끈 상태에서 브라우저가 기록한 LCP를 그대로 읽었습니다.

(수정 전 5회, 수정 후 10회 중앙값. 수정 후 두 상품 20회는 모두 304~656ms. 수정 전은 이미지 최적화가 이미 들어간 상태입니다)

이미지가 도착하는 시각은 그대로입니다. 바뀐 건 도착한 뒤 기다린 시간 하나로, 2초 남짓에서 0.3초 아래로 줄었습니다.

앞에서 쓴 Lighthouse 구간 분해로도 봤습니다. 상세 페이지 A의 Render Delay가 세 시점에서 이렇게 움직였습니다.

이미지를 6MB 줄였을 때는 그대로였고, 두 줄을 고치자 10초가 빠졌습니다.

이미지를 6MB 줄였을 때 Render Delay는 거의 그대로였는데, 두 줄을 고치자 10.65초에서 1.13초로 89% 줄었습니다. 약 9.4배 빨라진 셈입니다.

데스크톱 Lighthouse 점수는 상세 페이지 A가 78에서 92로, B가 80에서 93으로 올랐습니다. 같은 측정에서 브라우저가 실제로 기록한 LCP도 A는 1,531ms에서 452ms로, B는 1,126ms에서 415ms로 줄었습니다.

모바일 점수는 60에서 65로 5점 올랐을 뿐입니다. 시뮬레이션 LCP가 16초에서 8초로 반이 됐지만 Lighthouse는 LCP 항목에 4초면 50점, 2.5초면 90점을 줍니다. 8초는 여전히 0점 근처라 점수에는 거의 안 잡힙니다. 그래서 성과는 점수 대신 실측 LCP와 Render Delay로 봤습니다.

이번엔 측정 도구가 범인이었습니다

배포한 날 모바일 Lighthouse를 돌렸더니 10회 중 5회가 1.3~2.4초가 될 때까지 첫 화면을 그리지 못했습니다. 고친 코드가 뭔가 망가뜨린 줄 알았습니다.

전날 들어간 핫픽스로 상품 소개 이미지 일부가 원본 JPG(최대 5.6MB)로 돌아간 게 있어서 그걸 먼저 의심했습니다. 그 이미지를 막고 측정해도 똑같았습니다. 카테고리홈, 데스크톱, 실제 브라우저 30회 이상에서는 한 번도 나오지 않았습니다.

trace를 열어 보니 페이지는 0.39초에 이미 그림을 다 그려 둔 상태였습니다. 그런데 측정용 Chrome 안에서 브라우저 자체의 주소창 팝업 UI(chrome://omnibox-popup.top-chrome)가 그려지는 순간, 페이지 화면 출력이 0.8~1초 멈췄습니다. 그 기능을 끄는 플래그를 넣었습니다.

--chrome-flags="--headless=new --disable-features=WebUIOmniboxFullPopup,FullWebUIOmniboxFrame,WebUIOmniboxPopup"

플래그를 넣고 다시 측정한 16회는 모두 정상이었습니다.

자기 서비스에서 확인하는 법

같은 구조에 걸려 있는지는 10분 안에 확인할 수 있습니다.

① LCP를 구간별로 봅니다. Lighthouse를 돌리고 INSIGHTS에서 LCP breakdown을 엽니다. 네 구간이 표로 나오는데, Element render delay가 전체의 절반을 넘으면 해당됩니다.

이 인사이트는 실제 관측값이고 상단 점수판의 LCP는 시뮬레이션 추정치라서 둘의 시간이 10배쯤 차이 납니다. 헷갈리기 쉬우니 절대 시간 말고 구간 비율을 보세요. 추정 기준의 구간값이 필요하면 리포트 JSON의 largest-contentful-paint-element 감사를 직접 읽어야 합니다.

② 그 시점을 TTI와 비교합니다. Render Delay가 끝나는 시점이 TTI와 겹치면 hydration이 LCP를 붙잡고 있을 가능성이 큽니다. TTI는 리포트 화면에 나오지 않아서 리포트 JSON의 audits.interactive 값을 직접 봐야 합니다. 이 값은 시뮬레이션 추정치라 상단 점수판의 LCP와 비교하면 됩니다.

③ 서버가 내려준 HTML을 봅니다. curl을 쓰세요. 개발자도구의 Elements 탭은 이미 hydration이 끝난 결과를 보여주기 때문에 여기서는 opacity: 1로 보입니다.

curl -sL https://your-service.com/page \
  | grep -oE ']*(opacity:0|visibility:hidden)[^>]*>' | head -5

여기서 opacity:0이나 visibility:hidden이 잡히면 확정입니다.

걸렸다면 우선순위가 바뀝니다. 이미지를 더 줄여도 LCP는 거의 안 움직입니다. 대표 이미지 한 장만이라도 서버 HTML에서 보이게 하는 게 먼저입니다.

마무리

처음 세운 가설은 틀렸습니다. 이미지가 무거워서 느리다고 봤는데 상세 페이지의 대표 이미지는 5초 남짓에 이미 도착해 있었고, 나머지 12초는 JS를 기다리는 시간이었습니다. 이미지 최적화는 전송량을 줄였고 번들은 그 기다림을 조금 줄였습니다. 대표 이미지가 JS를 기다리지 않게 만든 건 컴포넌트 두 줄이었습니다.

다운로드가 병목이던 목록 페이지에서는 이미지를 줄인 만큼 빨라졌습니다. 그 구간을 줄이고 나니 거기서도 가장 긴 구간은 표시 대기였습니다.

세 수단을 한꺼번에 적용하고 측정했다면 “전부 적용했더니 1.8초 줄었습니다”로 끝났을 겁니다. LCP를 구간으로 쪼개지 않았다면 Render Delay를 못 봤을 테고 측정 도구를 의심하지 않았다면 고친 코드를 되돌렸을지도 모릅니다.

여기까지 읽어주셔서 감사합니다.

함께 읽으면 좋은 글

  • QA 티켓 280건, AI와 함께 처리한 기록
  • 여기어때 해외투어 프론트엔드 구축기록

이런건어때 파일 용량을 줄여도 LCP가 줄어들지 않는 이유? was originally published in 여기어때 기술블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Java4Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate a critical Java flaw
event_model_payload.summary:
GitLab has internally assessed the impact of Java4Shell, and concluded it is not exploitable in GitLab-managed infrastructure. Exploitation requires a specific combination of conditions, which we confirmed are not present in our production environment. A single component was found to contain the impacted bundle in its runtime environment, which we are proactively upgrading as a hardening measure.

On November 17, 2026, OpenJDK, the project that most Java runtimes are built from, fixed a memory corruption flaw known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS 8.1) in the optimized java.util.Base64 decoding used on recent x86-64 CPUs. Web servers and frameworks routinely decode Base64 values from users, such as authentication headers and cookies, before the application sees the request. Researchers have demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in the default configurations of several widely used Java products.

Upgrade Java to a fixed version now

To mitigate this issue, upgrade every Java runtime from 17.0.6 onward, including unsupported releases such as Java 18 and 24, to a build based on OpenJDK 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1, or to your distribution’s patched package. If you can’t upgrade right away, turn off the vulnerable optimization with the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option.

Here are fixed builds and packages as of November 19:

Vendor or distributionFixed build or package

Amazon Corretto17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2, 27.0.1.1.4

RHEL 10, 9, and 8No fix yet

Sources: the OpenJDK advisory, vendors’ release pages, and the Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of November 19, 2026.

How you apply the upgrade depends on where Java runs:

  1. Containers with a floating tag, such as amazoncorretto:21: Rebuild the image so it pulls the latest base image, then redeploy.
  2. Containers with a pinned tag: Change the tag to a fixed version, then redeploy.
  3. Hosts: Upgrade the package, then restart every Java process.

For containers, check that the new base image ships a fixed version. As of November 19, eclipse-temurin:21 and the images built on it, such as tomcat, still don't, so they need the workaround below until they do.

If you can’t upgrade yet, turn off the vulnerable optimization

Set the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics JVM option, and restart every Java process for it to take effect. Base64 decoding will then use the regular version, which doesn’t have the flaw, and is only slightly slower.

To apply it to every JVM a container starts, add it to the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable, keeping any value already set. In a shell script, such as the container’s entrypoint, add this line of code:

export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="${JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS:+$JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS }-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

To confirm the option is set, run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics in the container, which should print false.

Locate Java projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs Java needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as a CI tool, a build server, or a product that bundles its own JDK. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features: container scanning, GitLab Orbit, and a language filter. Use them in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds Java installed with apt, apk, or dnf. It reports the CVE once the CVE reaches the advisories in the scanner’s vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:  
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml  
   
container_scanning:  
  variables:  
    # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager  
    CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. Once the policy is on, the next pipeline in each project runs container scanning. After the scan completes, review the default branch’s results in the Vulnerability Report.

You can also set up merge request approval policies with container scanning. If a code change contains Java4Shell, the policy blocks the merge until the selected approvers approve it.

In addition, turn on CS_BINARY_SCAN to find Java runtimes that no package manager installed, such as the JDK archive the eclipse-temurin images unpack or a JDK bundled in an application. The default scan can’t see them because they have no package record. The binary scan identifies them and reports Java4Shell.

2. GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit indexes your projects, pipelines, security findings, and source code, including Java, into a context graph you can query. You can ask an agent to review an entire group. With Orbit enabled on the top-level group, an agent can list every project that contains Java code, including the projects that JDK container scanning misses. You can also ask Orbit which projects have open findings for CVE-2026-114938 once scans have run. Orbit indexes the default branch only and is generally available to Premium and Ultimate tiers on GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated.

3. Projects by language

GitLab detects the languages in each project’s default branch, so a language filter lists every project that contains Java or Kotlin code, one row per project, whatever build tool it uses. Open Explore > Projects and filter by language, then again for Kotlin. Alternatively, you can get the list through the REST API:

GET /groups//projects?with_programming_language=Java&include_subgroups=true

4. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning, Orbit, and the language filter show what your projects declare and build, but Java can also run outside your GitLab projects. It often runs in application servers and products installed on hosts by hand, in CI runners and build servers, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline.

Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. Note which hosts run on affected x86-64 CPUs. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters. It uses the same package-only detection as the container scanning in Step 1. Treat every Java runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo can run the discovery steps above for you: pass it the list of projects filtered by language, or ask it to find them through Orbit. From there, let agents do the repetitive work, while keeping humans in the loop to review and merge.

To have agents open the fixes for every affected project:

  1. Set up a flow trigger on the Assign event, so the Developer Flow starts when someone assigns an issue.
  2. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions.
  3. Use Agentic Chat to create an epic with one issue per affected project, and assign the Developer Flow to each. The flow opens a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version, or, where no fixed image exists yet, sets -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.
  4. Review and merge each merge request, then close the issue once the fixed version is deployed.

The merge request approval policy you set up with container scanning blocks any change that reintroduces a vulnerable Java version without approval. The scan execution policy keeps container scanning on in every project, so a regression appears in the vulnerability report.

event_model_payload.headline: Show image swatches for product options in the Catalog API
event_model_payload.summary:
The Catalog API can now return an image for each product option value, such as a color, so you can show buyers a picture of each choice instead of only its name. Swatches are available when you request full product details with get_product. The new field is optional, and existing integrations keep working without changes.

What changed

In a get_product response, an option value can include a swatch object. Each swatch has one field, image_url, which is the URL of an image that represents the option value. Not every option value has a swatch. When a value has no swatch data, the response omits swatch.

search_catalog and lookup_catalog don’t return swatches, and swatches aren’t part of a variant’s options array. You don’t need to change your agent profile to get them.

Who’s affected

You’re affected if your app or agent calls get_product and shows product options to buyers, for example in a variant picker on a product page. If you only call search_catalog or lookup_catalog, nothing changes.

What to do

No action is required. If you don’t read swatch, your integration keeps working as before.

To show swatches:

  1. Read product.options[].values[].swatch.image_url from the get_product response.
  2. Show the image beside the option value or in its place, and keep the label visible or available to screen readers.
  3. When a value has no swatch, or its image doesn’t load, show the label.
  4. Use available and exists to set each option’s state. Don’t treat a missing swatch as an unavailable option.

Related docs

  • Option swatches in the Global Catalog extension reference
  • get_product in the Global Catalog MCP reference

event_model_payload.headline: Function settings extensions can now report several errors at once
event_model_payload.summary:
Function settings extensions can now report several errors at once. When your s-function-settings onSubmit handler rejects with an AggregateError, the Shopify admin shows every error on discount and checkout rule pages instead of only one. No action is required.

What changed

Previously, the admin showed one error when your extension rejected the promise you passed to event.waitUntil() in onSubmit, using the message of that error.

Now you can reject with an AggregateError, and the admin shows the message of each entry in its errors list. Each entry is an Error, and you can give it a code string.

  • The admin shows up to 10 errors. Each message is trimmed to 300 characters, and duplicate messages appear once.
  • Your onError handler receives the same entries, with their codes, so you can mark the fields in your own UI.
  • An entry with no code, or a code that is empty or longer than 64 characters, gets a default code: UNKNOWN on discount pages and EXTENSION_ERROR on checkout rule pages.
  • Rejecting with a single Error still works and shows one error.

The onerror property of s-function-settings is now typed as the AggregateError it receives in @shopify/ui-extensions 2025-10, 2026-10, and the 2027-01 release candidate.

Who's affected

This applies to apps with a function settings extension on discount or checkout rule pages, built with Polaris web components on API version 2025-10 or later.

Extensions on earlier API versions keep the previous behavior and show a single message. Extensions that reject with a single Error also keep working as before.

Why this matters

When a merchant fills in several fields incorrectly, they now see every problem after one save. They do not have to fix one field, save, and then find the next error.

What to do

No action is required. To report several errors, reject with an AggregateError of Errors in your onSubmit handler:

function fieldError(code, message) {
  return Object.assign(new Error(message), {code});
}

async function save(settings) {
  const errors = [];
  if (!settings.minimumQuantity) {
    errors.push(fieldError('MINIMUM_QUANTITY_REQUIRED', 'Enter a minimum quantity.'));
  }
  if (settings.percentage > 100) {
    errors.push(fieldError('PERCENTAGE_TOO_HIGH', 'Percentage can be at most 100.'));
  }
  if (errors.length > 0) {
    throw new AggregateError(errors, 'Settings are not valid');
  }
  // apply your metafield changes here
}

 event.waitUntil(save(settings))}
  onError={(event) => {
    for (const error of event.error.errors) {
      console.log(error.code, error.message);
    }
  }}
>
  {/* your fields */}

This sample checks two fields and throws one AggregateError with an Error per invalid field. Replace the checks and codes with your own. To test your extension, save settings with several invalid fields on a development store and confirm that the admin lists each error.

event_model_payload.headline: MongoDB is a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms
event_model_payload.summary:
We’re pleased to announce that MongoDB has been recognized as a Leader in the recently released Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, Q4 2024.

The report—which highlights “Leaders, Strong Performers, Contenders, and Challengers” and is “an assessment of the top vendors in the market”—notes that “MongoDB is an excellent choice for organizations looking to enhance their document and NoSQL platforms with real-time insights by leveraging translytical capabilities.”

What are translytical capabilities?

So what are translytical capabilities? In short, modern applications use a growing number of data types for transactional, operational, and analytical uses. Developers can silo different data types and workloads into separate systems, but this causes architectural complexity and reduced agility for teams.

A better approach—and one that speeds development—is to leverage a single platform that can store and use multiple data types for different purposes. Forrester defines these “translytical data platforms” as “next-generation data solutions built on a single database engine to seamlessly support transactional, operational, and analytical workloads without compromising data integrity, performance, or real-time analytics.”

That’s why we built MongoDB Atlas as a modern database. It brings data like documents, vectors, streaming, and time-series together in one system so that you can run transactional, operational, and analytics workloads in one place.

How Forrester measured translytical capabilities

To measure providers, Forrester evaluated 15 of the most significant translytical data platform vendors against 26 criteria. These criteria span current offering and strategy, to market presence. Being recognized as a Leader is based on an organization’s scores in both current offering and strategy categories for criteria like vision and innovation.

Forrester gave MongoDB the highest possible scores across nine criteria, including:

  • Multimodel1

  • Search

  • Development Tools / API

  • Scale optimization

  • Streaming

  • Platform management

  • Roadmap

  • Adoption

  • Number of customers

According to the report, “MongoDB continues to expand its translytical market share by delivering new capabilities that enhance automation, intelligent memory tiering, and multimodel support, including vector, streaming, analytics, and integrated transactions.”

“Developers have been telling us for years that they need easy ways to work with all their data in one place,” said Jim Scharf, Chief Technology Officer at MongoDB. “That’s what continues to drive our strategy of making MongoDB Atlas the modern database. We’re excited to be recognized as a Leader in the new The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, and we will continue to support our customers’ growing needs for their data.”

What are MongoDB customers doing with translytical capabilities?

The Forrester report notes that organizations “use MongoDB to support real-time analytics, customer intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), and AI applications.” So, let’s look at a few examples in action.

Companies like Ignition started using MongoDB just for operational data—but, over time, expanded into using Atlas Vector Search for AI use cases. Meanwhile, Bosch Digital makes their IoT data easier to work with by bringing multiple data sources together in a single platform. And, Keller Williams uses MongoDB Charts to bring their analytics to where their transactional data is, making it faster to gather insights for their product teams.

Overall, customers are attracted to MongoDB because of how developer-friendly the platform is, and because it simplifies their lives by bringing their data together.

1 Multimodel is defined as support for storing and using various data types.

event_model_payload.summary:

When a customer opts in to store credit for an eligible subscription at checkout, Shopify applies the customer's store credit to each renewal first and charges the remaining balance to the saved payment method. The change is available in the GraphQL Admin API and the Customer Account API, and doesn't require any mandatory action.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API adds the following fields and inputs:

  • Selling plans: SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicy.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit shows whether subscriptions on a selling plan can use store credit. You set it through paymentConfiguration on SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicyInput, in sellingPlansToCreate and sellingPlansToUpdate on sellingPlanGroupCreate and sellingPlanGroupUpdate.
  • Contracts: SubscriptionContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit and SubscriptionBillingCycleEditedContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit show the contract's store credit setting.
  • Contract calculation: paymentConfiguration is a new optional input on SubscriptionContractCalculationContractCreateInput and SubscriptionContractCalculationContractUpdateInput. SubscriptionCalculatedContract.paymentConfiguration shows the value that the commit applies.
  • SubscriptionDraft: SubscriptionDraftInput.paymentConfiguration is available on subscriptionDraftUpdate, subscriptionContractCreate, and subscriptionContractAtomicCreate.

In the Customer Account API, SubscriptionContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit returns the store credit setting. Customer portals can display it, and the field is read-only.

The Customer Account API applies the following validation rules:

  • The API rejects allowStoreCredit: true when the contract has no lines.
  • The API rejects allowStoreCredit: true when any line's selling plan has store credit off. A fixed selling plan counts as store credit off.
  • The API accepts allowStoreCredit: true on lines that have no selling plan.
  • The API always accepts allowStoreCredit: false.

If a calculation fails validation, then the API returns an INVALID error on calculatedContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit. On a subscriptionDraftCommit, it returns an INVALID user error.

Who's affected

This change affects:

  • Apps that create or manage subscription selling plans or subscription contracts using the GraphQL Admin API.
  • Customer portals that read and display subscription contracts using the Customer Account API.

The new paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit fields are available in API version 2027-01 and later. Existing selling plans and contracts are unchanged, and their allowStoreCredit default value is false.

What to do

No action is required. Existing selling plans and subscriptions continue to work as before, and you only need to update your app if you want to add support for store credit.

To add store credit support in your app:

  1. Set allowStoreCredit on your selling plans through SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicyInput.paymentConfiguration.
  2. Set allowStoreCredit on your contracts, either directly through SubscriptionDraftInput or through contract calculations.
  3. After each calculation, read calculatedContract.paymentConfiguration.allowStoreCredit, and don't commit the calculation if the value differs from the value that you sent.

For implementation details, end-to-end examples, and request shapes, see Use store credit with subscriptions.

Related docs

  • Use store credit with subscriptions
  • About subscriptions
  • Admin API: SellingPlanRecurringBillingPolicy
  • Admin API: SubscriptionContract
  • Admin API: SubscriptionDraftInput
  • Admin API: SubscriptionCalculatedContract
  • Customer Account API: SubscriptionContract

event_model_payload.headline: RolloutChange now includes applyResult
event_model_payload.summary:
As of GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, the RolloutChange interface has an applyResult field. Applying a rollout makes a treatment's changes permanent for every buyer. applyResult shows the outcome of the latest attempt to apply each change, so your app can find changes that failed.

applyResult is null before the first attempt to apply the change. With an online access token, it's also null if the staff member can't read the changed resource. It uses the existing read_rollouts access scope.

query {
  rollout(id: "gid://shopify/Rollout/1") {
    treatments {
      changes(first: 10) {
        nodes {
          id
          applyResult {
            status
            completedAt
            errorCode
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

RolloutChangeApplyResult has three fields:

  • status: IN_PROGRESS, SUCCESS or FAILURE.
  • completedAt: when the attempt finished. It's null while in progress, or if the time wasn't recorded.
  • errorCode: why the change failed, when known: RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND, VALIDATION_FAILED, LIMIT_EXCEEDED, INVALID_CHANGE or INTERNAL_ERROR.

event_model_payload.headline: Expiring offline access tokens required for new custom apps as of December 1, 2026
event_model_payload.summary:
Starting December 1, 2026, every new custom app must request and use expiring offline access tokens for GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests. This has been required for new public apps since April 1, 2026. This update extends the requirement to new partner-created custom apps and merchant-created apps.

If you already request expiring offline tokens, you likely don’t need to change your app.

What changed

For apps created on or after December 1, 2026, Shopify requires expiring offline access tokens for Admin API calls:

  • New offline tokens that you obtain with the authorization code grant or token exchange must be expiring.
  • You request an expiring offline token by including expiring=1 in your token request and then storing and using the refresh token that Shopify returns.
  • Tokens that you obtain through the client credentials grant already expire after 24 hours, so this flow already meets the requirement.
  • Tokens that you obtain through application-only access already meet the requirement.

Existing custom apps and merchant-created apps that were set up before December 1, 2026 can keep using their existing offline tokens.

Who’s affected

The requirement for expiring offline access tokens applies to:

  • Custom apps created on or after December 1, 2026
  • Apps that merchants create on or after December 1, 2026

The following aren’t affected by this change:

  • Custom apps and merchant-created apps that were created before December 1, 2026
  • Public apps, which have already been required to use expiring offline tokens since April 1, 2026

Why this matters

Expiring offline access tokens limit how long a leaked token can be used. If an expiring token leaks, it stops working after a fixed amount of time unless your app refreshes it. A non-expiring token keeps working until the app is uninstalled or you rotate the app secret, which increases the risk from a leak.

What to do

  1. If your app uses token exchange or the authorization code grant:

    • Include expiring=1 in your token requests for offline access.
    • Store and use the refresh token that Shopify returns to obtain new access tokens when the current one expires.
    • If you use Shopify app templates or libraries, check that you’re on a recent version, because they already request expiring tokens by default.

  2. If your app uses the client credentials grant:

    • You don’t need to make any changes. Tokens from that grant already expire after 24 hours.

For setup details and examples, see the expiring offline access token guide in the Admin API docs: Use expiring offline access tokens.

event_model_payload.headline: Network access declarations are now required for apps that run on the online store
event_model_payload.summary:
We're adding network access declarations as a requirement to better protect merchants. Apps that run code on the online store must declare allowed_sources in the [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml.

Timeline

Shopify will reject deploys and delist apps that haven't added the required declarations as follows.

Public apps:

  • December 1, 2026: Shopify rejects deploys and Shopify App Store submissions. Merchants see a warning in the Shopify admin. Existing app versions keep working.
  • January 1, 2027: Shopify delists apps from the Shopify App Store and blocks new installs. Existing installs keep working.

Custom apps installed outside your organization:

  • December 1, 2026: Shopify rejects deploys.
  • January 1, 2027: Shopify blocks installs of your apps outside your organization until every app that's in scope declares its network access.

What apps are affected

Public apps, and custom apps that you install on stores outside your organization, are affected if they use any of the following features:

  • A theme app extension block or app embed.
  • Script tags on the online store.
  • An app proxy.
  • The write_themes access scope.
  • A web pixel with the write_open_pixels access scope.

What apps are unaffected

  • Apps that only write content, such as metafields, menus, or products.
  • Apps that have a checkout UI extension but none of the features listed above.
  • Custom apps that you install only on stores within your organization.
  • Apps that merchants create in the Dev Dashboard or in the Shopify admin.
  • Web pixels that run in the default strict sandbox.

Why we're making this change

Injected scripts can load code onto a storefront from any server. Declaring your app's servers helps Shopify spot suspicious requests, which protects your app and the merchants who use it.

What to do

  1. Add the servers that your app's code loads from or sends requests to, such as your API or CDN, to allowed_sources. If your app doesn't contact any external servers, then set allowed_sources = []. An empty list counts as a declaration.
  2. Optional: Add the hosts that your app links customers to, such as your app's own site, to allowed_navigation_hosts. This helps Shopify recognize links to sites that you trust, so customers are less likely to see an exit warning.
  3. Test your configuration on a dev store with the Network access testing preview. The preview covers the online store only.
  4. Run shopify app deploy, and then release the new version.

Here's an example configuration:

[network_access]
allowed_sources = ["https://api.app.example.com"]
allowed_navigation_hosts = ["app.example.com"]

For examples and troubleshooting, refer to Declare your app's network access. For every upcoming date, refer to Upcoming security deadlines.

event_model_payload.headline: Grafana Labs’ First Executive Briefing Center Coming to Ginza
event_model_payload.summary:
Grafana Labs does not have a headquarters office. Since its founding in 2014, it has been fully remote-first.

It began with three co-founders living on different continents, and today our team spans more than 50 countries.
From day one, the organization was designed with the assumption that everyone works remotely. Real-time meetings are kept to a minimum, information is shared through documentation, and we have cultivated a culture that trusts people to “work autonomously.” At its core lies the transparency and autonomy of open source.

And now, we are building the world’s first Executive Briefing Center (EBC) in Ginza, Tokyo.

A remote-first company creating a physical space—what does that mean?
This article is the first in a three-part series following the EBC launch project.
From the background of the concept to site selection, design philosophy, and even the demolition process, we will walk you through the journey.

Not an “office,” but an “EBC”

We do not call this place an “office.” It is an Executive Briefing Center, or EBC for short.

As a remote-first company, there is no need to commute to a fixed location every day. However, there has never been a place anywhere in the world where people can directly experience the Grafana product, or share the same physical space with customers and the community to engage with technology. The EBC is designed to serve three roles.



A place to experience the product


A space where customers can directly interact with Grafana solutions, experiencing how observability solves real challenges through demos and briefings—not through a screen, but through face-to-face conversations in the same space.



A starting point for innovation


A flexible space design that is not bound by fixed layouts, allowing the environment to adapt to different purposes and foster new ideas and use cases.

A hub for the community


A venue open for meetups and technical events, where people in the Grafana community can naturally gather and connect.


We are building the world’s first EBC in Japan—to meet the rapidly growing demand for observability in the Japanese market. And for the Grafana community that already exists here, having a physical hub carries significant meaning.

Because Grafana Labs is a company where employees around the world operate autonomously, we believe there is real value in creating a space for experiences that can only happen in person. We aim to create an open space—one where people feel that we are close to them.

Site selection — A space that embodies our culture

Two key requirements for the location

The search for a property began around April 2025. Led by Country Manager Andy Schwabecher, we explored multiple areas. There were two key requirements in the selection process.

First, the location needed to make customers feel that Grafana Labs is “right there with them.” It had to be open, accessible, and easy to drop by—a place where people could naturally engage with the Grafana solution. Not a space hidden behind security gates and reception procedures, but one that feels open and inviting. A building where customers might think, “Let’s just stop by.”

Second, the space needed to embody the way Grafana Labs works. For us, the concept of an “office” is fundamentally different from that of a typical Japanese company. It is not a place where people sit at assigned desks every day. It must be an open, flexible environment that does not contradict a remote-first way of working. It also needed to accommodate a skeleton ceiling and allow for a design that breaks away from conventional office norms.

Finding a place that satisfied both conditions was not easy.

A property once lost—and eventually secured

Around the summer of 2025, a building in Ginza was introduced by a broker. At the viewing stage, the team rated it highly, and it met all the conditions. However, during the consideration process, another tenant moved ahead, and the opportunity slipped away.

While continuing to search for other options, we received news a few months later that the original tenant had withdrawn, and the space was available again.

And so, after a long journey, we secured the current floor—about nine months after starting the search in April 2025.

Looking back, not compromising on finding a place that could physically express Grafana Labs’ culture—transparency, openness, and autonomy—was one of the most important decisions in shaping the EBC.

Design philosophy — Expressing Grafana’s culture through space

Skeleton ceiling and open interior

In a typical office or tenant space, ceilings are finished, and pipes and wiring are hidden.

At the EBC, we chose the opposite: a full skeleton ceiling. Exposed pipes and visible wiring. This itself is an expression of Grafana Labs’ philosophy of “making things visible.”

As a company whose core business is observability—the ability to see—we intentionally reflect that philosophy in the space itself.

Three areas and design principles

The space is broadly divided into three areas.

First, an area where visitors can casually experience Grafana Labs’ culture.A large screen displays content that introduces what kind of company Grafana Labs is and what we value.

Second, an area where visitors can directly experience Grafana solutions.A space where they can view demos, receive explanations, and engage in practical discussions—not through a screen, but together in the same place.

Third, private meeting rooms.Spaces designed for more in-depth conversations in a relaxed atmosphere.
Across all areas, the common design philosophy is to create a place where people can easily drop by and directly interact with Grafana Labs members. The goal is to provide a sense of comfort that helps visitors feel at ease.

Interior and flexibility

In selecting the interior layout and color scheme, we intentionally avoided the rigid feel of a typical office. Instead, we focused on creating a relaxed environment where conversations naturally emerge.
Furniture in the EBC is designed to be as movable as possible.

On a daily basis, the space includes an eight-person free-address desk (with monitors at each seat), window-side bench seating, and high tables. For meetups and community events, these can be moved to the sides, transforming the space into an open area that can accommodate gatherings of around 50 people.

Not fixed, but flexible. A space that changes form depending on its use—that is the core concept of the EBC design.

Meeting room names — Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)

Meeting room names — Amber, Jade, Mikage
There are three meeting rooms in total.
We utilized one existing room and added new partitions—retaining part of the original wall—to create three separate spaces.

For a remote-first company like Grafana Labs, having physical meeting rooms is itself a new experience.
Various ideas were considered, including place names like “Tokyo,” “Ginza,” and “Kyoto,” as well as festival-themed names like “Kanda” and “Tenjin.”

In the end, we chose names based on Japanese stones and minerals:

Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)

Minerals are formed deep underground over long periods of time. While their beauty is undeniable, what resonated most with the team was the weight of that time.

What we aim for in this space is to build long-term relationships with our customers—not one-time interactions, but connections that deepen over time.

There is also another meaning: these are names rooted in Japan. The sound itself feels familiar and naturally accepted.
As a global company, we wanted the space to feel grounded in Japan, and for that sense to be reflected even in the names.

Demolition — Walls removed, space revealed

Originally, this floor was divided into three separate rooms for different tenants. Air conditioning was already installed, making it move-in ready. To create an open, single-floor space, we began by demolishing the walls that separated the rooms. The ceiling was also replaced with a skeleton structure to better reflect Grafana’s open culture.

Floor plan before demolition: three rooms on one floor

Before demolition

After demolition

With two walls removed, the space opened up into a single, expansive area.

Current status and what’s next

As of March 2026, the demolition work has been completed.
The walls are gone, the ceiling has been stripped, and a large open floor now stretches across the space.
Structural work has been completed, and from here, full-scale interior construction based on the design will begin.

The target completion is late April.
After inspections and adjustments, operations are expected to begin in mid-May.
Starting next week, the space will begin to transform daily, with new walls, flooring, and equipment installation.

Coming next

Walls go up, floors are laid, wiring is installed, and monitors are set in place.
What once existed only on blueprints will take shape as a real, physical space.

In the next article, we will share an on-site construction report, coordination with designers and contractors, and behind-the-scenes insights into equipment selection—bringing you the reality of the build process.

event_model_payload.headline: Bring charts, queries, and context into one shareable document: Introducing Grafana Notebooks
event_model_payload.summary:
A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures. You have an error-rate chart in your dashboard, a query that narrows the failures to one payment provider, and an explanation you've been exploring with Grafana Assistant. To bring your teammate up to speed, you start collecting screenshots and query links, then write out how they connect.

That explanation is part of the analysis. Your teammate needs to see what supports the conclusion and where you're still making an assumption. As findings come from both your own exploration in Grafana and from AI-assisted work, having one place to examine them together becomes key.

Grafana Notebooks help you do just that, bringing charts, queries, and findings from Assistant together in one working document, so teammates can follow your reasoning and assess next steps. In this post, we’ll use the checkout example above to show how this works in practice, then look at how Notebooks can support rollout decisions and post-incident reviews.

How Notebooks work: develop your analysis in a working document

Through conversations with users, we've heard a recurring need for a lightweight place to work through a question and share the results. Notebooks give that work room to develop inside Grafana, from an initial observation to a recommendation someone can assess.

You can start with a panel you've already found. Select Add to notebook from its dashboard menu, or from the Add menu in Explore, and choose a new or existing notebook. Then add your explanation and reorder the blocks as the argument takes shape. Your edits save automatically.

Assistant can contribute to your working document, too. Add a visualization generated in an Assistant conversation directly to a notebook, whether you're using the side pane or Workspace. Once you're in the notebook, open the Assistant side pane to ask for changes to a visualization or help refining the document. You can also edit the content directly as your analysis develops.

Work through a question and share your conclusion

Let's revisit the checkout example. Your notebook starts with the error-rate panel and a question: could the latest payment-service deployment explain the increase?

Alongside the panel, you bring in an Explore query that narrows the errors to requests to one payment provider. You can refine that query in the notebook without changing the source dashboard, and can also set an absolute start and end time on the error-rate panel to keep readers focused on the period around the deployment.


You ask Assistant to chart payment-provider timeouts before and after the deployment, then add the visualization directly from the conversation to your notebook. Within the notebook, you open the Assistant side pane and ask, "Break this chart down by payment provider." In this example, the breakdown shows an increase for the provider you identified in Explore. You add a detail from the deployment notes: the release changed that provider's timeout setting. You explain why that connection deserves testing.

Before sharing, you put the suspected cause and proposed test near the top, with the supporting charts and explanation below. A reader can see what you're recommending, then follow the evidence. The next step is to reproduce the behavior with the previous and current timeout settings.

You share the notebook link with the payment-service team. A teammate with access can read the analysis and examine the queries as they plan the test. Their next action happens in the service's test environment, informed by the work you've brought together.

Support rollout decisions, post-incident reviews, and more

The same approach works for questions outside troubleshooting. For example, after a deployment intended to improve performance, you could bring together latency and resource-usage charts, explain the differences you observe, and document any trade-offs. Share the notebook with the service owners to help them decide whether to expand the rollout or make another change.

For a post-incident review, a notebook can bring relevant queries together with an account of what happened. Place your explanation beside the evidence so readers can understand the conclusions before discussing follow-up work. A finding about repeated timeouts, for example, might support a proposal to change retry behavior or add a load test.

Start with a question your team needs to answer

For your first notebook, choose a question you're already working through in Grafana. Add the evidence you've found, explain what you think it means, and make the next question or recommendation clear. Share it with the people whose expertise you need.

We're also exploring richer collaboration in Notebooks, including comments and live editing. Our ambition is to give people and agents more ways to develop their work together, with the evidence and discussion in the same place.

Notebooks are in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, as of the Grafana 13.3 release. Grafana Cloud access is rolling out over the coming weeks. 

For self-managed Grafana, follow the Notebooks guide to enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. Once available, create a notebook from the Notebooks page. You can also start with findings from an Assistant conversation.

Read the Notebooks guide for more details on setup and examples of adding content from dashboards, Explore, and Assistant.

event_model_payload.headline: How to Align Modern Payment Platforms with PCI DSS Using MongoDB Enterprise Advanced
event_model_payload.summary:
Payment platforms operate in a demanding environment. They must protect payment account data and support the teams that authorize transactions, investigate suspicious activity, and resolve exceptions. The more people and systems that can see sensitive data, the harder it is to control exposure. And the more data is locked away, the harder it can be to use in legitimate workflows. So how can you set up the platforms to ensure they protect that data while also giving the right people access?

Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a global security standard managed by the PCI Security Standards Council, provides a framework for protecting payment account data, restricting access, securing networks, and monitoring activity. Meeting those objectives is not a database-only exercise. It depends on how the application handles data, how the database server protects and governs it, and how the underlying infrastructure is configured and operated.

While the fully managed MongoDB Atlas platform can provide a foundation for organizations pursuing PCI DSS compliance, with MongoDB’s infrastructure-level certifications supporting the infrastructure layer, some organizations opt for a self-managed architecture to maintain direct operational control over their infrastructure and internal security policies. For self-managed deployments, MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides database security, governance, and encryption capabilities that can help support applicable PCI DSS objectives. Red Hat OpenShift provides configurable platform and network controls, while the MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) Operator manages MongoDB deployments on OpenShift.

Achieving alignment across this architecture requires a defense-in-depth model, which provides multiple overlapping layers of cybersecurity to protect data. While technical controls and reference architectures alone do not constitute formal compliance attestations, they provide the foundation needed to meet core PCI DSS objectives. The following sections walk through establishing this foundation across three complementary tiers—application, database, and infrastructure—before examining how they work together to protect sensitive payment workflows.

Start with the application layer

The application determines what payment data enters the platform, where it flows, and which business roles need it. In our reference payment service provider (PSP) demo, the application models two distinct workloads: high-throughput payment authorizations and post-transaction fraud investigations.  

This PSP demo application is designed to support deployment with either a fully managed MongoDB Atlas cluster or a self-managed MongoDB Enterprise Advanced deployment. Its core architecture, data models, and client-side encryption approach can be shared across both models, although configuration, integrations, and operational responsibilities may differ by environment. This dual compatibility gives organizations the flexibility to migrate workloads between cloud and on-premises environments as strategic needs evolve, eliminating infrastructure lock-in. Furthermore, it reinforces data sovereignty by allowing organizations to retain direct operational control over where cardholder data resides and how it is governed across hybrid architectures.

At the functional level, data minimization is enforced at the point of entry. Primary account numbers (PAN) are tokenized when downstream services do not need raw cardholder data, and sensitive authentication data (SAD) such as card verification value (CVV) never gets stored post-authorization. In addition, an isolated application programming interface (API) layer ensures that external clients never connect directly to the database tier.

These design choices reduce unnecessary exposure before data reaches storage. They also make the next layer more effective: The database can apply protection to the fields and workflows that genuinely need it, rather than compensating for an application that collects or shares too much.

Protect and govern data at the database layer

MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides security capabilities for self-managed MongoDB deployments. One relevant capability is queryable encryption (QE). It allows selected fields to remain encrypted in the database while supporting defined query patterns over those fields. In practical terms, an authorized payment or investigation workflow can look up protected information, such as an account reference, without the database storing that value in plaintext. The client driver encrypts selected fields and decrypts query results using keys from the configured key management service (KMS), meaning the database engine processes only ciphertext for supported query patterns. QE is field- and query-specific, so teams can choose which data must be searchable and validate the supported patterns for their deployment.

Encryption works alongside access governance. MongoDB role-based access control lets administrators assign built-in or custom roles so that application services, analysts, auditors, and database operators receive only the permissions they need. MongoDB also supports IP-based authentication restrictions for database users. These controls help answer two different questions:

  • What may this identity do? 

  • From which network locations may it connect?

Database auditing can complement these protections by recording selected database activity for review and investigation. The value comes from connecting audit policy to the organization’s monitoring and response processes, not simply turning on logging in isolation.

Enforce the environment at the infrastructure layer

The database and application still need a tightly controlled environment. OpenShift provides platform controls that teams can configure to isolate workloads and govern their runtime. Those controls include role-based access for cluster and project operations, security context constraints for pod privileges, and NetworkPolicies to limit which workloads can communicate. For example, a policy can allow the payment API to reach MongoDB while denying unrelated workloads access to the database network path.

The MongoDB controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) operator manages the cluster’s deployment, while Ops Manager provides management capabilities such as automation, monitoring, and backup according to the deployment configuration. These tools help platform and database teams operate the deployment consistently; they do not replace the need to set restrictive policies, manage identities and keys, or review the resulting configuration.

The following high-level view shows how the layers work together:

Figure 1. Payment platform stack, from underlying infrastructure to business applications. 

As shown above, these components align into a defense-in-depth model. The stack builds upward from the host infrastructure and immutable operating system (RHEL OS) to the OpenShift container platform, establishing a hardened foundation. On top of this platform, the MCK operator provides persistence for the encrypted data, Ops Manager orchestrates data automation, and the business payment microservices run isolated at the application tier. This layered view helps teams map controls across each tier to meet PCI DSS requirements.

How the layers support PCI DSS objectives

Application-level tokenization and data minimization can reduce how much sensitive data the platform handles. Queryable encryption can protect selected fields while preserving supported lookup workflows. Database roles and IP restrictions can narrow access to the database, while OpenShift policies can further limit which workloads and network paths reach it. Auditing and operational monitoring help teams review activity and investigate events. The value, ultimately, occurs when this all comes together seamlessly.

As illustrated in Figure 2, the reference PSP demo organizes these controls into clear architectural boundaries:

  • Perimeter and access control: External entities (client devices, wallet systems, and merchant systems) communicate exclusively over HTTPS through the service gateway. Identity and access policies are enforced at the security gateway using standards such as OAuth, OIDC, and JWT backed by general identity and access management (GIAM), preventing direct access to data stores from untrusted networks.

  • Protected core processing: The core system coordinates payment workflows and integrates directly with a key management service (such as AWS KMS) and MongoDB EA. This design ensures that field encryption occurs before persistence and that the database engine handles only ciphertext for configured search patterns.

  • Event decoupling and specialized services: By routing events through an event bus (Kafka) to dedicated providers for fraud detection (FDS) and anti-money laundering (AML), the platform isolates investigative workflows from the core payment engine, supporting workload separation and least-privilege data access.

Figure 2. Reference view of a PCI DSS-aligned payment demo integrated with MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on OpenShift.

Together, these controls can support PCI DSS objectives such as protecting stored account data, restricting access based on business need, maintaining secure network boundaries, and monitoring access. With a self-managed MongoDB EA deployment on OpenShift, the organization remains responsible for the full cardholder data environment, including infrastructure configuration, identity and key management, operational procedures, and evidence.

The payment service demo application makes this layered approach tangible. Its payment and investigation workflows provide concrete context for demonstrating how queryable encryption can protect selected sensitive fields while supporting defined searches, how MongoDB roles and IP-based restrictions narrow database access, and how OpenShift policies can limit paths between the application and data tiers. MCK and the Ops Manager provide deployment and operational tooling for sensitive data, tailored to the organization’s needs. These layers offer a starting point for building a self-managed payment environment with controls across the stack.

event_model_payload.headline: Atlas for Government: The Only FedRAMP® Class D Certified Cross-Cloud Operational Database
event_model_payload.summary:
Federal, state, and local agencies are under mounting pressure to modernize legacy systems, adopt AI, and protect sensitive data, all at the same time. Many of the databases that can currently handle an agency's most sensitive, high-impact workloads are native to a single cloud and run nowhere else, leaving agencies with a limited set of authorized options and little room to change course when missions, mandates, or threats shift.

MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era, and today we're extending it to the workloads where the stakes are highest: MongoDB Atlas for Government has achieved FedRAMP® Class D Certification. Formerly known as FedRAMP High, Class D is the highest level of assessment under the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP). Atlas for Government has also added support for Azure Government, expanding its existing support for AWS GovCloud and Commercial Regions and Google Cloud Assured Workloads.

Together, these milestones make MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) Certified cross-cloud operational database in the world. Public sector organizations and the independent software vendors (ISVs) that serve them can now run their most sensitive mission-critical workloads—including production AI applications built on real-time operational data—on a single platform and on the cloud provider of their choice, across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. To learn more, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page or the FedRAMP Marketplace page.

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of the MongoDB Atlas intelligent data platform built specifically for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It brings the core capabilities of MongoDB’s intelligent data platform to government, giving agencies a fully managed way to deploy, run, and scale mission-critical applications in the cloud, including transactional workloads, search, vector search for AI applications, and time series data, all within a single, unified data platform.

Atlas for Government is operated by MongoDB employees who are United States persons on U.S. soil, and all encryption within MongoDB-managed infrastructure is FIPS 140-3 validated. The platform maintains a 99.995% uptime SLA and has been generally available since 2021.

MongoDB Atlas for Government is already trusted across the federal government. MongoDB works with 13 U.S. Federal Cabinet-level agencies. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, agencies like these can bring even more sensitive, high-impact workloads to Atlas for Government. For example, a health agency could modernize benefits and eligibility systems that handle protected health information and personally identifiable information. A financial agency could run real-time fraud detection across high-volume transaction streams. And a civilian agency could build an AI application that lets analysts search policy and case records in natural language, without that data leaving a FedRAMP Class D (High) environment.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP provides the standardized authorization framework that cloud service providers (CSPs) must successfully navigate to demonstrate compliance with federal security requirements before hosting federal agency workloads. In 2026, FedRAMP moved away from labeling these standards Low, Moderate, and High, replacing them with a four-tier Certification Class system, A through D. FedRAMP Class D (High) is the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High, and it remains the most rigorous tier a CSP can achieve within the FedRAMP program.

FedRAMP Class D (High) certification is designed for cloud services that support an agency's high-impact systems, where a security failure could have severe or catastrophic consequences for operations, assets, or people. This includes systems tied to national security, law enforcement, and emergency response, as well as high-impact modernization initiatives across civilian agencies. Achieving this certification requires meeting hundreds of stringent security controls covering everything from access management to incident response.

MongoDB Atlas for Government achieved FedRAMP Moderate authorization in 2023 and has been a trusted, fully managed data platform for federal agencies and ISVs since then. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, that foundation is now extended to high-impact workloads, including production AI applications. Agencies can bring those workloads to the cloud on a platform that meets the security and compliance requirements for high-impact systems, and build secure, production-grade AI applications on top of them.

Freedom to run anywhere: Now spanning AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

With the addition of support for Azure Government, MongoDB Atlas for Government now runs across all three major cloud providers: AWS (both GovCloud and AWS commercial regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. This makes MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) certified, cross-cloud database in the world.

For public sector organizations, this cross-cloud support is about more than convenience. A database tied to a single cloud provider limits an agency's options if costs rise, a mission requirement changes, or a new mandate calls for a different cloud environment. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives agencies and ISVs the freedom to run their workloads on the cloud that best fits their needs today, and to change that decision later without rewriting their applications. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments (AWS GovCloud, Google Cloud Assured Workloads, and Azure Government), data can be distributed across providers to optimize for performance, cost, or resilience, and to strengthen disaster recovery with automatic failover across providers.

Getting started on Azure Government works the same way as it does on AWS GovCloud or Google Cloud Assured Workloads. Agencies and ISVs can create a project in Atlas for Government, designate it as a FedRAMP Class D (High) Gov Regions Only project, and select Azure as the cloud provider when creating a cluster.

Protecting data and powering AI at the highest level

FedRAMP Class D (High) sets a high bar for how a provider documents, assesses, and maintains its security program, but that is only one part of the picture. Agencies handling the country's most sensitive data also need assurance that the data itself stays protected, even if a system is compromised.

MongoDB Atlas for Government provides robust protection for sensitive data, supporting workloads that include Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), and Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) data. Data at rest is protected using database encryption with Customer Managed Keys, and data in transit is protected via TLS.

For organizations that require protection beyond the authorization boundary, MongoDB Queryable Encryption performs encryption and decryption client-side, so designated fields remain encrypted throughout their lifecycle, in transit, at rest, and in use. MongoDB, cloud operators, and even the organization's own database administrators never have access to keys or unencrypted data.

This same secure foundation enables agencies to deploy production AI applications in their high-impact environments. MongoDB Atlas for Government includes MongoDB Vector Search, allowing teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI-powered applications directly on top of their operational data. Instead of standing up a separate vector database and building a pipeline to keep it in sync, agencies can run transactional workloads, search, and vector search in a single, FedRAMP Class D-certified environment, reducing both complexity and risk.

How to get started with MongoDB Atlas for Government

With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification and support for Azure Government, MongoDB’s intelligent data platform for the AI era now reaches the public sector’s highest-stakes missions. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives public sector organizations and ISVs a secure, fully managed, and truly multi-cloud way to run their most sensitive workloads and build production AI applications.

To get started, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page, view the FedRAMP Marketplace listing, or refer to the Atlas for Government documentation for setup details.

FAQ

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of MongoDB Atlas built for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It is a fully managed, FedRAMP Class D (High) certified operational database.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP Class D (High) is the highest tier in FedRAMP’s four-tier Certification Class system and the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High. It is designed for cloud services that support high-impact government systems.

Which cloud providers does Atlas for Government support?

Atlas for Government runs on AWS (GovCloud and Commercial Regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments, data can be distributed across providers with automatic failover.

Can agencies build AI applications on Atlas for Government?

Yes. MongoDB Vector Search enables teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI applications directly on operational data, in a single FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment, without a separate vector database or sync pipeline.
