event_model_payload.headline: aiohttp proxy: auth, trust_env, SOCKS5, limits and rotation
event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on proxymint.

Set a proxy in Python aiohttp: proxy= per session or request, auth after the 3.14 proxy_auth deprecation, trust_env, SOCKS5, connector limits and each error.

TL;DR

  • Pass the proxy as proxy= and keep http:// even for HTTPS sites. ClientSession(proxy="http://USERNAME:PASSWORD@HOST:PORT") covers both, a proxy= on one get() overrides it, and the session form needs aiohttp 3.11 or later, so run pip show aiohttp before copying an old tutorial.
  • If your password has a /, # or ? in it, percent-encode it, or you get InvalidURL with the password printed in the message. Skip proxy_auth=BasicAuth(...) too: it warns on every call since 3.14, and its proxy_headers replacement works per request only and does nothing for plain-HTTP targets.
  • HTTPS_PROXY does nothing until you pass trust_env=True, and even then ALL_PROXY is skipped and an https:// value in HTTPS_PROXY is dropped with a log warning, so requests go direct without an error. An explicit proxy= saves you that hunt.
  • On an HTTPS site a 407 arrives as ClientHttpProxyError, not a status code, and because it subclasses ClientResponseError you catch it first; only plain http:// targets give you resp.status == 407.
  • For SOCKS5 you need aiohttp-socks, which rejects socks5h://. ProxyConnector.from_url("socks5://...") already sends the hostname to the proxy by default; rdns=False is what turns that off.

Key takeaways

  • Standardise on one proxy URL with quote(..., safe="") credentials. It works for HTTPS and plain-HTTP targets, on the session or per request, with no DeprecationWarning on 3.14.5.
  • Cap tunnels with TCPConnector(limit=N) and a semaphore of the same size. limit_per_host counts target hosts, not the proxy port, and requests queued for the pool burn their total timeout.
  • Set ClientTimeout yourself. The default is 300 seconds total, so a dead exit holds a slot for five minutes before anything fails.
  • Run the reused-vs-fresh exit test before trusting rotation. Keep-alive reuses one tunnel for 15 seconds, and force_close=True is the switch for a new tunnel per request.
  • Retry 429, 5xx and timeouts in the job, never 407 or 403. aiohttp has no built-in retry, and on per-GB plans every retry is extra traffic.

Read the full guide on proxymint, with the commands, tables and sources.

event_model_payload.headline: Is OpenClaw Worth Self-Hosting Over a Claude Pro or ChatGPT Subscription? A Security-First Look
event_model_payload.summary:
OpenClaw is worth self-hosting if you want an assistant that lives in your own messaging apps, keeps its memory and configuration on your server, and acts on your behalf. It is not worth it if you mostly chat in a browser tab, because Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus at about $20 a month gives you a polished app with no gateway to secure and no API bill to watch. The deciding factor is not price. It is whether you will actually lock down the three things a subscription handles for you: the gateway token, who can message your agent, and how much your API keys are allowed to spend.

TL;DR:

  • The browser-tab chatter (a student drafting essays and asking quick questions): stay on the subscription, because a flat fee with no infrastructure beats any setup you would have to maintain.
  • The messaging-first power user (a freelancer who lives in Telegram and wants an assistant there): self-host OpenClaw, because it meets you in the channel you already use and keeps conversation state on your own disk.
  • The homelab tinkerer (someone already running Docker on a mini PC): self-host OpenClaw behind a VPN or SSO proxy, because you already have the skills to handle token rotation and network isolation.
  • The light, occasional user (a parent asking a few questions a week): self-host with a hard provider spend cap, because pay-per-token usage at low volume can come in well under a flat monthly fee.
  • The heavy daily user (a developer running long agent sessions every day): keep the subscription or set strict budgets first, because API usage at high volume can cost more than $20 a month.
  • The privacy-focused household (a family that wants nothing kept on a vendor's chat history servers): self-host, but understand that your prompts still reach the model provider through the API.

The central tradeoff is simple: a subscription sells you convenience and a fixed bill, while OpenClaw gives you control and makes you responsible for every lock on the door.

Table of contents

  • What does OpenClaw actually do that a chat subscription does not?
  • How much does OpenClaw really cost compared with a $20 a month subscription?
  • Capping API key spend: provider limits, scoped keys and budget alerts
  • What does the gateway token protect, and where should it be stored?
  • Allowed origins, reverse proxies and keeping the Control UI off the open internet
  • How do you stop strangers from messaging your OpenClaw agent?
  • Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord and Slack: exposure compared channel by channel
  • What can the agent execute on your server, and how do you restrict it?
  • Is prompt injection through incoming messages a real risk?
  • Where should you run OpenClaw: home server, VPS or managed personal cloud?
  • Data sovereignty: what stays on your server and what still reaches the model provider
  • How do you rotate tokens and recover after a leaked API key?
  • Which OpenClaw setup fits your situation?
  • Key points

What does OpenClaw actually do that a chat subscription does not?

A Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus subscription gives you a chat window. You open the app, type, and read the reply. OpenClaw is an open source agent you run yourself. A long-running gateway process connects a model provider to your messaging apps and to tools on the machine it runs on. The model still does the thinking. OpenClaw decides where the conversation happens, what the agent can touch, and where its state is stored.

That difference changes your security job. A subscription has one way in: your account login. OpenClaw has several, and you own each of them.

Capability Chat subscription Self-hosted OpenClaw
Where you talk to it Vendor web and mobile apps Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack and a browser Control UI
Model access Fixed to one vendor's models Your own Anthropic or OpenAI API key, billed per token
Memory and configuration Stored in the vendor's account Stored as files on your server
Actions beyond chat Limited to the vendor's built-in tools Shell commands, browsing and installable skills on your host
Billing About $20 a month, flat Usage-based, with no ceiling unless you set one
Who secures access The vendor You: gateway token, channel allowlists, spend caps

Read that last row carefully. Each extra capability opens another way in. A messaging channel means strangers can find your bot. An API key means a leak turns straight into a bill. Shell access means a manipulated prompt can run commands on your server. The rest of this article covers how to close each of those doors before you cancel your subscription.

How much does OpenClaw really cost compared with a $20 a month subscription?

A subscription at about $20 a month comes to $240 a year and $720 over three years, whether you use it every day or forget it for a month. OpenClaw itself costs nothing to license. Its running cost has four parts, and only one is fixed.

  • API usage: you pay your provider per token, for input and output separately. Light use with short messages can cost a fraction of a flat fee. Long agent sessions are different: every turn resends the conversation history, and tool output gets fed back into the context, so the bill grows faster than your message count suggests.
  • Hosting: the agent needs an always-on machine. Plan for roughly 2 to 3 GB of RAM for the container stack. That might be a mini PC you already own, a small VPS billed monthly, or spare capacity on an existing home server.
  • Electricity or rental: a home box adds a small, steady power cost. A VPS adds a fixed monthly line item. Neither depends on how much you chat.
  • Your time: this is the cost most people leave out. Token rotation, updates, channel allowlists and checking the spend dashboard take real hours in the first month and a few minutes a week after that.

The honest comparison is not $20 against zero. It is $20 against a variable API bill plus hosting plus maintenance. If you already run a homelab, hosting is close to free, and the decision comes down to your token volume. If you would be renting a server just for OpenClaw, the subscription usually wins on cost alone. In that case, self-hosting has to be justified by control, not savings.

The variable part is also the risky part. An uncapped key has no ceiling, which is why the next section comes before any other hardening step.

Capping API key spend: provider limits, scoped keys and budget alerts

Do this before you connect a single messaging channel. A leaked or misused key costs money, and nothing in OpenClaw stops a runaway loop from reaching your provider. Your protection has to live on the provider's side, where the agent cannot override it.

  • A dedicated key for the agent: create a separate key just for OpenClaw. In the Anthropic Console, put it in its own workspace. On OpenAI, put it in its own project. Never reuse a key from your scripts or IDE. If the key leaks, you revoke one thing and nothing else breaks.
  • A spend limit equal to your old subscription: set a monthly limit on that workspace or project. $20 is a sensible first ceiling because it is exactly what you stopped paying. Raise it only after a full month of real usage data shows you need more.
  • Budget alerts below the limit: turn on notifications at about 50% and 80% of the cap. An alert in the first week of the month means a stuck session or an abusive sender, not heavy use.
  • A minimal prepaid balance: where your provider bills from prepaid credits, keep only a small balance loaded and turn off auto-reload. An empty balance is a hard stop no misconfiguration can get past.
  • Key storage outside the compose file: pass ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY through an environment file or a secret with restricted permissions, never committed to Git. A compose file pushed to a public repository is one of the most common ways keys leak.
  • Model restrictions where offered: if your provider lets you limit which models a key or project can call, block the most expensive tier. This stops a configuration slip from quietly switching every request to the priciest model.

A capped key turns the worst case from an open-ended bill into a known number.

What does the gateway token protect, and where should it be stored?

The gateway is the core of OpenClaw. It holds your API keys, your channel connections and the agent's tools. The gateway token is the shared secret the browser Control UI and other clients present to connect to it. Whoever holds the token can chat as you, change the configuration and trigger anything the agent is allowed to do. Treat it as a root password, not a convenience setting.

Generate it, don't invent it. openssl rand -hex 32 produces 64 hex characters, or 256 bits of randomness. A short memorable phrase is the weakest link in the whole setup.

Where the token lives matters as much as how strong it is. The same rules apply whether the gateway runs on a self-managed VPS, a home server, a NAS or a managed platform. Yundera is a managed Personal Cloud Server, built on CasaOS, that runs self-hosted apps as Docker containers on a server dedicated to the user.

Storage location Risk Recommendation
Hardcoded in docker-compose.yml Leaks with any Git push, backup share or screenshot Avoid entirely
.env file next to the compose file Readable by anyone with shell access to the host Acceptable with chmod 600 and kept out of Git
Docker secret or the platform's secret store Only exposed to the container that needs it Preferred for any server reachable from the internet
Browser tab session storage Cleared when the tab closes, but readable by scripts on that origin Fine for daily use; never paste the token into other sites
Password manager Safe at rest, only exposed when you copy it Keep the master copy here for rotation and recovery

Two habits close the remaining gaps. Never share the token in a chat channel the agent itself reads. Rotate it whenever someone who once had access no longer should.

Allowed origins, reverse proxies and keeping the Control UI off the open internet

The token proves who you are. The network layout decides who gets close enough to try it. A Control UI that anyone on the internet can reach invites token guessing, scanning and attacks on whatever bug appears in the next release. Make reaching the login screen hard, not just passing it.

  • Bind the gateway to localhost: publish the container port as 127.0.0.1:PORT:PORT, not just PORT:PORT. Docker's default publishes on every interface and can bypass host firewall rules like ufw. Binding to localhost forces all outside traffic through your proxy.
  • Exact allowed origins, never a wildcard: OpenClaw checks the browser's Origin header before it accepts a Control UI connection. List the exact HTTPS address you use, such as https://agent.example.com. A * entry lets any website your browser visits try to talk to your gateway.
  • TLS at a reverse proxy: put Caddy, nginx or Traefik in front and serve only HTTPS. Plain HTTP sends the token across the network in readable form on every connection. Caddy gets and renews certificates automatically, which removes the most common reason people skip TLS.
  • An authentication layer in front of the token: Authelia or Authentik as forward-auth means an attacker has to pass SSO, ideally with TOTP or a passkey, before they can even try the gateway token. Two independent secrets beat one strong one.
  • A VPN instead of a public hostname: if only you and your household use the Control UI, Tailscale or WireGuard removes the public endpoint completely. Messaging channels keep working, because Telegram and Discord connections are outbound from your server.
  • Rate limiting on the proxy: cap connection attempts per IP address. Even a 64-character token deserves protection from endless automated retries.

Pick one: a VPN or SSO. Doing neither is the mistake.

How do you stop strangers from messaging your OpenClaw agent?

A Telegram bot username or a WhatsApp number is discoverable. Bot names get scraped and numbers get guessed. Anyone who gets a message through spends your tokens and can use whatever tools the agent has. The default stance should be that nobody gets in until you have named them.

  • Pairing or allowlist, never open: OpenClaw's direct-message policy decides what happens when an unknown sender writes in. Pairing mode answers with a short code that you must approve on the server before any conversation starts. Allowlist mode drops everyone not listed. An open policy hands your agent, and your API budget, to the whole platform.
  • Stable numeric IDs, not display names: allowlist Telegram users by numeric user ID and WhatsApp contacts by full international number, for example +447700900123. Usernames and display names can be changed or copied. An ID cannot.
  • Groups off by default: adding the bot to a group exposes it to every member, including people who join later. If you do enable a group, list that specific group and require an explicit mention before the agent replies.
  • Pending pairing requests reviewed weekly: every unapproved code is someone who found your bot. A steady trickle of unknown requests is your early warning that the handle is known and the allowlist is the only thing holding.
  • Separate trust levels per person: your partner may need the agent for reminders, not shell commands. Give household members a less privileged agent profile instead of your full toolset.
  • Remove people promptly: when someone leaves the household or a project, delete their ID the same day. Stale allowlist entries outlive the trust they were based on.

Done right, a stranger's message gets dropped silently or answered only with a pairing code, at zero token cost.

Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord and Slack: exposure compared channel by channel

Every channel adds a credential to protect and a third party that sees your messages. Self-hosting the gateway does not change the fact that Telegram, Meta, Discord or Slack still relays every prompt you type. Choose your channels for their exposure, not just for convenience.

Channel What you expose Hardening priority
Telegram A bot token from BotFather and a public, searchable bot username. Bot chats are not end-to-end encrypted, so Telegram's servers can read them. Pairing or allowlist by numeric user ID. Revoke the token in BotFather if it leaks. Disable group joins unless needed.
WhatsApp A linked-device session on a real phone number, authorised by QR code. Whoever holds the session files can read and send as that number. Use a dedicated number, not your personal one. Protect the session directory like a password. Unlink from the phone if the server is compromised.
Discord A bot token from the Developer Portal, with the Message Content intent turned on. Messages are not end-to-end encrypted. Turn off "Public Bot" so only you can invite it. Restrict it to one private server and specific channels. Reset the token on any suspicion.
Slack Bot and app-level tokens installed in a workspace. Messages follow that workspace's retention and admin export policy. Install only in a workspace you control. Grant the narrowest scopes. Remember that workspace admins can export conversations.

The table points to a simple rule: start with one channel. Each extra channel doubles the places a token can leak and the allowlists you have to maintain. For most people moving off a subscription app, one Telegram bot with a strict allowlist covers daily use. Add a second channel only when a real need shows up.

What can the agent execute on your server, and how do you restrict it?

A chat subscription runs its tools on the vendor's machines. OpenClaw runs them on yours. Depending on configuration, the agent can run shell commands, read and write files, drive a browser and load installable skills. Whatever the container can reach, a bad instruction can reach too. On Yundera, a self-managed VPS, a home server or a NAS alike, the agent runs as a Docker container, so the container boundary is your main control.

  • Approval before execution: set shell commands to require your confirmation instead of running automatically. Each approval costs you a tap. In return, a manipulated prompt cannot quietly run curl … | sh while you sleep.
  • Deny by default, allow by need: turn off tool families you do not use. If you only want reminders and web lookups, the agent has no reason to keep shell or file-write access.
  • Never mount the Docker socket: mounting /var/run/docker.sock into the container is equivalent to giving the agent root on the host. No convenience feature is worth that.
  • A narrow workspace mount: give the agent one dedicated directory, not your home folder or /. Mount everything else read-only or leave it out entirely.
  • Drop privileges in compose: run as a non-root user and add cap_drop: [ALL] and security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]. These three lines remove most container-escape paths for free.
  • Hard resource limits: cap memory and CPU with mem_limit and cpus. A runaway loop then hits its own ceiling instead of starving your other services.
  • Vet skills like software installs: a third-party skill is code that runs with the agent's permissions. Read its source before enabling it, and pin a known version.

Approval prompts plus a minimal mount set cover most of the risk.

Is prompt injection through incoming messages a real risk?

Yes, and it is the risk a subscription user never has to think about. Prompt injection means text the model reads gets treated as instructions instead of data. Every model is open to it today, and no setting in OpenClaw removes it completely. What changes the outcome is what the agent can do once it has been fooled. In a browser chat, a successful injection produces a strange reply. In an agent with shell access and your API key, it can run commands or send messages as you.

Injection vector How it reaches the agent Mitigation
Web pages The agent browses or fetches a URL containing hidden instructions in text or HTML comments Require approval for any tool call that follows a browse, and keep shell off for browsing tasks
Forwarded messages You forward a stranger's message or email for a summary, and it carries embedded commands Summarise in a profile with no write tools. Treat forwarded content as hostile by default
Group chats Any member, including one who joined yesterday, posts text the agent reads Require an explicit mention and allowlist the group. Better still, keep groups disabled
Files and documents A PDF or README.md in the workspace includes instructions aimed at the model Mount untrusted files read-only and in a separate directory from the agent's own configuration
Third-party skills A skill's prompt text or tool descriptions steer the model toward actions it should not take Read the skill before enabling it and pin a known version

The useful mindset is containment, not prevention. Assume an injection will eventually succeed, then ask what a fooled agent could reach. If the answer is "one workspace folder, with no shell and capped spend", the damage stays small.

Where should you run OpenClaw: home server, VPS or managed personal cloud?

The gateway has to be always on, or messages sent to your bot overnight go unanswered. Each hosting choice also changes which of the earlier hardening steps carries the most weight.

  • Home server or mini PC: your hardware, your network, and no monthly rental. Telegram, Discord and Slack connect outbound, so the bot works behind ordinary NAT without forwarding any port. The weak points are power cuts, residential uplinks and the temptation to expose the Control UI with a quick port forward. Use a VPN instead.
  • Self-managed VPS: a public IP, high uptime and a fixed monthly bill. Within minutes of going live, the IP will see automated SSH and HTTP scans. Use key-only SSH, a default-deny firewall and the localhost binding from earlier. Note that the provider controls the hypervisor your session files and tokens sit on.
  • NAS: convenient if you already run one, but it usually holds your photos, documents and backups. An agent with a careless volume mount sits one path away from all of it. Keep its workspace on a separate share, and check that the CPU and RAM leave room for the agent.
  • Managed personal cloud such as Yundera: the app is installed from an app store in one click and reached on a public HTTPS subdomain through NSL.SH mesh routing, with no static IP, port forwarding or manual TLS setup. Data stays on a server dedicated to the user. A public subdomain still needs the token and SSO discipline from earlier, because reachable means discoverable.

A practical rule: if you already maintain a box that runs 24 hours a day, use it. If you would be buying hardware just for OpenClaw, compare that cost against two or three years of the $20 subscription first.

Data sovereignty: what stays on your server and what still reaches the model provider

Self-hosting OpenClaw does not make your prompts private. It moves the conversation archive, memory and configuration onto disks you control. The model provider still receives every prompt and every tool result it reasons over. That traffic is governed by the provider's API terms, which are separate from its consumer app terms, so read the retention and training clauses for the API specifically.

Advantages you actually gain:

  • Conversation history on your disk: transcripts and agent memory live as files in your volume, not in a vendor account that can be locked, changed or subpoenaed in one place.
  • Choice of hosting location: you decide the country and the machine, whether that is a home server, a NAS, a VPS in the EU or a dedicated server on Yundera.
  • Provider portability: switching between Anthropic and OpenAI is a key change, not an account migration. Your history stays where it is.
  • One deletion path: removing the volume and revoking the keys ends your local footprint, with no export request needed.

Checklist before you call it sovereign:

  • Provider API terms read: confirm the retention period and whether API data is used for training.
  • Channel relay accepted: Telegram, Discord and Slack still store or relay messages under their own policies.
  • Backups encrypted: a plain .tar.gz of the data volume on a cloud drive undoes the whole point.
  • Volume location known: you can name the physical machine and country where the agent's files sit.
  • Secrets kept separate from data: keys and tokens are not stored inside the backup archive itself.

What you own here is the archive and the control plane, not the inference.

How do you rotate tokens and recover after a leaked API key?

Assume a credential will leak eventually: a screenshot, a public repository, a compromised laptop. What matters is how fast you can revoke everything and bring the agent back. Practise this once while nothing is on fire, and time how long it takes.

Credential Revoke and reissue Routine rotation
Provider API key Delete it in the Anthropic Console or OpenAI dashboard, create a new key in the same workspace or project, then update the secret Every 90 days, and right away if your spend alert fires unexpectedly
Gateway token Generate a new one with openssl rand -hex 32, replace the secret and recreate the container with docker compose up -d Every 90 days, and whenever someone loses access
Telegram bot token Send /revoke to BotFather and pick the bot to get a fresh token Only on suspicion, since the token changes but the bot username stays
Discord bot token Use Reset Token on the bot's page in the Developer Portal Only on suspicion, or after a contributor leaves
WhatsApp session Log the device out under Linked devices on the phone, then relink with a new QR code After any server compromise or restore onto new hardware
Slack tokens Regenerate tokens or reinstall the app in the workspace When workspace membership changes significantly

After a real leak, order matters. Revoke the provider key first, because it is the only credential that costs money every minute it stays live. Next rotate the gateway token, because it grants control of everything else. Then reset the channel tokens. Finally, check the provider's usage log for calls you did not make, and look at the agent's recent transcripts for actions taken during the exposure window. If those transcripts show tool calls you did not approve, rebuild the container from a clean image instead of trusting the running one.

Which OpenClaw setup fits your situation?

Use your actual habits, not your ambitions, to choose. Most people overestimate how much agent capability they will use and underestimate how much upkeep it needs.

Profile Recommendation Main reason
Browser-only chatter Keep Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus A flat $20 a month buys a polished app with nothing to secure
Telegram-first freelancer Self-host, one channel, allowlist by numeric ID The assistant lives where you already work, with history on your disk
Homelab owner with a 24/7 box Self-host behind a VPN or SSO proxy Hosting cost is already paid and the network skills are already there
Light weekly user Self-host with a $20 provider spend cap Low token volume can cost less than the flat fee
Heavy daily agent user Keep the subscription or budget carefully Long sessions resend context and can exceed a flat plan
Family sharing one assistant Self-host with separate, less privileged profiles Per-person allowlists beat sharing one vendor login
Privacy-first, no third-party relays Self-host with the Control UI over a VPN only Avoids messaging-platform relays, though prompts still reach the model provider
No time for maintenance Keep the subscription Unrotated tokens and stale allowlists are worse than no agent

Next steps:

If you self-host:

  1. Create a dedicated provider key with a $20 monthly cap and alerts at 50% and 80%.
  2. Generate the gateway token, store it as a secret and bind the port to localhost.
  3. Connect one channel in pairing or allowlist mode, with shell approvals turned on.

If you stay on the subscription:

  1. Turn off chat history training in the app's privacy settings.
  2. Revisit self-hosting once your messaging or automation needs outgrow the app.

Key points

OpenClaw beats a chat subscription only when you want an agent in your own channels and you are willing to own every credential that a vendor used to manage for you.

Point Details
The cost is variable, not lower A subscription is a fixed $240 a year. OpenClaw is free to license, but you pay per-token API usage plus hosting plus your own time. Light users can come out ahead. Heavy agent users often do not, because every turn resends the growing context.
Spend caps come first A dedicated provider key in its own workspace or project, capped at the price of the plan you cancelled, turns a leaked key or a runaway loop into a bounded loss instead of an open-ended bill.
The gateway token is a root password Generate 256 bits of randomness, store it as a secret rather than in docker-compose.yml, and put a VPN or an SSO layer in front so attackers cannot reach the login screen in the first place.
Channels are public doors Bot usernames and phone numbers get found. Pairing or allowlist mode with stable numeric IDs, groups off by default, and one channel to start keep strangers from spending your tokens.
Containment beats prevention Prompt injection cannot be fully blocked. Approval before shell commands, no Docker socket, one narrow workspace mount and dropped capabilities limit what a fooled agent can actually do.
Sovereignty is partial Transcripts, memory and configuration stay on your disk. Prompts still reach the model provider and pass through messaging platforms, so read the API terms and encrypt your backups.

event_model_payload.headline: Deploy a LangGraph agent to a public URL
event_model_payload.summary:
You have a LangGraph graph that works in a notebook. Now someone else needs to call it: a teammate, a Telegram bot, a CRM that posts a question and waits for an answer. That means a web API, a server that stays up, pinned dependencies, a secret for your model key, and a URL that not everyone on the internet can spend your model budget through.

This walkthrough takes a small LangGraph agent from a folder on your laptop to a public HTTPS address on uagents8, then locks that address with a token. In our run on 28 October 2026 the agent was live 78 seconds after we created it; the build took about 38 of them.

What we're deploying

One graph, two nodes, one branch:

START --(the question is arithmetic)--> calculate --> END
START --(anything else)--------------> respond   --> END

calculate is a tool node in plain Python. respond is where your model goes; until you add one, it answers with a labelled stub, so the whole thing runs with no key and no network. The graph sits behind FastAPI with one route that matters, POST /ask.

import ast
import operator
import os
from typing import TypedDict

import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class State(TypedDict):
    question: str
    answer: str
    mode: str  # "tool", "stub" or "model"


_OPERATORS = {ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul, ast.Div: operator.truediv}


def _evaluate(node: ast.AST) -> float:
    """Evaluate + - * / and parentheses on numbers; anything else raises ValueError."""
    if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
        return _evaluate(node.body)
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
        return node.value
    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and isinstance(node.op, ast.USub):
        return -_evaluate(node.operand)
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in _OPERATORS:
        return _OPERATORS[type(node.op)](_evaluate(node.left), _evaluate(node.right))
    raise ValueError("unsupported expression")


def _arithmetic(question: str) -> str | None:
    """The expression inside `question`, if the whole question is just arithmetic."""
    expression = question.strip().lower().removeprefix("what is").strip().rstrip("?= ")
    if not expression or not any(ch.isdigit() for ch in expression):
        return None
    if any(ch not in "0123456789+-*/(). " for ch in expression):
        return None
    return expression


def route(state: State) -> str:
    return "calculate" if _arithmetic(state["question"]) else "respond"


def calculate(state: State) -> dict:
    expression = _arithmetic(state["question"]) or ""
    try:
        result = _evaluate(ast.parse(expression, mode="eval"))
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, ArithmeticError):
        return {"answer": f"I could not calculate {expression!r}.", "mode": "tool"}
    return {"answer": f"{expression} = {result:g}", "mode": "tool"}


def respond(state: State) -> dict:
    # Your model call goes here. The key comes from the environment, never from this file.
    return {"answer": f"[stub] You asked: {state['question']}", "mode": "stub"}


builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("calculate", calculate)
builder.add_node("respond", respond)
builder.add_conditional_edges(START, route, {"calculate": "calculate", "respond": "respond"})
builder.add_edge("calculate", END)
builder.add_edge("respond", END)
graph = builder.compile()

app = FastAPI()


class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=500)


@app.post("/ask")
def ask(body: Ask) -> dict:
    result = graph.invoke({"question": body.question, "answer": "", "mode": ""})
    return {"question": body.question, "answer": result["answer"], "mode": result["mode"]}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8000")))

_arithmetic and _evaluate accept + - * / and parentheses on numbers and nothing else, so user input never reaches eval. A malformed expression gets a polite answer, not a crash.

Three things the platform needs from your code

1. Listen on PORT, on 0.0.0.0. The last two lines do it. The platform sets PORT; a server bound to 127.0.0.1 runs fine and can never be reached.

2. Start listening before anything slow. The health check only asks whether the port accepts connections. It requests no route, so an API with only /ask is fine. It gives the port about 150 seconds to open. Load big models or indexes after the server is up, or lazily on the first request.

3. Pin every dependency. The build runs Python 3.12 with no compiler, so pick versions that ship wheels. In a clean virtual environment:

pip install fastapi uvicorn langgraph
pip freeze > requirements.txt

The sample pins fastapi==0.143.3, uvicorn==0.54.0 and langgraph==1.2.16. main.py and requirements.txt sit at the top level, and the platform runs python main.py. There is no build file to write: the platform works out the build from your code, and if your project already has its own build file at the top level, it uses that as written.

Deploy it

Push the folder to a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, or zip main.py and requirements.txt.

In the dashboard, press + Deploy Agent:

  1. Source: pick your Git provider and the repository. Every push to the branch redeploys. Or pick Code Archive and upload the zip.
  2. Configure: keep Continuous Service and choose a Resource size. Sizes are memory limits: T is 256 MB, S 512 MB, L 1 GB. In our run this agent used about 80 MB, so T is enough.
  3. Confirm, then Deploy agent.

The status screen moves from Building agent to Starting your agent to Running. Ours took 78 seconds, uploaded as a zip, with no model key. The agent's page then shows its public URL.

Call it 

curl -X POST https://<your-agent-url>/ask \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "what is 2+3*4?"}'

{"question": "what is 2+3*4?", "answer": "2+3*4 = 14", "mode": "tool"}

Ask it anything else and you get the stub, with "mode": "stub". That's your sign that the branch to the model is wired and waiting.

Add your model

Put your provider's client library in requirements.txt (pinned) and replace the body of respond() with the call. Then add the key in the agent's Settings → Environment Variables, with Sensitive switched on, and redeploy. A changed variable is picked up on the next deploy. The key never goes into the code or the repository.

Close the door: an access token

Here is the part most tutorials skip. Your agent now has a public URL, and behind it sits a model you pay for per token. Anyone who finds the URL can spend your budget.

Open the agent's Settings tab, find Access tokens and choose Generate agent token. Give it a name you'll recognise (crm, telegram-bot) and pick how long it stays valid: 7, 30 or 90 days, or no expiry. Copy it. It starts with uagt_live_ and is shown only once.


curl -X POST https://<your-agent-url>/ask \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer uagt_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "what is 6*7?"}'

A call without a valid token gets 401 Unauthorized before it reaches your code or your model. Once an agent has its first token, every caller needs one, so give your existing callers theirs before you generate it. One token per caller means you can revoke a leaked one without breaking the others.

When the deploy fails

It will, sooner or later: a package you installed locally and never pinned, a variable you renamed in one file and not the other, a server bound to localhost. The failed agent's page explains the error in plain language. If you press Fix with AI, it reads the error and your code, patches a copy, checks the patch before building it, and deploys the fixed copy as a new version. If that copy fails too, it makes one more attempt. Your repository is never changed, and you can restore the previous version in one click.

What it costs

Size T runs on every plan, from Builder at €19 a month (prices before VAT). Monthly plans start with a 14-day free trial of every feature. A card is required to prevent abuse, and nothing is charged unless you choose a plan to continue with. For the launch, LAUNCH30 takes 30% off the first three months on Builder or Growth, monthly billing, until 30 November; with the trial, the discount starts with your first payment, after the trial. Code from your laptop to a token-protected URL, in Europe.

Try it: https://uagents8.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=launch-2026-11&utm_content=devto-langgraph-article

event_model_payload.headline: Ubuntu 26.04 Upgrade with Ansible: Migrate 24.04 Fleets Safely
event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on kuryzhev.cloud

You have forty Ubuntu 24.04 servers in an inventory, a change window on Thursday, and a manager asking whether the Ubuntu 26.04 upgrade can be "just a playbook run". It can, if you treat it as a staged migration and not a bulk apt upgrade. This runbook shows how to drive do-release-upgrade from Ansible one host at a time, with checks before and after each step.

The timing matters now. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS was released on 2026-04-23, and the current point release is 26.04.1, according to the Ubuntu release cycle page. Ubuntu normally offers LTS-to-LTS upgrades to servers only once the first point release is out, so the supported upgrade path should now be open. Verify that on your own hosts with the check task shown below. It fails if no upgrade is offered yet.

Short answer: bring every host to fully patched 24.04 and take a snapshot. Then run a serial: 1 playbook that wraps do-release-upgrade in async, reboots, and asserts 26.04. Upgrade a canary first. Where you can, rebuild stateless hosts from a fresh 26.04 image instead. In-place upgrades carry the risk, and rebuilding avoids most of it.

What changed and who is affected

Every 24.04 host that you want on a supported LTS beyond its current cycle is affected. Ubuntu 24.04 is still supported, so this is a planned migration, not an emergency. Check the support dates for both releases on the release cycle page before you commit to a deadline.

The groups that need the most care:

  • Hosts with third-party apt repositories (Docker, PostgreSQL PGDG, Grafana, Jenkins). The upgrader disables third-party sources, and you must re-enable them for the new release.
  • Stateful hosts such as databases, where a major library and service-version jump happens in the same reboot.
  • Jenkins agents. Jenkins LTS 2.555.1+ requires Java 21 or 25 on the controller and on every agent JVM. Confirm that the Java package your agents use exists on the new release (upgrade guide).
  • Control nodes. ansible-core 2.22 is the current release (2.22.0, released 2026-11-02). Check the Ansible documentation for the supported target-Python matrix. A new release usually ships a newer system Python, and that is the interpreter Ansible uses on the target.

Read the official 26.04 release notes for removed or replaced packages before you start. This article does not list package-level changes, because they are version-specific and you should take them from Canonical.

Before/after config

The common failure is a playbook set that hardcodes the old release name in repository definitions and package pins. First, the "before" pattern, which breaks the moment the host is on a new release:

# BEFORE: roles/docker/tasks/main.yml (breaks after the upgrade)
- name: Add Docker repo
  ansible.builtin.apt_repository:
    repo: "deb [arch=amd64] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu noble stable"  # hardcoded codename
    filename: docker

🧪 Lab — try this in your browser

  • EOL Countdown — Check when your Kubernetes, PostgreSQL, Node.js, Ubuntu… versions lose support. Paste command output or add versions — get status, days left and calendar reminders.

The "after" version derives the codename from facts and gates on the release, so the same role works on both sides of the migration. It also writes a deb822 .sources file with a Signed-By key, which matches Docker's current install method. The deb822_repository module needs python3-debian on the target. Remove any old docker.list file so you do not end up with duplicate sources.

# AFTER: codename comes from facts, not from the file
- name: Add Docker repo for the running release
  ansible.builtin.deb822_repository:
    name: docker
    types: deb
    uris: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu
    suites: "{{ "{{" }} ansible_facts['distribution_release'] }}"
    components: stable
    architectures: "{{ "{{" }} 'amd64' if ansible_facts['architecture'] == 'x86_64' else 'arm64' }}"
    signed_by: https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg
  when: ansible_facts['distribution_version'] is version('24.04', '>=')

- name: Refresh apt cache
  ansible.builtin.apt:
    update_cache: true

Before you upgrade, confirm that each vendor actually publishes a repository for the new codename. Docker Engine 29, for example, is installed from Docker's own repo, so check the Docker install docs for supported releases. If a vendor has not published one yet, that host group waits.

Step-by-step Ubuntu 26.04 upgrade

Run this against a one-host canary group first. The playbook does the following:

  • Refuses to touch anything that is not 24.04.
  • Patches fully and forces the LTS prompt policy.
  • Runs the upgrader with async, so a dropped SSH session does not kill it.
  • Asserts the new release after the final reboot.
# upgrade-2604.yml
- name: Upgrade Ubuntu 24.04 to 26.04
  hosts: upgrade_wave
  become: true
  serial: 1                  # one host at a time
  max_fail_percentage: 0     # stop the whole run on the first failure
  tasks:
    - name: Refuse anything that is not 24.04
      ansible.builtin.assert:
        that: ansible_facts['distribution_version'] == '24.04'

    # Take your snapshot here (cloud API, hypervisor, LVM). Ansible cannot undo this upgrade.

    - name: Fully patch 24.04 first
      ansible.builtin.apt:
        update_cache: true
        upgrade: dist
        autoremove: true

    - name: Check for pending reboot
      ansible.builtin.stat:
        path: /var/run/reboot-required
      register: reboot_flag

    - name: Reboot into the final 24.04 kernel
      ansible.builtin.reboot:
      when: reboot_flag.stat.exists

    - name: Allow LTS upgrades
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /etc/update-manager/release-upgrades
        regexp: '^Prompt='
        line: 'Prompt=lts'

    - name: Confirm an upgrade is offered (fails if none is)
      ansible.builtin.command: do-release-upgrade --check-dist-upgrade-only
      changed_when: false

    - name: Run the release upgrade
      ansible.builtin.command: do-release-upgrade -f DistUpgradeViewNonInteractive
      environment:
        DEBIAN_FRONTEND: noninteractive
      async: 5400            # 90 minutes ceiling
      poll: 30

    - name: Reboot into 26.04
      ansible.builtin.reboot:
        reboot_timeout: 900

    - name: Refresh facts after the upgrade
      ansible.builtin.setup:

    - name: Assert the host is now on 26.04
      ansible.builtin.assert:
        that: ansible_facts['distribution_version'] == '26.04'

Run it with a canary limit. The --diff flag prints file changes, such as the lineinfile edit, as they are applied:

ansible-playbook -i inventory.yml upgrade-2604.yml --limit canary01 --diff
# then widen: --limit 'upgrade_wave:!canary01'

Watch out for non-interactive config-file handling. The non-interactive frontend avoids prompts, which means modified conffiles are resolved automatically. Afterward, review /var/log/dist-upgrade/ and any *.dpkg-new or *.dpkg-old files. Check the Ubuntu Server documentation on upgrades for the exact semantics on your version.

Verify and roll back

Do not rely only on the playbook's green status. Verify the result independently, per host, with an ad-hoc run:

ansible upgrade_wave -b -m ansible.builtin.shell -a \
  '. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_ID" && systemctl --failed --no-legend | wc -l && apt-get check && uname -r'
# expect: 26.04 / 0 failed units / apt-get check silent / a new kernel version

Then run your application-level checks:

  • HTTP health endpoints.
  • Database replication state.
  • Prometheus up for the host's targets.
  • The alert dashboard in Grafana.

A host that boots but has lost its exporter is a quiet failure worth checking for explicitly.

Rollback is a restore, not a downgrade. Ubuntu does not support downgrading a release in place. Your real rollback options are:

  • Restore the pre-upgrade snapshot or image. This is fast, but you lose data written since the snapshot.
  • Rebuild the host from a 24.04 image and re-run your configuration playbooks. This is clean, but it needs your Ansible to be idempotent.
  • Fail traffic over to an untouched replica, for stateful tiers.

That is why serial: 1 and max_fail_percentage: 0 matter. They cap the blast radius at one host. The cost is wall-clock time. Forty hosts, each with two reboots and a long package run, need a long window. For stateless fleets, replacing instances with fresh 26.04 images is often simpler and lower-risk than upgrading in place, especially if image builds are already automated.

Gotchas after the switch

Third-party repositories stay disabled. The upgrader comments out or disables external sources. Re-run your repo roles (the "after" version above). Then confirm with apt-cache policy docker-ce that the candidate comes from the vendor and not from Ubuntu's archive.

Python on the target can change. Your tasks may rely on system Python modules such as python3-apt, python3-debian, or python3-docker. If so, re-run your baseline role first. Leave ansible_python_interpreter on auto discovery unless you have a reason to pin it. Check the ansible-core 2.22 documentation for the supported target-Python versions before you upgrade the control node and the targets together.

Leftover 24.04 package pins. Roles that pin exact versions (postgresql-16=...) will fail or hold packages back. PostgreSQL 18 is the current major, but a major database upgrade is a separate project, so do not combine it with the OS jump. Keep the same major version across the OS upgrade if the package is available, for example from PGDG. Move the database afterward.

Agents and runtimes. Re-check the Java version on Jenkins agents, and rerun your hardening role. Sysctl, SSH, and firewall defaults can differ between releases. Diff your rendered sshd -T output against a pre-upgrade capture.

Finally, record the result in your inventory so later plays can gate on it, for example with an os_release: "26.04" host variable. More runbooks of this kind live on kuryzhev.cloud.

Related

  • Migrate Playbooks to ansible-core 2.22 Without Breaking Collections
  • Ansible Rolling Deployment: 6 Tips for Zero-Downtime Releases
  • Ansible server bootstrap locks you out of new hosts: fix

event_model_payload.headline: Functions in Python
event_model_payload.summary:
1. What is a Function in Python?

  • A function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, we can define a function once and call it whenever needed.

  • Functions help to reduce code repetition, improve code readability, and make programs easier to maintain.

  • Python provides the def keyword to define a function.

Syntax: 

def function_name():
    # function body
    statements

Example: 

def greet():
    print("Hello, Welcome to Python")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python

Explanation:

  • def is the keyword used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • The statements inside the function form the function body.
  • greet() is the function call used to execute the function.

2. Why Do We Use Functions?

Functions provide several advantages:

  1. Code Reusability – Write code once and use it multiple times.
  2. Code Readability – Makes the program easier to understand.
  3. Code Organization – Divides a large program into smaller parts.
  4. Easy Maintenance – Changes can be made in one place.
  5. Avoid Code Repetition – Reduces duplicate code.

3. Types of Functions in Python

Python functions can be classified into two main types:

  1. Built-in Functions
  2. User-defined Functions

1. Built-in Functions

Built-in functions are predefined functions provided by Python. We can use them directly without defining them.

Some commonly used built-in functions are:

Function Description
print() Displays output
input() Gets input from the user
len() Returns the length
type() Returns the data type

Example:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

print(len(numbers))

Output:

4

2. User-defined Functions

User-defined functions are functions created by programmers to perform specific tasks.

The def keyword is used to create user-defined functions.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    print(a + b)

add()

Output:

30

4. Types of User-defined Functions Based on Arguments and Return Values

Based on arguments and return values, functions can be divided into four types.

1. Function Without Arguments and Without Return Value

This function does not accept any arguments and does not return any value.

Example:

def display():
    print("Welcome to Python")

display()

Output:

Welcome to Python

2. Function With Arguments and Without Return Value

This function accepts arguments but does not return any value.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

add(10, 20)

Output:

30

Here, a and b receive the values passed during the function call.

3. Function Without Arguments and With Return Value

This function does not accept arguments but returns a value using the return keyword.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    return a + b

result = add()
print(result)

Output:

30

Here, the function calculates the result and sends it back to the caller using return.

4. Function With Arguments and With Return Value

This function accepts arguments and returns a result.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(10, 20)
print(result)

Output:

30

This is one of the most commonly used function types in Python.

Conclusion

Functions are an important concept in Python programming. They help developers write reusable, organized, and maintainable code.

Understanding function definitions, arguments, parameters, return statements provides a strong foundation for developing Python applications.

event_model_payload.headline: How to tell whether a physics simulation blew up during RL training
event_model_payload.summary:
When you train a policy across thousands of parallel simulated worlds, a few of them will explode: a body starts inside the floor, an energy spike throws parts across the scene, a value turns into NaN. If those worlds keep feeding observations and rewards, the policy learns from garbage and you find out hours later. This walkthrough shows how to catch them with Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning that grades every world as it runs.

pip install alloy-engine

1. Three worlds, one of them broken on purpose 

import numpy as np
import alloy

z = np.array([0.3, 0.0, 0.6])        # world 1 starts with its cube half inside the ground
pos = np.stack([np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3), z], axis=1)
scene = alloy.Scene(worlds=3, dt=0.01)
scene.add_ground()
scene.add_box("block", size=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1), pos=pos, mass=0.2)
sim = alloy.build(scene, device="cpu")
sim.run(0.8)
for w, row in enumerate(sim.health()["worlds"]):
    flags = [f for f in row["flags"] if f != "DET_DOWNGRADED"]
    print(w, row["severity"], flags)

0 OK []
1 INVALID ['PEN_WARN', 'PEN_FAIL', 'ENERGY_JUMP', 'LATCHED', 'START_PEN']
2 OK []

Every world gets a grade: OK, DEGRADED or INVALID. World 1 started with its cube overlapping the ground, so it was flagged for penetration and an energy jump, then frozen at its last good state while the other two worlds carried on.

2. Trust the check, not the picture 

check = sim.check()
print(check["ok"])
print(sim.state(["block"])["block.pos"][:, 2].round(2))
for p in check["problems"]:
    print(p["world"], p["level"], p["check"])

False
[0.05 0.   0.05]
1 fail start_overlap
1 error health
1 error penetration
0 warn health
2 warn health

The frozen world sits calmly at z = 0, which looks fine in a render. check()["ok"] is the value to trust, and each problem names its world and the check that failed. The warn rows for worlds 0 and 2 record a flag that fired during the landing and cleared; those worlds stay OK.

3. In a training environment it is automatic

With Alloy's Gymnasium-style vector environments you do not reset anything by hand. A frozen world ends its episode, returns zero reward and observation, and starts again, and the environment counts it:

import numpy as np
import alloy.envs

env = alloy.envs.make("GripperLift-v0", num_envs=4)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
for _ in range(20):
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.xp.asarray(np.zeros((4, 3), np.float32)))
print(np.asarray(info["invalid"]).tolist(), np.asarray(env.invalid_episodes).tolist())

info["invalid"] marks the worlds frozen on this step and env.invalid_episodes counts frozen episodes per world. Log that count during training: a rising number means the task or the physics settings need attention.

Keep in mind

  • The health check does not catch every overlap between rigid bodies and robot parts, and a fast body can pass through a thin static part before any flag fires.
  • A GPU run does not repeat bit for bit once bodies touch in more than one place.
  • The docs keep the full list of limits.

Links

  • Docs page this is based on: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/answers/did-my-simulation-blow-up/
  • Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16312

event_model_payload.headline: Stress-Tested in Public: Four Outside Runs Against the Receipt Standard This Week
event_model_payload.summary:
Stress-Tested in Public: Four Outside Runs Against the Receipt Standard This Week

I publish a standard and a server. The useful days are not the ones where I say the record holds. They are the days where strangers try to break it with their own code, in public, and print what happened. Four of those runs landed within a few hours of each other, on the night of November 18, 2026. Every claim below links the primary artifact, so you do not have to take my word for any of it.

Run one: the Merkle vectors, two constructions

An independent implementer who maintains uibc-core took the Merkle test vectors from the AER-1 corpus and ran them against two constructions: the one specified in section 8.1 of draft-zambo-aer1-26, and his own project's tree. The AER-1 construction reproduced all nine expected roots. His construction reproduced none of them. We then re-ran both constructions independently, from the draft text on one side and his published code on the other, and got the same split: 9/9 against 0/9.

The divergence is not a mystery and nobody had to guess at it. It is three named parameters. His tree prefixes leaves and nodes with RFC 6962 style domain separation bytes; AER-1 hashes unprefixed. His tree splits at the largest power of two; AER-1 duplicates the odd node at each level. His tree returns an all-zero digest for an empty input; the AER-1 corpus root for the empty tree is the SHA-256 of the empty input itself. His own verdict stands in his report: the Merkle mapping stays partial, with the reason measured instead of asserted, and he has offered to add the section 8.1 construction to his codebase as a named profile.

The corpus he ran against is public, and the vector file hashes to the value the index publishes: https://zambo.dev/aer1/corpus.json

Run two: a pilot kit, run by someone else

EslaM-X maintains a verifiable approval receipt profile in the agentic commerce work. This week he shipped a pilot kit for it: fifteen rows covering approvals, tampered mirrors, surcharged executions, unpinned keys, replays, and conflicts, with the rule that the run only exits clean if every row lands where the kit says it should. Then he made the offer in public: we run the kit and publish the report, he maps every outcome in it to AER-1's verdicts line by line within three days, and any row where the two disagree becomes a test vector in the corpus.

We cloned his repository and ran the kit twice. Exit 0 both times, 15/15 rows landing as stated, including the three rows he flagged himself before we ran anything: a tampered mirror refused on its identifier before the signature was consulted, a surcharged execution declined with the offending field named, and an unpinned key scored NOT_CHECKED instead of VERIFIED. The full report, with the row table, is on the discussion thread, and his mapping clock runs to about November 22:

https://github.com/agentic-commerce-protocol/agentic-commerce-protocol/discussions/328#discussioncomment-19722647

Run three: the scenarios that were described but never committed

The longest running argument in the MCP lost-response thread is what a client should do when a response disappears mid-call. Arjun had argued that two scenarios in a shared lab tree, one for recovery and one for a nonce-only retry, had been described in a comment weeks ago but never actually committed. The lab's author answered in the thread overnight: Arjun was right about the tree. The scenarios are committed now, and the lab ran them at three batches of twenty runs each.

The recovery scenario recovers the stored original result on the operation key, with exactly one committed effect in every run. The nonce-only scenario rejects the retry and leaves the original outcome unresolved, still with exactly one committed effect, and the lab now uses the wording Arjun suggested for that case: a rejected retry does not mean the original operation failed. Sixty runs per scenario, all passing, published by the person who had the most reason to want the earlier description to have been enough:

https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/issues/3394#issuecomment-7000766569

Run four: a failure scenario turned into a test

On a smolagents pull request that fixes parallel tool calls being lost when a consumer stops early, a reviewer had proposed the hard case in words: three calls in the pool, the first succeeds, the second is released to fail, the third succeeds, and then the consumer either closes early or runs into the error. A second engineer turned that paragraph into a deterministic test: event-gated, no sleeps, no model calls, no external effects. Both cases fail against the parent code and pass against the fix, with all three calls recorded, the successful ones exactly once, and no observation fabricated for the failed one. Eleven tests pass in the selection:

https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents/pull/3209#issuecomment-7002533938

What the four runs have in common

None of these people work for me. Two of them were arguing with positions I hold, one was correcting his own tree in public, and one was testing someone else's fix. What they share is a method: state the claim narrowly, run it where everyone can see, and print the result either way.

That method is the whole design. A Zambo receipt proves the saved result was not changed after it was saved. It does not prove the work was right, and it says so. Anyone can test the narrow claim the same way these four runs tested theirs: open a receipt, take its canonical bytes, recompute the digest, and compare. event_model_payload.headline: I built a 37-line static site generator. Then I ran it on real markdown.
event_model_payload.summary:
I have a small pile of side projects, and one of them is staticgen: a static site generator in Python with no dependencies at all. The goal was not to replace Hugo. The goal was to understand it.

The first version is 37 lines. It reads a folder of markdown, turns it into HTML, and drops it into a template:

def render(post_md, template):
    lines = post_md.strip().split("\n")
    out = []
    for line in lines:
        if line.startswith("# "):
            out.append("
" + line[2:] + "
")
        elif line.startswith("## "):
            out.append("
" + line[3:] + "
")
        else:
            line = line.replace("**", "", 1).replace("**", "", 1)
            out.append("
" + line + "
")
    body = "\n".join(out)
    title = lines[0].lstrip("# ").strip()
    return template.replace(TITLE, title).replace(BODY, body)

It worked on the one test post I wrote. Then I fed it something realistic, and it fell apart in four ways worth knowing about.

1. The bold replacement eats exactly one pair

That .replace("**", ..., 1) chain is a neat trick that breaks the moment a line has two bold runs. Actual output from the code above, on Some **bold** and **more bold** here.:

Some bold and **more bold** here.

The first ** became , the second became , and the remaining four asterisks were left alone. Any line with more than one bold span renders literally.

The fix is not a better loop over replace. It is one regex pass that consumes both cases:

BOLD = re.compile(r"\*\*(.+?)\*\*")
line = BOLD.sub(r"\1", line)

.+? is lazy, so it matches the shortest run between two delimiters. That handles one pair or ten, and it fails visibly instead of silently leaving artifacts.

2. Nothing is escaped

This line went straight through:

a < b && c > d

A naked < makes browsers guess, and the guess is not always what you want. Escape first, then add markup:

import html
line = html.escape(line, quote=False)

Do it before the bold pass, otherwise you escape your own tags. Order matters here, and it stays hidden until a post mentions generics or a comparison operator.

3. Every blank line becomes an empty paragraph 



Some bold here.

Harmless-looking, annoying in practice: it adds gaps you cannot style away without an :empty rule, and it bloats the HTML of ordinary prose. Skip blank lines and let them separate paragraphs instead:

if not line.strip():
    continue

4. Fenced code blocks get mangled, which is the real bug

A fenced block came out as three paragraphs, and markdown inside the code was interpreted. The fence markers ended up wrapped in

tags, and **not bold** was bolded inside what should have been literal code.

For a developer blog this is fatal. Code samples are the content. A line-by-line renderer with no state cannot handle it, so the renderer needs a mode switch:

in_code = False
for line in lines:
    if line.startswith("```"):
        out.append("
" if not in_code else "
")
        in_code = not in_code
        continue
    if in_code:
        out.append(html.escape(line))
        continue
    ...

That is the whole lesson of the project, and it is the same lesson every time I have written a small parser: the naive version is not wrong about the concept, it is wrong about state. Bold spans, fences, lists, and escaping all need to know what came before.

Where it stands

staticgen is now about 90 lines, still dependency-free, and it builds my posts without surprises. It has a --template flag and a sample post in posts/. It is not a Hugo competitor: no incremental builds, no taxonomies, no front matter beyond a leading # heading.

What it gave me was cheap. Two hours, and now I know exactly why the markdown pipeline in every tool I use is more complicated than it looks.

If you want the same exercise, pick the smallest tool you rely on and rewrite the dumb version of it. The bugs will teach you more than the docs.

event_model_payload.headline: Run Mobilerun with local and cheap models Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenRouter
event_model_payload.summary:
Every step a phone agent takes is a model call. Read the screen, pick one action, tap, repeat. A simple task can be 10 of those. A test suite can be thousands.

So the first question people ask after getting Mobilerun working is always the same: can I run this on something cheaper? Or on my own machine, with no API key at all?

Yes. The open-source Mobilerun framework doesn't care where the model lives. This post shows what runs where, the exact local setup with Ollama and Qwen, the hosted setup for DeepSeek and OpenRouter, and what actually changes your results.

The problem with "which model is best?"

You'll find plenty of opinions about which model is best for phone agents. You won't find a published Mobilerun benchmark broken out by Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen and OpenRouter. We haven't published one yet either.

That matters, because the answer depends on things only you know: your tasks, your device, your hardware, and whether you run with vision. So instead of a ranking, we'll give you the setup for each option and a simple way to measure them on your own work.

What runs where

The Mobilerun framework runs on your machine. It controls an Android device through Portal and ADB. The LLM provider is a separate choice you make in config or on the command line.

Here's how the options split:

  • Ollama runs inference locally. No model API key.
  • DeepSeek is a hosted API. It uses DEEPSEEK_API_KEY.
  • OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to many models. It uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
  • Qwen is a model family, not a provider. You can run Qwen locally through Ollama, and Qwen models are also available through hosted providers like OpenRouter.

Install and run it locally with Ollama and Qwen

You need Python 3.11 to 3.13. Python 3.14 isn't supported yet, and the docs warn that installing on 3.14 silently falls back to an old version. You also need ADB and an Android device with USB debugging on.

Install the framework:

Install Ollama, connect your Android device, then set up Portal and check the connection.

mobilerun setupmobilerun pingCopy

If ping prints "Portal is installed and accessible. You're good to go!", you're ready. Pull the model and run a task:

ollama pull qwen3:8bmobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider Ollama --model qwen3:8b --base_url http://localhost:11434Copy

That's the whole loop running on your hardware. The framework talks to Ollama at localhost:11434, and no request leaves your machine for inference.

Pass --provider and --model together. The CLI guide is clear that passing only one makes the run fail before the agent starts.

To make Ollama the default instead of typing flags every time, add a profile to your config file. Mobilerun creates it at ~/.config/droidrun/config.yaml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/droidrun/config.yaml on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\droidrun\droidrun\config.yaml on Windows. Yes, the folder still says droidrun. You can also point MOBILERUN_CONFIG or --config at your own file.

One Ollama detail worth knowing: Mobilerun sets the context size itself. The default context_window is 32,768, which keeps most models on the GPU. Setting it to -1 asks for the model's full context, which preallocates the whole KV cache and can spill onto your CPU.

DeepSeek and OpenRouter: hosted, pay per call

For the hosted options, set the key and pick the provider and model with CLI flags.

DeepSeek:

export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider DeepSeek --model deepseek-flashCopy

OpenRouter, here with a hosted Qwen model:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider OpenRouter --model qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

Or save them as profiles so every run uses them:

llm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: DeepSeek    model: deepseek-flashllm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: OpenRouter    model: qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

A note on mobilerun configure. The wizard's provider list today is gemini, openai, anthropic, xai, ollama, openai_like, minimax and zai. DeepSeek and OpenRouter aren't in it as named options, so use the CLI flags or the YAML profile for those. Model IDs change often on both services, so check DeepSeek's and OpenRouter's model lists before you copy ours.

What affects your results

Swapping the model is one line. Whether the task finishes is a different story. These are the four things that change the outcome.

Accessibility tree by default. Out of the box, the agent reads Android's accessibility tree, a structured list of what's on screen with text and bounds. No screenshots. That works with text-only models, including qwen3:8b.

--vision adds screenshots. With vision on, the agent gets a screenshot alongside the tree on every step. That needs a vision-capable model. If you test vision on a local model, pull one that accepts images. For local vision models that downsize images in a way Mobilerun can't detect, the docs suggest capping the screenshot so tap coordinates stay accurate:

agent:  model_screenshot_max_side: 1280Copy

There's also --vision-only, which drops the tree and drives the device from screenshots alone.

Native tool calling vs the fallback protocol. Mobilerun uses native tool calling where the model supports it. For other models, it falls back to a text protocol where the model writes tool calls as XML and the framework parses them. In v0.7.4 the native path covers providers like DeepSeek, OpenAI and xAI. Ollama and OpenRouter go through the fallback. If a model writes broken tool-call markup three times in a row, the run stops, and smaller models hit this more often.

Your hardware. With Ollama, speed is your GPU, your RAM and the model size. The same model can feel quick on one laptop and painful on another.

Success and speed will vary with the model, the task, the device and the hardware. That's why the next section exists.

Some tips to keep the numbers honest:

  • Run mobilerun --version and record it. Results change between releases.
  • Keep --steps the same across runs. The default is 15, and complex tasks may need more.
  • Turn on --tracing to see tokens per step, or use --debug and --save-trajectory action to see where a run went wrong.
  • Count completed tasks, not tokens. A cheap model that fails half the time isn't cheap.

On cost: Ollama removes per-call model API fees, but local hardware still has a cost. The GPU, the power and the machine that's busy while it runs all count. Hosted APIs flip that. No hardware to own, but you pay for every call.

Honest limits

  • There are no published per-provider Mobilerun benchmarks yet. Anyone giving you a confident ranking is guessing.
  • Small local models are more likely to drift from the tool-call format, especially on busy screens.
  • qwen3:8b is a text model. Keep --vision off with it, or switch to a vision-capable model.
  • The framework is the open-source, bring-your-own-device path. You manage the phone, ADB, Portal and the model.

Don't want to manage a device?

If you'd rather skip the phone and the ADB setup, Mobilerun Cloud gives you hosted devices and a managed agent behind an API. You send a task, it runs on a phone in the cloud. If you want to keep your own model and your own device, the open-source framework will always let you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I run Mobilerun with no API key at all? Is Qwen a provider?

Which model is the cheapest per task? Can I use DeepSeek or OpenRouter from mobilerun configure? 

The takeaway

The model is your choice, and the right one is the one that finishes your tasks on your hardware. Measure it, don't guess it. If you'd rather not manage a device at all, start at cloud.mobilerun.ai.

Docs: Quickstart · CLI and providers · Ollama profiles · Vision mode

Also Read:

  • Running an AI Agent on Your Android Device
  • How to Turn Old Android Phones into AI Agents (Complete Guide)
  • How to connect your mobile device to Mobilerun cloud
