Give every user visibility into their own usage. Individual users on GitLab.com can now track their own GitLab Credits consumption over time, filtered by product and date range, without relying on an administrator’s report.

Keep your budget flexible with GitLab Flex

As you discover where agents deliver the most value, your spending priorities will evolve too.

GitLab Flex brings seats and GitLab Credits together under one annual commitment, with flexibility to adjust your monthly allocation within your agreement. It helps you direct your investment toward the capabilities your teams need as adoption grows.

More value from each credit, combined with more flexibility in how you use your budget, gives you room to expand without treating every new use case as a separate investment decision.

If you opt out before December 18, you keep your current request rates until your next renewal or for 12 months, whichever comes first. event_model_payload.headline: The best way to use your coding agents with GitLab
event_model_payload.summary:
Say you and your team already use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Devin, or OpenCode to write code. Maybe even more than one of them.

What happens next depends on everyone’s personal setup.

Some have their agent review changes, watch CI pipelines and security checks, with a different approach to follow up when something breaks. Others do it by hand. When those steps depend on each engineer’s setup, skill, or time to follow up, even changes in the same project move at different speeds and get different levels of scrutiny.

We paired each one of these coding agents to create a recommended configuration that makes your best engineering practices the default for the whole team.

  • One bar for every change. You set security, architecture, and engineering standards once in GitLab. Duo reviews changes against your review instructions, and GitLab enforces required pipelines, security checks, and approvals before merge, whether a coding agent or a person wrote the change.
  • Give agents the context they need. Duo can work from the repository, merge request discussion, CI logs, and scanner results. Your team doesn’t have to piece that context back together every time work moves between tools or people.
  • Delegation without handing over keys. Composite identity ties every agent action to the agent and the person who started it, and limits access to what both are allowed to do.
  • Leave a record the next engineer can use. Reviews, pipeline results, and approvals stay with the merge request. A pipeline fix can link back to its Duo session. Anyone picking up the work can see what ran and what still needs attention without reconstructing someone else’s agent conversation.
  • Your models, your cloud. Pick the model for each agentic flow from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or open-weight providers, and change it when a better one ships.

What’s new

Your coding agent writes the code. GitLab Duo does the work that starts at the merge request and follows through to deployment.

You can now set up code review, pipeline repair, and security triage together from your coding session. The GitLab Duo setup skill connects your agent to GitLab and configures automatic review and failed-pipeline repair. On the Ultimate tier, you can also opt in to security triage and remediation. The skill tells you what, if anything, still needs your attention.

Once configured, the work keeps running in GitLab even if you close your editor. When you come back, the optional MR follow-up skill checks what’s already running and brings review and pipeline feedback back into your coding session.

For a deep dive on how to use our new skills, please see our detailed guide here.

What you and your team get

Give every eligible MR a separate review for 25¢

Your coding agent can check its own work before it pushes. Duo gives the change a second look when the MR is marked ready and posts feedback on the diff. A review costs a flat $0.25 at list price, so 1,000 reviews cost $250. Anthropic's Code Review averages $15–$25 a review, so the same volume would cost $15,000 or more. That makes a first pass practical even for routine changes.

Then ask your agent to read the comments, fix the ones you agree with, and reply on each thread.

Turn security findings into fixes you can verify

On Ultimate, Duo flags likely false positives from static application security testing and secret detection and opens MRs with fixes for eligible SAST findings, usually about 10 minutes after a scan. Your team gets a proposed change it can test, scan, and review under the same rules as any other change.

Start investigating when CI goes red

When a pipeline fails, an automation starts Fix CI/CD Pipeline while you're on to something else, and links the session on the MR. Duo suggests a change, opens a fix MR, or explains what it found if it can't propose a reliable fix. The fix still has to pass CI. While Duo works on the fix on GitLab, your coding harness can also collaborate with Duo to review the proposed fix, commit a change to the MR, and watch for the pipeline to pass.

Take an MR to merge, with policy-based approvals

The MR follow-up skill checks the review threads, failed jobs, and conflicts on an MR, and works through them from your agent. Your agent can resolve a merge conflict in your checkout, or hand it to the Developer flow to resolve in GitLab. The skill stops when only approvals are left.

Then your approval rules decide what merges, for agent changes and people alike. Approval policies can require a person to approve every MR, or add approvers when a scan finds a vulnerability. Pipeline execution policies make required jobs run. Tool approval guardrails can make an agent ask a person before a sensitive action. Tool calls that go through GitLab’s MCP server can be viewed in Audit events when storage is enabled. If you let Duo approve MRs, its approval doesn't count toward required approvals.

Hand an issue to GitLab Duo and get back a merge request

Ask your agent to hand an assigned issue to the Developer flow. The flow runs in GitLab, reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens an MR in your name. You keep working locally, and nobody has to copy the issue and the code history into a prompt.

How to get started

Paste this into your coding agent:

event_model_payload.headline: Turn Slack conversations into trusted software, faster
event_model_payload.summary:
Most software starts as a conversation: a customer requests a new capability, a product manager weighs it against the roadmap, an engineer checks feasibility, and a security lead asks what it touches.

Then someone has to turn it into work. They reread the thread, retype the decisions into an issue, and hope they didn’t miss an important detail buried in a reply. The conversation moves fast; the handoff between both teams and tools is where it slows.

AI agents are uniquely equipped for that handoff: reading a long, many-voiced discussion and turning it into structured work. That leaves people free to collaborate while agents produce the output.

GitLab for Slack now adds agentic capabilities and is generally available for GitLab.com users in GitLab 19.6, with support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated to follow. Mention @GitLab in a thread in your team's channels, and the agent reads the conversation, finds what already exists, turns decisions into tracked work, and starts the agent flows that carry it to production. Work starts in Slack and lands in GitLab, where it's governed, tracked, and delivered.

"Teams make decisions in Slack every day, and the best agents are the ones that can act on that context. GitLab for Slack lets agents read the conversation, take action across the software lifecycle in GitLab, and bring the results back to the thread. Teams can go from a quick discussion to planned, reviewed, and shipped work without switching tools."

– Katie Steigman, Vice President Product Management, Slack

Slack is the front door, GitLab does the work

GitLab for Slack connects the interface where your team discusses the work to the platform where your software ships. Your team’s conversation in Slack itself becomes the agent's input, so no decision gets lost between the thread and the first commit.

The agent also looks beyond the thread. When you mention @GitLab, it can read the messages in the channel where you mentioned it, so its response reflects the whole discussion and not only the replies under one message. You can also ask it to catch you up first, for example: “@GitLab, summarize #channel for me.”

It works in both directions. GitLab context (what's been built, what's tracked, whether a merge request is ready, etc.) also shows up in the conversation. The conversation becomes issues, merge requests, and running agent flows, with results posted back to the thread.

If your team already uses the GitLab for Slack app on GitLab.com, reinstall it today to add these agent capabilities. There's nothing new to learn; you just mention @GitLab.

Use it where your team works

Debate it in the channel. Draft it in your DM. GitLab for Slack works in both places:

  • Public and private channels: Bring the agent into team discussions and turn decisions into tracked work where everyone can see it.
  • Your own DM: Get a private space to ask questions, check on a merge request, or draft an issue before you share anything with the team.

One thread, every role

GitLab for Slack works for everyone who shapes the work, including people who never write code:

  • Product managers turn a decision into scoped work before the meeting ends.
  • Designers send their notes straight to the people and agents doing the work.
  • Sales and customer teams bring a customer request into a team channel and follow it to production.
  • Security and platform teams confirm agent work passes review before it ships.
  • Engineers check what exists before building it again, without leaving the conversation.

Watch GitLab for Slack in action:

Governed from the first mention

An agent that acts from a chat thread is only useful if you can trust what it does. The conversation happens in Slack; the work and every control stay in GitLab.

  • Agents act only when asked. In channels, GitLab acts only when someone mentions @GitLab. In your own DM, it answers you and only you.
  • Internal conversations only. GitLab for Slack doesn't run in external (Slack Connect) channels, so project context isn't exposed to people outside your organization.
  • Requests run as you. Each request uses the requester's linked GitLab account, scoped to their existing permissions. If you don't have access to a project in GitLab, the agent can't access it for you in Slack.
  • Context stays in scope. The agent reads the surrounding context only from the channel where it was mentioned. Anything it does in GitLab still follows your permissions.
  • Actions are on the record. Each request creates an agent session in GitLab. Merge requests go through the same reviews, approval rules, and audit trail as any other change.
  • Costs stay visible. Usage draws from your GitLab Credits, so admins can track and cap it like any other agent work.

This is the model behind GitLab's governed software factory: agents speed up the work, and source control, security, and governance keep it trustworthy. Slack is one more way into that factory, not a way around it.

Get started

GitLab for Slack is now generally available on GitLab.com — just reinstall the GitLab for Slack app to get the new capabilities. Support for GitLab Self-Managed and GitLab Dedicated will follow in an upcoming release.

Help us shape what's next

We have a lot more planned for GitLab for Slack, and we want your feedback to guide it. Every agent response in Slack includes a thumbs up/down button, so you can tell us what worked and what didn't without leaving the thread.

event_model_payload.headline: Keep recurring work moving with scheduled automations
event_model_payload.summary:
Every engineering team has work that needs regular attention, like triaging new issues or investigating incidents. Among DevSecOps professionals using AI tools, 43% say automating repetitive tasks has created the most efficiency, according to GitLab’s Global DevSecOps report. But agents still rely on a human to kick off the workflow or an event trigger to fire, and without a record of what ran and why, no one can trace how the work got done.

With scheduled automations, in beta in GitLab 19.6, flows in GitLab Duo Agent Platform handle routine tasks on a schedule your team sets and keep a history of what ran. Scheduled automations are a building block of the governed software factory, where agents and flows work autonomously within controls set by your team.

Put routine work on a schedule

Relying on a person or an event to start automated work limits efficiency gains and makes timing unpredictable. When the person responsible is out, the work waits, and when there’s no event, it never starts. Scheduled automations give routine work a dependable rhythm.

You can already run event-based automations in GitLab Duo Agent Platform, triggered by activities like a merge request or a mention in a comment. Scheduled automations start the work on a recurring schedule, with no event needed. Describe the task in plain language, set the cadence once, and the automation runs on its own at the times you choose, with run counts and success rates your team can review.

Triage new issues daily to keep your backlog organized, or schedule a flow to check CI health incidents every hour and comment with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.

You can set a schedule from every 15 minutes to every month, at the time of day and in the timezone that meets the needs of your group. Because automations in GitLab drive the work your whole team depends on, each one runs at the project level.

See how to schedule an automation, from describing the task to reviewing its first run:

Control and transparency for every run

As agents take on more of the work around your code, teams need to know which agent acted, what permissions it had, and what it did. Without a verifiable identity and a record of every change, no one can say which agent made a change or why it ran, and every review or audit starts with reconstruction. It’s hard to scale agentic work when you can’t see what agents or flows already did.

Scheduled automations offer the controls a team needs to trust what runs on its own. Each automation runs as a dedicated service account with scoped permissions, so your team can tell agent work from human work in the audit events. Audit events also record changes to every automation, so your team knows what ran, what happened, and who changed it.

A redesigned Automations page, previously labeled Triggers, brings scheduled and event-based automations together in one place, with run volume, success rate, and session details for each, so your team can see details of what ran and what happened. If a run fails, the page shows the reason, and you can open the session to see exactly what the agent did.

A foundation of the governed software factory

The governed software factory is a connected system for moving software from idea to production under your organization’s own policy and standards, with an evidence chain that records how every change got there.

Scheduled automations add a critical piece to that foundation by automating work into the factory on a regular basis. A weekly scan for vulnerabilities can create work items for the factory to act on, and every automation runs as its own service account with scoped permissions, so its actions stay easy to identify.

Scheduling the right work keeps the factory moving, saves your team time, and leaves a record they can trust. Creating one of these automations is a good place to start:

  • CI health investigation - An hourly check of open incidents that comments with the likely root cause, so the investigation is underway before anyone opens the issue.
  • Issue triage - A morning review of new issues that decides whether each is a bug or a feature and adds a label, so the backlog stays organized.
  • Stale work report - A weekly report that lists the open issues with no activity in the last 30 days in a new issue, so stuck work gets a second look.
  • Duplicate spotting - A daily check of new issues that comments with any open issues that look like the same request, so duplicates get linked before anyone triages them twice.
  • Weekly digest - A Friday summary of what closed and merged that week, written in plain language for people outside engineering and posted as a new issue, so stakeholders know what shipped without reading MR titles.

Try scheduled automations today

Scheduled automations are available now in beta in GitLab 19.6. Like other flows on GitLab Duo Agent Platform, scheduled automations use GitLab Credits. To try one, turn on experimental and beta features, choose a routine your team repeats, like one of the recommendations above, and put it on a schedule.

If you’re new to GitLab Duo Agent Platform, start a free trial. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription.

event_model_payload.headline: Rotate a leaked GitLab token and let GitLab Duo fix the code
event_model_payload.summary:
Secret detection alerts you when an active personal access token (PAT) is exposed in your default branch. Acting on that finding is harder: revoking the token breaks dependent pipelines, and replacing it safely takes several manual steps. While the finding waits in your vulnerability report, the token stays live.

Starting in GitLab 19.6 in beta for GitLab Ultimate, you can remediate a leaked GitLab PAT directly from the vulnerability page. Select Rotate and fix, and GitLab revokes the token, stores a replacement in GitLab Secrets Manager, and uses GitLab Duo Agent Platform to open a merge request (MR) to update your CI/CD jobs. You review and merge the MR. GitLab never exposes the new token value to you or your agents.

Why leaked tokens stay active after detection

Imagine that secret detection flags an active PAT in deploy.sh:

export GITLAB_TOKEN="glpat-..."

Fixing this manually requires tracking down the token's owner, revoking it, generating a replacement with matching scopes, storing it securely, and opening MRs to update your scripts and CI/CD jobs.

Because this process is tedious, remediations often stall or go wrong:

  • The finding ages: Nobody wants to break the pipeline, so the finding sits in the vulnerability report while the token remains active.
  • The fix stops halfway: Someone revokes the token immediately, breaking the build. In a rush to recover, they paste a replacement into a less secure CI/CD variable.
  • The new token leaks: Someone shares the replacement token in a chat thread so a teammate can configure it.

In the gap between detected and rotated, the token still works for anyone who can read the repository.

Rotate and fix in a snap

The Rotate and fix function closes this gap by combining secret detection and validity checks, GitLab Secrets Manager, and GitLab Duo Agent Platform.

When you open an active PAT finding and select AI actions > Fix with AI > Rotate and fix, GitLab:

  1. Revokes the leaked token and creates a replacement with the same name, scopes, and duration (reset from the rotation date).
  2. Stores the new value as a project secret in Secrets Manager, available to all branches and environments.
  3. Marks the token as inactive on the vulnerability.
  4. Starts a GitLab Duo Developer Flow session, which opens an MR to remove the hardcoded token and configure your CI/CD jobs to read the secret.

You review the MR, merge it, and resolve the vulnerability.

Update the code without exposing the new token

Rotation finishes before the agent starts, so GitLab Duo never sees the new token. By the time GitLab Duo reads the file to remove the hardcoded credential, the value is revoked and the replacement is safely stored in Secrets Manager. The agent receives only the vulnerability and its file location, the new secret's name, and your username so it can assign the MR to you. GitLab Duo then updates your pipeline configuration:

deploy:
  secrets:
    GITLAB_TOKEN:
      gitlab_secrets_manager:
        name: ROTATED_GITLAB_TOKEN_123
      file: false
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh

Your script continues using GITLAB_TOKEN, which Secrets Manager injects at runtime.

What to know before you implement

  • Availability: This beta feature requires GitLab Ultimate 19.6 or later. It is enabled by default on GitLab.com, available behind the secrets_manager_pat_rotation feature flag on GitLab Self-Managed, and not yet available on GitLab Dedicated.
  • Supported secret types: Rotation supports GitLab PATs, including fine-grained PATs. It doesn't yet cover other secrets that secret detection finds, such as cloud provider keys.
  • Immediate and irreversible: The leaked token stops working right away, and you can't undo the rotation. Scripts outside GitLab CI/CD and jobs in other projects that used the old token need a new token, because the new secret is scoped only to the current project and its raw value cannot be retrieved.
  • Ownership rules: On GitLab.com, you can rotate only your own tokens. On GitLab Self-Managed, administrators can also rotate tokens belonging to other users.
  • Independent of AI: If the GitLab Duo session cannot start, GitLab still rotates the old token and stores the replacement so you can update the code manually.

For role requirements, required settings, and step-by-step instructions, see the leaked token rotation documentation.

Automate rotation across a group

Rotating tokens one by one doesn't scale across large organizations. Rotate and fix makes two API calls: the projectSecretCreateFromLeakedToken GraphQL mutation, which rotates the token and stores the secret, and a request that starts the GitLab Duo Developer Flow.

We packaged both calls into leaked-token-rotation-automation, a dependency-free Python CLI and CI/CD component that batch-rotates tokens across an entire group:

  • Active vulnerability findings: Rotates active leaked PATs across your group's repositories and opens an MR for each finding. On GitLab.com, it rotates your own tokens and lists other users' tokens in the report for follow-up. On GitLab Self-Managed, an administrator can rotate every user's tokens.
  • Tokens in CI/CD variables: Secret detection doesn't scan project CI/CD variables, and any project Maintainer can read a variable that isn't hidden. The tool finds GitLab PATs in those variables, rotates them, and stores the new values in Secrets Manager. If any jobs use the variable, GitLab Duo opens an MR to update them. Each token rotates itself using its own api or self_rotate scope, so this command also works on tokens that belong to other users. It skips group, instance, file-type, and hidden variables.

Every run defaults to dry-run mode (pass --apply to execute), stops after 10 rotations (configurable with --limit), and never includes token values in reports. See the project README for installation instructions, CI/CD component usage, and required token scopes.

Getting started

To try this out, you need GitLab Ultimate, GitLab Duo Agent Platform, and Secrets Manager, which you can evaluate with a free 30-day trial. Each rotation consumes GitLab Credits for the Developer Flow session and for the stored secret and each CI/CD job that reads it.

  1. Review the prerequisites and troubleshooting guide to ensure validity checks and Developer Flow are enabled. On GitLab Self-Managed, also enable the secrets_manager_pat_rotation feature flag.
  2. Open an active PAT finding in your vulnerability report, select AI actions > Fix with AI > Rotate and fix, and review the resulting merge request.
  3. Run the leaked-token-rotation-automation tool in dry-run mode to preview which tokens you can rotate across your group.

What's next

We’re building a migration workflow into GitLab that imports sensitive CI/CD variables into GitLab Secrets Manager, with no values to re-enter. GitLab will automatically find variables that look like credentials and apply default access policies to the ones you choose to migrate. GitLab Duo will then open a merge request that updates your pipeline configuration, so all you have to do is review and merge.

event_model_payload.headline: Bring Live MongoDB Atlas Data Into Microsoft 365 Copilot
event_model_payload.summary:
The federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas gives organizations a governed way to bring live operational data into the flow of work across Copilot experiences.

To operate efficiently, businesses require timely information about the systems that underpin their organizations. For example, they need to be able to answer questions like: Which incidents are open? Which orders are delayed? What fields and data types are present in the customer collection? The answers they need often live in operational applications built on MongoDB Atlas, while the questions are asked in the productivity tools people use every day.

To help close that gap, MongoDB is excited to introduce a federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas. Now generally available, the connector enables users to ask Microsoft 365 Copilot questions about live data in MongoDB Atlas, bringing operational context into the same experience where people collaborate, analyze information, and make decisions.

The connector surfaces MongoDB Atlas data across Microsoft Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, Researcher in Copilot, Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Word, Excel, and Teams, with additional experiences planned to follow.

Bring operational data into the flow of work

The connector brings MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Copilot through MongoDB’s managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. When a user asks a relevant question, Copilot can query Atlas in real time—instead of relying on a static copy of the data.

This creates a more direct path from a business question to the information needed to answer it, and helps users—who may not have MongoDB expertise—access and analyze live operational data through an AI assistant.

Now, business users can use conversational prompts to:

  • Retrieve live business data without writing database queries.

  • Find and filter customers, transactions, products, orders, content, or operational events.

  • Get quick counts and key performance indicators, such as the number of delayed orders or high-value customers.

  • Summarize and rank data to identify top categories, products, regions, trends, averages, and other business insights.

For example, a user might ask Copilot to summarize the open incidents in an Atlas cluster supporting a payments application, identify delayed orders, or describe the fields and data types in the customer collection for a loyalty service. By industry, a supply chain team can investigate inventory, shipment, and warehouse exceptions. A financial services team can explore customer records, fraud alerts, and transaction investigations. And a retailer can ask questions about orders, loyalty, customer service, and personalization.

The connector can also help power business copilots and agents. Organizations can ground Copilot and other AI assistants in current MongoDB Atlas data for customer service, sales, operations, and decision support, bringing live operational context into the workflows where teams already work.

Connect to live data without migrating or indexing it

Organizations using MongoDB Atlas do not need to migrate their operational data, re-platform their applications, or rebuild their integrations to use the connector.

To do so, an administrator simply approves and enables the connector in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Users then sign in, and their existing Atlas permissions carry through to each query.

MongoDB Atlas remains the system of record. The connector queries Atlas directly rather than indexing a copy of Atlas data into Microsoft 365, so the information returned to users reflects the current state of the underlying application data.

This federated approach helps organizations connect their productivity layer to operational data while keeping that data in the environment where it is managed.

Put governance into every interaction

Making operational data more accessible requires controls that organizations can understand and manage. The connector is designed to support that approach through:

  • Permission-aware access: Each query runs as the signed-in user and honors the permissions already defined in MongoDB Atlas.

  • Administrator control: Admins approve the connector and can manage deployment through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

  • Read-only access: The connector is designed for read-only interaction with Atlas data.

  • Auditability: Administrators can audit connector activity in Microsoft Purview.

  • No separate search index: The connector queries Atlas on demand instead of indexing a copy of Atlas data in Microsoft 365.

Together, these controls give organizations a practical way to make operational information available through Copilot without giving up the governance model around the source data.

A foundation for more productive work

AI-powered productivity depends on access to relevant business context. By connecting Microsoft Copilot and other AI assistants to live MongoDB Atlas data through a federated connection, MongoDB and Microsoft are helping organizations make operational information easier to use without adding a data-movement project or another application to maintain. Users can get answers, summaries, and insights from live data through natural language, while technical teams retain control over the underlying systems and permissions.

For organizations already running MongoDB Atlas on Azure and Microsoft 365 Copilot, the connector provides a way to build on existing investments. Teams can explore high-value operational questions, validate measurable business outcomes, and develop repeatable patterns for bringing current data into everyday decisions.

The result is a simpler path from question to context to action—grounded in the systems organizations already use and governed by the permissions they already have.

event_model_payload.headline: App Events: Send events from Admin UI extensions and embedded apps
event_model_payload.summary:
Admin UI extensions and embedded apps can now send app events to Shopify with shopify.appEvents.emit(). At Editions, we launched app events for Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions. This release adds the Shopify admin, so you can now track app usage across all three surfaces. This is a new, optional API, so no action is required.

What changed

shopify.appEvents.emit() is now available on two more surfaces:

  • Admin UI extensions: Extensions that use API version 2027-01 or later can call shopify.appEvents.emit(). Extensions that you preview with shopify app dev can also send events.
  • Embedded apps (App Home): Apps that use App Bridge can call the same method from the app's pages in the Shopify admin.

The method takes an event handle and an optional object of attributes:

shopify.appEvents.emit("description_generated", {
  word_count: 120,
  placement: "product_details",
});

Shopify adds your app and the shop to each event, so you do not need an access token or a shop ID. Do not include data in attributes that could identify an individual, such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, staff member IDs, or customer IDs.

Events that Shopify accepts are visible in the Dev Dashboard logs, together with the events that your app backend sends. Events do not identify the extension that sent them or the staff member who used it.

Each Admin UI extension can send a burst of up to 20 events, then 2 events per second. An embedded app has the same limit, shared across the app in one Shopify admin tab. Events from Admin UI extensions and embedded apps are not processed for billing. To report usage for Shopify App Pricing, send a billing event from your app backend.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that have Admin UI extensions on API version 2027-01 or later, and to embedded apps that use App Bridge. Embedded apps do not need a specific API version. Admin UI extensions on earlier API versions do not have shopify.appEvents.

On should-render targets and data targets, emit() sends nothing and resolves {success: false, error: 'Emit is unavailable.'}. An embedded app gets the same result where the Shopify admin does not offer App Events.

What to do

No action is required as existing apps and extensions will continue to work without changes. If you want to send events from the Shopify admin, do these steps:

  1. For an Admin UI extension, set api_version = "2027-01" or later in shopify.extension.toml.
  2. Call shopify.appEvents.emit() with an event handle and optional attributes.
  3. Run shopify app dev and use the extension or app in a development store.
  4. Check the result of emit(). If success is false, read error for the cause.
  5. Open Logs in the Dev Dashboard to confirm that your events arrive.

Related docs

  • Send events from Admin UI extensions
  • Send events from embedded apps with App Bridge
  • Monitoring and logs in the Dev Dashboard

event_model_payload.headline: Build Once, Grow Freely: Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite
event_model_payload.summary:
Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run.

In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls.

MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together.

How Atlas Infinite works

A new deployment option within MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Infinite separates compute from storage so each scales independently and rapidly. Storage moves into a fully managed layer that handles replication, durability, and backup across availability zones, so compute no longer has to carry the data with it.

The impact is dramatic. Read replicas come online in minutes because there's no data to copy. A single shard holds up to 128 TB, so you no longer shard just to add disk space. You only pay for the data you store, not capacity provisioned in advance, so a small team never has to buy a bigger compute tier just to get more disk. And it’s all driven by the same MongoDB API, drivers, and tooling, so your application doesn’t need to change.

The separation of storage and compute matters most where agentic applications grow fastest: the retrieval layer. Every answer an assistant gives and every step an agent takes starts with a search over your data, and the data behind that search, especially vector embeddings, can grow large quickly. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search running natively on Atlas Infinite, that data lives on the same foundation as the rest of your application and can grow without re-architecture. Build your agentic workload once and keep scaling it on the same foundation as demand grows.

Figure 1. Compute and storage as independent layers in Atlas Infinite.

Retrieval, built into the database

Many retrieval stacks are cobbled together from disconnected components—a database, a search engine, and a vector database—which means running all of those separate parts, plus managing the pipelines that keep everything in sync. On Atlas Infinite, retrieval is part of the platform, so there are fewer pieces to build, secure, and maintain. Here is what that looks like:

  • One platform, nothing to stitch together: On Atlas Infinite, your database and retrieval work together seamlessly, with no separate search engine or vector database to stand up, sync, or monitor. MongoDB Atlas keeps your indexes in sync with your data automatically, so there is no pipeline for your team to build or maintain, and no extra systems to copy sensitive data into or secure. With Atlas Infinite, retrieval is built in, alongside the ability to scale to absorb unpredictable demand with zero waste.
  • Start small, never outgrow your data platform: A team can start with a 5 GB prototype that includes semantic search and keep building on the same foundation. Rather than sizing and maintaining two infrastructures, storage grows automatically with your data, billed only for what you store. The operational data behind your search has room to grow to petabyte scale on Atlas Infinite, with no re-platforming when the application takes off.
  • Agent memory and context retrieval: Give agents one place to store and retrieve context, history, and state alongside your operational data. Support thousands of agents hitting your retrieval layer while also persisting agent memory and context within a single, durable system that scales when they need it.

Figure 2. Search and Vector Search run alongside the database on Atlas Infinite, with indexes kept in sync automatically and data stored once in Atlas-managed storage.

How Atlas Infinite handles your largest text and vector workloads

Separating compute from storage in the database also changes the scaling behavior and economics of large retrieval workloads. Text and vector data lives in the database first, where it drives storage requirements. Because Atlas Infinite manages that storage separately from compute, the economics come down to one property of the data: how well it compresses.

Databases shrink data on disk with compression, which works by finding repetition. Text is full of repetition: common words, repeated field names, predictable structure. Text in MongoDB typically compresses to about 40% of its original size. An embedding is an array of decimal values with almost no repetition, so it shrinks by only about 13%. In practice, a vector takes up as much space on disk as it does in your application.

How each deployment option stores that data

Atlas Core uses attached storage volumes. Each node in a replica set keeps a full copy of the data on its own disk, provisioned ahead of time with room to grow, and compute and storage come in matched tiers. That gives every node complete isolation and predictable performance, and it's the right fit for many workloads, especially ones where data and query load grow together.

Vector workloads tend to be storage-driven because high-dimension embeddings are so large. A RAG knowledge base can hold hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings, which drives up storage needs relative to query volume. On Atlas Core, storage can drive scaling decisions: once you outgrow a tier’s maximum disk size, you have to move up a tier to get more storage, even if you don’t need more compute, and very large datasets eventually call for sharding.

On Atlas Infinite, compute and storage scale independently. Storage is billed per logical (uncompressed) GB of data you store, metered hourly. Replication across availability zones happens inside the storage layer and isn't billed separately. There's no headroom to provision, and because a shard holds up to 128 TB, a growing dataset doesn't push you to a larger compute tier or to more shards. Because embeddings barely compress, their logical size and their size on disk are nearly the same, so you pay only for the data you store and nothing for the copies and headroom underneath it. As vector collections grow to hundreds of millions of documents, that billing model becomes an advantage.

Here is an example. For a collection with 100 million documents, each with a 1,024-dimension float32 embedding and about 1 KB of other fields, storage is roughly 500 GB uncompressed. Assuming moderate query traffic, an M30 cluster tier’s compute is sufficient.

On Atlas Core, since embeddings barely compress, the data shrinks to ~435 GB on disk. Each node also needs space for the oplog and room for the collection to grow. At 1.3× headroom, that comes to about 565 GB per node, more than the 512 GB an M30 supports, so the cluster has to move up to an M40 for the disk. On Atlas Infinite, the cluster stays at the compute tier its queries need, and storage is billed once on the 500 GB it holds. With storage billed once and no tier-up for disk, the total monthly cost of this deployment, Search Nodes included, comes out about 25% lower than on Core. At 1 billion vectors (about 5 TB), it is about 30% lower, and the gap keeps widening as vector data grows. These figures are modeled on list prices in US East, with Search Nodes sized to the smallest tier that fits the index, so your results will vary.

Where the difference is smaller

Text-heavy search workloads also see a TCO benefit on Atlas Infinite, around 5% to 10% cost reduction at multi-terabyte scale. Text compresses well, so Core's storage cost per GB is already low. The advantage of Atlas Infinite comes from deferring early tier-ups and delaying sharding for disk. Under 500 GB, the two deployment options are roughly even on cost, so a smaller workload gets Atlas Infinite’s room to grow without paying more for it. Choose the deployment option based on the elasticity and growth you expect.

Get started with Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite

MongoDB Search and Vector Search are available on Atlas Infinite in public preview on AWS. Choose Atlas Infinite as the deployment option for your next workload, add a search index the way you would on Atlas Core, and keep building on the same foundation as your application grows. Whether you’re prototyping an AI feature or running a large production application, you can start small and keep going. Start with the Atlas Infinite documentation.

event_model_payload.headline: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB
event_model_payload.summary:
Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

  • Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.

  • Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.

  • Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

Why do sessions need a database?

Say a team deploys its Strands agent as an AWS Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation runs in a disposable environment (i.e., a scratchpad for the agent). There may be no local disk, and no guarantee that the next invocation lands on the same instance, so the state tied to one process is invisible to the next.

With this integration, every agent session is saved in MongoDB. Each invocation loads the session by its ID and carries on, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. Long-term memories the agent saves to MongoDBMemoryStore persist beyond the session, so they’re available the next time that user returns.

Figure 1. Stateless agent architecture keeps state out of the agent process.

Two Lambda instances serve consecutive turns of the same session. Both read and write the session via MongoDBStorage and long-term memory via MongoDBMemoryStore, so neither depends on the other's local state. That matters most for enterprises with many teams running Strands agents across different machines. They get one MongoDB-backed foundation for agent state and memory, instead of building and maintaining separate systems to store and retrieve sessions and memory.

What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

  • Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place.

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

  • No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op. For example, if the agent extracts "Prefers metric units and a 24-hour clock" a second time, the store keeps the copy it already has, with its original timestamp and expiry. This means that, as a developer, you don’t need to write your own deduplication logic, and your memory store stays clean, regardless of how often the agent re-extracts the same fact.

  • Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata. This isolation is enforced by the package, not by the server, so where a tenant boundary is also a compliance boundary, give each tenant its own database or collection, with credentials restricted to it, and MongoDB enforces the boundary itself.

  • Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

How it works

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

As you can see above, the query and the stored fact share no words, but the store still finds it. This path needs an Atlas cluster with an embedding model registered. If you already produce your own embeddings, the store can index and query them instead; the README covers the additional code required.

Figure 2. Without an embedding pipeline, memory is just text in and text out. Atlas generates and stores the embeddings and embeds each query before running $vectorSearch.

store.add() writes plain text and returns. Atlas embeds it in the background, and embeds each search query the same way before running $vectorSearch. Bringing your own embedding model is optional.

Sessions and memory together: One connection config serves both. Hand them to the agent and let the SDK wire them up:

The storage= parameter makes MongoDB the default backend for five SDK subsystems, including sessions, context offloading, and transcripts. The SDK's SnapshotSessionManager saves the conversation under its session ID, and any agent built with that ID restores it. MemoryManager gives the model a tool to search memory and, with add_tool_config=True, one to save to it. There's no MongoDB-specific session class to learn.

Figure 3. After a Strands agent is wired to MongoDB, it can save and restore conversations and search long-term memory without any MongoDB-specific session code.

Three agent parameters do the wiring. storage= points the SDK's storage subsystems at MongoDBStorage, session_manager= saves and restores the conversation by session ID, and memory_manager= gives the model search and save tools backed by MongoDBMemoryStore.

Get started today!

strands-mongodb requires Python 3.10 or later and strands-agents 1.54.0 or later. MongoDBStorage works on any MongoDB deployment; memory search with Automated Embedding needs MongoDB Atlas. Install it with the following commands:

Moving from the mongodb_memory tool or a community MongoDB package? MIGRATION has the field mapping and a copy script.

Explore the source, open issues, or contribute on GitHub. 

The README covers connection options, the full configuration reference, and index privileges.

Linked resources:

  • Strands memory overview

  • Strands storage documentation

  • Strands session management documentation

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications
event_model_payload.summary:
We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm.

This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts.

What is the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context.

Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember context.

What types of memory does an AI application need?

An AI application needs five kinds of memory, each kept for a different length of time and retrieved differently. This integration automatically categorizes each type of memory and stores it in MongoDB Atlas; here are short definitions of the five memory types:

  • Session: The conversation an application or agent has in each session. This helps the application follow what the user just said.

  • Semantic: Facts about people, entities, and preferences, so users don't have to repeat themselves.

  • Procedural: Workflows and instructions, so the application carries out tasks the way you've defined them.

  • Episodic: Key events and outcomes, so the application can recall what happened before. Kept for one year of inactivity by default.

  • Scratchpad: Temporary notes for work in progress. They expire after an hour and can be promoted to episodic memory if they turn out to matter.

Semantic and procedural memories are versioned, so history is preserved when a fact changes. The semantic, procedural, and episodic tiers use MongoDB Vector Search, which finds stored memories by semantic meaning rather than by exact keywords.

This integration automatically creates the vector indexes and detects embedding dimensions at startup. Developers can use any AI SDK embedding model to create vector indexes, including Voyage AI, OpenAI, Cohere, or Google.

Figure 1. How the integration works with MongoDB Atlas and the Vercel SDK interface.

How should memory age?

Each category of memory has its own retention policy, so short-lived notes expire quickly, and long-term facts are stored for longer. The MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration ships with defaults for every category, which developers can customize if they desire.

Effective memory retention requires a balance. Keeping memories indefinitely can decrease retrieval performance and increase costs, while deleting them too early can cause applications to forget important context. This integration includes features to help developers easily set the right balance:

  • Retention modes: Choose none (never expire), ttl (expire after a set time), ttl+importance (expire after a set time unless the memory is marked important), or dynamic, where you define your own forgetting time period.
  • Model-driven forgetting: With memory_forget, the model can delete a specific memory when a user says "forget that." Removal usually happens within about 60 seconds.

Because the memory is stored in MongoDB Atlas, application operational data, its memory, and the vector search that retrieves it run on one platform. Developers can secure, monitor, and scale a single database without bolting on a separate vector store or memory service alongside it.

What changes when you run the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration in production?

This production release gives developers greater controls over their data and flexibility in how they use the integration:

  • Reliable session history: By default, the model decides when to save and read conversation turns, so it can occasionally skip one. For production, you can use the AI SDK hooks so that the application’s own code loads and saves the transcript at every turn. Every user, assistant, and tool message is saved exactly once.

  • Separate data per customer: Developers can add a filter field, such as tenant_id, to the application’s vector indexes to limit each search to a single customer's memories.

  • Application names and layout: Developers can rename collections and indexes to match the existing application schema or turn off indexing for unused categories. 

  • Open source: The package is licensed under Apache 2.0 and works with any AI SDK model.

Get started today

Developers can add memory to an existing Vercel AI SDK project in three steps. This integration works with AI SDK v6 and v7 and requires a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

  1. Install the package and its peer dependencies: npm install @mongodb-developer/vercel-ai-memory ai mongodb

  2. Create a memory instance with an Atlas connection string and an embedding model.

  3. Pass the memory tools to the application, scoped to a user and session.

From there, the model decides when to save and when to search for memories.

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing the MongoDB Google ADK Integration: Durable Memory for Agent State
event_model_payload.summary:
We’re excited to announce the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, which provides developers with the building blocks they need to create durable memory for agent state.

As agents move from prototypes to real-world applications, they need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over a long time. However, developers still need to build their own tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state. 

This integration gives developers a cohesive, ADK-native experience for using MongoDB as the data platform for agents.

What is the Google ADK?

The Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

Google ADK offers developers an extensive set of tools for creating, deploying, assessing, and scaling agents, enabling developers to build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows.

How does the MongoDB Google ADK Integration help?

Developers can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. With MongoDB as the data layer, developers can keep the data their agents search over, the conversation state that needs to survive a restart or a scaled-out instance, and the memories agents build over time, all in the same place as the rest of their application data. That means no separate database to stand up for retrieval, no pipeline syncing app data into a different memory index, and no added latency pulling context from another system before the agent can respond.

ADK supplies the agent framework and tool interface; this integration provides the data and persistence layer beneath it, so developers can easily take an agent from prototype to production. These agents can maintain conversation and session memory independent of any single machine, and carry a user's history across sessions.

Providing a unified agent architecture

At the core of this integration is Google ADK 2.0, which serves as the code-first orchestration layer for multi-agent systems. ADK 2.0 provides the deployment framework, while MongoDB provides session and memory storage for agents.

Integrating directly with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, ADK 2.0 eliminates the need for custom routing logic by providing standardized tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry, and enterprise access controls out of the box. Developers can use Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for low-latency execution.

Figure 1. The MongoDB Google ADK Integration adds session and memory storage for single or multi-agent workflows.

How do Sessions and Memory storage work?

Great agent experiences improve with context. This integration introduces MongoDbSessionService to persist sessions, events, and application-, user-, and session-scoped state to MongoDB.

This means developers can build agents that retain the context needed for longer-running and multi-turn interactions. The session service includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications safely manage concurrent updates, while configurable collections make it easier to fit the service into existing data architectures.

The following Python code shows how you can add MongoDbSessionService to your agent:

For agents that need memory beyond a single session, MongoDBMemoryService ingests session events into MongoDB collections and recalls relevant memories through keyword matching. Memory ingestion is idempotent, which prevents duplicates when a session is added again.

Together, these services help agents become more useful over time without requiring developers to stitch together separate systems for retrieval, state, and memory.

How does MongoDB Search help agents with data retrieval?

Having memory for agent state is essential, but agents also need fast access to the operational data they search over, the same product catalogs, documents, and records your application already queries. This is where MongoDB's built-in search capabilities come in. MongoDB Vector Search leverages Voyage AI's embedding models, which are the same engine backing MemoryService's semantic retrieval in this integration.

Developers can also perform hybrid search by combining vector search with full-text search using the $rankFusion aggregation stage.

This gives agents access to the right information and context at the right time, delivering better responses in production. Whether you are building product discovery, knowledge assistants, support experiences, or domain-specific copilots, agents can automatically leverage semantic and hybrid retrieval to ground their responses in your data.

The application owns the database connection, database name, and search configuration. The agent gets focused tools to call, without exposing those operational details in its context.

The following Python code shows how to add MongoDB Search to your agents:

Using MongoDB as the operational data store, the memory layer for agent state, and the search engine over both, developers get one platform instead of three, on whatever deployment they run it on. There's no separate vector database to stand up, no search engine to sync against a second copy of the data, and no added latency from hopping between systems before the agent can respond.

Which deployment versions does this integration support?

The integration supports MongoDB Atlas and self-managed MongoDB 8.0+ deployments for vector and hybrid search. Developers can provide a connection string or bring an existing PyMongo client, and configure search behavior through MongoDbToolSettings, including index names, embedding fields, limits, and candidate counts.

That flexibility makes it possible to align the integration with existing data models, deployment choices, and performance requirements.

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents
event_model_payload.summary:
The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore.

Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027).

What is the Claude Agent SessionStore?

But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store.

That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn.

That is the gap the MongoDB Session Adapter closes.

This is especially useful for enterprises that have multiple teams developing agents across many machines, who need session storage that survives host failures, scales as the agent fleet increases, and enforces the same access controls and retention rules as the rest of their data estate, not a bolt-on system built solely for agent memory.

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter gives Claude agents durable session storage: a record of the conversation and its action history that lets an agent pick back up exactly where it left off, whether that's on the same laptop, a different server, or any server in a distributed deployment.

The adapter helps cover three crucial areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: Whether a different backend instance picks up a conversation after a restart or a user resumes on a different device, session state doesn't live on the machine that started it. Because every step is mirrored to MongoDB as it happens, any instance in your deployment can resume exactly where the last one left off.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container gets rescheduled mid-conversation, nothing is lost. Entries are written to MongoDB as they occur, not batched or cached locally, so whichever instance picks the session back up sees the same state as the failed one, up to the last completed step.

  • Retention and auditability: Many teams need to retain agent transcripts to meet internal data-retention or audit requirements. Instead of standing up a separate system just for that, session data lives in the MongoDB cluster you're already operating, under the same access controls and backup policies as the rest of your data.

How it works

This adapter implements the Claude Agent SDK's session storage interface directly, so you can mirror session transcripts to MongoDB in a few lines in ClaudeAgentOptions:

That's it. Every session started with these options is stored in MongoDB and can be resumed across machines. Each agent writes locally; MongoDB makes the conversation portable between app instances.

Figure 1. How the adapter allows you to access agent session transcripts mirrored in MongoDB.
