Erasure requests will now be processed 5 days after the request was submitted, regardless of when the customer's most recent order was placed. For recipients of gift cards that have been scheduled to send, the erasure request will remain in a pending state until the gift card has been delivered.

This update simplifies the overall experience for managing customer data requests.

event_model_payload.headline: Updated B2B location access in the Customer Account API
event_model_payload.summary:
We've changed what B2B customers can read on all versions of the Customer Account API. Customers now read only the company data and the orders for companies that they belong to.

Company location access

The schema doesn't change. Some fields now return null, an empty list, or fewer results.

CompanyContact.locations returns an empty list unless the contact belongs to the current customer. The current customer reads the locations that they have a role in from their contact's locations field, from Company.locations, and from companyLocation(id:).

On a CompanyLocation where the current customer has no role, the following fields return null or an empty list:

  • Tax field: taxIdentifier.
  • Contact fields: contacts and roleAssignments.

Orders after a customer is removed from a company

When a merchant removes a customer from a company, order(id:) and draftOrder(id:) refuse that company's orders and draft orders. customer.orders and customer.draftOrders exclude the orders and draft orders for that company. The customer's personal orders are still listed.

What you need to do

If your app reads a location's tax or contact data through another contact's locations or through an order's purchasingEntity, then expect null or an empty list for locations where the customer has no role. If your app shows a customer's order history, then the history omits the orders that the customer placed for a company that they no longer belong to. You don't need to change your queries.

event_model_payload.headline: Storefront MCP policies and FAQs tool is being deprecated in favor of UCP MCP Ask tool
event_model_payload.summary:
Storefront MCP search_shop_policies_and_faqs is deprecated. Migrate to UCP MCP's ask_business tool by January 15, 2027.

What's changing

The search_shop_policies_and_faqs tool on the Storefront MCP server (https://{shop}.myshopify.com/api/mcp) is deprecated in favor of the UCP Ask MCP tool.

UCP MCP implements the UCP ask capability (dev.ucp.common.ask) and exposes the following tool at the https://{shop-domain}/api/ucp/mcp endpoint:

  • ask_business: Answer a buyer's question about the store's policies and services, using the store's knowledge base and policies.

The deprecated tool will be maintained until January 15, 2027, but all documentation will refer to Ask MCP.

What you should do

If you're building with search_shop_policies_and_faqs:

  • Migrate calls to ask_business, and update endpoints to use https://{shop-domain}/api/ucp/mcp.
  • Include a meta object carrying ucp-agent.profile in every request. Your agent profile must declare dev.ucp.common.ask.
  • Send the question in ask.query, and optional buyer context (such as country or preferred language) in ask.context.
  • Note that ask_business returns a written answer in result.structuredContent.answer.plain, not raw knowledge base facts or full policy text. Update any code that parses the old response.
  • Use tools/list to check whether a store offers ask_business for your agent profile.

See the documentation for Ask MCP (https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/ask) for more details.

event_model_payload.headline: Remove your app from the Shopify App Store yourself
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now start sunsetting your app and remove it from the Shopify App Store yourself, from the Partner Dashboard. You no longer need to contact Shopify Support.

What's new

  • In the Partner Dashboard, go to Apps > your app > Distribution, and click Remove from App Store.
  • Choose a sunset date at least 30 days from now. This gives your merchants time to prepare and find an alternative.
  • Shopify removes your app from the Shopify App Store right away. Merchants can no longer find or install it there.

Removing your app from the Shopify App Store can't be undone. To list the app again, you need to submit it for review as a new app.

What happens to existing merchants

Removing your app from the Shopify App Store doesn't immediately affect merchants who already have it installed. They can keep using your app until your scheduled sunset date, when your app is sunset and removed from their stores.

Shopify doesn't email your merchants, cancel their charges, or uninstall your app for you. Before your sunset date, you're responsible for:

  • Telling your merchants about the sunset and reminding them before the sunset date
  • Cancelling app subscriptions with appSubscriptionCancel
  • Uninstalling your app from any remaining stores with appUninstall

Related docs

  • Sunsetting your app

event_model_payload.headline: Declare that your app uses only expiring Admin API tokens
event_model_payload.summary:
Turn on the Admin API token expiry card from your app’s Settings page in the Dev Dashboard and any API requests made from your app to the GraphQL or REST Admin API must use expiring tokens. Requests made with non-expiring tokens will be rejected.

What changed

When you enable Admin API token expiry for an app, it applies across every store where that app is installed. GraphQL and REST Admin API requests then fail if they use either:

  • A non‑expiring offline access token
  • A delegate access token with more than 24 hours remaining before expiry

Enforcement can take up to 30 minutes to take effect. Enabling the setting doesn’t migrate or revoke existing tokens.

You can turn the setting off if you encounter issues. Turning it off doesn’t change the April 1, 2027 enforcement deadline for public apps or the December 1, 2026 requirement for custom apps.

Who’s affected

This setting is available for all app types in the Dev Dashboard. It affects an app only after you turn it on for that app.

Expiring tokens are required for all apps:

  • **December 1, 2026: ** Custom apps created on or after must use expiring tokens.
  • January 1, 2027: Public apps that still use non-expiring offline access tokens are delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • April 1, 2027: Shopify rejects a GraphQL Admin API or REST Admin API request that presents a non-expiring offline token, and merchants lose access to your app until they re-authenticate.

What to do

We recommend turning on Admin API token expiry to give you peace of mind that your migration is complete ahead of the deadlines.

  1. Complete your migration using the Admin API token expiry migration guide, then review your app’s GraphQL and REST logs for affected requests. The Dev Dashboard highlights potential token‑expiry issues detected in the last 14 days, though detection can lag by a day.
  2. Open your app in the Dev Dashboard, go to Settings, and select Turn on in the Admin API token expiry card. Confirm that you understand that requests that don’t meet token‑expiry requirements will fail.
  3. Allow up to 30 minutes for enforcement to take effect. Then check your app’s workflows and logs for rejected requests, including requests from background jobs, to confirm that your app handles expiring tokens correctly.

event_model_payload.headline: Market.metafields matches keys in any case as of Storefront API version 2027-01
event_model_payload.summary:
As of Storefront API version 2027-01, the metafields field on the Market object matches each requested key in any case, as Market.metafield already does. This is a breaking change for apps and custom storefronts that request a market metafield key in a different case from the stored key, or that read a key that the buyer's markets store that differ by letter case. If your app does either, review its Market.metafields queries before you move it to 2027-01.

What changed

In version 2027-01, Market.metafields returns a metafield when the requested key matches the stored key in any case. In earlier versions, Market.metafields returns a metafield only when the requested key and the stored key have the same case.

For example, a market stores a metafield with the namespace custom and the key colour:

  • In version 2026-10 and earlier, the entry for { namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" } is null.
  • In version 2027-01, the entry returns the stored metafield.

Who's affected

The change applies to apps and custom storefronts that query metafields on a Market object, from Localization.market or Country.market, with Storefront API version 2027-01 or later. Your app is affected only if one of these conditions is true:

  • It requests a key in a different case from the key that the market stores.
  • The buyer's markets store the same key in different cases.

Your app isn't affected if it requests each key in the case that the markets store it, or if it uses only Market.metafield, which already matches keys in any case. Versions 2026-10 and earlier don't change.

Why this matters

In earlier versions, Market.metafield and Market.metafields can return different results for the same key: Market.metafield finds the metafield, and Market.metafields returns null. In 2027-01, both fields return the same metafield, so your storefront shows the same value whichever field it queries.

What to do

Market.metafield already matches keys case-insensitively, and it returns the metafield from the buyer's most specific market. So on the version that you use today, Market.metafield returns the result that Market.metafields returns in 2027-01. You can compare the two fields to find out whether the change affects your app.

  1. For each market metafield that your app reads, query Market.metafield and Market.metafields with the same namespace and key, and compare the results.
  2. If the results are the same for every key, then you don't need to make changes.
  3. If a result is different, then check whether the difference has a material impact on your app or your storefront.
  4. If it does, then update your app and your metafields so that they don't depend on the case of keys. For example, request each key in the case that your markets store it, and use one case for each key on every market.
query CompareMarketMetafields @inContext(country: CA) {
  localization {
    market {
      metafield(namespace: "custom", key: "Colour") {
        key
        value
      }
      metafields(identifiers: [{ namespace: "custom", key: "Colour" }]) {
        key
        value
      }
    }
  }
}

Related docs

  • Market object in the Storefront API
  • Storefront API 2027-01 reference
  • Retrieve metafields with the Storefront API
  • About Shopify API versioning

event_model_payload.headline: Market metafields break ties between equally specific markets by market handle
event_model_payload.summary: When a buyer matches two or more equally specific markets that set the same metafield, Market.metafield and Market.metafields now return the value from the market with the lowest handle, instead of the value that was updated most recently. This behavior change applies to the Storefront API, Liquid, and Function APIs on every API version. If your app or theme reads market metafields on stores with overlapping markets, check which value buyers get in a tie.

event_model_payload.headline: IP allowlists are now required for custom apps installed outside your organization
event_model_payload.summary:
We're enhancing protection of merchants by requiring IP allowlists for custom apps, if those apps are installed on stores outside of the organization that owns them.

  • Starting November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET: Apps must have an IP allowlist for new installs.
  • Starting January 1, 2027 at 11:59 PM ET: Allowlists are required for existing installs.

What apps are affected

  • Custom apps installed on stores outside the organization that owns the app.
  • Partners who own multiple apps. From January 1, 2027, one app without an allowlist affects your ability to install any app on stores outside your organization.

What apps are unaffected

  • Apps installed only on stores within your own organization
  • Apps created by merchants either in the Dev Dashboard or in the admin
  • Public apps, which are covered by a separate requirement

Why we're making this change

Leaked tokens can be used from any network location. IP allowlists reduce the impact of a credential leak by limiting the networks from which your app can invoke the Admin API.

What to do

Configure your app's allowed IPs in the Dev Dashboard:

  • If your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses, configure your IP allowlist based on static IPs or CIDR range.
  • If your app's egress IP addresses are dynamic, allow your hosting provider's ASNs and list the countries your app runs in.

Audit every app you've installed on stores outside your organization, and configure an allowlist on each one before January 1, 2027.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

event_model_payload.headline: App security updates: Thank you, plus what's required next
event_model_payload.summary:
Thanks to you, we've already seen the vast majority of apps that run bulk operations adopt an IP allowlist. That's a big step toward keeping merchants protected heading into the busiest weeks of the year.

Here's what's required, what's new, and what's coming next.

Action required

  • All public apps that call the Admin API: Turn on an IP allowlist by November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. Apps without one will be delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working. For apps that are delisted, we'll relist apps automatically once they add an IP allowlist. Set up your IP allowlist
  • Bulk operations: We're beginning enforcement on bulk queries and mutations from public apps without an IP allowlist. Turn on your allowlist to restore them.
  • Enable bulk operations for partner-created apps: Before your app can run bulk queries or bulk mutations, enable them from API access requests in the Partner Dashboard. If your app doesn't start a bulk query or mutation for 31 days, you'll need to enable it again. Read the changelog
  • Custom apps installed outside your organization also need an IP allowlist: These apps need an IP allowlist for new installs from November 20, 2026, and for existing installs from January 1, 2027. From January 1, one app without an allowlist blocks you from installing any of your apps on stores outside your organization. Apps installed only within your organization, and apps created by merchants, aren't affected. Read the changelog

New this week

  • You can now use IP addresses and ASNs together. Your allowlist can include IP addresses, CIDR ranges and your hosting provider's ASNs at the same time, with up to 250 IP addresses or ranges. A request is allowed if it matches any entry. Country restrictions apply only to ASNs. For the strongest protection, use specific IP addresses wherever you can. Read the changelog

Coming soon

  • MFA on every partner account. Starting next week, multi-factor authentication will be required on all partner accounts. We recommend passkeys. Turn on MFA now so it doesn't interrupt your work later. Protect the accounts that control your app

Get help

If you see something suspicious, tell us right away at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You're responsible for fixing it and notifying affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security questions, contact Shopify Support.

Everything lives in the App Security Hub, and we answer questions on the App Security board in the developer community.

event_model_payload.headline: App IP allowlists now support IP addresses and ASNs together, and up to 250 IPs
event_model_payload.summary:
Your app's IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard can now include IP addresses and autonomous system numbers (ASNs) in the same allowlist. This helps apps whose requests come from a mix of static and dynamic IP addresses. You can also now configure up to 250 IP addresses or ranges, up from 100.

What changed

The IP allowlist section of your app's Settings page no longer makes you choose between IP addresses and networks. You can enter up to 250 addresses or ranges in IP addresses or CIDR ranges, up to 10 ASNs in Networks (ASN), or both. Under Limit ASNs to countries, you can choose up to 10 countries. Countries limit only your ASNs, not your IP addresses.

Requests are allowed if they match one of your configured IPs or ASNs. Requests from outside your allowlist fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

IP allowlists will soon be required for all public and custom apps. Shopify strongly recommends all apps use an IP allowlist.

Allow specific IP addresses wherever you can. This is the most secure option, because only your own servers can use your app's access tokens. An ASN allows every address on your hosting provider's network, including addresses used by the provider's other customers. Add ASNs only for requests that come from dynamic addresses, such as serverless functions, and limit them to the countries your app runs in.

Before you turn on enforcement, test your updated allowlist against recent traffic.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

event_model_payload.headline: Amazon EventBridge webhook payload size limit increased to 1 MB
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now receive webhook and Events payloads up to 1 MB (1,000,000 bytes) through Amazon EventBridge, up from 256 KB. This increase applies automatically across all API versions, and you don't need to update your existing subscriptions.

What changed

Previously, Amazon EventBridge deliveries capped payloads at 256 KB:

  • Classic webhook payloads over 256 KB fell back to a minimal {"id": ...} body, requiring a follow-up Admin API request to fetch the full resource.
  • Events payloads over 256 KB used large-payload overflow and delivered a temporary payload_url download link instead of the inline payload.

Shopify now sends raw UTF-8 payloads up to 1,000,000 bytes directly to your Amazon EventBridge partner event source, leaving headroom under EventBridge's 1 MiB entry cap for the source, detail-type, and detail envelope. Large resources such as products with many variants or orders with many line items now arrive inline, reducing follow-up Admin API requests and payload_url downloads in your app.

Payloads over 1,000,000 bytes keep the existing fallback behavior: classic webhooks send {"id": ...}, and Events deliveries send a stub payload with payload_url, payload_size_bytes, and expires_at.

What to do

No action is required. Existing EventBridge subscriptions configured in shopify.app.toml or through the GraphQL Admin API (eventBridgeWebhookSubscriptionCreate and webhookSubscriptionCreate) automatically receive inline payloads up to 1 MB across all API versions.

To review how your app handles large deliveries:

  • Keep fallback handling in place for payloads that exceed 1 MB ({"id": ...} for classic webhooks and payload_url for Events), or narrow payloads with include_fields and targeted Events [events.subscription] query selections.
  • Verify that the downstream AWS targets attached to your EventBridge rules accept events up to 1 MB, or configure an EventBridge input transformer if a target enforces a smaller quota.

event_model_payload.headline: Admin-created custom apps now appear in the Dev Dashboard
event_model_payload.summary:
Custom apps created in the Shopify admin are moving to the Dev Dashboard, where you can view their logs and set up an IP allowlist. Existing integrations keep working.

What changed

Custom apps that merchants or staff created in the Shopify admin now appear in the Dev Dashboard. Manage existing admin-created custom apps in the Dev Dashboard, including credentials and logs.

Existing apps and integrations keep working:

  • Apps stay installed with their existing access scopes and webhook subscriptions.
  • Existing Admin API access tokens continue to work.

In the Dev Dashboard, these apps now have access to:

  • Configure IP restrictions to control which IP addresses can use the app’s credentials.
  • Inspect API and webhook logs to investigate unexpected activity and troubleshoot integration issues.

The migration doesn’t automatically replace any existing tokens or enable IP restrictions.

For more on building and managing apps in the Dev Dashboard, see the dev docs

Who’s affected

This change applies to custom apps that were created in the Shopify admin, including apps transferred to a merchant. These custom apps will now appear in the merchant’s Dev Dashboard.

Public apps and other app types that you already managed in the Dev Dashboard are not affected.

Why this matters

Managing all app types in the Dev Dashboard gives you:

  • Centralized control over app credentials and authentication.
  • IP restrictions that reduce the risk of credential misuse.
  • Logs for API calls and webhook deliveries that make it easier to audit traffic and debug issues.

This helps you secure existing integrations without breaking them and gives you better visibility into app behavior.

What to do

No immediate action is required for your apps to keep working. To improve security and observability, you should:

  1. Review each migrated custom app in the Dev Dashboard and confirm that it appears with the expected installation and scopes.
  2. Enable IP restrictions for each app where you can safely limit traffic to known IP addresses.
  3. Use the API and webhook logs in the Dev Dashboard to confirm that requests and deliveries look as expected after any changes.

After you enable IP restrictions, monitor the logs for a period of time to confirm that all integrations continue to function as expected.

event_model_payload.headline: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
event_model_payload.summary: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

event_model_payload.headline: Engineering AI Discover
event_model_payload.summary:
The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer

By Varun Khaitan, Peng Ren, Gary Tang, Itay Teller, Atif Faheem, Nipun Kumar, Donnie DeBoer, Eduardo Lundgren, Matteo Rinaldi, Raghav Bakshi

We recently introduced AI Discover, a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see.

Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline.

This post covers the challenges we designed for and the key decisions we made along the way.

Why an intelligence layer?

Every Netflix page combines recommendations with rules. We pick titles a member may enjoy, and eligibility, maturity and safety rules decide what can appear. An experience built on LLMs needs the same rules, plus code that decides when to call an LLM and how to handle its output. That code is called an agent harness, and it’s the core of our intelligence layer.

The simplest implementation hands the entire request to an LLM and lets it pick the titles, write the labels and decide what happens next. However, that leaves us relying on probabilistic output where we need governed results, because every turn in AI Discover ends on a screen in someone’s living room. At our scale, even rare failures happen many times a day. A member sees every slow call, unavailable title or off-brand line. Seven challenges shaped our design:

  1. Fitting LLMs into a product and architecture designed without them. Traditional recommenders rank titles based on past behavior. LLMs can do more: understand what a member is asking for and plan how to respond. Our existing experience would leave most of that unused.
  2. Keeping recommendations grounded. Every pick must be a real, available title from our changing catalog. Retrieval and rankers work in tandem with LLMs to choose titles that fit the member’s taste and intent.
  3. Working with slow, unpredictable LLMs. LLM calls are the slowest and most expensive part of the system. Tail latencies can spike, and the output may not be what you asked for. So we use LLMs selectively, treat what they return as untrusted input and test performance and quality before anything ships.
  4. Adapting to fast-changing models, tools and prompts. Modeling and engineering solutions keep evolving, so the product can’t depend on any single model, tool or prompt.
  5. Building for TV. Typing on a TV is hard, so members rely on the remote, and the app should respond to every press right away on widely varying hardware. TV apps also update slowly, so changes have to ship without an app release. A typical TV request returns in moments, while multi-step generation can take several seconds.
  6. Holding a safety and reliability bar at scale. Members always get a page, even when an LLM call fails or yields poor results. Their choices and our content standards hold on every request, and when something breaks, structured records show why.
  7. Learning from what members say alongside what we already know. Recommendations have always learned from viewing behavior. AI Discover also lets members tell us what they want, and that has to shape what they see next.

System Architecture

When a member picks a theme, the TV app sends the request to the Page Server, which builds pages for all Netflix apps and hands the request asynchronously to the intelligence layer. At a high level, this new layer has two components: a controller and an executor.

The controller decides what to run. It gathers the context needed for each request, including real-time signals such as the time of day. It then settles on a plan, either an established one or a new one drafted by its planner, validates it and retrieves only the member details that this plan requires from Memory Hub, our per-member memory store. These details may include member taste summaries generated by MemberLLM, our in-house language model for personalized recommendations, or feedback shared by the member. We talk more about Memory Hub and member taste summaries later.

A plan is a graph of approved steps, each running a capability. A capability is a named unit of work that can have multiple versions and belongs to a family such as retrieval, ranking, generation or packaging. It declares its inputs and outputs, the context it may see and what happens if it fails.

Capability declarations make a plan verifiable. Before execution, the controller validates the graph: every step is approved, every input has a producer, nothing loops and the plan ends in exactly one page. Afterward, the controller checks the result before it’s served.

The executor runs the plan. Steps pass typed outputs to each other through the declared contracts, so each receives exactly what it asked for. Independent steps run in parallel, each with its own deadline and appropriate fallback behaviors. Some steps are optimized LLM calls with one task each, such as writing row titles or suggesting next themes, and they act only within the validated plan. Checks before the run and contracts during it give us governed execution, where every action stays within limits set in code.

Both parts write to the request records, the traces we use offline to evaluate and improve the system.

Key Decisions

Each challenge led to one decision. Here’s what we chose and what it bought us.

1. Design the product and architecture around LLMs

We reimagined the experience around LLMs. The easier path would have been to drop them in as rankers, keep today’s latency budgets and precompute where necessary. AI Discover is built on a back-and-forth around themes a member can steer, which gives LLMs work only they can do: generating themes, explaining rows, summarizing taste and helping choose the titles that fit the member and the moment. Members pick themes with the remote, so they never have to type. On the TV, those themes and explanations get their own native UI elements. Behind the screen, LLMs can draft plans, and asynchronous serving gives multi-step agentic orchestration the time it needs.

This opens up experiences our traditional stack couldn’t support on its own.

2. Make existing systems composable

Keeping recommendations grounded meant building on the systems that already know our catalog and members. Most capabilities wrap complex, proven Netflix systems such as search, large-scale ranking and catalog metadata access. Some of them may run their own agents in the future.

Reshaping them took careful work, because agentic orchestration challenges many long-standing assumptions of distributed systems. A capability now has to work in combinations no one designed, for a caller that chooses to call it at runtime. Each one needs a clear purpose and a semantic interface, and shaping it means deciding how much to combine into a single step and how much to leave to the planner. Too fine, and the planner has more ways to go wrong; too coarse, and it loses room to compose richer plans.

In return, the planner gets building blocks it can mix in new ways, and connecting services takes far less manual wiring. Because plans can only use these blocks, even one drafted on the fly stays grounded in our catalog and member taste.

3. Plan first, then execute

To contain LLM latency and errors, we plan every request before anything runs. The familiar way to let an agent use tools is a loop: reason, call a tool, read the result, reason again. It’s flexible, but you can’t tell up front how many steps it will take or whether it has gone down a wrong path. In agent terms, ours is a plan-and-execute agent: an LLM can propose the path, but code decides whether it runs.

Plans come from two places: established plans we’ve already tested, and plans an LLM drafts on the fly. A router we control decides which one is served. Either way, the plan passes the same checks before it runs. If the planner is slow or its plan fails a check, we fall back to a tested plan.

This allows for adaptive planning. The planner can find new ways to serve a request, and we can balance cost, latency and quality for each task, from a lean single-call plan to a richer multi-step one.

4. Stay model and capability agnostic

The best model or capability for a task today may be second-best, or overkill, in a few months, so we built the system to switch between them. We assign each task to the model or capability version that fits it. Today that’s a per-task setting we can override live. Only some steps in a request use an LLM.

That only works if switching is easy. All the LLMs we use sit behind one common interface. Before we switch, each candidate is scored on the same tasks by automated checks and LLM judges, so every swap is a measured change.

Much of the system’s behavior lives in server-side prompts and configuration, so we can swap models, tools and capabilities without new code or a TV app release.

Upgrades get cheap and experiments get easy. Moving to a better model, ranker or retrieval system is a plan or setting change, not a migration, so each component can keep improving without a large investment.

5. Make page generation asynchronous

Inference keeps getting faster, but member expectations rise just as quickly: richer responses, more context and more of the page shaped by LLMs. The line between what feels instant and what’s worth waiting for will keep shifting, so we built the asynchronous path as a first-class way of serving.

Most of a TV app is synchronous: press a button, get a page. Generative work breaks that pattern. Holding one request open for many seconds across services would tie up too many threads. So requests that involve generation are asynchronous. The press returns right away with an acknowledgement, and the TV switches to a thinking state that explains what’s being prepared. Meanwhile, the executor runs the plan in the background. When the result is ready, the server notifies the TV, which then fetches it.

Slow generation no longer slows anything else. The serving path stays healthy however long a turn takes, and every press still gets immediate feedback on screen.

6. Enforce safety in code

Some rules must hold no matter what an LLM writes: content and maturity standards, what each step can access, and what a member has asked us not to show them. Putting those rules in a prompt makes them probabilistic, so we enforce them in code. Generated text is cleaned up before it reaches the screen. The planner sees a stripped-down request, and member details are limited to what the validated plan needs.

For example, the planner decides which inputs each step needs, such as the profile’s maturity rating for retrieval. Instead of writing parameter values directly, it uses placeholders. After the plan passes validation, the controller fills them with values from the request, matched by declared type. This also protects against prompt injection.

Each request also leaves a structured record: the plan, each step and its outcome, and which rules applied. When a page misses, we can tell whether the plan, the data, a rule or the model was at fault. The same records feed our offline evaluation and replay.

Together, these rules and records let an experiment ship at the same safety and privacy bar as the rest of the product.

7. Remember what members tell us

A taste summary is a short profile of what a member enjoys, such as favorite genres, tone and recurring themes. MemberLLM generates it ahead of time from the member’s viewing history, which keeps that LLM work off the request path. It helps us further personalize their page, and steps that write themes and explanations receive it as context, so their wording reflects the member. We’ll cover MemberLLM in more detail in an upcoming post.

In AI Discover, members can also tune their recommendations and tell us directly what they want. Those choices apply right away and carry across visits, and they give us a new signal alongside what we already know about their taste. This is a first step toward remembering more about each member, from their preferences to the habits that show up over time and the corners of the catalog they like to explore. We keep it all in Memory Hub, our persistent, low-latency memory store, next to their taste summaries, and we can add new kinds of memory as we need them. We apply these memories to later requests where they’re relevant, together with real-time context.

The member holds the remote

In this version, members interact by selecting themes and using tuning options such as “don’t recommend.” There’s no free-text input or open-ended chat. That keeps the LLM’s job narrow by design.

  • The usual protections still apply. Profile settings and our safety and privacy policies hold here as everywhere else.
  • Generated text was tested before launch. We ran safety evaluations on theme labels, row titles and explanations to make sure they meet our standards.

What’s next

It would have been faster to let an LLM do everything and stop there. The intelligence layer gave us an AI-native product, grounded building blocks, adaptive planning, quicker experimentation, asynchronous generation, governed execution and agent memory for tunable personalization. While AI Discover is its first experience, we designed it with more in mind.

We’ve organized our efforts to answer two questions:

  • How much do members want to shape their recommendations? Whether they’d rather steer or lean back, and how much, which kinds of themes help, and how we should blend what members tell us with our existing personalization systems.
  • What tradeoffs does this technology bring? How cost and latency hold up in production as we ramp traffic, how long members will wait for generated results, and whether errors came from the model, the harness or our existing systems. Multi-turn sessions also need different evaluation and observability than single requests.

Longer term, our goal is a system that improves itself, starting from the record each request leaves behind. Today we replay past requests against a new prompt, model or rule to see what changes, and we judge each change with automated checks, LLM judges and human evaluations. Eventually, we want the system to propose improvements, test them safely and keep only what proves better, within our privacy and data-use policies. As LLMs improve, more of the work may move into them, and the intelligence layer lets us move that line deliberately.

This is part of a bigger shift. Recommendation systems have long learned quietly from what members watch and answered with ranked rows. LLMs let them listen and respond, and members may increasingly expect that. We’ll keep exploring what that means for discovery on Netflix.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank Adi Suresh, Akash Katipally, Allan Johns, Becks Wood, Bhargav Mangipudi, Carrie Santiago, Chris Martin, Claire Campbell, Corey Waldin, Dana Sittler, Daneo Zhang, David Leen, Devon Bryant, Dharamendra Kumar, Dharini Chandrasekaran, Ebony Turner, Federico Roa, Gianfranco Cuoco, Guru Tahasildar, Haley Clanton, Haresh Chudgar, Ivan Provalov, James Schultz, JingXu Yang, Josie Shaw, Kamelia Aryafar, Kate Cummings, Kathleen Garrity, Kelley Robinson, Kevin Du, Kevin O’Connor, Kyla Moore, Kyle Lind, Laura Matsuura, Leah Cusella, Lingyi Liu, Lingyong Wang, Mallory Walkup, Matthew Pereira, Michael Galassi, Minsu Jang, Moumita Bhattacharya, Paran Jain, Paul Lee, Qusai Al-Rabadi, Scarlet Chen, Sergi Perez, Sriram Rao, Stephen Shaw, Sura Elamurugu, Varad Pathak, Yesu Feng, Zainab Mahar Mir, and Zhongli Cheng for their contributions to this work.
