event_model_payload.headline: GitHub Actions 모니터링의 빈칸: Exporter로 ARC Runner 관측하기
event_model_payload.summary:
안녕하세요, 당근 SRE팀 딜리버리 파트에서 일하고 있는 Uno(우노)예요. 딜리버리 파트는 Kubernetes 환경 기반의 사내 배포 플랫폼 Kontrol을 운영하고 GitHub Actions 중심의 전사 CI 시스템을 관리해요. 이번 글에서는 GitHub Actions를 운영하며 Job의 대기 현황과 Job을 실행 중인 Runner를 파악하기 위해 exporter를 만들고 개선한 과정을 소개할게요.

exporter를 소개하기에 앞서 GitHub Actions의 구조를 간단히 살펴볼게요. GitHub Actions에서는 push나 Pull Request 같은 이벤트가 발생했을 때 실행할 작업의 흐름을 Workflow로 정의해요. 하나의 Workflow는 테스트, 빌드처럼 여러 Job으로 나뉘어 각 Job은 Runner라는 실행 환경에 배정되어 실행되고 할당 가능한 Runner가 없으면 Job은 배정될 때까지 대기해요.

name: Simple                    # 1. Workflow: 자동화 작업 정의
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:               
  run_shell_command:            # 2. Job: Runner 배정 및 실행 단위
    name: Actions are amazing
    runs-on: arc-test-runner
    steps:                      # 3. Step: 작업 실행 절차 및 명령
      - name: Say hello
        run: |
          echo "Hello!"

GitHub Actions의 Job을 실행하는 Runner는 크게 GitHub이 관리하는 GitHub-hosted Runner와 GitHub 외부에서 운영하는 self-hosted Runner 두 가지로 나뉘어요. 당근은 Kubernetes 환경에서 직접 운영하는 self-hosted Runner를 주로 사용하고 이 Runner는 ARC(Actions Runner Controller)라는 Kubernetes 오퍼레이터로 관리해요.

ARC는 Runner Scale Set 단위로 Runner를 관리하고 대기 중인 Job 수에 맞춰 Runner 수를 조절해요. Runner Scale Set에는 Runner의 이미지와 리소스 및 최소, 최대 수를 설정할 수 있고 Workflow의 runs-on에 Runner Scale Set을 지정하면 해당 Runner에 Job이 배정돼요.

Runner 수가 자동으로 조절되지만 모든 Job이 즉시 실행되지는 않고 GitHub 장애가 발생하거나 Job 요청이 급증해 실행이 지연되면 Queued 상태로 표시돼요. ARC로 Runner를 운영하면서 가장 자주 받은 문의도 “GitHub Action이 Queued 상태로 실행되지 않아요.”였어요.

하지만 상황 파악을 위한 데이터가 부족해서 GitHub 상태 페이지에 공지가 올라오기를 기다리거나 ARC가 기본적으로 제공하는 메트릭으로 원인을 추측할 수밖에 없었어요.

ARC 기본 메트릭으로 Runner와 Job의 집계 현황은 볼 수 있지만 Runner를 기다리는 Job 개수와 대기 시간, 어떤 Job이 어느 Runner Pod에서 실행되는지는 파악하기 어려웠어요. 이런 정보를 확인할 수 있다면 Job 실행을 기다리는 개발자분들께 현재 상황을 더 명확하게 안내할 수 있을 거라고 생각했고 해결책을 찾던 중 Runner Pod에 Job 정보를 라벨로 추가하자는 ARC 이슈를 발견했어요. 하지만 이 방식은 컨트롤러 변경과 권한 추가가 필요해 적용까지 시간이 걸릴 수 있었고 라벨을 메트릭으로 수집하는 구성도 따로 마련해야 해서 다른 방법을 찾아야 했어요.

⁠그래서 Runner Pod와 Job의 관계뿐만 아니라 대기 중인 Job까지 살펴볼 수 있도록 action-runner-job-exporter를 만들었어요. exporter는 Runner Pod에 Job 이름을 붙이는 Collector, Runner를 기다리는 Job을 추적하는 Webhook, Webhook의 상태를 저장하는 StateStore까지 세 개의 바이너리로 구성했어요. 지금부터 각 구성 요소를 만든 과정과 운영하며 개선한 내용을 소개할게요.

배경: ARC Runner가 생성되고 Job을 배정받기까지

Collector가 Runner와 Job을 어떻게 연결하는지 살펴보기 전에 ARC에서 Runner Pod가 생성되고 Job을 배정받는 과정을 먼저 알아볼게요.

  1. 각 Runner Scale Set의 Listener Pod는 GitHub과 세션을 맺고 새로운 Job 배정을 기다려요.
  2. 저장소에서 Workflow가 실행되면 GitHub은 각 Job의 runs-on에 맞는 Runner Scale Set에 Job을 배정해요.
  3. Listener는 배정된 Job과 최소·최대 Runner 설정을 바탕으로 필요한 Runner 수를 계산해서 EphemeralRunnerSet의 replicas를 변경해요.
  4. ARC가 필요한 수만큼 EphemeralRunner를 생성하고 GitHub에서 일회용 등록 설정(JIT config)을 받아와 Runner Pod를 띄워요.
  5. Runner Pod가 GitHub에 등록되면 GitHub은 해당 Runner에 Job을 배정해요.
  6. Job이 시작되면 Listener가 Job 배정 정보를 받아 해당 EphemeralRunner의 status 필드에 저장소와 Job 정보를 업데이트해요.
  7. Job이 끝나면 Runner 프로세스가 종료되고 ARC가 Runner 관련 리소스를 정리해요.

ARC가 필요한 수만큼 Runner를 생성하면 각 Runner에 어떤 Job을 배정할지는 GitHub이 결정해요. Runner Pod는 특정 Job을 위해 생성되지 않으므로 Pod 이름만으로는 어떤 Job이 배정되었는지 알 수 없고 Listener가 EphemeralRunner의 status를 갱신해야 배정된 Job을 확인할 수 있어요.

Collector: Runner Pod에 Job 이름 붙이기

exporter를 만든 목표는 개발자분들이 GitHub Actions의 상태를 문의하시기 전에 SRE가 GitHub Actions의 이상 징후를 먼저 파악하는 것이었어요. 그래서 가장 먼저 Runner Pod에서 어떤 Job을 실행하고 있는지 확인하고 싶었어요. Pod 라벨과 기존 메트릭에는 Job 정보가 없었지만 EphemeralRunner와 Runner Pod의 이름이 같다는 점을 이용하면 status에 기록된 Job 정보를 해당 Pod와 연결할 수 있다고 생각했어요.

이 아이디어로 Pod와 Job의 관계를 메트릭으로 확인할 수 있도록 첫 번째 바이너리인 Collector를 만들었어요. Collector는 Kubernetes informer로 EphemeralRunner의 생성, 변경, 삭제를 지켜보며 최신 상태를 메모리 캐시에 저장하고 이 캐시를 읽어 아래 메트릭을 제공해요.

arc_runner_job_info{namespace, pod, runner_name, repository, job_name, workflow_ref, workflow_run_id}

Collector는 Job이 시작되어 status.jobRepositoryName이 채워진 Runner에 대해서만 이 메트릭을 제공해요. workflow_run_id 라벨은 여러 Job을 이어서 작업을 정의하는 Workflow를 가리키는 값이라 https://github.com///actions/runs/로 실행 페이지 링크를 바로 만들 수 있게 구성했어요.

Prometheus가 메트릭을 수집할 때 exporter Pod의 라벨과 이름이 겹쳐서 Runner Pod의 이름은 exported_pod에, Namespace는 exported_namespace에 담겨 있어요. 이 라벨을 컨테이너의 CPU, 메모리, 네트워크 사용량 메트릭(container_.*)에 있는 pod, namespace 라벨과 연결하면 사용량에 저장소와 Job 이름을 붙일 수 있어요. 덕분에 대시보드에서 실행된 Job마다 Runner Pod를 연결해서 Job의 리소스 사용량을 바로 확인할 수 있게 되었어요.

다만 Job이 종료되어도 EphemeralRunner가 정리되기 전까지는 status에 Job 정보가 남아있어요. 그래서 메트릭에 보이는 Job은 지금 실행 중인 Job이 아니라 ‘Runner가 배정받은 Job’으로 해석해야 해요.

Webhook: Runner를 기다리는 Job 가시화하기

status 필드는 Runner가 Job을 배정받고 실행을 시작한 뒤에 채워지기 때문에 GitHub Queue에서 Runner를 기다리는 Job은 Collector로 확인할 수 없었고 대기 중인 Job이 얼마나 쌓여있는지도 파악하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 GitHub Organization에 workflow_job 웹훅을 설정하고 Job 상태가 바뀔 때마다 이벤트를 받는 두 번째 바이너리, Webhook을 만들었어요. 웹훅 이벤트는 ARC Listener를 거치지 않고 GitHub에서 직접 전달되기 때문에 Listener에 문제가 생겨도 웹훅이 정상적으로 전달된다면 대기 중인 Job을 확인할 수 있어요.

workflow_job 이벤트로 확인할 수 있는 주요 Job 상태는 다음과 같고 일반적으로 Job은 queued → in_progress → completed 순서로 진행돼요.

  • waiting: 배포 환경 승인 등 보호 규칙을 기다리는 상태로 Runner를 기다리는 상태와 구분해요.
  • queued: 실행을 기다리는 상태로 보통 Runner 할당을 기다려요.
  • in_progress: Runner에 배정되어 실행 중인 상태예요.
  • completed: 실행이 종료된 상태로 성공, 실패, 취소를 모두 포함해요.

Webhook은 job_id를 키로 Job 상태를 메모리에 저장하고 이를 집계해 메트릭을 제공해요.

  • github_workflow_jobs_queued: 실행을 기다리는 Job 수
  • github_workflow_jobs_in_progress: 실행 중인 Job 수
  • github_workflow_job_queued_seconds: Job이 생성된 시각
  • github_workflow_job_queue_duration_seconds: Job이 Runner를 배정받기까지 기다린 시간을 담은 히스토그램

github_workflow_job_queued_seconds에는 대기 시간 대신 Job이 생성된 시각을 Unix time으로 담았어요. time() - github_workflow_job_queued_seconds로 현재 대기 시간을 계산할 수 있어서 exporter가 값을 계속 갱신할 필요가 없고 Job이 Runner에 배정되어 실행을 시작하면 해당 Job은 메트릭에서 사라져요.

GitHub 웹훅 이벤트는 순서대로 도착한다는 보장이 없어요. 그래서 Job 상태가 queued → in_progress → completed 방향으로만 변경된다는 전제로 이미 in_progress, completed인 Job에 늦게 도착한 queued 이벤트는 무시해요. 완료된 Job도 상태 맵에서 바로 삭제하면 늦게 도착한 이벤트 때문에 새로운 대기 Job으로 잘못 집계될 수 있어요. 그래서 완료된 Job은 바로 삭제하지 않고 일정 시간 동안 완료 표시(tombstone)로 남겨두었어요.

Webhook으로 대기 중인 Job이 얼마나 쌓여 있는지 확인하고 Job이 대량으로 밀릴 때는 메트릭을 통해 정확한 상태를 공유할 수 있었어요.

이후에 일정 시간 이상 대기하는 Job 수가 임계치를 넘으면 알림이 오도록 설정했어요. 더하여 Runner Scale Set의 Runner 수가 maxRunners의 90%에 도달할 때도 알림을 보내 ARC 설정으로 인한 병목을 살펴볼 수 있게 했어요.

StateStore: Webhook이 재시작해도 상태를 잃지 않게

처음 만든 Webhook은 Job 상태를 메모리에만 저장해서 배포하거나 재시작하면 대기 중이던 Job의 상태를 잃어버렸어요. 상태를 S3에 저장해 두고 복원하는 방법도 있지만 Webhook은 GitHub 이벤트를 받기 위해 인터넷에 노출되어 있어서 S3 권한을 부여하고 싶지 않았어요.

그래서 세 번째 바이너리인 StateStore를 만들었어요. Webhook이 침해되더라도 공격자가 S3 권한을 직접 사용하기 어렵도록 S3 권한은 사내망에 있는 StateStore에만 부여하고 스냅샷 저장을 맡겼어요.

롤아웃 중에는 일시적으로 이전 버전과 새 버전 Pod가 함께 실행되기 때문에 S3 조건부 쓰기(ETag / If-Match)로 서로의 저장 내용을 덮어쓰지 않게 했어요.

운영 개선: 잘못 집계된 Job 상태 바로잡기

#1 completed Job이 queued로 집계된 문제

어느 날 Runner를 오래 기다리는 Job이 72개라는 알림이 울렸지만 실제로는 모두 몇 시간 전에 완료된 상태였어요. 원인을 추적해보니 Webhook이 재시작되면서 오래된 스냅샷을 복원했고 이미 완료된 Job이 대기 중인 것으로 집계된 거였어요.

당시 Webhook은 진행 중인 Job의 상태와 완료된 Job의 tombstone, 중복 제거에 사용하는 Delivery ID(X-GitHub-Delivery)의 보관 기간과 스냅샷 복원 유효기간을 모두 기본값이 6시간인 --webhook-ttl 하나로 관리하고 있었어요. 그 결과 상태 맵에 6시간 치 기록이 쌓였어요. 스냅샷 크기 상한은 진행 중인 Job의 상태만 저장할 것을 고려해 8MiB로 여유 있게 설정했는데 스냅샷이 이 상한을 넘으면서 문제가 발생했어요.

  1. 스냅샷 저장 중단: Delivery ID와 tombstone이 쌓이면서 스냅샷 크기가 8MiB로 늘었고 이후 스냅샷 저장이 중단되었어요.
  2. Webhook 재시작: 상태 맵을 메모리에 보관하던 Webhook Pod가 메모리 limit 0.2GB를 넘겨 OOMKilled 됐어요.
  3. 오래된 상태 복원: 새 Pod는 2시간 44분 전에 저장된 스냅샷에서 Job 상태 16,097개를 복원했어요. 스냅샷 복원 유효기간이 6시간이어서 오래된 스냅샷이지만 복원 대상에 포함됐어요.
  4. 완료된 Job이 대기 중으로 집계: 스냅샷 저장이 중단된 뒤 수신한 completed 이벤트는 종료된 Pod의 메모리에만 남아 있었어요. 새 Pod에는 이 이벤트가 반영되지 않아 이미 완료된 Job을 queued 상태로 집계했어요.

잘못 복원된 Job은 이후 상태를 갱신할 이벤트가 오지 않아 대기 시간만 늘어났고 이후에 보관 기간인 6시간이 지나 상태가 한꺼번에 삭제되면서 알림도 해제됐어요.

데이터별로 보관 기간 분리하기

같은 문제가 반복되지 않도록 데이터 종류에 따라 보관 기간을 나누고 스냅샷 복원 유효기간도 별도로 설정했어요. 진행 중인 Job은 오래 추적할 수 있도록 보관하되 tombstone과 Delivery ID는 보관 기간을 줄였어요. 스냅샷은 오래될수록 실제 상태와 달라질 가능성이 커지기 때문에 복원 유효기간을 짧게 설정했어요.

  • --webhook-ttl 6시간: 진행 중인 Job
  • --tombstone-ttl 1시간(현재 3시간): completed Job과 waiting Job의 tombstone
  • --dedup-ttl 10분: Delivery ID (X-GitHub-Delivery)
  • --snapshot-max-age 10분: 스냅샷 복원 유효기간

알림을 받았을 당시 상태 맵의 항목 16,097개 중 진행 중인 Job은 175개뿐이었고 나머지 대부분은 tombstone이었어요. 그래서 tombstone 보관 기간을 1시간으로 줄이자 스냅샷 크기도 8MiB에서 약 0.66MiB로 줄어드는 걸 확인할 수 있었어요.

그리고 이벤트 카운터만으로는 전송이 끊긴 것인지, 원래 이벤트가 적은 시간대인지 구분하기 어려웠어요. 그래서 스냅샷 저장이나 웹훅 수신이 멈춘 상황을 살펴볼 수 있도록 마지막 스냅샷 저장 시각, 시작 시 복원한 Job 수와 스냅샷의 저장 경과 시간, 마지막 웹훅 수신 시각을 메트릭으로 추가했어요.

#2 실패한 웹훅 이벤트 재전송하기

GitHub은 실패한 웹훅을 자동으로 재전송하지 않아요. Webhook이 내려가 있거나 일시적인 네트워크 문제로 in_progress나 completed 이벤트를 놓치면 해당 Job은 보관 기간인 6시간 동안 대기 중이거나 실행 중인 상태로 남을 수 있어요.

이 점을 보완하기 위해 StateStore가 GitHub App으로 5분마다 Organization 웹훅의 전송 기록을 확인하도록 했어요. 최근 30분 안에 전송에 실패한 workflow_job 이벤트 중 in_progress와 completed는 재전송을 요청해요. queued와 waiting은 늦게 도착해 상태를 잘못 집계할 가능성을 고려해 제외했어요. 같은 이벤트가 중복 처리되지 않도록 Delivery ID도 확인해요.

#3 GitHub의 실제 상태로 Webhook의 Job 상태 바로잡기

재전송만으로 해결되지 않는 경우도 있었어요. 이미 성공한 Job 수십 개가 queued 상태로 남아 있는 일이 발생했는데 queued 이벤트가 Job 생성 후 한 시간 넘게 늦게 도착하고 그사이 당시 보관 기간이 1시간이었던 tombstone이 삭제되어 Webhook이 이를 새로운 대기 Job으로 인지한 것이 문제였어요.

같은 시각 GitHub Status에서 웹훅 전송 지연과 관련된 장애를 확인하며 원인은 파악했지만 이미 잘못 집계된 상태를 바로잡을 방법이 필요했어요. 그래서 일정 시간 동안 상태가 바뀌지 않은 Job은 리컨사일(reconcile)을 통해 GitHub의 실제 상태와 동기화하기로 했어요.

  • Webhook은 1분마다 10분 넘게 이벤트가 없는 queued, in_progress Job의 상태를 StateStore를 통해 Actions API로 확인해요. GitHub에서 Job이 완료된 것으로 확인되면 completed로, 실행 중이면 in_progress로, 승인을 기다리는 상태면 waiting으로 상태를 갱신해요. 상태는 queued → in_progress → completed 방향으로만 변경된다는 전제를 지키며 여전히 queued라면 상태를 유지해 실제 대기 중인 Job의 알림은 그대로 유지해요. 조회하는 사이 웹훅 이벤트가 도착하면 해당 이벤트에 따라 상태를 업데이트해요.
  • StateStore가 사용하던 GitHub App에 Actions: read 권한을 추가해서 조회해요. rate limit을 고려하여 매 주기마다 가장 오래전에 확인한 Job부터 최대 50개를 조회해서 Job 조회는 시간당 최대 3,000번으로 제한해요.
tombstone 보관 기간 늘리기

리컨사일 배포 후 5분 동안 완료된 Job 244개가 정리되었고 오래 대기 중이던 Job은 30개에서 4개로 줄었어요. 하지만 당일 오후에도 queued 이벤트가 70~112분씩 늦게 도착하면서 리컨사일 대상이 되기 전까지 약 10분 동안 Job 30여개가 알림에 걸렸어요. 그래서 --tombstone-ttl 기본값을 1시간에서 3시간으로 늘리고 3시간보다 늦게 도착하는 이벤트로 잘못 집계된 상태는 리컨사일로 정리하도록 개선했어요.

활용 사례: 메트릭으로 적절한 Runner 선택하고 병목 찾기

#1 Job별 사용량을 고려한 Runner 선택

Collector로 Runner Pod의 리소스 사용량에 Job 이름을 붙이면서 Job마다 실제로 사용하는 CPU와 메모리를 확인할 수 있게 되었어요. 이 사용량을 Runner에 설정된 리소스 요청량(request)과 비교하면 각 Job이 필요한 크기의 Runner를 사용하고 있는지 판단할 수 있어요.

필요 이상으로 큰 Runner를 사용하면 리소스가 낭비될 뿐 아니라 리소스를 확보하는 데 시간이 걸려 Pod 스케줄링이 늦어질 수도 있어요. 그래서 Job에 맞는 Runner를 선택할 수 있도록 이 데이터를 바탕으로 Job별 권장 Runner를 보여 주는 대시보드도 운영하고 있어요.

#2 GitHub 장애가 아닌 ARC 설정으로 인한 지연 탐지

Runner를 기다리는 Job이 계속 쌓이면서 대기 시간 알림이 울렸고 Webhook Queue 대시보드에서도 대기 중인 Job이 늘어나는 것을 확인할 수 있었어요.

먼저 GitHub 장애 여부를 확인했지만 공지된 장애는 없었고 Runner 등록 설정(JIT config)을 가져오는 호출의 중앙값도 0.57초로 평소와 비슷했어요. 그래서 ARC 쪽을 살펴보니 Runner의 생성과 정리를 담당하는 EphemeralRunner 컨트롤러의 작업 큐(workqueue_depth)가 평소보다 훨씬 높아져 있었어요.

작업을 처리하는 worker 수(controller_runtime_active_workers)는 6시간 동안 2에 머물러 있었는데 이 값은 동시 처리 수 설정인 runnerMaxConcurrentReconciles의 기본값(0.12.x 기준)이에요. 작업 처리 시간도 p99 기준 0.9초에서 8~10초로 늘어나 있었어요. worker가 두 개뿐인 상황에서 GitHub 호출 지연까지 발생하자 컨트롤러가 작업을 제때 처리하지 못하고 있음을 확인했어요.

이 병목 때문에 새 Runner를 만드는 작업이 큐에서 밀리면서 Pod 생성도 늦어졌어요. 한 Runner Scale Set에서는 생성을 기다리는 Runner가 258개였지만 Pod는 약 150개뿐이었어요. Runner 정리도 지연되면서 이미 종료된 Pod 95개와 삭제 중인 Runner 55개가 maxRunners 한도를 계속 차지하고 있었어요.

컨트롤러의 처리량을 늘리기 위해 runnerMaxConcurrentReconciles를 2에서 5로 상향 조정하니 약 10분 만에 컨트롤러 큐는 669에서 233으로, 대기 Job은 380에서 168로 줄었고 Runner Scale Set의 대기 Runner도 224에서 61로 감소했어요. 작업 처리 시간의 p99는 여전히 11초로 높았지만 동시 처리 수를 늘린 뒤 밀려 있던 작업이 줄어들었어요. Webhook 메트릭으로 Job 대기 상황을 파악하고 ARC 컨트롤러 메트릭을 함께 살펴본 덕분에 병목이 컨트롤러의 처리량에 있다는 점을 짚을 수 있었어요.

마무리: 보이지 않던 Job의 상태를 살펴볼 수 있게 되기까지

처음에는 GitHub Actions를 ARC로 직접 운영하더라도 GitHub에 의존하는 부분이 커서 장애가 발생했을 때 개발자분들께 상황을 안내하고자 메트릭 수집을 목표로 시작했어요. 그런데 Job의 상태를 살펴볼 수 있게 되면서 장애 안내뿐 아니라 Runner 사용량을 파악하고 지연 원인을 찾아 병목을 개선하는 데에도 활용하고 있어요.

GitHub Actions와 ARC를 운영하며 Job과 Runner의 상태를 파악하기 위해 비슷한 고민을 하고 계신 분들께 이 글이 도움이 되었으면 좋겠어요. 읽어주셔서 감사합니다.

GitHub Actions 모니터링의 빈칸: Exporter로 ARC Runner 관측하기 was originally published in 당근 기술 블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Closing the GitHub Actions Monitoring Gap: Observing ARC Runners with an Exporter
event_model_payload.summary:
Hi, I’m Uno from the Delivery part of Karrot’s SRE team. Our team’s mission is to run Kontrol, our internal deployment platform on Kubernetes, and manage the company-wide CI system that mostly relies on GitHub Actions. In this post I’ll introduce the exporter we built to see which Jobs are waiting and which Runner is running each Job. I’ll also share how we improved it in production.

A Workflow defines what happens when an event such as a push or pull request occurs. Each Workflow is split into Jobs such as test and build that run on execution environments called Runners. If no Runner is free, a Job waits until one becomes available.

name: Simple                    # 1. Workflow: defines the automation
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  run_shell_command:            # 2. Job: the unit that gets a Runner and runs
    name: Actions are amazing
    runs-on: arc-test-runner
    steps:                      # 3. Step: the commands the Job executes
      - name: Say hello
        run: |
          echo "Hello!"

Runners can be GitHub-hosted or self-hosted. At Karrot we mainly use self-hosted Runners on our own Kubernetes clusters. These are managed by a Kubernetes operator called ARC (Actions Runner Controller).

ARC organizes Runners into groups called Runner Scale Sets and scales each set according to Job demand. Each set defines the Runner image and resources, along with minimum and maximum Runner counts. A Workflow can specify a Runner Scale Set in runs-on so its Jobs are assigned to Runners in that set.

Even with autoscaling, Jobs don’t always start immediately. A GitHub outage or a spike in Job requests can leave them stuck in the Queued state. While operating ARC, we often heard developers say, “My Action is stuck in Queued and won’t run.”

Answering that question wasn’t easy with the data we had. We often had to wait for an announcement on GitHub’s status page or infer the cause from ARC’s built-in metrics.

ARC’s built-in metrics show aggregate counts of Runners and Jobs, but they don’t tell us how many Jobs are waiting for a Runner, how long they’ve been waiting, or which Runner Pod is running a given Job. With that information, we could give developers a better understanding of what was happening with their Jobs.

While looking for a solution, we found an issue in the ARC repository proposing to add Job information to Runner Pods as labels. Adopting that approach would require controller changes and additional permissions, as well as a separate setup to collect the labels as metrics, so we decided to build our own solution.

We built action-runner-job-exporter to connect Runner Pods to their Assigned Jobs and track Jobs still waiting for a Runner. There are three key components for the exporter, which are separate binaries. Collector associates Job names with Runner Pods, Webhook tracks waiting Jobs, and StateStore persists Webhook's state.

How ARC Runners work

Before getting into the exporter, let’s look at how ARC creates a Runner Pod and how a Job reaches it.

  1. Each Runner Scale Set has a Listener Pod that keeps a session open with GitHub and waits for new Job assignments.
  2. A Workflow starts in a repository, and GitHub assigns each Job to the Runner Scale Set that matches its runs-on.
  3. The Listener works out how many Runners are needed from the assigned Jobs and the min/max Runner settings, then updates the replicas of the EphemeralRunnerSet.
  4. ARC creates that many EphemeralRunner resources, fetches a one-time registration config (JIT config) from GitHub for each, and starts the Runner Pods.
  5. Once a Runner Pod registers with GitHub, GitHub assigns a Job to it.
  6. After the Job starts, the Listener receives the assignment and writes the repository and Job details into the status field of that EphemeralRunner.
  7. The Runner process exits after the Job finishes and ARC cleans up the Runner’s resources.

ARC creates the Runners and GitHub decides which Job goes to each one. Because Runner Pods aren’t created for a specific Job, the Pod name alone doesn’t tell us which Job it’s running. That becomes visible only after the Listener updates the EphemeralRunner status.

Collector: Mapping Jobs to Runner Pods

We wanted SREs to detect GitHub Actions delays before developers had to ask about them. We started by finding a way to see which Job each Runner Pod was running. Neither Pod labels nor existing metrics carried that information, but an EphemeralRunner and its Runner Pod share the same name. We could use that name to match the Job information in the status to the right Pod.

Our first binary, Collector, exposes that relationship as a metric. It uses a Kubernetes informer to watch EphemeralRunner creations, updates, and deletions, keeping the latest state in an in-memory cache. From that cache, it serves the following metric.

arc_runner_job_info{namespace, pod, runner_name, repository, job_name, workflow_ref, workflow_run_id}

Collector emits this metric only after a Runner’s Job has started and status.jobRepositoryName is populated. The workflow_run_id label identifies the Workflow run, letting us link directly to its page at https://github.com///actions/runs/.

The pod and namespace labels on this metric collide with those of the exporter Pod itself during a Prometheus scrape. As a result, the Runner Pod name appears in exported_pod and its namespace in exported_namespace. We join those labels with pod and namespace on container resource metrics (container_.*) to attach repository and Job names to CPU, memory, and network usage. The resulting dashboard links each Job to its Runner Pod and shows how many resources it used.

Job information remains in the status after the Job ends until the EphemeralRunner is cleaned up. The metric therefore shows the Job assigned to each Runner even if the Job has already finished.

Webhook: Tracking queued Jobs

Collector filled one gap, but the status field is populated only after a Runner receives a Job and starts running it. Jobs still waiting in GitHub’s queue remained invisible, so we couldn’t tell how many were piling up.

To make those Jobs visible, we added a second binary called Webhook. It receives workflow_job events from our GitHub Organization whenever a Job's state changes. Because the events come directly from GitHub rather than through the ARC Listener, we can see waiting Jobs even when the Listener has problems, as long as GitHub delivers the webhooks.

A Job typically progresses through queued → in_progress → completed. The main Job states in workflow_job events are described below.

  • waiting: Waiting for a protection rule, such as a deployment environment approval, to be satisfied. This is different from waiting for a Runner.
  • queued: Waiting to run, usually for a Runner.
  • in_progress: Assigned to a Runner and running.
  • completed: Finished. Includes success, failure, and cancellation.

Webhook keeps Job state in memory using job_id as the key and exposes the following metrics.

  • github_workflow_jobs_queued: number of Jobs waiting to run
  • github_workflow_jobs_in_progress: number of running Jobs
  • github_workflow_job_queued_seconds: when the Job was created
  • github_workflow_job_queue_duration_seconds: histogram of how long Jobs waited before getting a Runner

Rather than storing a wait duration, github_workflow_job_queued_seconds holds the Job's creation time as a Unix timestamp. We can calculate the current wait time with time() - github_workflow_job_queued_seconds without the exporter having to keep updating the value. Once a Job is assigned to a Runner and starts running, it is removed from the metric.

Because GitHub doesn’t guarantee that webhook events arrive in order, we treat Job state as moving only queued → in_progress → completed. Late queued events are ignored for Jobs already in_progress or completed. To make that possible even after a Job finishes, we keep completed Jobs in the state map for a while as markers called tombstones. Removing them immediately could cause a late event to be counted as a new waiting Job.

With Webhook showing us how many Jobs were waiting, we could share more accurate status updates when delays affected many Jobs.

We also set up alerts for when too many Jobs have been waiting longer than a certain time and when a Runner Scale Set reaches 90% of its maxRunners. These alerts help us detect delays and investigate potential bottlenecks in our ARC configuration.

StateStore: Preserving Webhook state

The first version of Webhook kept Job state only in memory, so it lost track of waiting Jobs whenever it was deployed or restarted. Saving and restoring the state through S3 was one option, but Webhook is exposed to the internet to receive GitHub events, and we didn’t want to grant it S3 permissions.

Instead, we built a third binary called StateStore. It runs on the internal network and handles snapshots as the only component with S3 permissions. This separation makes it harder for an attacker to use those permissions directly if Webhook is compromised.

During a rollout, old and new Pods briefly run together. We use S3 conditional writes (ETag / If-Match) to keep them from overwriting each other's snapshots.

Fixing Job state errors

#1 Stale snapshots

One day an alert reported that 72 Jobs had been waiting a long time for a Runner, even though all of them had completed hours earlier. We traced the miscount to a Webhook restart that had restored an old snapshot.

At the time, --webhook-ttl (default 6h) controlled several things at once: retention of in-progress Job state, tombstones for finished Jobs, and Delivery IDs (X-GitHub-Delivery) used for deduplication. It also set the maximum age of a snapshot that could be restored. As a result, six hours' worth of records accumulated in the state map. We had set an 8MiB snapshot size limit, assuming it would only need to store in-progress Jobs, but eventually the snapshot outgrew it.

  1. Snapshots stopped saving: Delivery IDs and tombstones piled up until the snapshot hit 8MiB, and saving stopped.
  2. Webhook restarted: The Webhook Pod held the whole state map in memory. It went over its memory limit and got OOMKilled.
  3. Stale state restored: The new Pod restored 16,097 Job states from a snapshot saved 2 hours and 44 minutes earlier. The snapshot was old, but the 6-hour restore window still allowed it.
  4. Finished Jobs counted as waiting: completed events received after snapshots stopped saving only existed in the dead Pod's memory. The new Pod never saw them, so it counted those finished Jobs as queued.

No further events arrived to correct those restored Jobs, so their apparent wait times kept increasing. The alert cleared only after the 6-hour retention period passed and their state was deleted all at once.

Separate retention for each kind of data

We split retention by data type and set a separate limit for snapshot restore. In-progress Jobs are retained long enough to be tracked while tombstones and Delivery IDs have shorter retention periods. We also kept the restore window short because older snapshots are more likely to diverge from the actual state.

  • --webhook-ttl 6h: In-progress Jobs
  • --tombstone-ttl 1h(now 3h): Tombstones for completed and waiting Jobs
  • --dedup-ttl 10m: Delivery ID (X-GitHub-Delivery)
  • --snapshot-max-age 10m: Max age of a snapshot that can be restored

Only 175 of the 16,097 entries in the state map were in-progress Jobs at the time of the alert; most of the rest were tombstones. Reducing tombstone retention to one hour shrank the snapshot from 8MiB to about 0.66MiB.

We also found that event counters alone made it hard to distinguish stopped delivery from low traffic. To detect stalls, we added metrics for the last snapshot save and the last webhook received. At startup we now record the number of Jobs restored and the snapshot’s age as well.

#2 Failed webhook deliveries

Another source of incorrect state is a missed event. GitHub doesn’t automatically retry failed webhooks, so if Webhook is down or a temporary network issue causes it to miss an in_progress or completed event, the Job can remain in a waiting or running state for the entire 6-hour retention period.

To recover from failed deliveries, StateStore uses a GitHub App to check the Organization’s webhook delivery log every 5 minutes. It requests redelivery of in_progress and completed workflow_job events that failed in the last 30 minutes. We exclude queued and waiting events because they could cause incorrect counts if they arrive late. We also check Delivery IDs to avoid processing the same event twice.

#3 Reconciling Job states

Redelivery couldn’t solve every case. At one point, dozens of Jobs that had already succeeded still appeared as queued. GitHub Status reported a webhook-related incident around the same time.

Their queued events had arrived more than an hour after the Jobs were created, but with the tombstone retention set to one hour, the tombstones have already been expired by the time the events arrived. This lead to misunderstanding the events as new waiting jobs.

We still needed a way to correct the miscount, so we decided to reconcile Jobs whose state hadn’t changed for a certain period with their actual state on GitHub.

  • Every minute Webhook checks queued and in_progress Jobs with no event for over 10 minutes against the Actions API through StateStore. It updates their state from GitHub to completed, in_progress, while keeping transitions forward-only along queued → in_progress → completed. Jobs still queued keep their alerts. Events received during a lookup update the state as usual.
  • The lookups use StateStore’s existing GitHub App with the Actions: read permission added. Each cycle checks at most 50 Jobs starting with the least recently checked. That caps lookups at 3,000 an hour and keeps us within rate limits.
Keeping tombstones longer

Within 5 minutes of deploying the reconciliation logic, 244 completed Jobs were cleaned up and the number of long-waiting Jobs dropped from 30 to 4. Later that afternoon, though, queued events kept arriving 70 to 112 minutes late, causing about 30 Jobs to trigger the alert for roughly 10 minutes before they became eligible for reconcile. We raised the --tombstone-ttl default from 1 hour to 3 hours, leaving reconcile to clean up miscounts caused by events arriving more than 3 hours late.

Runner sizing and bottlenecks

#1 Right-sizing Runners

Collector linked Job names to Runner Pod resource usage so we could see how much CPU and memory each Job actually used. Comparing that usage with the Runner’s configured resource requests helps us determine whether the Runner is right-sized for the Job.

An unnecessarily large Runner wastes resources and can delay Pod scheduling while the cluster secures them. To help teams choose an appropriate sized runner, we use this data in a dashboard that recommends a Runner for each Job.

#2 ARC controller bottleneck

In another incident, the wait-time alert fired as Jobs waiting for Runners accumulated, and we could see the queue growing on the Webhook Queue dashboard.

We first checked for a GitHub outage, but nothing had been announced, and the call that fetches the Runner registration config (JIT config) had a normal median latency of 0.57 seconds. The problem turned up in ARC instead. The work queue (workqueue_depth) of the EphemeralRunner controller, which creates and cleans up Runners, had risen far above its usual level.

The number of workers processing that queue (controller_runtime_active_workers) had been stuck at 2 for 6 hours, the default value of runnerMaxConcurrentReconciles as of 0.12.x. Meanwhile, p99 processing time had risen from 0.9 seconds to 8–10 seconds. The controller couldn't process its work fast enough with only two workers and slower GitHub calls.

Work to create new Runners sat in the controller queue and slowed Pod creation. In one Runner Scale Set, 258 Runners were waiting to be created while only about 150 Pods existed. Cleanup was delayed too. As a result, 95 already-terminated Pods and 55 Runners being deleted continued to count against maxRunners.

We raised runnerMaxConcurrentReconciles from 2 to 5 to give the controller more throughput. Within about 10 minutes, the controller queue fell from 669 to 233, waiting Jobs went from 380 to 168, and Runners waiting in the Runner Scale Set dropped from 224 to 61. Although p99 processing time was still high at 11 seconds, increasing concurrency reduced the backlog. Comparing Webhook's Job wait-time metrics with ARC's controller metrics had helped us identify controller throughput as the bottleneck.

Conclusion

Even though we operate ARC ourselves, running GitHub Actions inevitably depends on GitHub. We originally collected these metrics to keep developers informed during outages, but once Job states were visible, we found other uses for them too. They now help us size Runners appropriately and track down the sources of delays and bottlenecks.

I hope our experience helps you better understand what’s happening with your Jobs and Runners when using GitHub Actions with the ARC. Thanks for reading.

Closing the GitHub Actions Monitoring Gap: Observing ARC Runners with an Exporter was originally published in 당근 기술 블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: De-identifying text at scale: How Airbnb protects personal data in AI training
event_model_payload.summary:
Here’s how Airbnb detects and replaces personal data in messages, reviews, and support chats before it reaches a model.

By: Emelin Flores, Alex Klimov, Lee Formyduval, Bahador Nooraei

Introduction

Airbnb is built on trust. Every night that a guest books a stay, or a host welcomes someone into their home, that trust is backed by information they’ve shared with us, which includes personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, home location, current location, and payment details.

We now use transaction information to train machine learning models. Before we do so, we remove PII to minimize the number of copies of this information and prevent leakage into and through our models.

As we’ve written before, Airbnb maintains a shared taxonomy as to what constitutes PII, from commonly used fields such as names and card numbers to less frequently used fields such as precise location coordinates. We use de-identification to remove PII and replace it with simulated data that’s as realistic as possible to maximize its usefulness for ML model training.

Decisions relating to user privacy start as policy. These policies are set and maintained by Airbnb’s Privacy Architecture team, with engagement from Legal, Policy, and Engineering. Engineering then implements policy decisions as code.

This post focuses on text de-identification. We’ll describe the OSS library we chose to start with, the changes we made to create a functional system for Airbnb, and how we confirm that the system is working.

1. Choosing Presidio as the foundation

Many organizations are concerned with protecting PII, so there’s a lot of existing best practice and tested code out there that we can use. We chose Presidio, an open-source library originally developed by Microsoft and recently transitioned to community governance.

We needed to meet demanding requirements:

  • On-premises hosting, to keep data on our infrastructure
  • General-purpose functionality and high degree of modularity, for maximum extensibility
  • Multilingual support, for our global user base
  • PII detection and obfuscation separate, but within a single framework, for manageability and consistency
  • Support for redaction, masking, and realistic replacement
  • Consistent fake values within a run (ie, the same name repeatedly produces the same fake result)

Presidio meets these requirements well, especially regarding modularity. Functional elements such as PII recognizers, natural language processing (NLP) engines, and operators are all pluggable. We bypassed alternatives such as managed cloud services, since hosting is not on-premises, and standalone recognizers, known as named entity recognition (NER) models, since they only address part of the problem we needed to solve.

1.1 Deployment and distribution

Presidio ships as a Python package, and each consumer imports it in-process rather than calling a service we operate. Raw personal data is de-identified inside the calling process, so no separate service holds it and the data flow stays simple. It also removes a central bottleneck, since jobs run independently wherever compute is available. The decision is reversible: the same library wraps into a service if the need arises.

The tradeoff is distribution. The library only protects data if every pipeline calls it, on the current version, with a compliant configuration. Models at Airbnb train through a shared machine learning (ML) workflow orchestrator, so the library ships as a reusable pipeline step. A team supplies only its data schema, marking which columns carry personal data; we own the recognizers, operators, language handling, and runtime environment. The resulting dataset is tagged as de-identified, and that tag follows the data into the model registry, where it is designed to gate deployment to production. Each run records the library version and configuration used, so registered models can be traced back to the datasets that produced them.

2. How it works

Presidio runs text through two stages. The Analyzer finds spans that look like personal data, then labels each span with an entity type and a confidence score; the Anonymizer decides what replaces each span. Everything we build sits inside the Analyzer or the Anonymizer.

2.1 The Analyzer

The Analyzer is a collection of recognizers for personal data, each responsible for one entity type, such as a name or a phone number. Recognizers differ in how they decide that a span of text is an entity of interest to this capability, and we use three kinds.

For a pattern-based recognizer, detection quality depends on both a regex and a context-word list. For an NER-based one, it depends on the model behind it, so the model choices discussed later affect only some of our recognizers.

Recognizers run independently, so two different recognizers can claim text strings that overlap, or in which one is nested within another. A LISTING_ID matched inside an EMAIL_ADDRESS is one common case. Overlaps pass through the Analyzer untouched and are resolved in the Anonymizer as a configurable step before any operator runs.

Language detection is a prerequisite. Recognizers and models are language-specific, so it’s important that language detection be accurate. Names and addresses are short and carry few language cues, so we detect language on the whole record, or take it from the record’s locale metadata when it exists. If neither gives a confident answer, we use a more conservative configuration rather than taking the risk of using a model that might be for the wrong language.

Pattern-based recognizers. We support Presidio’s standard entity types alongside Airbnb-specific ones such as LISTING_ID and AIRBNB_GIFT_CARD, which no general-purpose model knows about. We defined Airbnb-specific recognizers as PatternRecognizers. For an identifier that’s just a run of digits, shape alone can’t settle the match. A gift card number, a credit card number valid against the widely used Luhn algorithm, and a listing ID all look the same. Presidio’s context words supply the deciding signal, so “listing” appearing a few tokens before a number raises the LISTING_ID score above the other candidates.

But stock context matching is single-token, so “gift card” declared as context never fires, and “card” alone fires just as readily next to a credit card. We extended the enhancer with a phrase pass, an ordered contiguous multi-word match in the tokens before a candidate, scored above a single-word hit, so the recognizer whose specific phrase appears wins the span.

NER-based recognizers. Names and street addresses have no structural pattern, so detecting them depends on a model. Presidio’s default NLP engine is spaCy, which is fast, mature, cheap at scale, and requires no training from us. Its generic NER tags any location it sees, including cities, landmarks, and neighborhoods, while the detail that identifies a person is a street address with a house number. On our benchmark those broad tags never resolved to the full address span.

We replaced spaCy for PERSON and LOCATION with recognizers built on GLiNER, a zero-shot NER model that takes an entity description at inference time. That lets us ask specifically for a street address instead of any place name, and precision improved for both entity types.

We evaluate newer backends the same way, and GLiNER2 is wired into the harness as a candidate. We adopt one for a given recognizer only when the benchmark shows a gain.

Configurable detection. Score thresholds and entity scope are set per recognizer and per consumer, because different consumers want different answers from the same text. A pipeline feeding raw text into training wants a low threshold and accepts false positives. On already-reviewed data, a consumer can trade recall for fewer unnecessary redactions. Consumers can also limit detection to the entity types present in their data.

2.2 The Anonymizer

The Anonymizer operates on the Analyzer’s output, a set of detected entities whose overlaps are unresolved. Settling those is its first job, and how it settles them is configurable. For each surviving span it then applies an operator, a transformation that decides what replaces the original value.

Presidio’s default operators leave a document full of placeholder tokens or blank gaps, and both tell a downstream model far less than realistic-looking text does. Most of our work on the Anonymizer went into closing that gap.

Faker-based values. For most entity types we use the faker library to generate realistic fake values, so a real name becomes another plausible name rather than . This matters for downstream utility, since a model training on de-identified text should still see content that reads like the original. Placeholder tokens signal that something was removed, and that signal is itself a pattern a model might learn, resulting in mis-training.

Custom fakers. Two things push us off the stock library. The first is that some matches shouldn’t be faked at all. A listing’s own URL is structural, non-personal data that consumers need intact, and a generic URL faker can’t tell it apart from any other site.

The second is that the library’s assumptions don’t always hold. Some locales’ card-network tables are so narrow that faking a card number in the text’s own language fails, so we pin the card faking to a locale with full coverage. Keeping a real country and area code while faking the rest of a phone number needs a library that parses phone-number structure, not a locale-based generator. And where an identifier format has a reserved or never-issued range, the fakes are drawn from it, so they can’t collide with real values.

Keeping fake values consistent — and unlinkable. Two properties have to hold at once, and they pull against each other. Across separate runs, de-identifying the same input must produce different fake values, so the fakes themselves are designed not to become a fingerprint tying two de-identified outputs back to each other. Within a single run, the same real value must always map to the same fake, or the dataset stops being internally coherent — the same person mentioned twice in one record needs the same fake name both times.

A globally shared random state can’t give you both, so each fake is seeded from the real value plus a secret unique to the run. We don’t store a real-to-fake mapping.

Configurable de-identification. Which operator applies to which entity type is configurable per model and use case, mirroring the configurable detection in §2.1 above. A pipeline feeding text into model training wants the faker-based operators for anything that needs to be read naturally. A use case where a human is reviewing flagged output might prefer a mask, so the reviewer can still recognize what kind of value it was. The same engine also covers structured columns. Identifiers are hashed with a caller-supplied salt — a secret mixed into each value before hashing — so the same value maps to the same hash within a run, and the hash can’t be reproduced without the salt. Coordinates are truncated to a precision set by Privacy, keeping most of the geographic signal without pinpointing a location. Our 64-bit internal IDs, the numeric keys for listings, reservations, and similar records, go through format-preserving encryption, so that the output is another valid ID of the same width and range, so a de-identified table passes the same schema checks as the original.

3. Evaluating and iterating on de-identification quality

Everything above, the recognizer split, spaCy versus GLiNER and GLiNER2, the phrase-context layer, are design decisions, not proof. We hold those decisions to measurement along three dimensions, because optimizing for any one produces a system that fails in a specific, predictable way.

Recall is how much real personal data the system finds; a miss is a leak, not a rounding error. Precision is how much of what it flags is actually personal data; over-redaction turns legitimate text into noise a model can’t learn from. Throughput is detection speed at pipeline scale. When recall and precision have to be traded, we weigh recall, because our users’ privacy is our top priority.

An aggregate score is exactly where the failure that matters most goes to hide, so every metric is reported per entity type and per language, with the number of labeled instances behind it, and a table of which entity type claimed spans that belonged to another. One identifier swallowing another’s spans is a different fix from a recognizer that simply misses, and invisible in an aggregate.

The benchmark scores the overlap-resolved spans the library actually emits, not the Analyzer’s raw candidates — a phone-shaped ZIP code inside a correctly detected address never reaches the output, so it shouldn’t count against phone-number precision. Measuring the product rather than an intermediate keeps the numbers aligned with what downstream teams see.

Because the harness takes the NER backend as a parameter, spaCy, GLiNER, and GLiNER2 are scored on the same golden sets side by side; that comparison is why GLiNER owns PERSON and LOCATION today and GLiNER2 remains a candidate. A new language works the same way — the spaCy model, context phrases, and locale-aware fakers are the easy part; it ships when a labeled dataset in that language exists to score it against.

When a gap surfaces, it gets folded into the benchmark, so the datasets expand rather than standing as a fixed snapshot. And before any release, we run the full framework against the deployed version and the candidate side by side; a version ships only when no language or entity type that has worked in the past has regressed.

That comparison, run against a benchmark that keeps getting harder, is what “good enough” means here: not a number hit once, but a bar the next version has to clear again, every time.

What’s next / conclusion

When our community shares information with us, we use the least possible amount in our ML models. De-identification is how we keep our models useful; it isn’t a single control we turned on, but a library, a set of configurable defaults and a benchmark that keeps getting harder. It is built so a team training a model on text doesn’t have to make privacy decisions from scratch, and so that the decisions they inherit are ones we can point to evidence for.

Getting detection working was an important milestone, but there is still plenty of work to be done. There are always new languages we can add, and new LLM-based recognizers arise that we can include in the platform. So far, we are only shipping our work on text, but we have already started on de-identifying other media as well.

If this type of work interests you, check out some of our related positions!

Acknowledgments

Thanks to Airbnb’s Privacy and MLI teams for making de-identification a shared default; to Bill Meng and Iman Saleh for grounding the requirements in privacy regulation; to Shunbao Chen for driving adoption by ML practitioners; to Manman Fan for improving detection quality; to Varun Sagar and Joe Rutherford for keeping the work on track across teams; and to Jessica Simon and Zoya Sultana for their leadership and support.

event_model_payload.headline: Scheduling the removal of the kube-proxy IPVS backend
event_model_payload.summary:
The ipvs backend for kube-proxy was an experiment in providing a service proxy implementation with better performance than the iptables backend. While it succeeded in that goal, the kernel IPVS API has turned out to be a bad match for the Kubernetes Services API, and the ipvs backend was never able to implement all of the edge cases of Kubernetes Service functionality correctly.

In Kubernetes 1.29, the project introduced the nftables backend for kube-proxy, which became GA in 1.33. Part of the plan behind adding the nftables backend was the idea that it would eventually replace both the iptables and ipvs backends. Because the ipvs backend in particular is complex, not 100% feature complete, and architecturally quite different from the other two backends (and thus more work to maintain), Kubernetes SIG Network decided to officially deprecate it as of Kubernetes 1.35. Although it currently remains available in kube-proxy (with a warning about its deprecation), we (Kubernetes SIG Network) now plan to remove it in Kubernetes 1.40. All ipvs users should therefore be planning to migrate to either the nftables or iptables backends.

Why was the ipvs backend written?

The ipvs backend was originally designed to fix two different kinds of performance problems in the iptables backend:

  • First, iptables had problems with data plane latency (the speed at which clients could establish new connections to services), because kube-proxy would write a separate iptables rule to match each service IP, so every new connection would need to be matched against a long series of rules that was O(n) in the number of services in the cluster.

  • Second, it had an even larger problem with control plane latency (the speed at which kube-proxy could process changes to services and endpoints and update the data plane rules), because kube-proxy would rewrite the entire iptables ruleset every time any service or endpoint changed. While the list of rules itself was only O(n) in the total number of endpoints, the amount of time, RAM, and CPU that it took to process the updated ruleset grew faster than that. In very large clusters, kube-proxy would use 100% of one CPU all the time just to process iptables updates. (In fact, the control plane scaling problem was bad enough that for most users it was not even possible to grow the cluster to the size where the data plane scaling problem became noticeable.)

The ipvs backend solved both of these scaling problems. The data plane problem was solved mostly automatically, because the kernel IPVS subsystem uses hash tables rather than linear lookup. The control-plane problem was solved by not rewriting the entire ruleset on every update. (The kernel IPVS API doesn’t have a way of doing batch updates anyway, so this was essentially forced.)

Why is the ipvs backend now being deprecated?

Almost from the start, the ipvs backend also had problems.

The first version didn’t have 100% compatibility with the iptables backend, but it was assumed that this would be fixed over time. Unfortunately, the original authors moved on to other things outside the Kubernetes ecosystem (as inevitably sometimes happens in open source), and it took a while to find new people interested in maintaining the code.

Meanwhile, as people began using the ipvs backend in larger and larger clusters, its own scaling problems started to emerge. In particular, the lack of batch update operations in the IPVS API meant that while the ipvs backend was faster than iptables when making a few small changes, it was potentially slower when making a large number of changes at once. And because the IPVS API is fairly limited in what it can do, kube-proxy's ipvs backend needed to fall back to using iptables to implement various features of Kubernetes Services beyond basic "load balancing", making it run into some of the same scaling problems the iptables backend has. While the ipvs backend tried to mitigate this by using ipset for some of its rules, this again ran into the problem of not having a batch update API. Additionally, the fact that the ipvs backend uses iptables means that it has the same long-term support problem as the iptables backend: Red Hat's plan to remove the iptables API entirely from Red Hat Enterprise Linux means the ipvs kube-proxy backend will also no longer be available to Kubernetes users on RHEL.

What about IPVS schedulers?

Beyond performance, the other reason some users were excited about the ipvs backend was the ability to pick from among various IPVS "schedulers" for distributing traffic to endpoints, rather than relying on the simple random selection used by iptables (and nftables).

Unfortunately, the way IPVS is used by kube-proxy prevents it from being able to use most of the IPVS schedulers in a useful way. The problem is that kube-proxy is a distributed service that runs on all nodes in the cluster, but the kube-proxy processes on different nodes do not share their IPVS scheduler state, so each node picks endpoints without knowing what is happening with clients on any other node. Even the schedulers that are designed to work in a distributed way generally don't work better than random selection in the context of kube-proxy. For example, the mh scheduler uses Maglev Hashing to select endpoints, which theoretically allows for extremely efficient distributed load balancing. But that efficiency is only in the context of a specific sort of two-layer load-balancer design, and kube-proxy does not have the right architecture to be able to act as either of the two layers in that design.

Switching away from ipvs

Switching to nftables

If you are running Kubernetes 1.36 or later, and your nodes are running a Linux distribution with kernel 5.13 or later, and you use the ipvs proxy mode, then Kubernetes recommends switching to the nftables mode of kube-proxy. (Although the nftables backend is GA —and fully usable—as of Kubernetes 1.33, there have been some performance- and scaling-related fixes since then that that weren't backported to releases earlier than 1.36.)

The nftables backend is fully supported, feature-complete, and even has very slightly better performance than ipvs:

(Taller bars represent longer latency. The "p50" group is the average connection establishment latency. Note that even the largest numbers in this graph are quite tiny; the point is not to claim that nftables is (noticeably) faster than ipvs, just to show that, unlike iptables, it's not slower.)

Switching is as easy as changing the kube-proxy configuration and restarting kube-proxy. For example, in clusters deployed via kubeadm, change mode: ipvs to mode: nftables in the kube-proxy ConfigMap and then restart the kube-proxy pods, as described in the documentation on reconfiguring a kubeadm cluster. (If you are overriding other ipvs-specific kube-proxy configuration, you will also need to change those options to the corresponding nftables ones.)

Switching to iptables: "It's Not As Slow As You Think!"

If you can't switch to nftables, either because you are on an older version of Kubernetes, or because your cluster runs on an older Linux distribution that isn't new enough to support the nftables backend, you may be able to just switch to the iptables backend, which has improved greatly since the original creation of the ipvs backend in 2017:

  • The generated ruleset has been optimized to remove redundant and irrelevant rules (#57461, #60306, #96959, #108251), reducing data plane latency.

  • The code that generates the ruleset has been optimized to do fewer allocations, and to avoid unnecessarily recomputing the same information multiple times (#65755, #65902, #67948, #85617, #90103, #97238), reducing CPU and memory usage when resyncing.

  • Rather than doing “check the current state of the rules, then update them to the new state”, iptables kube-proxy now does “assume the current state is correct, update to the new state based on that assumption, and only explicitly check the current state if that update fails”. This greatly improves the resyncing speed, because it turns out that even reading the iptables ruleset is extremely slow in large clusters (#81517, #110334, #114181).

  • To the extent possible within the constraints of the iptables APIs, kube-proxy’s iptables backend now only updates iptables rules for services/endpoints that have changed since the last sync, rather than rewriting the entire ruleset every time (#110268 / KEP-3453).

The net result of this is that the iptables backend of 2026, while still not as good as the ipvs backend, is at least much better than the iptables backend of 2017 was, and many people who found iptables unusable in the past would not have problems with it now.

As with switching to nftables, switching to iptables is mostly just a matter of updating your kube-proxy configuration, although for technical reasons, in this case we recommend that you reboot each node after changing the kube-proxy configuration, rather than merely restarting kube-proxy.

Learn more

  • KEP-5495 gives the full timeline and plan for kube-proxy IPVS deprecation.

  • The blog post "NFTables mode for kube-proxy" has more information about nftables mode and its performance relative to ipvs and iptables.

event_model_payload.headline: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs
event_model_payload.summary:
A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out.

Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly.

To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. 

“When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.”

In this post, we’ll explore how full-text search speeds up log investigations. You can also learn more in the ObservabilityCON 2026 talk below.

Why labels alone only get you so far

Historically, Loki only indexed labels, then scanned every line in the selected streams. That is fast when the selector and the time range are already narrow. Searching a wide selector over a long window for one request ID means reading all of those lines. If you've run Loki at scale, you've probably reached for one of these techniques to avoid that scan:

  • Put the whole or partial ID in a label. This is an obvious fix, but it creates high cardinality. Request IDs and user IDs make so many unique streams that ingestion and query performance suffer and eventually hit configured limits. Loki's cardinality guidance warns against this for good reason.

  • Shrink the time range and guess. This works if you already know roughly when something happened. During an incident, or with a ticket that came in days later, you usually don't.

  • Send some logs to a separate full-text index. That means running a second system, paying to index every field, and making engineers switch tools mid-investigation.

Full-text search removes that tradeoff. The secondary index tells Loki which data can contain a literal string, so Loki reads only that data and skips the rest. That makes a big difference in how much data a query scans and how fast it returns.

And it does this without the overhead of a traditional inverted index. The Logline technology behind it adds approximately 10% to compute costs and 10% to storage at Grafana Cloud scale with the current capabilities. Much of that cost is offset by the query compute Loki saves by reading less data.

Loki also stays schemaless. You keep your labels and your ingestion pipelines, whether that's Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, or another supported client, and you keep writing LogQL. For supported queries, searches that used to time out can now return in seconds or less.

Find answers faster with full-text search 

Full-text search accelerates several LogQL patterns used for needle-in-a-haystack lookups:

  • Exact string matches, using |=.

  • Literal regex searches, using |~, including case-sensitive searches and case-insensitive searches with (?i).

  • Label filter expressions over structured metadata and label attributes, such as | transaction_id="12345".

  • Post-parser literal expressions over extracted attributes, such as | json | transaction_id="12345".

Some advanced regex constructions are not supported; see the full-text search documentation for details.

These patterns above support investigations ranging from following a transaction ID to tracking down an intermittent error. Here’s how faster lookups help engineers and AI agents follow those leads.

Trace one ID across weeks of logs

Most needle-in-a-haystack searches start from a single identifier: a customer ID from a support ticket, a failing transaction from a payment alert, or a trace ID copied from a slow span.

With full-text search, the line filter you already use is the fast path:

{service="payments"} |= "txn-123456"

Loki no longer has to read every chunk in the stream selector across the whole time range. The index sends it to the data that can contain txn-123456. You can search a wider time range with a broader stream selector and still get results fast enough to stay focused.

Anyone on the on-call rotation can paste an ID, set a long time range, and get an answer. You no longer need a Loki expert to make that query efficient.

Hunt down rare and intermittent errors

Some of the hardest incidents to investigate never show up on a dashboard. An error shows up a few times a day on a few hosts, and the only evidence is a specific string buried in the logs.

Full-text search speeds up literal and case-insensitive searches, so you can look across services for rare errors without knowing in advance where they'll appear:

{service="api"} |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You can also combine literals to narrow results while staying on the fast path:

{service="api"} |= "txn-123456" |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"

You find the first occurrence of an intermittent failure faster, which makes it easier to tie that failure to a deploy, a dependency, or a specific customer.

Speed up AI-driven investigations 

Fast lookups matter even more as AI agents take on more of the investigation work. AI-driven investigations often run many queries in a row: an agent checks a hypothesis, searches for an ID, follows it into another service, and searches again. 

Faster needle-in-a-haystack queries mean each of those steps returns sooner, so the investigation keeps moving.

Get started

If you use Grafana Cloud Logs, full-text search is available now at no additional cost. You don't need to change ingestion, redesign labels, or learn a new query language.

Try full-text search in your stack, or create a free Grafana Cloud account to get started today.  

To run your first search:

  1. Open Explore in your Grafana Cloud stack and choose your Grafana Cloud Logs data source.

  2. Pick a stream selector and add a line filter for a value you'd normally search for, such as a request ID, customer ID, or error string.

  3. Set a longer time range than you'd usually risk, such as the last few days or weeks, and run the query.

For supported query patterns and best practices, see the full-text search documentation.

Faster search is one way we’re helping teams get more value from their logs. At ObservabilityCON 2026, we also announced Adaptive Logs updates to give you more control over storage costs. To learn more, check out this on-demand talk from the event.

event_model_payload.headline: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience
event_model_payload.summary:
Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7.

We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. 

In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below.

Starting with why

“Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella Meadows

At Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible.

Meanwhile, over the last year, the product design team has worked with our engineers to build new interaction patterns to support AI solutions like Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace. Building these patterns opened the door to curiosity, and we started experimenting with new visual forms, colors, shapes, and effects that laid the groundwork for the refresh.

Through this work, our approach to UI style and aesthetics evolved, and so did our purpose: alongside supporting new workflows and use cases, we wanted to bring greater consistency to interactions and design patterns across Grafana. This refresh is the first step toward that goal.

Visual styling and usability

“The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its usefulness.” – Dieter Rams

So why invest in visual styling? To stay relevant? To facilitate sales conversations? Because it looks cool?

All of those reasons are valid, but at Grafana Labs, product designers are utilitarians first. We believe digital products should exist with a clear purpose and function in mind. We think each color, font style, and line should establish a clear information hierarchy and help users quickly understand what's on the page, ultimately making our product easier to use.

As more workflows shift to terminals and agentic chat interfaces, we believe investing in visual style now is foundational to Grafana’s future usability. When fewer user journeys rely on a traditional UI, those that do must emphasize clarity and consistency.

What’s new: a closer look 

This first phase of the refresh focuses on making the Grafana UI clearer and more consistent across workflows and components, while giving you time to adapt to the changes. Here are some of the highlights:

  • New default light and dark themes: These themes use completely new color palettes with improved accessibility compliance by design.

  • Increased consistency across components: We have started to reduce the amount of available UI components and their variants. This means users only need to learn an interaction or a pattern once, and can then leverage it across the entire platform.

  • New font styles, borders, and shadows: By overhauling our visual primitives to work in a proportional and scalable way, we create layers of hierarchy and visual information. As part of our audits, we noticed that many areas of the UI competed for users’ attention. We’re moving to a state where you can immediately understand what’s most important on a page, so you can complete tasks faster and more efficiently. You’ll notice these changes across the building blocks of Grafana, including cards, panels, and drawers.

We’re rolling out the visual refresh gradually so Grafana contributors and users have time to adapt without disrupting critical workflows. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Existing navigation stays the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. 

To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous styling at any time.

For a full list of changes in the public preview, please visit our documentation.

Curiosity, monitoring, and feedback

"There are three key practices needed in order to build and maintain a circle of competence: curiosity and a desire to learn, monitoring, and feedback." – Shane Parrish & Rhiannon Beaubien

Curiosity is a key attribute of product designers at Grafana Labs and we knew that unifying the look and feel across Grafana meant making choices that could elicit strong reactions. This is why learning, gathering feedback, and monitoring the response have been central to our process.

We could have spent a year working on what we think is a perfect new visual styling, running hundreds of internal iterations, but instead we started with early internal dogfooding of the refreshed UI. This led to honest discussions and opinions from Grafanistas across the company, helping us iterate the visual refresh rapidly into a version we could not have achieved without working openly. 

Now, with the refresh in public preview, your feedback is central to how we’ll continue to refine our visual styling. Through our community Slack and a temporary in-app survey, you can tell us directly what’s working, what needs improvement, and what we might have missed. We monitor and discuss this feedback in the open, helping to amplify your voice and share it across the organization. Your responses will be integral to shaping future iterations of the refresh.

We can’t wait to hear what you think, and to continue our evolution toward a bolder visual experience for all Grafana users.
