event_model_payload.headline: Any agent anywhere: How to use Grafana Cloud with Claude, Cursor, and any other AI agent
event_model_payload.summary:
AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks. But to be truly useful in production, these agents need access to more than code. They also need observability data and context to understand what's happening across your systems, investigate problems, and help you take action.

At Grafana Labs, we believe that context should be available wherever you work. That’s one of the core ideas behind Grafana Cloud as the open agentic observability platform: the flexibility to work with your observability data through the AI agents you prefer—whether it’s Grafana Assistant, a coding agent in your IDE, or a tool you’ve built yourself—so you can investigate and troubleshoot issues without switching tools.

In this post, we'll explore how to bring Grafana Cloud into your agentic workflows using tools like the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx, with practical examples along the way. You can also check out our ObservabilityCON 2026 talk in the video below to learn more.

Three ways to use Grafana Cloud with AI agents

There are multiple ways to bring Grafana Cloud observability data and context into your AI workflows, depending on where and how you prefer to work:

  • Work directly in Grafana Cloud: Use Grafana Assistant, the AI-powered assistant built into Grafana Cloud, to investigate issues and interact with your observability data.

  • Connect your preferred AI agent: Use the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring Grafana Cloud data into compatible tools such as Claude, ChatGPT, and Codex.

  • Work with coding agents and scripts: Use gcx, the Grafana Cloud command-line tool, to give coding agents access to observability data directly from their working environment.

Whether you're working directly in Grafana Cloud with Grafana Assistant or using your own AI agents, you can choose the approach that works best for you. Let's look at how the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx make that possible outside of Grafana Cloud.

Investigate an alert from your phone with Claude and Grafana Cloud MCP server

Imagine you're waiting in line at a coffee shop when a Slack message arrives from your director of engineering. Something is wrong with the frontend, and they need your help.

Your laptop is still in your backpack, but you don't necessarily need it to start investigating. With Claude connected to the Grafana Cloud MCP server, you can pull out your phone and ask a simple question: "Why is the frontend slow? Is there anything firing?"

Claude can use Grafana Cloud data to answer your question directly in the conversation. In this example, it confirms that an alert is firing, shows a chart of the relevant signal, and identifies which pages are affected.

You can then ask a follow-up question: how is this affecting the health of the frontend, and what's causing the problem? Again, Claude can return a visual Grafana Cloud view directly in the conversation, giving you more context about the health of your frontend application and helping you determine where to investigate next.

All of this happens without leaving the conversation or opening your laptop. By the time you get your coffee, you've already confirmed the issue and started exploring its impact.

How it works: The Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP Apps

This experience is powered by two capabilities: the Grafana Cloud MCP server and MCP Apps.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources. The Grafana Cloud MCP server makes your Grafana Cloud observability data available to compatible agents, allowing them to query alerts, dashboards, and telemetry to help answer questions and investigate issues.

That means you can interact with Grafana Cloud data from the AI tools you already use, rather than rely exclusively on the assistant built into your observability platform.

MCP Apps take this a step further by bringing interactive Grafana Cloud views directly into your AI conversations. Instead of returning only a text description of an issue, an agent can display relevant visualizations, such as firing alerts and frontend health, alongside the conversation.

These views are delivered by the Grafana Cloud MCP server and can appear in MCP clients that support them.

To learn more, see the Grafana Cloud MCP server documentation. 

Continue your investigation in Cursor with Grafana Cloud context and gcx

Now imagine you've grabbed your coffee and opened your laptop. You want to take a closer look at the frontend performance issue and get some help from your coding agent.

You navigate to Grafana Cloud Frontend Observability, where a dashboard shows elevated time to first byte (TTFB), one of the symptoms of the slowdown.

You could manually copy the relevant queries, filters, and time range into your coding agent and explain what you're looking at. But Grafana Cloud provides a simpler way to hand off that context.

From a panel on the dashboard, you can click a button that automatically gathers the relevant information, including the query, filters, and time range. Then you select your agent of choice—Cursor, in this example—and send the context directly to it.

Now Cursor has the same starting context you were using in Grafana Cloud. Instead of explaining the issue from scratch, you can immediately ask it to compare the affected pods with healthy ones. Cursor uses gcx to query Grafana Cloud and begin investigating the differences.

This lets you continue investigating in the environment where you're already working, with the relevant observability context carried over from Grafana Cloud.

How it works: Give coding agents access to Grafana Cloud with gcx

gcx is the Grafana Cloud command-line tool. It provides a way for developers and coding agents to interact with Grafana Cloud directly from a terminal. Because coding agents can execute shell commands, they can also use gcx to access observability data as part of their investigations.

gcx includes curated agent skills that help coding agents understand how to use Grafana Cloud data for common tasks, without requiring step-by-step instructions. Agents can also discover available commands and use them to explore different parts of a system, including services, databases, and frontend sessions.

For example, gcx provides commands to:

  • Explore application services: Inspect services and their operations to understand application behavior.

  • Investigate databases: List and inspect database instances as part of a performance investigation.

  • Examine frontend activity: Access frontend application information and sessions to understand the end-user experience.

Here's an example of available commands, with arguments omitted:

gcx
├─ appo11y
│  ├─ services get
│  └─ services list-operations
├─ dbo11y
│  ├─ instances list
│  └─ instances get
└─ frontend
   ├─ apps list
   └─ sessions get

In our example, gcx gives Cursor a way to look beyond the original alert and query additional observability data to guide its investigation. And because gcx works from the command line, this approach isn't limited to Cursor. Other coding agents that can execute shell commands can use it too, making it possible to incorporate Grafana Cloud data into existing development and automation workflows.

To learn more and get started, visit the gcx repository on GitHub.

Bring it all together: Investigate issues in Slack with an open source agent

What if you'd rather investigate an issue without leaving Slack? You can also connect an open source agent like Hermes to Grafana Cloud using both gcx and the Grafana Cloud MCP server.

For example, imagine your team reports a drop in completed bank transfers, even though traffic looks normal. You can ask Hermes directly in Slack to investigate the issue, providing the affected application, time window, and relevant context.

Hermes can then use gcx commands and MCP tools to investigate the underlying requests, examine user sessions, and compare the results with an earlier time window. From there, it can report its findings back in the Slack thread, with supporting Grafana Cloud links, potential causes, and recommended next steps.

Wrapping up

With Grafana Cloud, you choose the agent, the model, the provider, and where you work. Grafana Cloud then gives your agent access to the observability context and tools it needs to help investigate issues, identify root causes, and take action.

Ready to try it yourself? Here are three ways to get started:

  1. Start with Grafana Assistant to investigate and troubleshoot directly in Grafana Cloud.

  2. Connect your preferred agent through the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring observability data into compatible AI tools.

  3. Explore gcx to bring Grafana Cloud into your coding agents, scripts, and terminal-based workflows.

event_model_payload.headline: Building an Agentic Warehouse Management System—Part 3: Tools, Decisions, and Actions
event_model_payload.summary:
If you haven’t read the first two parts yet, I recommend starting with Part 1: Where AI Agents Add Value and Part 2: Designing and Planning the Agent. There, we introduced the WMS scenario, discussed where an AI agent can add value, and built the first stages of the implementation with Java and Spring AI.

In this third and final part, we will build on the execution plan created in Part 2 and focus on the remaining stages of the agent workflow. We will see how each task is executed using controlled tools, how operational and business context is gathered, how the replenishment decision is made, and how the agent acts on that decision when necessary.

From plan to execution

Let’s revisit the complete agent flow. The first stages: Define the Agent, Trigger the Agent, and Plan, were covered in the previous article. Now we will focus on executing the tasks, using the available tools, gathering context, and making the replenishment decision.

Figure 1. Agent Lifecycle: Execute, Decide, and Complete.

Execute tasks with controlled tools

With the execution plan created in Part 2, the AgentRunner starts processing the tasks one at a time. For each task, the runner reads its description and capability, executes it, stores the result, and then continues with the next task:

Before executing a task, the runner selects only the tools associated with its capability:

When the task is executed, the executor receives the current goal, the results produced by previous tasks, the current task, and only the tools available for its capability:

The result of each completed task becomes part of the context available to the tasks that follow. This allows the agent to progressively gather the information it needs before making the replenishment decision.

At the same time, the capability assigned to each task defines which tools are available during its execution. This preserves the boundaries we established earlier: an ANALYSIS task, for example, can inspect information from the WMS, but it does not have access to tools that create a replenishment request.

Figure 2. Agent running.

Accessing operational data

During ANALYSIS tasks, the agent can use controlled tools to retrieve operational data from the WMS, such as inventory, invoice movements, stock movements, and pending replenishments.

For example, one of the available tools retrieves the stock movements generated by an outbound invoice:

With Spring AI, methods like this can be exposed to the model using annotations such as @Tool and @ToolParam. The executor can then call them when the current task requires that information.

The complete application exposes additional tools for retrieving inventory, invoice movements, pending replenishments, and other operational data. We will not cover each one here, but they follow the same idea.

Retrieving depositor policies

The depositor policies are also accessed through a dedicated tool exposed by the POLICY capability. In our application, each depositor can register business rules through the Depositor Policies page. For example, a policy may define a seven-day lead time or require at least 500 units per replenishment request:

Figure 3. Depositor policies screen.

These policies are stored as natural-language documents, which allows us to retrieve them using semantic search instead of relying solely on exact keywords. For example:

When a policy is stored, its text is converted into an embedding using the configured Voyage AI embedding model and added to the vector store. During a POLICY task, the agent can ask a question based on the context collected so far:

This gives us a simple Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) flow: the question is used to retrieve the most relevant policies, which are then added to the execution:

Figure 4. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline for policy lookup.

The retrieval uses semantic search:

and is filtered by depositor and knowledge type:

Together with the results from the ANALYSIS tasks, these policies give the agent the operational and business context required to decide whether replenishment is needed.

Decide

After the ANALYSIS and POLICY tasks are completed, the DECISION task uses the collected context to determine whether replenishment is required. The result ends with one of two tokens:

This gives the AgentRunner a simple way to determine whether the remaining tasks should continue:

If replenishment is not required, the remaining REPLENISHMENT and NOTIFICATION tasks are marked as SKIPPED, and the execution is completed:

Figure 5. Agent skipped task.

The runner marks those tasks as SKIPPED and completes the execution:

If replenishment is required, the execution continues with the next tasks in the plan.

Act

Once replenishment is required, the agent can use the action tools exposed by the application.

The REPLENISHMENT task can create a replenishment request:

Again: The tool does not replace the existing WMS logic. It gives the agent a controlled way to request the operation, while validation and persistence remain inside the application services.

Once created, the replenishment ID can be used by the NOTIFICATION task to prepare the depositor email draft:

At this point, the agent has made the decision and performed the actions required by it.

Complete

When there are no more tasks to execute, the agent run is completed, and a summary is generated:

Figure 6. Agent finished process.

If a replenishment request was created, it is now available on the Replenishments page for review:

Figure 7. Replenishments review dashboard.

This completes the flow: the agent gathers context through controlled tools, decides whether replenishment is necessary, and acts only when required.

Next steps

During a single execution, the agent uses the results of previous tasks as context for the tasks that follow. A natural next step would be to give the agent memory across different executions.

For example, before creating a new replenishment request, the agent could look at previous AgentRun records and use relevant outcomes from similar situations:

The last three requests for 500 units of this product were rejected. Approved requests were usually between 200 and 300 units. Based on the current consumption, I will request 250 units.

This would allow the agent to use not only the context of the current execution, but also relevant information from previous ones. One possible evolution would be to retrieve similar past executions and add them to the agent context before making a new decision.

There are many other directions in which this agent could evolve, but this is a good example of how the same design can gradually become more context-aware over time.

Conclusion

The main goal of this series was to show how an AI agent can add value in scenarios where business decisions depend on multiple sources of context and increasingly complex rules. Our replenishment example is only a small glimpse of what this approach can support in a real Warehouse Management System.

In Part 1, we explored where an AI agent can add value in a WMS. In Part 2, we translated that design into Java and Spring AI by defining the agent, its capabilities, and its execution plan.

In this third and final part, we completed the flow: tasks were executed through controlled tools, operational data and depositor policies were added to the context, and the agent used that information to decide whether replenishment was required and act when necessary.

The main idea remains the same: the application defines what the agent is allowed to do, while the agent decides what to do within those boundaries.

Explore our MongoDB JVM Showcase repository for more Java examples and use cases. If you find it useful, consider giving it a ⭐.

event_model_payload.headline: Why Actionable Banking Is the Critical Stepping Stone to Full Autonomy
event_model_payload.summary:
Almost nothing is as important to someone today as their financial health. Most of us want to stay on top of what's happening with our bank accounts, like when a deposit clears so we can pay bills, if we're reaching our credit card limit, or if we have finally paid off that 30-year mortgage and can free up funds for that dream vacation or paying for our kid's college tuition. But we don't always get immediate feedback when transactions happen. That information often sits on the backend within our banks, and then days or weeks later we may get an email or alert with advice on investing or creating a payment plan.

But with actionable banking, this all becomes immediate. With the help of agentic AI, banks’ customers can quickly have a better understanding of steps they can take to make an investment or curb their spending with AI-powered insights. And people have said they want this.

In fact, in a survey conducted by Personetics of 2,000 bank customers(1), 70% said they strongly want their bank to proactively analyze their financial situation and 84% said they would likely switch to a bank that offers timely, relevant advice.

Actionable banking is also the safest first step toward autonomous banking. The agents act on events, but a human still makes the decision. MongoDB Atlas makes this possible by turning banking events into real-time triggers, unifying customer context in one platform, and keeping an auditable record of every agent action.

A three-step ladder: From passive to autonomous banking

Actionable banking serves as the bridge between legacy banking and fully autonomous finance:

Figure 1. The three-step ladder from passive to autonomous banking.

  • Passive banking: The customer initiates the interaction, most likely in response to a marketing campaign.
  • Actionable banking: The bank takes a proactive approach based on real-time event analysis. Agents act on events, but the customer still makes the decision.
  • Autonomous banking: A personal finance agent acts on its own, within limits the customer has set in advance and can revoke at any time.

The gap between actionable and autonomous is not the model. It is evidence: A bank can only grant agents a mandate once it can show what each agent saw, decided, and did, and who authorized it. Actionable banking is how that evidence gets logged into the corresponding audit trail.

Actionable banking also imposes a behavioral change. A dedicated agent will be continuously monitoring personal banking information, so its success will depend heavily on the guardrails implemented by the bank, in line with the customer's consent. More importantly, it should comply with data protection and AI regulations. Policymakers are moving fast to propose frameworks that incentivize innovation with the right controls in place. In the end, actionable banking's goal is to recommend the "best course of action" based on specific triggered events, but the customer is the one who decides and has the final word, which safeguards trust.

Below are three actionable agentic workflows and a reference architecture built on MongoDB Atlas and Atlas Agent Engine.

Three banking events, three agentic workflows

Every workflow starts with the Personal Finance Agent, which listens to daily banking activity through event-driven notifications. When a significant event arrives—a large deposit, an overdue card balance, a new mortgage—the agent opens an agentic workflow, hands the work to specialist agents, and returns a proposal the customer can discuss.

Figure 2. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive investments.

Proactive investment. A large deposit is the clearest signal of idle money. McKinsey estimates(2) that $23 trillion of the $170 trillion in consumer deposits worldwide sits in accounts paying zero or close to zero interest. The risk profile is not a formality; the EU requires the MiFID II suitability assessment before investment advice. So a risk assessment agent's output must be stored as evidence, not just passed along in a prompt. While the personal finance agent is responsible for the interaction and agreement with the customer, the wealth advisory agent is specialized in private banking, bringing the right proposal to the customer.

Figure 3. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive lending.

Proactive lending. An overdue card balance is both a credit risk and a moment of customer stress. Moving the balance to a cheaper installment loan costs the bank card margin, but keeps the customer and lowers its credit risk. Creditworthiness assessment of individuals is a high-risk use under the EU AI Act, so this workflow needs the strictest human oversight of the three. A credit risk officer needs to review, approve, and have all the arguments at hand for situations where customers and regulators would demand an explanation. A single agent with lending expertise can handle both risk assessment and advisory.

Figure 4. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive added-value services.

Proactive added-value services. A new mortgage changes the terms of what the customer needs to protect. The insurance agent reads the mortgage conditions and proposes an insurance policy with the proper coverage, as an optional offer and never as a condition of the loan.

Each workflow ends in "push and discuss," not "execute." That is what makes it actionable rather than autonomous.

Actionable banking reference architecture on MongoDB

Figure 5. Actionable banking reference architecture.

Systems of record write into MongoDB Atlas, which holds the operational view of each customer. Change streams turn business moments into events for the personal finance agent. Specialist agents run on Atlas Agent Engine, sharing customer context through a common memory layer with per-agent access controls. Every agent action and tool call is recorded in a single, immutable audit trail. The customer's decision flows back as memory for the next interaction and as evidence for the regulator.

The business case for actionable banking

McKinsey(3) estimates that banks that fail to adapt to agentic AI could see global profit pools fall by about $170 billion, or roughly 9%, as customers' own agents start moving idle money. Actionable banking is both the defense and the offense: The bank's agent makes the better offer before someone else's agent does.

Why banking agent projects stall and what the platform must fix

Banks are not short of agent pilots; they are short of agents in production. Gartner(4) expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 over cost, unclear value, or weak risk controls. Actionable banking runs into three engineering problems behind those numbers.

Atlas Agent Engine(5), in public preview since September of 2026, unifies runtime, memory, and governance in one layer, with sandboxed execution and agent identity built in. It is neutral across models and frameworks and built on open standards such as MCP and A2A, so a personal finance agent can delegate to specialist agents without tying the bank to one vendor's model or cloud. Paysafe is already exploring an agent engine-based agent so its analysts stop stitching together data from multiple systems by hand when investigating unusual payment activity.

A change in behavior, not only in technology

Actionable banking is largely an engineering pattern. Autonomous banking also requires a shift in trust and behavior. Customers must delegate, banks must accept accountability for agents that act, and regulators must be satisfied that both are safe.

The relationship manager becomes an agent. The attention of a private banker, someone who notices the bonus, the new mortgage, and the missed payment, has always been rationed by cost. A personal agent makes it available to every customer, around the clock, with memory of every conversation. Banks that get this right keep the relationship with the customer. Those that don’t may end up as the infrastructure for another party’s agent.

Trust is the ultimate mandate. The most critical challenge is not technical. Delegating decision-making authority to an agent—and granting it permission to act on behalf of an organization or an individual—turns machines into active economic participants. That is a disruptive behavioral change for customers, regulators, and banks alike. Banks have always sold trust; in autonomous banking, they must also prove it, action by action and mandate by mandate.

Start simply with one event, one workflow, or one governed proposal. That is the first step toward autonomous banking, and the data platform underneath decides how far you can take it.

Sources:

  • (1)New Research Shows Surging Consumer Demand for AI-Banking Services, According to Personetics Global Survey
  • (2)Customer use of AI agents will depress profits: McKinsey | American Banker
  • (3)Bank profits face $170bn hit from AI - McKinsey
  • (4)Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027
  • (5)MongoDB Launches Atlas Agent Engine to Put AI Agents in Production Without a New Stack

event_model_payload.headline: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
event_model_payload.summary:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Build with Workflow SDK 5

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK:

Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK, now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks.

event_model_payload.headline: orderCreate line items support custom IDs
event_model_payload.summary:
The variantIdentifier field on orderCreate line items is now available in GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 and later. Previously, it was only available in the unstable version. You can use it to identify a product variant by its ID or by a custom ID, such as a listing ID from another system that you store in a metafield. This is an additive change to the 2027-01 release candidate, so no action is required.

What changed

In version 2027-01, OrderCreateLineItemInput includes the variantIdentifier field. Provide exactly one of the following:

  • id: the global ID of the product variant.
  • customId: the namespace, key and value of an id metafield on the product variant. If you omit namespace, your app-reserved namespace is used.

Use variantIdentifier instead of variantId and productId. If a line item sets variantIdentifier together with either of those fields, then orderCreate returns a user error with the INVALID code.

To look up variants by custom ID, the store needs a metafield definition of type id for product variants, and your app must be able to read it. If the definition doesn't exist, then orderCreate returns an INVALID user error saying that the definition is required.

If no variant in the store matches an identifier, then orderCreate returns a user error with the VARIANT_IDENTIFIER_NOT_FOUND code for that line item, and doesn't create the order. Line items that use variantId work as before.

Who's affected

The change applies to apps that create orders with orderCreate. It's most useful for sales channels and integrations that identify products by an ID from an external system.

  • API version 2027-01 and later include variantIdentifier.
  • API version 2026-10 and earlier don't include it.
  • Apps that already use variantIdentifier on unstable can move to 2027-01 without changing their requests.

variantIdentifier needs no access scopes beyond those that orderCreate already requires. Custom ID lookups only find metafields that your app can read.

What to do

No action is required. To start using custom IDs on order line items:

  1. Check that the store has a metafield definition of type id for product variants, and that each variant stores its external ID in that metafield.
  2. Update your app to API version 2027-01.
  3. Pass variantIdentifier on each line item that you identify by custom ID:
mutation {
  orderCreate(order: {
    lineItems: [{
      variantIdentifier: {
        customId: { namespace: "custom", key: "listing_id", value: "LST-10045" }
      }
      quantity: 1
    }]
  }) {
    order { id lineItems(first: 1) { nodes { variant { id } } } }
    userErrors { field message code }
  }
}

This example creates an order for the variant whose custom.listing_id metafield is LST-10045. Replace the namespace, key and value with your own metafield definition and external ID, and add the other order fields that your app normally sends.

  1. Test in a development store. Create an order with a known custom ID and check that the line item refers to the expected variant. Then send an unknown value and check that userErrors returns VARIANT_IDENTIFIER_NOT_FOUND.

Why this matters

Until now, an app that knew a variant only by an external ID had two options. It could keep its own mapping from external IDs to Shopify variant IDs, or it could look up each variant with productVariantByIdentifier before calling orderCreate. Now you can pass the external ID in the same request that creates the order.

Related docs

  • Working with custom IDs
  • orderCreate mutation
  • OrderCreateLineItemInput reference

event_model_payload.headline: IP allowlists are now required for public apps
event_model_payload.summary:
We're enhancing protection of merchants by adding IP allowlist configuration as a requirement for public apps. All public apps using bulk operations must configure an allowlist by November 12, 2026, and all other public apps must configure an allowlist by November 20, 2026.

If an app is not migrated by these dates:

  • November 12, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET.: Bulk operations from public apps without an IP allowlist will fail to execute.
  • November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET: Public apps without an IP allowlist will be delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs.

What apps are affected

All public apps.

What apps are unaffected

  • Custom apps
  • Apps created by merchants either in the Dev Dashboard or in the admin

Why we're making this change

Leaked tokens can be used from any network location. IP allowlists reduce the impact of a credential leak by limiting the networks from which your app can invoke the Admin API.

What to do

Configure your app's allowed IPs in the Dev Dashboard:

  • If your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses, configure your IP allowlist based on static IPs or CIDR range.
  • If your app's egress IP addresses are dynamic, allow your hosting provider's ASNs and list the countries your app runs in.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

What if my app makes Admin API calls from merchant infrastructure?

You should move as quickly as possible to an architecture that better limits exposure of Admin API tokens. You may submit a request for an extension to the deadlines above.

event_model_payload.headline: What’s new with Grafana variables: less clutter, easier reuse across dashboards, and more
event_model_payload.summary:
Template variables are one of the most used features in Grafana, providing users with a dropdown to turn one dashboard into hundreds: pick a different cluster, region, or service, and every panel updates.

For most of Grafana's history, variables had a single home at the top of the dashboard. Each dashboard had one flat list of variables, and that list was shared by every panel on it. But as dashboards grew in size and number, those controls became harder to organize and maintain. The top of a dashboard could get crowded with dropdowns that only applied to certain panels, while shared controls were copied across dashboards and had to be updated individually.

To address these challenges, we’ve rolled out two new features in Grafana: 

  • Section-level variables for rows and tabs (generally available): these variables let you place controls near the panels they affect, reducing clutter at the top of the dashboard. 

  • Cross-dashboard variables (public preview): these are variables you can define once and reuse across dashboards, keeping configurations consistent and easier to maintain.

In this post, we’ll take a closer look at each variable type, its use cases, and how to get started. 

Section-level variables: define and manage variables by row or tab

Section-level variables let you define variables and filters for a specific row or tab, so they apply only to the panels inside that section. Placing a control next to the panels it affects makes it clear what a selection will change, and it keeps the top of the dashboard uncluttered.

Let’s say you want two $instance dropdowns, one for your API gateway panels and one for your database panels. Traditionally, with one flat namespace, you’d end up with names like $api_instance and $db_instance, or you’d split the dashboard into two.

Now, with section-level variables, the API gateway section and the database section can each have its own $instance variable with its own query and selected value. Both sections still share the dashboard time range, and nothing else on the dashboard changes.

Here’s how section-level variables work:

  • Resolution goes from nearest to farthest. When a panel uses a variable, Grafana first checks the section the panel is in for a matching variable, then any parent sections (rows and tabs can nest), then the dashboard. 

  • Filters work, too. You can add Filter and Group by controls at the section level, so a section can filter by its own labels.

  • The query editor knows about scope. Autocomplete only suggests variables the panel you're editing can actually see.

  • Restructuring is safe. If you ungroup a row or tab, its section variables move up a level instead of disappearing.

To add a section-level variable, edit the dashboard, select a row or tab, and open Variables in the options pane. 

Cross-dashboard variables: define and manage variables across multiple dashboards 

Section variables solved scope inside a dashboard. The bigger request has always been scope across dashboards.

Cross-dashboard variables let you define shared controls once and reuse them across dashboards, reducing duplicate work and keeping configurations consistent.

They come in two scopes:

  • Global variables are defined at the organization level and can be used on any dashboard.

  • Folder variables are defined on a folder and can be used on the dashboards in that folder.

Here's what cross-dashboard variables looks like in practice: say, for example, a few team dashboards all use the same environment picker with the values dev, staging, and prod. With a cross-dashboard variable, you define environment once. When you add a new environment, or change the query behind it, every dashboard that uses the variable gets the update, without needing to edit each dashboard individually.

Cross-dashboard variables achieve this by separating two things: the definition (the variable's type, query, and options) is shared and managed in one place, while the value someone selects (for example, prod) is chosen on each dashboard as they use it.

Managing cross-dashboard variables

Go to Dashboards > Variables to create, edit, move, and delete cross-dashboard variables. The editor is the same one you already use for dashboard variables, with the same types (Query, Custom, Data source, Text, and so on). The only new field is Folder:

  • Leave it at the root to create a global variable.

  • Pick a folder to create a folder variable.

To change a variable's scope, move it between folders or move it to the root.

Choosing variables per dashboard

A dashboard doesn't use any cross-dashboard variables until you choose them. In the dashboard's settings, pick which global and folder variables it should use:

  • Specific variables: only the ones you pick appear on the dashboard. Variables created later in that scope don't appear until you add them.

  • All variables in a scope: every global variable, or every variable in the dashboard's folder, appears. New ones show up automatically.

Precedence: nearest scope wins

With four places a variable can come from, there's one simple rule: the nearest definition wins.

If a dashboard defines its own region, it overrides the global region. A section can override both.

On the dashboard, cross-dashboard variables appear alongside the dashboard's own variables and work the same way: you can select values, sync them to the URL, and use them in queries, titles, and links. In edit mode, they're read-only on the dashboard. To change the definition, go to Dashboards > Variables.

Managing cross-dashboard variables as code

Under the product name, a cross-dashboard variable is a Variable resource with its own API. It isn't stored inside any dashboard, but it is tied to dashboards: it lives in the dashboard API group (dashboard.grafana.app) next to Dashboard, and it does nothing until a dashboard opts into it.

Because it's a separate resource, it's served by the same Kubernetes-style API platform as v2 dashboards and folders. You can create, list, and update variables like any other Grafana resource, without touching a dashboard.

A Variable uses the same shape as a variable inside a dashboard, so anything you already know about dashboard variable JSON carries over:

{
  "apiVersion": "dashboard.grafana.app/v2beta1",
  "kind": "Variable",
  "metadata": {
    "annotations": {
      "grafana.app/folder": ""
    }
  },
  "spec": {
    "kind": "CustomVariable",
    "spec": {
      "name": "environment",
      "query": "dev,staging,prod",
      "current": { "text": "prod", "value": "prod" },
      "description": "Deployment environment"
    }
  }
}

Leave out the grafana.app/folder annotation to make it global.

During the public preview, Variable is served at v2beta1.  It will move to v2 when cross-dashboard variables reach general availability.

Provisioning with Terraform

Because Variable is a standard API resource, you can manage it with the Grafana Terraform provider's grafana_apps_generic_resource. Here's a folder, a folder variable, and a dashboard that opts into it, all in one Terraform configuration:

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_folder" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "folder.grafana.app/v1"
    kind       = "Folder"
    metadata   = { name = "payments" }
    spec       = { title = "Payments" }
  }
}

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_env" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "dashboard.grafana.app/v2beta1"
    kind       = "Variable"
    metadata = {
      annotations = {
        "grafana.app/folder" = "payments"
      }
    }
    spec = {
      kind = "CustomVariable"
      spec = {
        name    = "environment"
        query   = "dev,staging,prod"
        current = { text = "prod", value = "prod" }
      }
    }
  }

  depends_on = [grafana_apps_generic_resource.payments_folder]
}

resource "grafana_apps_generic_resource" "payments_overview" {
  manifest = {
    apiVersion = "dashboard.grafana.app/v2"
    kind       = "Dashboard"
    metadata = {
      name = "payments-overview"
      annotations = {
        "grafana.app/folder"                     = "payments"
        "grafana.app/useCrossDashboardVariables" = jsonencode({
          global = ["region"]
          folder = ["environment"]
        })
      }
    }
    spec = {
      title = "Payments overview"
      # ... panels and layout
    }
  }

  depends_on = [grafana_apps_generic_resource.payments_env]
}

The opt-in setting also works naturally as code. Leave out the annotation, and the dashboard uses no cross-dashboard variables. List names, and it uses exactly those. Nothing appears on a provisioned dashboard unless the config says so.

The same API also works with kubectl, curl, or any tool that talks to Grafana's /apis endpoints.

Wrapping up

These updates mean Grafana variables have one consistent model, from a single section of a dashboard to your whole organization:

Variable scope

Defined on

event_model_payload.headline: The recommended GitLab configuration for agentic engineering
event_model_payload.summary:
Agents keep getting better at more than drafting code. Teams already use them to move work through review, repair pipelines, and push changes toward merge. That speed only helps if every change is based on the software lifecycle context that lives in a unified platform and still passes the same gates your organization trusts. Without it, context, controls, and evidence fragment across people and tools into a shadow software factory.

Identity, policy, CI pipelines, security, approvals, and audits have to travel with the change from plan through merge and into production. A local harness alone does not hold that full picture. Your coding harness and GitLab Duo Agent Platform are built to work in tandem, so coding agents can move quickly while GitLab certifies their work on the way to production.

Software teams get to use different coding tools and agents they prefer, while their GitLab instance makes sure that every change is safe to ship. GitLab stays cloud-neutral, model-neutral, and agent-neutral, so you keep the harnesses, models, and deployment path that fit your organization.

Let us show you how to configure your agentic engineering environment to drive greater automation throughout your workflow. You stay in the harness you already use and connect to GitLab Duo Agent Platform once with a skill. Longer, repository-aware workflows run on GitLab, and every merge request still hits the same reviews, pipelines, scans, and approval policies.

In this article, we will focus on Claude Code as the local harness because that’s what we see most of our customers using but this same flow can apply to the local harness of your choosing, including Duo CLI.

How to configure your agentic engineering environment

If you already do most of your coding in a local harness, keep working there and wire it to GitLab Duo Agent Platform. From the terminal, you can direct lifecycle work to agentic workflows that run inside GitLab:

  • Picking up an issue and opening a merge request
  • Reviewing every MR as it lands
  • Resolving merge conflicts
  • Repairing a pipeline that just failed
  • With GitLab Ultimate, triaging and fixing security findings once code lands

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and others become the place from where you direct that work.

Part 1 is the setup:

Install the GitLab Duo setup skill, ask Claude Code to run it, and it sets up your whole top-level group with the necessary settings, the flows, an automation in every project, and the MCP connection.

Part 2 walks through four workflows:

You can try them as soon as the setup is done, each driven from Claude Code:

  1. Find an issue assigned to you and hand it to the Developer flow.
  2. Get automated code reviews on your merge requests, act on the findings without leaving your harness, and resolve any conflicts that pop up.
  3. Use an automation to fix a failed pipeline.
  4. On Ultimate, triage and fix security findings with the security flows.

When you want an even tighter loop:

The MR followup skill guides your local harness through the steps above even faster. The skill helps local agents monitor progress on the repo-side and take actions on your behalf to speed things along.

What you get from the combined path:

  • Move faster: Automatic review, pipeline repair, and (on Ultimate) security triage keep changes moving without leaving your harness.
  • Build trust: The same engineering and security standards apply to every MR, with oversight and an audit trail in GitLab.
  • Reduce complexity: Automate the handoff between your harness and GitLab so lifecycle work shares one context, one set of gates, and one audit trail.

What you need before you start:

  • A GitLab.com top-level group with GitLab Credits (Premium and Ultimate groups get access to promotional free credits each month for each user). The security workflow in Use Case 4 requires Ultimate licensing for your GitLab instance.
  • A project in that group with a pipeline, a few open issues, and an open merge request or two, so the workflows have something to act on.
  • The Owner role on the top-level group, so the skill can set up the whole group. If you're a Maintainer on the project but not a group owner, the skill sets up just that project and lists what to ask your Owner.
  • Claude Code installed and signed in, plus git and the GitLab CLI (glab, signed in with glab auth login ), which the skill uses to read and change settings.

Part 1: Guided setup with a skill

The GitLab Duo setup skill accelerates the connection from inside your harness. You install the skill once, ask Claude Code to set up GitLab Duo. The skill sets up your group as it turns on group-wide Duo Agent Platform workflows, creates the Fix CI/CD Pipeline automation where needed, connects to GitLab MCP server, and reports anything left for you to finish.

Install the skill

git clone https://gitlab.com/gitlab-da/projects/agentic-eng-config.git

cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-duo-setup ~/.claude/skills/

cp -R agentic-eng-config/skills/gitlab-mr-followup ~/.claude/skills/

Then Claude Code picks it up in the running session. If it isn't listed, restart Claude Code. You can add the skill to .claude/skills/ inside the repo so teammates can use it too.

Run the skill

In your project directory, start Claude Code and invoke the skill with a slash command:

/gitlab-duo-setup

Note: Different harnesses can have a different syntax for invoking skills.

What happens

Before it changes anything, the skill reads your top-level group and its projects and shows you one plan: every change and what it covers (the groups or projects). Group changes reach every downstream project and every member, and the plan says so. It waits for your yes, and you can drop any line. Then it:

  1. Turns on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and flow execution for the group, and adds the Code Review, Duo Developer, and Fix CI/CD Pipeline flows to the group's flows. Flows you already have stay on.
  2. Turns on automatic code review for the group, which carries down to every project.
  3. Creates an automation in every project with CI/CD that runs Fix CI/CD Pipeline when a pipeline fails. Projects that already have one are skipped, so running the skill twice is safe.
  4. Adds the GitLab MCP server to Claude Code, user-level or project-level as you prefer, and walks you through signing in in the browser.
  5. Verifies by calling list_duo_agents_and_flows. A successful call proves the sign-in worked, and the flows it returns prove the settings took.
  6. On Ultimate, asks one optional question: Do you also want GitLab to triage and fix security findings? Say "yes" and Use Case 4 will cover what gets turned on. Say "no" and the setup is done.
  7. Ends with a short report and links for anything it couldn't do. Blockers may be runners, if a project has none that can run flows, or push rules, if your group enforces them.

Why use a skill for setup

A skill sets things up in the same place you already direct agent work. You stay in your preferred coding harness, approve a plan, and wire Duo Agent Platform for group-wide automation without breaking out of that loop.

It's also harness-neutral by design (the repo's AGENTS.md requires it), so the same skill works whether your team is on Claude Code today and something else next quarter.

If the GitLab tools don't show up

Run /mcp and check that GitLab shows as connected. Connected but no tools? Restart Claude Code; new servers load at session start.

A 403 when you sign in usually means MCP client access is off for your top-level group: A group Owner turns on Allow connection to GitLab under the group's Settings > General > Permissions and group features. If two GitLab entries, user and project scope, show duplicate tools, keep one.

Part 2: Four workflows, all run from your terminal

With the GitLab MCP server connected in Part 1, Claude Code can now find your issues, start a flow, read review threads and pipeline status, and reply on a thread over that single OAuth connection. Server instructions help Claude Code propose the right agentic workflow within Duo Agent Platform, and each call comes with an AI audit event for your platform team.

The agent reads issues and merge request context through these tools, allowing the coding harness to access GitLab artifacts you trust. Context then builds in layers: local files in the harness, then issue and MR context over MCP, and finally Duo Agent Platform flows with full repo context and your gates.

Use Case 1: Hand an issue to the Developer flow

The first thing most people want from an agent is simple: Take the issue I was assigned this morning and come back with a merge request.

GitLab automations allow work items to be automatically handled by an agent through events: issue creation, assignment or mentions of an agent, status changes, and more. If you have the GitLab MCP connection in place, you can manage that work from the terminal as well. Either way, once something is assigned to an agent in GitLab Duo Agent Platform, the work is executed within your GitLab instance so you can keep working on other things.

Find the work

In Claude Code, ask something like:

What issues are assigned to me in ? Summarize each in a line.

Claude calls the GitLab MCP server's work item tools, filters your assignments, and gives you the list. You pick one. If the issue is thin, this is also where you'd ask Claude to read the linked files or recent commits through the repository tools so you can sharpen the description before handing it off; a clearer goal produces a better MR.

Hand it off

Ask Claude to assign the Developer flow to an issue.

Can you pick up Issue 1 and assign it to the Developer flow in GitLab?

Claude calls the server's Start Duo session tool with the project, the Developer flow, and a goal it writes from the issue, and hands you back a session link.

From here the work happens in GitLab, not on your machine. This frees you up to keep working locally without disrupting the agent. The session runs as a CI job on a runner. The flow reads the issue and the repository, writes the change, and opens a merge request. The MR is attributed to you, not to the service account, so it shows up in your activity and your review queue like any other MR you authored.

Use Case 2: Automated code review

From the harness, open or push an MR and let Duo Agent Platform review it on GitLab. You read findings and iterate locally while the review and verification stay on the merge request. GitLab Code Review flow reviews every merge request in your group as soon as the MR is marked ready. Once turned on, it enables agentic reviews and approvals.

On new groups and projects, Code Review flow is on by default, so those features are active out of the box. On existing groups and projects, you can run the setup skill to turn it on.

To check or change it for one project, go to Settings > Merge requests > GitLab Duo Code Review > Enable automatic reviews by GitLab Duo. There you can also choose to Start a new review on push so every commit to the MR branch gets a follow-up review that builds on the earlier one.

What a review looks like

When you or your agent creates an MR, GitLab Duo is added as a reviewer and runs a two-stage review: a pre-scan that pulls related files, tests and dependencies from the repo, then the review itself. It leaves inline threads with specific, actionable findings plus a summary.

With the beta approvals setting (also on the project's Merge requests settings page) turned on, GitLab Duo approves the MR when it finds nothing or requests changes when it does.

Tune it for your repo

Two files let you shape reviews without touching settings: mr-review-instructions.yaml for custom review instructions (focus areas, standards, per-path rules) and .gitlab/duo/mr-review-automated-rules.yaml to exclude MRs by target branch, source branch, or author, for example, bot-authored dependency bumps. As you identify improvements, keep updating these instructions to make reviews more efficient over time.

Work the feedback locally

Ask your agent:

Does MR 1 have feedback for me to review?

Claude Code reads Duo's Code Review threads through the MCP Server and summarizes them for you. You can ask it to follow through by fixing the ones it agrees with and reply in the threads to resolve them. Claude will make those changes locally, push them, and comment on each thread as the user. If you have the start a new review on push setting turned on, Duo will run another review to verify those changes. If a finding comes with a code suggestion, you can apply via MCP.

Long-running agentic work and verification stay on the merge request. Quick iteration stays in your local checkout.

Resolve a merge conflict

While a merge request waits for review, its target branch keeps moving. Eventually, this can lead to a conflict on your branch. You can clear it from Claude Code in two ways.

  1. Let Claude resolve it in your checkout: MR 1 conflicts with its target branch. Resolve the conflict and get the pipeline green.
  2. Or hand it over to Duo Developer on GitLab: MR 1 has a merge conflict. Can you ask the Developer flow in GitLab to resolve it?

If you use Claude Code to resolve it, it will go through the conflict locally and use any preferences in your Agents.MD or skills to resolve it. If you use GitLab Duo Developer flow, you can leave it to work on it in the cloud and move on to your next task.

Use Case 3: Fix a failed pipeline with an automation

From the harness you can watch the merge request, while Duo Agent Platform can start the automated Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow when a job fails, with the same repo context and merge gates as any other change.

An automation watches for a failed pipeline and starts the Fix CI/CD Pipeline flow for you. By the time you notice the pipeline failure, a fix is usually already waiting.

Check the automation

Automations live at AI > Automations in each project. If you ran the skill, the fixed pipeline automation will already be there, along with some other automations that come out of the box. To create one by hand (Maintainer or Owner):

  1. Select New automation and give it a name, for example Fix failed pipelines.
  2. Under Runs with, select Fix CI/CD Pipeline. (Developer is selected by default if it's enabled; change it.)
  3. Under Runs when, select Add trigger > On an event, choose Pipeline events, and under Run when select Failed.
  4. Select Add event, then Create.

What happens on a failure

When a pipeline fails, the flow starts a session. If the pipeline belongs to an open merge request, it posts a system note on the MR with a link to the session. It reads the job logs, the MR diff, and the repository, then:

  • If the fix is inside the MR's diff, it applies inline code suggestions on the source branch. You review and apply them from the MR, or pull the branch and apply them locally.
  • If the fix needs files outside the diff, or the pipeline has no open MR, it opens a new merge request with the change.
  • If it can't determine a reliable fix, or the failure is security-sensitive, it posts a comment that describes the failure and next steps so you can decide how to proceed.

Make it fit your project

The flow reads AGENTS.md, so you can tell it how to format commit messages, which labels to put on MRs it opens, how to treat specific failure classes, and when to stop retrying the same fix. One known limit: The flow sees only the last 150 KiB of a job log, so noisy jobs may need a summary step at the end.

Close the loop from Claude Code

The flow leaves a system note and its suggestions on the MR, so start from the MR.

On MR 17, did Fix Pipeline create a new MR or leave suggestions? Show me the diff and the reasoning.

Decide whether to merge the MR or apply the suggestions. The MR followup skill can also help you take the MR all the way to merge and guide you through the process.

/gitlab-mr-followup Take MR 1 through to merge.

Use Case 4: Triage and fix security findings (Ultimate)

For GitLab Ultimate + Duo Agent Platform users, three out-of-the-box agents can also help eliminate security debt that builds up once code lands: Secret False Positive Detection, SAST False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability. These security flows take findings from your scanners, score them for false positives, and open merge requests that fix the real ones. The flows work on findings from scans of your default branch (and other tracked branches), after code has merged.

Turn it on

If you said yes to the setup skill's security question, the skill then:

  • Adds the SAST False Positive Detection, Secret Detection False Positive Detection, and Resolve SAST Vulnerability flows to the group, keeping every flow you already have.
  • Applies the Secret Detection and SAST scan profile to projects that don't scan yet, without editing any .gitlab-ci.yml. The scans run in merge request pipelines, so if your tests only run in branch pipelines, check that a failing test still blocks the merge request.
  • Enables the flows to run the Standard preset: triage and fixes run automatically after every scan, for Medium findings and above, with up to 15 open fix merge requests per project.

If anything in this step fails, the skill stops there and leaves the setup from Part 1 as it is. Credits scale with the number of findings, so if you'd rather see results and cost first, ask for the Conservative preset when the skill shows its plan: on demand, for High and Critical findings, with at most five open fix merge requests.

Automated resolution out-of-the-box

After turning these on, agents will flag SAST and Secrets false positives for you and generate merge requests to address SAST vulnerabilities automatically, reducing developer time spent on security and eliminating application security risk more efficiently. Expect triage and the first fix MR about 10 minutes after the scan finishes.

The Security Review flow and the Vulnerability Context flow can help you dig deeper into findings that aren’t automatically addressed.

Review before you merge

Treat the agent-created MRs like any other. You can use the Code Review flow on the fix MRs too. Security Review, which reviews merge request changes for business logic vulnerabilities, is also available. The skill mentions it but sets it up only if you ask, because it needs experiment and beta features turned on for the whole group.

Take your software factory to the next level

Advanced governance, flexible model deployment, and comprehensive lifecycle context ensure your automated software factory remains secure, adaptable, and fully informed.

Governance that applies to every merge request

To ensure control and compliance as agents take on writing more code, it’s important to build guardrails that live alongside your code. With this integration, developers cut the handoff cost between the place they code and the place they ship, while building trust in their agentic workflows with consistent controls and evidence. In GitLab:

  • Merge request approval policies apply organization-wide rules to every merge request.
  • Pipeline execution policies make sure required jobs run, whatever a project's own pipeline configuration says.
  • Composite identity ties every agent action to both the agent's service account and the person who started it, so the audit trail always shows who asked for what.
  • Tool approval guardrails let administrators require a person's approval before an agent takes a sensitive action.

These controls already protect production for any enterprise that cares about security and governance. The same rules now cover agents, with no separate rulebook to maintain.

Model and cloud choice that stays under your control

The best model for a given job keeps changing. Teams should be able to take advantage of that without rebuilding how they ship software.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform is cloud-, agent-, and model-neutral. Group owners choose the model for each agent and flow, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open-weight providers, and can update it as new models arrive. On GitLab Self-Managed, GitLab Duo Self-Hosted runs models through Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, or the organization’s own infrastructure.

Whatever the model, the same approval policies, pipeline requirements, and audit trail apply to every merge request. Each organization picks the models that fit its needs, budget, and data rules, without tying how it ships software to one vendor’s roadmap.

Lifecycle context that cuts agent retries

An agent working one merge request sees only that merge request: the diff, the failing job log, and the review comments. It can't see that the same job fails in other projects. It can't see which services depend on the code it just changed, or who owns them. Without the full lifecycle picture, agents guess, then retry, then burn tokens on work that never ships.

GitLab Orbit, now generally available, is a context graph of the software lifecycle. It connects code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with your permissions intact. Agents get that context before they call a change safe to merge.

Developers and agents can also see which services, jobs, and environments a change touches across the group. In GitLab's internal testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries while discovering an answer, and used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.

Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents connect to Orbit through MCP or the GitLab CLI, so the context you build once serves every agent you add.

One governed path from code to production

With this integration, customers keep the coding harness their teams already use and enable GitLab Duo Agent Platform on the path to production. From the same terminal, they can hand issues into merge requests, get automated review on every MR, clear merge conflicts, let a failed pipeline start its own fix, and clear their security backlog. Every change still hits the same identity, policy, CI pipelines, security, approvals, and audit rules that their organization already trusts. That is the move from a shadow software factory to a governed software factory with the tools, models, and deployment path that fit how you work.

The GitLab Duo setup skill is how that connection starts. Install it in your harness, invoke it once, and review a single plan before anything changes. After you approve, the skill turns on Duo Agent Platform for your group, adds the Code Review, Fix CI/CD Pipeline, and Developer flows, creates the failed-pipeline automation where it is needed, connects the GitLab MCP server, and verifies the sign-in. It ends with a short report and links for anything left for you or your group Owner. From there, the four workflows in this guide run from the same terminal, and the MR followup skill is available when you want the loop even tighter.

New to GitLab Duo Agent Platform? Start a free trial. Already on Premium or Ultimate? Turn on Duo Agent Platform and use the GitLab Credits included with your subscription. Then clone the GitLab Duo setup skill, run it from the harness you already use, and take the first workflow for a spin on a real project.

event_model_payload.headline: The Pentagon wants to know who checks code when AI writes it
event_model_payload.summary:
The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise. DoW Instruction 8430.01, “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems the department has approved. Here’s what the instruction asks of your team, and how GitLab helps you address it.

What is DoW Instruction 8430.01?

Issued by DoW CIO Kirsten Davies, DoW Instruction 8430.01 applies to every DoW organization and to any acquisition program that includes software, regardless of cost. The instruction sets policy and procedures for modernizing and managing software, with an emphasis on delivering capabilities faster. It directs teams to automate testing and security scanning, reuse what already works, and produce evidence as software is built.

The instruction also encourages teams to use AI, calling AI-assisted development a major force multiplier for speed and quality. However, it attaches three conditions: AI’s role is traceable, its code is verified so developers stay accountable, and government data stays within approved boundaries. Each condition changes what a software platform has to do.

Three requirements that shape AI in delivery

While DoW Instruction 8430.01 covers a wide scope, the three conditions mentioned above show how software platforms must adapt. Here they are in more detail.

1. Traceability: Know what AI touched

Software on DoW networks needs proof of what’s in it and how it was built. When AI is involved, the proof has to cover AI, too: which models, which versions, and which datasets were used to write or test the code.

In GitLab, that record lives beside your code. Dependency Scanning produces your software bill of materials, and audit events and deployment records are generated as part of delivery. Agents in GitLab Duo Agent Platform act through their own service account, tied to the developer who started them, so a commit shows up as the agent acting on behalf of a named person. The commit then lands in the same audit log as everything else, where your SIEM can filter it as AI activity. Because the evidence stays in the platform, you can change models under managed policy without erasing the history.

2. Verification: Check what AI writes

Accelerated delivery cannot compromise security, safety, or supply chain integrity. AI-generated or AI-modified code is unverified input, and a person must approve changes to security-critical functions (a flaw that lets an attacker in) or safety-critical ones (a flaw that can cost lives or platforms). As the instruction states, “Developers and development teams remain fully accountable for the security, functionality, and integrity of any code generated or modified using AI.”

In GitLab, your scans, tests, and approval rules run in the same pipeline for every change, whether a developer or an agent writes the code. Merge request approval policies can require a named reviewer whenever a change touches protected paths or introduces a vulnerability, and protected branches mean an agent can propose but can’t merge past the people you’ve designated.

Dependency Scanning Auto-Remediation (currently in beta) is one example of an agent doing the work while your reviewers still sign off. It proposes dependency upgrades and build fixes, and those proposals wait at your existing approval gates like any other merge request. When GitLab orchestrates agents across several steps, a flow can carry a change through review, tests, scans, and approvals on its own, pausing for a human to sign off before a merge or deploy. Every flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so speed doesn’t mean skipped steps. For teams deciding how much autonomy to give agents, the GitLab Security Standard defines five stages (authorize, isolate, verify, release, and respond) that agents must clear before that autonomy is granted. Those stages are mapped to NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) and SP 800-53 controls.

3. Data boundaries: Control where AI runs

AI systems must respect data boundaries without compromising intellectual property or classified context. Approved AI services must guarantee that government data and prompts aren’t used to train external models, and non-public DoW information stays on approved DoW systems. That means controlling which models are used and where they are hosted.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform Self-Hosted runs on infrastructure you control, including air-gapped networks. You choose the supported models, on premises or in a private cloud, and can swap them without rebuilding workflows. Requests route through an AI Gateway you deploy yourself, so prompts and responses stay in your environment. For GitLab Dedicated for Government customers, this is the standard setup: You run the AI Gateway in your own environment, connected to the model provider of your choice.
